6c8174c3d48e.text: Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was elected to a fourth, nonconsecutive term in the nation's presidential election according to early results released Sunday evening. Why it matters: Lula's victory deals a setback to Brazil's right-wing populist movement and preserves a major counterweight to President Trump 's influence in Latin America, with tensions over trade and tariffs threatening to persist. Lula, the incumbent candidate, was facing Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro . Flávio was widely seen as the heir to the nation's right-wing populist movement. The big picture: The election has been shaped by the impact of U.S. tariffs, climate change and the Amazon rainforest, 60% of which is in Brazil. Bolsonaro campaigned on public security and tackling corruption, presenting himself as a continuation of his father's political legacy, while Lula emphasized defending Brazilian sovereignty against U.S. pressure. Yet substantive policy debate was limited, with both candidates focusing instead on corruption allegations levied against the opposing camp, wrote Matthew Taylor, a Brazil politics expert at American University. Zoom in: After the U.S. imposed additional 25% tariffs on some Brazilian goods this summer, Lula accused Bolsonaro of being "Trump's candidate" and the U.S. president of wanting to "colonize" Brazil. Lula has enacted climate policies aimed at reversing environmental deregulation under the previous administration, while Bolsonaro denied climate change and pledged to continue his father's political legacy. Amazon deforestation has fallen 71% since 2022, the year before Lula returned to office, reaching its lowest annual level on record in 2026. Yet Lula's environmental record is complicated by his support for expanded oil development. Lula defeated Jair Bolsonaro in the previous election. The elder Bolsonaro is now serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup to overturn the 2022 election, though he remains under house arrest due to health problems.

- Published
George McMaster's farming career started with milking eight cows in a byre, relying on his eyes to spot any health issues in his cattle.
He still watches his now-300-strong herd, but via a feed from an AI camera in the milking parlour at the farm near Islandmagee in County Antrim.
The device uses an algorithm which assigns each cow its own ID, records a short video of the animal every day, analyses it and flags any changes - often before they are visible to the human eye.
For the third generation farmer, it is "absolutely incredible to move from all hand-done to sitting on the phone, watching what's happening outside".
Making everyone happy
It is just one example of how technology is changing the traditional profession.
George's son Jack, who is taking over the farm, jumped at the chance to get involved with the CattleEye app when a local developer approached him.
He, too, is astonished by the potential.
"There's cows there we would never have thought of as lame when we were just watching them every day, but whenever the camera's watching they're picking them up so much earlier, any emergencies that we have, to check cows before they lose condition and get sick," he said.
"And if cows are in better health, we get more milk and they're happier - happy cows make happy farmers."
Simplifying business
Caleb Howard is using technology to manage his 90 Jersey cows on the farm near Coagh in County Tyrone.
They filter in and out of a robotic milking machine when they want to, rather than being herded in at set times.
Like the McMasters, he thinks "everything is going down the robotic route" to improve efficiency.
But historically in a place like rural Tyrone, that has come with its own challenges.
Getting high-speed broadband was a game-changer for him - he has been able to open a farm shop with an electronic payment system.
"Ten years ago, in our area, phone signal was rubbish, the broadband wasn't great, it was just like a slightly faster dial-up," he said.
"So now everything is much simpler and much easier-used when you've got a good internet connection."
Project Stratum was set up to deliver high-speed broadband to areas like the one Howard lives in.
Colin Hutchinson from Fibrus, which delivered the project, said it had had a "massive" economic impact.
"Being online and having good broadband access is really crucial now," he said.
"And it's enabling businesses like this to thrive in really rural locations."
'Facebook for cows'
Robert Smyth runs a herd of 100 dairy cows in another rural location, near Randalstown in County Antrim.
For four years now, he has used the FarmDrive app to run the business.
"It's so much handier - beforehand you're writing things down, bits of paperwork in the cattle house and writing them down in the office, whereas now you just do it at that time," he said.
"And then whenever you have inspections coming up, all you have to do is go into your compliance section, select reports, and there's your reports for your medicine, for your meal records, for everything.
"The AI really should be looking towards how to manage your farm better and how to reduce your inputs and increase your outputs."
Developer Gareth McDonald describes FarmDrive as "Facebook for cows". Each animal gets a profile with all her records in one place and a photo can be added.
He comes from a farming background and studied computer science.
Although he is passionate about the technology, he does not believe it will replace humans.
"It's allowing us to work a lot more quickly and efficiently, and on the farming side, it's basically allowing the farmer to see the right information at the right time, where it's kind of that adviser to the farmer," he said.
"We're very much of the opinion we don't want the AI making the decision for the farmer."
Data-driven industry
Almost a century ago, County Down-born inventor Harry Ferguson transformed the farming industry when he developed the linkage system still used in tractors today.
Former president of the Ulster Farmers' Union Ian Marshall says AI is similarly revolutionary.
While the industry has always relied on data, he believes technology will drive how information is used.
"When we take all the datasets, then I think we can deliver on the three pillars of sustainability - economic, environmental and social," he said.
"So I think that because we've got so much data and so much digitalisation in the industry, that farmers will certainly use this to their advantage and can meet their targets, meet their objectives and meet the obligations whilst delivering good quality, sustainable food."

Rapper Nicki Minaj said US President Donald Trump has "changed the energy of the country" as she joined him at a Michigan rally to stump for Republicans ahead of the nationwide midterm elections.
"He's given us a future to look forward to," she said, after Trump praised her figure and called her on stage to speak.
Minaj has called herself Trump's "number one fan" despite criticising some of his policies in his first term.
In Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is locked in a tight race with Republican Mike Rogers with just over a week to go before the midterms. Former President Barack Obama held a rally - one of the first in this cycle - with the Democrat on Saturday.
Democrats are also aggressively hitting the campaign trail, with close elections taking place on 3 November which will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency.
In his remarks on Sunday, Trump focused on El-Sayed's Muslim faith and background, alleging that he will "invite jihadists" into America if he wins.
El-Sayed has criticised similar remarks by Trump as Islamophobic, saying in an ad to voters last week that the US president "thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor's office".
In Port Huron on Sunday, Minaj, wearing a gold-coloured Gucci-branded suit, led the crowd in chanting Trump's name, and the names of Republican candidates in Michigan.
"We really need all these great people to be elected, because this is a major turning point for our country," she said.
"She never looked more beautiful," Trump said as she left the stage. "She gets it. She's smart," he added.
Earlier in his speech, Trump praised the rear end of one male Republican candidate before turning the crowd's attention to Minaj.
"By the way, I looked at a beautiful ass before," he segued. "Nicki Minaj. That's hard to miss."
He then asked her to "stand up" as the crowd cheered, and added that he hoped she was not "insulted" by his remark.
The Super Bass singer had accompanied Trump to the state aboard Air Force One. She filmed a video with an aide - which was posted to X -on the president's plane, pretending to be interviewing for the White House press secretary role.
The position is currently open after Katie Zacharia left five days after a shaky public debut.
The Trinidad and Tobago-born rapper has thrown her star power behind Trump a few times before, including on his allegations that Christians face persecution in Nigeria and his "gold card" visa, which offers applicants residency and a path to US citizenship.

The partner set to take over leadership of Weil, Gotshal & Manges has held talks to leave the firm for a rival, a move that would compound ongoing talent drain at one of Wall Streetâs top dealmaking and restructuring shops.
Ramona Nee, Weilâs co-managing partner, has had discussions to join Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, according to people familiar with the matter. Nee, an adviser to big private equity firms including Advent, was slated to take over as Weilâs sole chair in January.
Weil declined to comment. Nee did not return a request for comment. Her departure is not guaranteed and the talks could fall apart, the people said.
If she does leave, she would follow a flood of Weilâs top talent out the door and the breakdown of merger talks with crosstown rival Willkie Farr & Gallagher. Rainmaker Michael Aiello defected to Cravath, Swaine & Moore with a team of partners. It would be likely that a sizable portion of Weilâs Boston partnership would leave with her, according to one person familiar with the matter who is close with many of Weilâs top Boston lawyers.
Nee had told Weil partners she would not take the chair job, which was announced last spring, according to a person briefed on the communication. The Financial Times earlier reported that decision.
Remaining and former Weil lawyers place blame on Aielloâs departure â and Neeâs possible departure â at the feet of executive partner Barry Wolf, who has helmed the firm to some success for more than a decade but in recent years has failed to convince senior partners that Weil has a vision for a world where AI and outsize pay packages upend the perceived usefulness of high-end legal advice.
Aielloâs departure came as a result, in part, because top Weil leaders including Wolf failed to lay out a convincing long-term vision for the firm, according to a person familiar with his thinking.

8cac775fae01.text: A student-led protest movement has ended the 14-year rule of Serbia's right-wing party, former President Aleksandar Vučić conceded Sunday. Why it matters: The historic upset sidelines a Balkan strongman who courted President Trump's family and allies, raising questions about future U.S. relations with a country that has balanced ties with Russia and the West. Vučić 's outreach has included the president's son Donald Trump Jr. and longtime ally Richard Grenell, while a proposed development involving Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner became embroiled in controversy. The big picture: The movement's electoral breakthrough reflects a broader wave of youth activism in Europe, where young people have mobilized over corruption, education and economic pressures. The victory could usher in democratic reforms in Serbia, where Vučić consolidated power. Driving the news: Vučić said Sunday evening it was "clear" that his Serbian Progressive Party had lost to the student-backed electoral movement, although official results had yet to be announced, according to translations of his announcement . He projected the Student List would win between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-seat parliament, compared with 105 for his coalition. Cardiologist Ilija Srdanović heads the Student List, though the grassroots movement emphasized its decentralized leadership. The result echoes the student-led movement that helped topple Slobodan Milošević in 2000 , with Serbians reviving that era's "He's finished!" rallying cry as they celebrated Sunday. Context: The movement emerged from mass protests after the November 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad that killed 16 people, fueling public anger over alleged government corruption. It subsequently evolved into an electoral movement campaigning for accountability and institutional reform. What's next: The Student List must choose a prime minister and form a government while Serbia faces a separate presidential election in December to replace Vučić.

The trials, which will continue until mid-November, aim to replicate results from Singapore that demonstrated the wolbachia parasiteâs effectiveness in reducing dengue cases by 70%; wolbachiaâs significant advantage is the ability to bypass regulations against gene editing, which â by sowing male populations with a so-called âlethal geneâ that prevents viable offspring â has also shown promise in checking mosquito-borne illnesses.

A software developer became so frustrated by the amount of rubbish he saw dumped along roadsides that he built an AI-powered "litter dashcam" to expose the scale of the problem.
Robin Bennett, from Shrewsbury, developed the Roadside Litter app after noticing what he believed was a growing amount of litter while driving around the county.
The technology has already logged more than 3,000 litter reports in Shropshire and more than 28,000 across the UK.
He is now sharing the data with anti-litter campaign group Clean Up Britain in the hope it will encourage action, while Shropshire Council said it was exploring ways to improve litter management on some of the county's busiest roads.
Bennett, who runs a software company in Telford, said he found the amount of rubbish on local roads "really depressing" and wanted to understand whether the issue was unique to Shropshire or part of a wider national problem.
After approaching Clean Up Britain to ask how he could help, he went on to develop what he describes as a "litter dashcam" that records rubbish spotted from a vehicle.
"My software company's created an app, which essentially is a litter dashcam," he said.
"The app records the litter that it sees."
Mounted on a vehicle dashboard, the app automatically takes a photograph every 10 seconds, identifying visible litter and grading it against a national standard before uploading the information.
Bennett said: "I've got a phone holder stuck to the dashboard, I've put my phone in securely.
"I start it and that's it, you don't have to touch the screen, and the screen will go black in a minute so it's not distracting in any way.
"Every 10 seconds it takes a photo, it looks at the litter it can see by the side of the road and it grades it according to a national standard."
The app had recorded more than 3,000 reports in Shropshire and more than 28,000 nationwide, Bennett said.
He added litter was particularly common near convenience stores, fast-food outlets and motorway service stations.
"People pick up a bag of fast food and just throw the bag out the window," he added.
Bennett said he hoped the data collected by the app would help build a clearer picture of the problem and encourage authorities to do more to tackle roadside litter.
A spokesperson for Shropshire Council said the authority recognised the importance of maintaining a clean and attractive highway network and was engaging with National Highways to explore opportunities to improve litter management on the A5 and A49.

A discarded microwave, a mattress sodden by the rain and even a pile of used syringes. The reality of illegally dumped waste sits before me in a colossal mound next to the side of a motorway.
For the team I'm with, this is a jigsaw waiting to be pieced together and solved as they try to identify the criminal culprits.
It does not take long for Anthony Horan and Ashley Hanley from North East Lincolnshire Council to find answers within the mountain of waste on the side of the Brocklesby Interchange near Grimsby.
They tell me it is a goldmine of clues.
"I'm gobsmacked at the amount of evidence in this one," Anthony Horan, who works as a senior environmental health practitioner for the authority.
"I'm disgusted at the needles. I've never found this amount ever."
A number of times during the interview we pause after spotting a syringe close to our feet. Some are hidden under items, others are in plain sight.
About 20 are collected to be destroyed.
The team tells me this is exactly why they wear protective equipment.
Meanwhile, a picture starts to emerge as letters with different names and addresses - all miles outside the area - are fished out and photographed.
Horan tells me if evidence which identifies a person is found, they will be questioned.
If found liable, they could be fined if they have not properly undergone a "domestic duty of care".
"A lot of people think enviro-crime or fly-tipping is a victimless crime," Horan says. "It's not, there's many victims."
Horan says people often employ a "man with a van" to dispose of their waste, but frequently the person hired just dumps it.
If the waste is found dumped on private land, the owner will have to pay for its removal. Councils only pay if it is on public land.
Wearing thick gloves, environmental enforcement officer Hanley continues to dig through the dump.
I ask him about rogue waste removers and his advice for people wanting to get rid of waste.
"I would advise people to take the right precautions, make sure that they're giving it to somebody who has a waste carriage licence," Hanley says.
"Make sure that you're taking it to a proper waste facility if you're doing it yourself," he adds.
The Environment Agency says waste criminals "scar our environment and communities".
It says: "Illegal waste dumping is a crime that costs the public purse Â£1bn a year. We know the challenges and are working hard to overcome them."
It encourages the public to report suspected waste crime to its incident hotline or via its website.
In August, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said fines for fly-tipping would increase from Â£300 to Â£5,000 and offenders could be given up to nine points on their driving licence.
Across the Humber Bridge, I meet Hull City Council's Streetscene team as they arrive at a fly-tip in the middle of a housing estate.
Under this authority, the fines for fly-tipping are higher at Â£1,000.
As teams drag mattresses and wooden planks onto the truck, they tell a similarly frustrated story.
"It's all over the city and now it's on the rise," says Mike, one of the men clearing the waste.
"We've got a job to do so we have to clear it and move on to the next fly-tip and do the same again."
Carl Wilson, the team manager, tells me this location is a hotspot and criminals will be back soon enough.
"This will all get cleared away and then in a couple of weeks they'll probably do it again," Carl says.
"That's why you need this evidence to catch them, to stop them, to put it to a stop."
The authority tells me they often visit hotspots to deliver letters to residents on how to properly dispose of waste to prevent fly-tipping.
Back near Grimsby, I ask the North East Lincolnshire team what their message is to fly-tippers or people considering dumping their waste.
Horan is stern.
"Don't do it because we'll catch you," he says. "We don't want to be doing this, we want you to do the correct thing."
Additional reporting by Alice Toon

- Published
On 19 July about 18 tonnes of plastic nurdles, consisting of about one billion tiny balls, spilled into the River Tyne after a crash between ships at the Port of Tyne.
It is believed to be the worst recorded incident of its type in Europe.
In the months since, teams of volunteers have joined in efforts to collect the microplastics that continue to wash up on north-east England's coast.
But several questions remain. So what do we know about the spill right now - and what are we still waiting to find out?
What actually happened on 19 July?
A wind turbine installation vessel called the Wind Orca collided with a container ship berthed at the Port of Tyne.
A gantry crane on the quayside collapsed and ended up lying across the ship.
Two containers on the BG Orange were full of nurdles. These are pre-production plastic pellets, about the size of a lentil, which are used as the raw material to manufacture nearly all everyday plastic goods.
About 18 tonnes of these pellets spilled into the water because of the crash.
Who was at fault?
This is still being investigated.
Northumbria Police said it was investigating the collision and so far, no-one has been arrested. The Marine Accident Investigation Branch is also investigating.
The Port of Tyne previously said it, along with others, had asked the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) to consider enforcing safer transportation methods for nurdles, something environmental groups have long called for.
How much of the nurdles can actually be recovered?
By the end of September about 28% of the nurdles had been recovered, according to scientists.
But the Port of Tyne, the Environment Agency and the North East Mayoral Strategic Authority (MSA) said the numbers of nurdles washing up ashore had already "reduced significantly" by then and numbers were continuing to fall.
They said they believed the full recovery of the 18 tonnes was not achievable. When asked what percentage recovery rate would be considered a success, the bodies said they would measure success via various metrics including shoreline surveys.
Where will the nurdles go?
The pellets from the spill have been found along the English coast from Northumberland to North Yorkshire.
On Friday the Danish Environment Protection Agency confirmed pellets found on the country's western coast had also likely originated from the Tyne spill.
Dr Matthew Perks at Newcastle University and his colleagues are monitoring the movement of the nurdles and examining how the pellets may deteriorate in water.
The team's modelling so far suggests about one in eight of the billion nurdles remain in the Tyne estuary and high river flows could flush these microplastics downstream in the autumn.
Perks said this was a crucial opportunity to collect the pellets.
Nevertheless he said it was unclear how far some of the nurdles could really travel.
"As time goes by, it becomes more difficult to pinpoint the areas where these nodules are likely to be," he said.
It is also unclear when the nurdles will start breaking down into nanoplastics. "That will change the way they behave," he said.
What is the impact on wildlife?
Long story short â we do not know yet.
Professor Bhavani Narayanaswamy at the Scottish Association for Marine Science said it could be months or years before we understood the full impact of the spill.
She said the nurdles could affect wildlife in various ways, including getting stuck in animal digestive tracts and adsorbing chemicals which then may be toxic to wildlife when ingested.
Prof Narayanaswamy said there was little research on the long-term impact of plastic pollution on animals compared with its immediate effects.
Dan Turner, who coordinates the North East England Beached Bird Survey, said the group had collected several dead birds along the coast which they would be testing for nurdles next month.
"It is quite possible that the seabirds have mistaken the plastic for fish eggs," he previously told the BBC.
Who is paying for the clean-up?
Recovery is largely being paid for by insurers representing BG Orange, which was carrying the pellets, as well as local councils and the Port of Tyne.
Thousands of volunteers have also been involved in the clean-up.
Councils have been told to record their costs so they can seek compensation from the insurers of those ultimately found responsible.
And how long will it last for?
The multi-agency group, consisting of the North East MSA, Port of Tyne and the EA, said the nurdle recovery programme was continuing but it had increasingly moved away from "large-scale clean-up activity" towards "targeted recovery and monitoring".
Environmental charity Fidra said it was unclear how long the clean-up would need to continue, considering the fact that nurdles could stay in water for years.
It said a long-term plan was required to tackle the pollution and the plans should be "adequately resourced" with responsibility clearly defined.
Is it still worth going to beach cleans?
Volunteer Lou Shackleton said there was still a core group of individuals who gave up their spare time to monitor and recover nurdles on local beach.
She said the group needed all the help they could get.
"If you're happy to wrap up against the rain and the wind... come and join us," she said.

A convicted murderer serving a life sentence in Australia has lost his bid to overturn a ban on prisoners consuming Vegemite - the salty yeast-based spread that has become a national symbol.
Andre McKechnie argued that the ban, in place since 2006, denied him the right to "enjoy his culture as an Australian".
Authorities in the state of Victoria say inmates may use the strong-smelling paste to disguise contraband substances or to brew alcohol behind bars.
And on Monday, a Supreme Court judge rejected McKechnie's appeal, saying the prisoner's "cultural rights are limited primarily by the fact he has been sentenced to a term of imprisonment".
In his lawsuit against Victoria's Department of Justice and Corrections, the agency which manages the state's prisons, McKechnie, 54, said the ban on the spread breached law requiring prisons to provide food that allowed inmates to maintain their health and well-being but the judge said that had not been proven.
McKechnie was handed a life sentence for stabbing a property developer to death in Queensland in the 1990s. He served part of his sentence in Queensland before being transferred to Victoria.
During the hearing, the court heard evidence from Corrections Victoria that the smell of vegemite can distract sniffer dogs trying to detect drugs being brought into prison.
The product is also banned in jails in Queensland, South Australia and Tasmania.
A much-loved breakfast spread for some, Vegemite has acquired controversial accolades since it first hit shop shelves in Australia in 1923.
The thick, brown spread was invented in the Victorian capital of Melbourne more than a century ago as an alternative to the British spread Marmite.
It sparked an international dispute in April last year when an Australian cafe owner in Canada was told to remove jars of the condiment from his shelves as it did not comply with local health regulations.
Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese intervened in the row, saying it was "rather odd" that Canada allowed the sale of Vegemite's "rubbish" rival product Marmite. The cafe owner was later allowed to continue selling the spread.

The New York Times article appeared on September 24, 2025, under the headline The Billionaire, the Psychedelics and the Best-Selling Memoir.
The 4,980-word investigation by Katherine Rosman and Elisabeth Egan captured a wave of discomfort that had rippled from New Yorkâs publishing world to Amarillo, Texasâ police department about a bestselling memoir by a billionaire pillar of Manhattan society. Amy Griffinâs The Tell told the story of a woman whose perfect exterior masked childhood trauma, and how the drug MDMA helped her remember and ultimately move past childhood sexual abuse.
The Times story turned her success into a parable about class and Americaâs new ultrarich. Most damagingly, the Times discussed the possibility that Griffinâs memory of sexual abuse might have been borrowed from a classmate who attested that stories in The Tell were âeerily similar to the abuse she herself enduredâ in middle school from a different teacher.
Some of Griffinâs friends suggested she shrug off the bad press. But she was livid, consumed by it, friends said. It was intensely personal: In the days after the story, there had even been an exchange of Snap messages between Rosmanâs son, a student at the University of Southern California, and a friend of one of Griffinâs children. The messages, reviewed by Semafor, were heated but respectful.
The weekend after the story published, Griffin and her husband John Griffin, whose hedge fund was the source of their billions, were in the safe space of the superagent Ari Emanuelâs annual Aspen retreat, âThe Weekend.â A person seated with Griffin in Aspen recalled her saying the Times had sought to destroy her life and her familyâs.
Then Griffin said something that shocked her interlocutor, the person recalled: By calling into question Griffinâs account, Rosman had made her and her childrenâs life miserable â and she would do the same to the Times reporterâs son.
Griffin, through a spokesperson, heatedly disputed the claim: âAmy Griffin has never threatened Katherine Rosmanâs children or taken any action to harm Ms. Rosman or her family. These allegations are categorically false,â the spokesperson said.
The spokesperson cited the exchange of Snap messages after the story published. âAt an event shortly after publication, Mrs. Griffin was upset about the impact on her daughter and expressed those feelings in a conversation with a friend. Her words were later taken out of context and mischaracterized as a threat she never made.â
The person who heard Griffinâs comments in Aspen understood them as a threat, and said they felt obliged to act.
The person asked a mutual contact to warn Rosman, according to three people familiar with that exchange.
Rosman, in turn, alerted her employer. Then The New York Timesâ general counsel, David McCraw, spoke to Griffinâs lawyer, Tom Clare, though the two men offered somewhat different versions of what was said.
Thereâs no indication Griffin ever took any action against Rosmanâs son.
But Griffinâs focus on the Times story and other fallout has, acquaintances say, continued. The classmate, Joleene Altum, sued Griffin for emotional distress and invasion of privacy, and Griffin countersued for defamation in a bitter, ongoing legal battle. Itâs been covered breathlessly on Instagram and by celebrity media â led by the former Access Hollywood host Billy Bush, who last Monday on his podcast described being confronted by Griffin at a wedding on the Hawaiian island of Lanai.
âIn my opinion,â he said, Griffin âis a woman who has become unhinged, tearing down innocent people, trying to ruin lives and careers,â he said. âShe has attempted to blackball people from schools. Sheâs threatened to bankrupt media publications and individuals, including me.â
Griffin has also continued to focus her ire on Rosman, who didnât provide a comment to Semafor for this story. Months after the disputed exchange at Aspen, Griffin spoke to a person in a position to influence admissions at a major American university, a person with direct knowledge of their conversation confirmed.
In the conversation, Griffin asked the person to use that influence to deny admission to Rosmanâs children, the person with direct knowledge of their conversation said. Rosmanâs daughter is a senior in high school. The person did not act on the request, they said.
âMrs. Griffin has never contacted anyone associated with any university or school regarding Ms. Rosmanâs children,â Griffinâs spokesperson said.
âIf these troubling reports are accurate, this is a stunning abuse of power and influence wielded against the family of a journalist doing her job to report the news and follow the facts, simply because the subject of that reporting didnât like the coverage,â New York Times spokesman Charlie Stadtmiller said in a statement. âThe Timesâs reporting of Sept. 2025 was a careful, fair and above all accurate pursuit of the facts that probed important questions about memory, the past, traumatic events and the state of memoir publishing.â
Benâs view
Itâs tempting to see this story âÂ as the Times did âÂ as a parable of a billionaire class that has lost all moral moorings. But as I spoke to people in and around Griffinâs gilded circle, it was the opposite: Members of her social world were shocked by the suggestion sheâd take revenge on a journalistâs children, and most found it wildly out of character. Some I spoke to said they couldnât believe she meant what she said. One sought to warn Rosman, and the other did not act on Griffinâs alleged suggestion to attempt to intervene in Rosmanâs daughterâs college application.
Indeed, even as Americaâs emotional and capricious billionaires inspire terror in its professional and middle classes, they seem at times more vulnerable to negative media attention than anyone else. For the second time in three weeks, Indian cartoonist Satish Acharya found himself effectively invisible on Instagram in his own country.
The 55-year-old discovered on Tuesday that his account had once again been briefly blocked in India, allegedly with no explanation from the platform.
Just a few weeks ago, another cartoonist, Manjul, had found that Instagram had restricted a post criticising India's election commission over its controversial revision of voter rolls. His profile remained accessible.
The cases have raised concerns about the use of legal orders to restrict political satire in India, with cartoonists saying they are often given little explanation for why their work has been blocked.
Acharaya's account was first restricted from 28 September to 6 October, when users in India could neither find his profile through search nor access it through a web link.
Anyone trying to access his profile saw a message saying it was unavailable under India's Information Technology Rules.
The rules allow authorities and courts to order social media platforms to remove or restrict content.
The government says they help tackle unlawful material, but artists and free-speech advocates warn they can stifle India's rich tradition of political satire.
"Meta platforms have been restricting the reach of my cartoons for some years," Acharya told the BBC. "But when my entire profile was restricted in India, I was a little sad."
He wrote to Meta, Instagram's parent company, but received no reply. He says he was preparing to go to court when his account became accessible again in early October, only to be blocked again earlier this week for three days.
In a statement, Meta told the BBC that it may temporarily restrict accounts to comply with India's IT Rules but did not explain the specific reasons for restricting Acharya's account or Manjul's post.
Critics say the restrictions come as humour and satire play an increasingly visible role in political dissent in India, particularly among younger people.
Memes and Gen-Z humour helped fuel protests over education and jobs in July, which led to the resignation of India's education minister. Online debate has also intensified over a controversial revision of voter rolls that removed 130 million names.
The political significance of social media has not been lost on the government. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has urged ministers to strengthen their online presence and connect with younger audiences.
At the same time, technology policy expert Prateek Waghre says the government is increasingly using legal orders to regulate online content.
The Indian Express reported, external that government agencies sent nearly 195,000 blocking and content-restriction orders to platforms including Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July through the federal government's Sahyog portal.
The figures, obtained through a right-to-information request, do not show how many posts were ultimately restricted or removed. The BBC has not seen the original response.
Waghre says that some platforms, particularly Meta, "seem more willing to comply", he says, while X appears more willing to push back. But limited public data makes comparisons difficult. Meta declined to comment on his assessment.
The government has also reportedly sought greater scrutiny of how social media platforms recommend content.
Earlier this week, several media outlets reported, external that authorities had asked Meta to ensure its systems did not steer users towards "a single or limited set of narratives" and strengthen checks on content that could "cause public disorder or incite violence".
The BBC has sought comment from India's IT ministry on the restrictions and reported instructions to Meta but has not received a response.
Of course, political satire has a long history in India - as do attempts to curb it.
Cartoons have been a fixture of Indian journalism since independence, with RK Laxman's Common Man becoming one of its most recognisable characters.
But cartoonists have also faced censorship. During the Emergency in the 1970s, when civil liberties were suspended and the press was tightly controlled, Abu Abraham continued drawing, even as dozens of his cartoons were stamped "not passed by censors".
In 2012, cartoonist Aseem Trivedi was arrested on sedition charges over cartoons allegedly mocking the Indian constitution. The charges were later dropped.
Today, concerns about restrictions on political expression extend beyond cartoonists. India ranks 157th in Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index, while critics accuse the government of putting growing pressure on independent media. The government rejects the criticism, saying India's media remains free and vibrant.
Comedians have also faced controversy over political satire. Kunal Kamra, known for his jokes about Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his party, has faced threats, cancelled shows and legal action.
For cartoonists, however, challenging those in power is central to their work.
"We are among the default opposition," says Sandeep Adhwaryu, a cartoonist at a leading Indian newspaper.
"The nature of the craft is to oppose," he says, adding that cartoonists, like journalists, must question whoever holds power.
Acharya says he has followed that principle throughout his career. Before 2014, many of his cartoons targeted the Congress-led government and were shared by BJP leaders.
"I never faced official restrictions on my cartoons during the previous governments, though there would be some trolling occasionally," he says.
Now, with the BJP in power, much of his satire is directed at Modi's government.
Social media has allowed independent cartoonists like Acharya to reach audiences without relying on newspapers or other traditional outlets.

Until a few years ago many of us may have been blissfully unaware of what a data centre was.
These giant, warehouse-like buildings power virtually all our internet activity, from our web searches and emails to movie downloads and online banking.
They are at the heart of the AI boom, housing the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run services like ChatGPT and Claude.
But the speed at which they're growing, the enormous amount of electricity they consume and concerns about their environmental impact are fuelling a public backlash around the world.
In the US, they've become a huge issue ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, with both Republicans and opposition Democrats coming out against their development.
It's putting opponents of data centre expansion on a collision course with US President Donald Trump, who has dismissed the pushback as a "sick conspiracy", even as public anger grows.
Here's what you need to know about the data centre boom, and why opposition is growing.
They are growing rapidly
There are about 12,250 data centres around the world, according to Data Center Map, external, a company that tracks both operational and pre-operational sites.
That's up sharply from 2021, when there were around 8,000, external operational sites.
As the chart below shows, data centres are most densely clustered in the US which has 4,767 sites. It is followed by Europe, where the UK and Germany lead.
Data centres have typically been located near to cities where it's easier to access high voltage power lines or water resources for cooling. But as they get bigger, more are being built in rural areas.
But when it comes to actual capacity, the US is ahead by a much larger margin, with China in second place and Europe lagging far behind.
This gap is set to widen in the coming years, leading some to warn Europe risks missing out on the potential economic benefits of the AI boom, external.
They are getting bigger
Data centres vary wildly in size, ranging from ones that fit inside a garden shed to others covering vast expanses of land.
The world's largest operational data centre is widely reported to be one run by China Telecom in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, covering an area of approximately one million square metres (10.7 million sq ft). That is equivalent to about 140 Fifa football pitches.
However, much larger sites are under construction as the graphic below shows.
All these sites are being built exclusively to provide the immense computing power needed to run AI services.
For instance, Colossus 2, which is part of the wider Colossus campus, will house hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips made by tech giant Nvidia.
It will also be used to train xAI's chatbot Grok. Elon Musk's company will use 41 methane gas turbines to help power the site, which activists say could "significantly increase" local air pollution, external. Local regulators say the turbines will meet air quality standards.
They use more electricity than France
The pressure data centres put on local resources has sparked increasing concern. These facilities can use significant amounts of water to cool their systems, which could lead to water shortages, some experts say.
Data centres worldwide are also thought to consume more electricity than the whole of France, as the chart below shows.
This growing hunger for power is driving up carbon emissions, analysis shows, while putting pressure on local grids, which some fear could push up energy prices.
With others worried about the noise data centres make and the space they take up, a public backlash is gathering steam.
Some 16 US states have proposed laws to ban or temporarily block new facilities, and it could be a key issue in November's midterm elections.
Outside the US, opposition to data centres has emerged in countries like Mexico, France, Indonesia and the UK.
But they can boost jobs
But supporters say data centres are critical to national security, and the development of AI.
They also say they are good for the economy, external, attracting investment, generating tax revenue and creating jobs in areas like construction.
A recent report by the Brookings Center, external suggests data centres do create local jobs, although fewer than industry advocates claim.
The type of data centre matters too. So-called hyperscale facilities - massive sites owned and run by tech giants like Amazon and Microsoft - have a bigger positive effect on jobs, it found.
But "colocation" facilities, which lease space to remote tenants without a local presence, brought fewer benefits.
As the debate over their merits intensifies, the data centre rollout continues.
This year, the tech industry is expected to spend a combined $765bn, external ($544bn) on AI infrastructure in 2026, with this topping $1tn next year.
But as concerns about the environmental impact grow, the tech industry is exploring alternatives.
One idea is to put data centres in space, external or on the Moon, where they could harness abundant solar energy.
Others predict that more AI processing could eventually be carried out by the hardware already inside our computers and smartphones, reducing the need for vast data centres altogether.
Additional reporting and design by Erwan Rivault, Matt Faraci and Dominic Bailey.

Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships - the first time an Olympic federation has chosen to stage a global event in Russia since the country's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022.
The International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) announced its decision on Sunday, four months after confirming Russian athletes would again be eligible to compete in its events.
In July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) provisionally lifted a suspension on the Russian Olympic Committee.
That suspension had been imposed following the country's invasion of Ukraine.
The IOC's subsequent decision potentially opened the way for Russian athletes to compete for their country at the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.
The IWF announced the host cities of four world championships at junior, youth and senior levels, awarding the 2029 senior event to Ahmedabad in India.
"All the bids we received were excellent and we are sure that the championships in your respective countries will be a huge success," said IWF general secretary Jose Quinones.
No world championships in an Olympic sport, summer or winter, have been held in Russia since the start of the war in Ukraine.
The 2025 World Aquatics Championships, initially awarded to the Russian city of Kazan, were instead moved to Singapore.
Moscow has not held the World Weightlifting Championships since 1983.
The Russian Weightlifting Federation said: "[We are] the first Olympic sports federation to succeed in bringing a top-level official competition back to the country in many years."
Federation president Aleksandr Vinokurov thanked the IWF in a post on Telegram "for their trust", with the championships also serving as a qualifying event for the 2032 Olympic Games in Brisbane, Australia.
"Russia has all the necessary experience and capabilities to host competitions of the highest level," he said.
"Moscow has repeatedly staged major international sporting events and has modern infrastructure."
In announcing its decision in July to provisionally lift Russia's suspension, the IOC said that no decision had been taken on whether Russia could display their flag, colours and anthem at the Olympic âGames.
The IOC said it would continue to "not organise IOC events in Russia or invite Russian government or state officials to its events".
Some Russian athletes competed at the 2024 Paris Olympic Games and this year's Winter Olympics in Milan as neutrals.
Ukraine filed an appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) requesting that the IOC decision to lift its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee be annulled.
The IOC's move decision came after the International Paralympic Committee had already ended Russia's exile from global sports events, with the country's athletes allowed to compete under their national flag at the Winter Paralympics.
Five Ukrainian athletes are listed to compete in the 2026 IWF World Championships in Ningbo, China, which are scheduled to take place from 27 October to 8 November.

US singer Chris Brown has avoided jail after striking a man twice in the head with a glass tequila bottle in a London nightclub.
The R&B star was given an eight-month prison sentence, suspended for 12 months, over the attack at private members' club Tape in Mayfair, in the early hours of 19 February 2023.
Brown's vocal coach, rapper Omololu Akinlolu, who joined the attack, was sentenced to four months imprisonment, suspended for 12 months. Both men, who had pleaded guilty to affray, were also ordered to pay Â£1,500 costs.
Judge Tony Baumgartner said Brown's use of the glass bottle to hit the victim twice over the head "was plainly dangerous", adding that the violence of the attack was "intense".
The sentence means Brown will not be imprisoned unless he commits another offence during the 12-month period of suspension.
The court heard Brown's attack on music producer Abraham 'Abe' Diaw left the victim in need of hospital treatment for his injuries.
In sentencing, Judge Baumgartner said: "The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous, it carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained."
CCTV footage was shown where Brown struck Diaw four times with the bottle, connecting twice with his head, and then hitting his shoulder.
Sentencing Brown, Judge Baumgartner said: "This was not planned violence. It was nevertheless serious violence by two people in a crowded nightclub."
The judge told Brown: "Violence of this kind in a crowded nightclub is serious, it creates an obvious risk, not only to the person against whom it is directed, but also to others nearby."
He added that Brown's conduct was "particularly dangerous" and that he had to be "physically pulled away" from the attack.
The judge said Brown's fame, commercial success and professional standing "do not entitle you to special treatment - the law applies equally to everyone".
But judge Baumgartner also said he had noted Brown's guilty plea, compliance with bail conditions, and the impact a custodial sentence would have on Brown's children, and said the singer's "risk of further offending is low".
Brown and Akinlolu pleaded guilty to a charge of affray at Southwark Crown Court in July.
The singer had been due to face a trial on more serious charges, which he denied, and which were subsequently dropped.
These were assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm, and having an offensive weapon.
Following Brown and Akinlolu's guilty pleas, the CPS released a statement outlining that Brown had approached Diaw on the dance floor, hitting him over the head with a glass bottle twice, before Akinlolu then punched Diaw in the head.
"They continued their assault whilst the victim attempted to flee through the club," the CPS said. "The victim was kicked while he was seated defenceless on the floor."
On Monday, the court was shown three pieces of CCTV footage from inside Tape nightclub on the night of the attack.
The attack lasted no more than 20 seconds, but Brown could be seen hitting the victim four times with a tequila bottle, twice to the head.
Prosecutor, Heidi Stonecliffe KC, described the weapon as a "heavy square-shaped tequila bottle" and said Diaw was approached by Brown at around 03:00.
The footage showed that the nightclub was very small and packed at the time.
The defence described Chris Brown as a "dedicated and a loving father of four children," someone who is "positive and present".
The singer is described as having lived "a good and law-abiding life" since his last conviction in 2013.
The events in Tape nightclub were described by the defence as a "short and deeply regretted incident".
Brown's defence lawyer told the court that he apologises to all those present at the club at the time of the attack.
"This is an ugly and unattractive incident," Sallie Bennett-Jenkins KC said.
"It is, however, an incident which was very short-lived, lasting something more than 17 seconds but no more than 20.
"It is something which undoubtedly would have caused distress to those who are present and for which Mr Brown... offers a profound apology to all those present."
The court heard Akinlolu "genuinely believed" that Brown was "under attack" when he joined the attack, punching Diaw.
Brown was described as being like a "brother" to Akinlolu, his lawyer Laurie-Anne Power KC told the court.
She added: "He genuinely believed him to be under attack and became involved, and thereafter accepts his initial involvement very quickly evolved into the events he has pleaded guilty to."
Diaw was taken to St Mary's Hospital in London after the attack. Ms Stonecliffe KC said he was discharged with "pain relief and a diagnosis of head injury and superficial injury of the knee".
An MRI scan taken in early March showed a "high grade injury to a ligament on the inner side of the left knee", the court heard.
Defending Brown, Ms Bennett-Jenkins KC said there was a "relatively low level of force" and disputed how significant the injuries were.
The defence argued that the attack left no fractures or broken skin and there was an absence of serious injuries.
Diaw, the victim, was "not supportive of the prosecution" and "withdrew" his support some time after the incident, the court heard.
Brown and Akinlolu stood up and faced one another and clasped hands after the judge concluded his sentencing remarks before walking out of the glass dock.
There were loud cheers outside the court as Chris Brown left the building as he appeared to stop to sign an autograph.
After the sentencing, Brown shared a video from inside his car on his Instagram story, showing him looking out the window before turning to the camera and giving a thumbs-up.
Affray is an offence under the Public Order Act and a person is deemed guilty in law if they use or threaten "unlawful violence towards another" with their behaviour, leading someone to fear for their personal safety.

Anthropic has said artificial intelligence could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.
The company behind AI chatbot Claude revealed losses of more than $80.7bn (Â£60.5bn) in the first half of the year. It said it generated revenue of $16.3bn over the same period.
The number of shares to be released and their price range is yet to be determined.
Anthropic's valuation when it goes public has been expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which this summer was the biggest-ever stock listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion.
Ahead of its public listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.
It said that advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".
Anthropic, which was founded just five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five other co-founders, announced its intention to go public in June.
Its most significant rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit, saying it, too, intended to go public. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.
After the companies had decided on such plans, a wave of cyber-security and other types of technological breaches occurred involving their AI agents, or AI bots that are designed to operate somewhat autonomously.
Current and former staff of both companies also gained public attention with new warnings that AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect the whole of humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.
In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.
In its financial filings, Anthropic detailed losses that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".
"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.
Anthropic said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT. It will be the first true AI company to go public, marking a test for the future of the technology.
Tech companies have been heavily investing in costly AI infrastructure and tools, like data centres and the informational models that underly all AI technology, pouring more than $1tn into the efforts over the last year alone.

Brazil's President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office in a dramatic comeback over his right-wing challenger FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro.
Left-wing leader Lula took 51.79% of votes, becoming the first president since the return to civilian rule in 1985 to win an election after losing the first round of voting.
Lula told celebratory crowds this election is a "loss for negativity, lies", later adding "long live democracy".
FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, who is the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, has so far refused to recognise the result and called for it to be annulled, which experts say is unlikely.
In an unprecedented move, polls were also extended for two hours on Sunday evening after both candidates made requests for different reasons.
Lula's team had argued that voters in SÃ£o Paulo and Bahia could not get to the polling stations because of a lack of buses, while Senator Bolsonaro's campaign cited heavy rain in some areas in the south of the country and in SÃ£o Paulo as the reason for their request.
The decision - issued by the Supreme Court just as polling stations were due to close - meant that some had already shut and were not able to re-open.
Supreme Court President Kassio Nunes Marques - appointed by the older Bolsonaro - confirmed Lula's victory and said that the voting extension did not cause issues for the count or the electoral process.
Lula secured 51.79% of the vote against Bolsonaro's 48.21% - a difference of 4.4 million votes between the two candidates.
The result came as a surprise after Bolsonaro - who has the backing of his father - won the first round of voting on 4 October with 47% of votes ahead of Lula's 45%.
But Lula's camp gained momentum ahead of election day, focusing on boosting voter turnout after 33 million people did not vote in round one.
Sunday saw the largest drop in abstention between the first and second rounds of a presidential election since 1989.
As disconsolate Bolsonaro supporters left the house in BrasÃlia where their candidate had been watching the result, Lula took to the streets in SÃ£o Paulo to celebrate and address his supporters.
"This, my fourth term, will be the best of any president in the history of this country", the former metal worker said. "It will be the one in which I listen most to the Brazilian people."
Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin told him: "You, for the second time, have saved Brazilian democracy."
Bolsonaro, who had been poised to give a victory speech, said the result should be annulled, calling it "inexplicable" and "impossible".
But electoral law experts have told BBC Brasil that the chances of the results being annulled are remote.
Fernando Neisser from the Institute of Lawyers of SÃ£o Paulo (Iasp) said it would be "difficult from a legal standpoint" given that the margin of victory was relatively large, and would depend on the "narrative" his lawyers put forward.
Expert Alberto Rollo said that dates for presidential elections in Brazil are fixed and determined by the constitution, which would add another complication to getting it annulled.
Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, has already been president for three non-consecutive terms, serving two terms between January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023.
His win makes him the first in Brazilian history to secure a fourth term, which will last until 2030.
But this has been a bitterly fought campaign and the new term - set to start on 5 January - comes amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from US President Donald Trump.
Referring to what Trump has called the "Donroe Doctrine" - which seeks to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere - Lula used his victory speech to insist that Brazil "will not accept being anyone's backyard".
Trump has previously shown support for Bolsonaro's father Jair, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted of a coup attempt after losing the 2022 elections to Lula. FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro met Trump at the White House earlier this year to bid for his support.
Lula has also bucked a wider trend in Latin America, where voters in countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia have put right-wing candidates and parties in power.
While Trump has yet to react, other world leaders have been congratulating Lula on his win.
Ecuador President Daniel Noboa Azin said the region had "common enemies, shared challenges, and much to gain when we work together."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said "democracy and multilateralism" had won. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez - also a left-wing leader - called it a "great victory", saying "the comeback of global progressivism has just begun". French President Emmanuel Macron said the two nations should work "in service of a more just world".
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa called Lula's victory one for the "global south and progressive forces throughout the world".
Additional reporting by VinÃcius de S. Mendes, BBC Brasil

e1209836ac27.text: Anthropic's IPO filing includes an extensive list of extreme warnings — including the chance its own technology could put humanity at risk. Why it matters: These are the wildest IPO risk factors in history, a jarring collision of Wall Street legalese and what some see as Silicon Valley sci-fi, including catastrophic threats to humanity, blackmailing AI models, and $750 billion in computing commitments. Driving the news: Anthropic's prospectus includes over 90 pages of risk factors, which make up about a third of the paperwork overall. Among the most eye-popping, the company warns: 💥 AI could post "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," and could try to manipulate humans; 🔎 Models are becoming harder to monitor as they're getting better at circumventing oversight, and the pace of autonomous work alone could exceed the ability of human reviewers to monitor actions; 💰 AI models generally, including its own, have exhibited behavior resembling blackmail, including attempts to resist being shut down. Zoom in: Anthropic also disclosed that four of its models gained unauthorized access to real third-party systems during cybersecurity evaluations. In one incident, a model used a discovered password to gain administrator access, collected additional credentials, changed system settings and accessed an individual's personal information. Anthropic said it found no evidence that the models pursued goals beyond their assigned tasks or attempted to evade oversight. The big picture: Every company has to lay out risks for their investors to consider when they go public. But Anthropic is the first in modern history to go to such existential extremes. Friction point: The company also acknowledged that its success depends in large part on its ability to develop the best frontier intelligence. It admits that could butt up against safety practices, adding that model capabilities may then "advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement" corresponding safety measures. That underscores a fundamental tension critics have warned about: As Anthropic scales and faces pressure from public market investors to build better models than its competitors, its commercial ambitions could increasingly clash with its safety commitments. By the numbers: The risk factors also include the more typical financial cautions. Anthropic has committed hundreds of billions of dollars to cloud computing and equipment leases, even as customers can reduce their usage relatively quickly. Some agreements require minimum payments regardless of demand, and the company warns that failing to meet certain obligations could trigger defaults elsewhere, potentially accelerating debt repayments and jeopardizing access to computing infrastructure. Anthropic also acknowledges that it previously underestimated its compute needs. But overestimating future demand could leave it paying for expensive, underutilized infrastructure. The bottom line: Anthropic's IPO paperwork is an unusually candid warning about the risks of building a business around technology that its creator acknowledges may become increasingly difficult to control.

Then the students came World Oct 26, 2026 9:52 AM EDT BELGRADE, Serbia (AP) — Serbia's populist strongman Aleksandar Vucic dominated the Balkan country's politics for 14 years. Then came the students. The long-ruling authoritarian leader on Sunday conceded the defeat of his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party to a grassroots movement of university students in a parliamentary election. The students had led protests for almost two years before unseating him in a historic change of government. READ MORE: From France to Albania, how social unrest is fueling protests across Europe The 56-year-old political veteran easily outplayed political opponents in the past and thought he could do it again. Ahead of Sunday's ballot he pulled a maneuver in the style of his ally Russian President Vladimir Putin when he resigned the presidency to pursue a bid to become the prime minister. Vucic then launched a fierce campaign involving favorable around-the-clock coverage on state media and attacks on opponents. He handed out cash to voters and promised higher pensions, new roads and cheaper medicines. It didn't work. The diverse youth movement's message that rampant corruption, cronyism and organized crime under Vucic were eating away at the country resonated widely with voters. The student protests first started in 2024 after a collapsed canopy at a renovated train station in Serbia's north killed 16 people, triggering claims that graft-fueled negligence led to poor construction work and eventually to the crash. Defiant, Vucic on Sunday blamed his defeat on foreign interference. "I want people to know," he said. "This was the verification of a revolution that they carried out directly with support of different European countries and the deep American state, the one that is also against President (Donald) Trump." Vucic began his career as an ultranationalist During a political career spanning more than 30 years, Vucic morphed from being an extreme nationalist who supported aggression against non-Serbs in the former Yugoslavia to a populist who shifted his preferences to balance between global powers and influences. During the wars in the 1990s, Vucic was one of the radical party leaders who advocated the creation of a "Greater Serbia" that would include territories in Croatia and Bosnia where minority Serbs live. Those policies are widely blamed for bloody conflicts that killed over 100,000 people and displaced millions. Vucic was known for fiery speeches, including one in Serbia's parliament where he said that for each Serb killed in the Bosnian war, 100 Bosnian Muslims must die. He later said that he didn't mean it literally. As information minister in the late 1990s, Vucic oversaw media critical of then-President Slobodan Milosevic slapped with heavy fines or shut down. He shifted away from ultranationalism to a proclaimed pro-EU stance on the eve of his party's electoral win in 2012. He embraced Europe for a time In office, Vucic positioned himself as pro-European and pro-Russian, and as an admirer of Trump. Ahead of the decisive ballot, however, Vucic re-embraced his hard right roots and turned to Putin again as he struggled to restore his shaken voter base. Vucic defied the EU last month by allowing a hero's funeral in Belgrade for Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb army commander convicted of genocide by a U.N. court in the Netherlands. "It is no coincidence that Vladimir Putin said he hopes that I will be the prime minister," Vucic boasted days ahead of the ballot, ditching the proclaimed pro-EU position that helped his populist party come to power in 2012. Vucic's fall draws varied reactions in Russia Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov expressed hope Monday that the post-Vucic government will retain friendly relations with Russia. Vucic had refused to join EU sanctions against Moscow over the war in Ukraine despite formally seeking membership for Serbia in the 27-nation bloc. READ MORE: Serbians protest real estate project linked to Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner "We highly value the contribution Mr. Vucic has made to the development of our bilateral relations," Peskov said. "We intend to continue doing everything possible to help the development of our relations with Belgrade," Peskov said. "But, as you know, it takes two to tango." Konstantin Kosachev, a deputy speaker of the upper house, the Federation Council, said that the Serbian elections' outcome could signal that "there would be one sovereign country less in Europe." But Konstantin Malofeyev, a hawkish tycoon who sponsors a virulently nationalistic media outlet, welcomed Vucic's defeat, denouncing him as a hypocrite who has tried to maneuver between Russia and the West. "The Serbian people have delivered a historic verdict on the Vucic regime," Malofeyev said on his Telegram channel. "The era of political hypocrisy and duplicity is drawing to a close." Vucic controlled Serbia for 14 years In the past 14 years, Vucic served as a deputy prime minister, the prime minister and president. As president for nearly 10 years, Vucic turned the largely ceremonial post into the center of power in the country. He was known for frequent addresses to the nation and appearances in pro-government media. "He is a competitor who has mastered a technology of governing that is based on stick and carrot, and the idea that nobody but him is right," Dejan Pavlovic, a professor in the Faculty of Political Sciences at the University of Belgrade, told The Associated Press recently.
