The EU goal of reducing global deforestation could have damaging consequences for Ethiopiaâs coffee sector and wider economy, a think tank said. Some 15 million people in the country widely considered to be the birthplace of coffee are involved in the industry, which sends 30% of its output to the EU, according to London-based ODI Global.
The blocâs new rules, due to come into force at the start of next year, will require exporters of certain commodities â including coffee and cocoa â to prove they are deforestation-free. The change is placing tough traceability and mapping burdens on producers. Coffee growing in Ethiopia is dominated by smallholders, whose beans are mixed together and sold on. Difficulties in tracing their origin could result in 60% of these growers being excluded from the European market, ODI Global estimated.
Ethiopiaâs coffee authority is compiling data, but the process is not complete. In order to reverse historical deforestation, the country has also committed to planting 8 billion new trees this year, though the project has faced questions over verification and survival rates.

c017ca788b0c.text:
Kodal Minerals plans to expand its lithium business across West Africa, betting the gold-rich region can become a major supplier of the battery metal, Reuters reported.
The London-listed miner began producing lithium last year in Mali, in a joint venture with Chinese mining company Hainan Mining. Kodal has now agreed to acquire up to 80% of the Asamankese lithium exploration project in Ghana.
Africa is attracting investment from major miners as China and Western governments compete to secure minerals for clean energy and advanced technologies. Lithium, used in rechargeable batteries for electric vehicles, electronics, and electricity storage, has drawn more than $2 billion in Chinese investment to Zimbabwe, Africaâs largest producer, since 2021.

f1fc080e7d22.text:
A US solar energy provider plans to grow its Africa operations by adding facilities in Nigeria that will serve more than 30,000 people in the oil-rich, but electricity-poor, Niger Delta region. Deployment of grids backed by battery storage systems is ongoing, with a full launch slated for next year.
Atlanta-based Renewvia Energy recently raised $3 million from debt investors for one phase of the planned expansion, CEO Trey Jarrard told Semafor. It had previously tapped a Nigerian government grant tied to the World Bank-led Mission 300 project to connect 300 million Africans to electricity by 2030.
Solar minigrids have presented African households and businesses with a viable alternative to unreliable fossil-fuel-powered national grids strained by under-investment. Imports of Chinese solar equipment are at a new high, suggesting an enthusiastic take up. Nigeria, where about three in 10 people live without access to electricity, has introduced a $750 million fund to help private companies connect 17.5 million residents to a power source.

d4715b6a03be.text:
Swazi chef Sanza Sandile is using food to combat anti-migrant sentiment in South Africa. His Yeoville Dinner Club, found on the main street of the immigrant-rich inner Johannesburg neighborhood, is now in its 10th year.
The menus for the family-style meals unapologetically embrace the cultures and cuisines from across the continent and beyond, challenging the xenophobia stoked by some politicians, which has resulted in many migrant-owned restaurants seeing trade plummet.
Sandile, whose mother fled the apartheid regime, and who was raised partly by an uncle who took part in the armed struggle against the white-minority government, has spent years gathering recipes from around the world, believing food can invoke memory and inspire integration.

509bb65dda04.text:
Private Infrastructure Development Group, a multilateral financier backed by several Western countries, is planning to invest about $1 billion a year in Africa and Asia until 2030, its CEO said. Philippe Valahu told Bloomberg the money would primarily be pumped into renewable energy.
PIDG operates in 24 sub-Saharan African countries, including Angola, Ethiopia, Kenya, and South Africa. Valahuâs comments come as four of PIDGâs five funders â the UK, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Australia, and Sweden â trim their aid funding, raising concerns about how the group will sustain its pace of investment.
The project pipeline could be seen as helping to fill a hole in renewable energy funding after the Trump administration shut down Power Africa â a government-led initiative aimed at doubling African electricity access â pulled its share of investment planned for South Africaâs just energy transition, and has pressed the World Bank to back gas.

160643e67406.text: By — Eléonore Hughes, Associated Press Eléonore Hughes, Associated Press By — Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press By — Anna-Catherine Brigida, Associated Press Anna-Catherine Brigida, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/incumbent-lula-is-declared-winner-of-brazils-election-as-bolsonaro-rejects-results Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Incumbent Lula is declared winner of Brazil's election as Bolsonaro rejects results World Oct 26, 2026 9:19 AM EDT RIO DE JANEIRO (AP) — Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of U.S. President Donald Trump, was reelected Sunday in a result that provides relief to critics of widening U.S. influence in Latin America. WATCH: Brazil's high-stakes presidential runoff could reshape country's future With 100% of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that the soon to be 81-year-old Lula had a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, giving him 51.8% of the total vote. Bolsonaro quickly refused to concede defeat and asked for the election results to be annulled after an evening of chaos at some polling places that followed a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours. Bolsonaro is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, whom Lula defeated to take the presidency in 2022. Lula's triumph bucks a regional trend of victories for right-of-center presidential candidates allied with Trump. It also means Latin America's largest economy, with a GDP of $2.6 trillion per year, will likely continue defying Trump's demands, despite the pressure of increased tariffs. Lula says Brazil is 'not anyone's backyard' A video published by Lula's campaign shows the veteran leader celebrating with First Lady Rosângela da Silva and allies after his runoff victory was confirmed by Brazil's electoral court. Wearing star-shaped red glasses, he kissed his wife. Speaking to his supporters, thousands of whom gathered on Sao Paulo's main artery and in Rio de Janeiro's Cinelandia Square, Lula expressed his gratitude to the Brazilian people, and pledged to respect all Brazilians, regardless of gender or religion. He also attacked Bolsonaro. "This was a defeat for denialism and lies. I must confess that every time I attended a debate, I felt embarrassed," he said. He also doubled down on his commitment to Brazil's sovereignty. "Either the homeland remains free, or we die for Brazil," he said. "This country will not accept being anyone's backyard." In Rio de Janeiro, cars beeped their horns and a woman dressed in red — the color of Lula supporters — shouted "You lost! Cry harder!" to four men in yellow and green sipping beers, Bolsonaro's signature colors. A huge roar echoed in the street as the result was confirmed. Rodrigo Valentim, a 51-year-old businessman and supporter of Bolsonaro, said that another Lula government would harm the economy. He pointed to financial markets' positive reaction to the result of the first round, when Bolsonaro bested Lula. "I don't understand how people can vote for Lula," he said. "The country is collapsing." Lula is set to begin his fourth non-consecutive term as president on Jan. 5, 2027. Bolsonaro rejects results after confusion at polling places The electoral court's announcement ended an evening of confusion at polling places after Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ruled three minutes before the scheduled end of voting to keep polls open for two more hours, following requests by both candidates. Lula's request came after issues with buses that provide transportation to polls in Sao Paulo and Salvador, two cities that tend to favor the incumbent. Bolsonaro's request was due to heavy rains in Brazil's south, where he is favored. The decision delayed tallying the votes by two hours. It was unclear how many polling stations stayed open after the scheduled closing time. Polling stations in Brasilia and Rio de Janeiro closed shortly after the original 5 p.m. deadline, reporters for The Associated Press observed. READ MORE: Brazil's Lula warns against foreign interference in elections, urges leaders to respond to global conflicts Bolsonaro, whose father is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup after he lost the 2022 presidential election to Lula, pointed out that Zanin is Lula's former lawyer and criticized him for "changing the rules of the game in the middle of the game." "It's impossible to recognize the results of the election in the context of these things that happened," he said. It's not clear if Bolsonaro's complaint could meet the legal threshold to annul the results. Bolsonaro also has the right to request a recount if he has evidence of fraud, but that might not change the results. The president of the electoral court, Kassio Nunes Marques, who was appointed to the Supreme Court by former President Bolsonaro, said that the extension of voting hours did not impact results. Joao Pedro Padua, a law professor at the Fluminense Federal University, said that Bolsonaro can file a lawsuit directly with the country's electoral authorities or the Supreme Court, asking for the elections to be declared null and void. "But there isn't much legal basis for that," Padua said. "The extension of voting hours is unusual, but for it to invalidate the elections, the candidate would have to prove that it affected voters' ability to freely express their will. There doesn't seem to have been any such impact." Lula overcame concerns about security and cost of living Bolsonaro bested Lula by more than 2.2 million votes in the first round of the election earlier this month. Sunday night's victory by Lula marked the first time since Brazil's military dictatorship ended in 1985 that the second-highest vote-getter in the first-round elections won the presidency. Lula faced a tough reelection battle because of concerns about the cost of living and security. Bolsonaro mad

dbaefed69ac5.text:
Senegalâs government is locked in a budget standoff with parliament as the oil price crisis triggered by the war in Iran strains the heavily indebted West African countryâs finances. The revised 2026 budget, which sets spending at about $13 billion, would cut public investment while increasing energy subsidies. The bill is due before lawmakers on Tuesday, after the finance committee rejected it.
Parliament Speaker Ousmane Sonko, who leads the largest party in the legislature, said the budget sacrifices essential investment and demanded greater transparency over government finances. Sonko, who was fired as premier in May, has clashed with his successor over how to manage the countryâs debt. Prime Minister Ahmadou Al Aminou LÃ´ said the government would use âinstitutional and constitutional toolsâ to end the impasse if the deadlock persists.
The government owed about $44 billion at the end of 2025, equivalent to roughly 100% of the countryâs GDP, and is negotiating with creditors over repayment terms. It is also seeking to restore support from the IMF, which suspended its previous loan program after billions of dollars in unreported government debt came to light in 2024. A new $2.2 billion program agreed in principle in September still awaits final approval.

ea38e62c6961.text:
The UAE is contending with an oil spill off its shores, the most visible example of the risks of attacks on tankers and a threat to an already fragile tourist season. Beaches are closed across the northern UAE, including in Ras Al Khaimah, where the Wynn Al Marjan Island is set to open next year. In the days before the spill was announced, residents complained of fuel-like odors pervading areas of Dubai and north.
This was not the first oil spill of the war: A tanker ran aground near Omanâs southeastern coast, leaving a slick covering about 6.5 times the land area of Manhattan, and Iran had an oil spill off Qeshm Island near a breeding ground for endangered hawksbill sea turtles, Bloomberg reported.

32b14846d8fb.text:
For years, Qatar has faced accusations of supporting Hamas, the Muslim Brotherhood, and Iran, and using Al Jazeera and American universities to spread its agenda. While Doha has influence among Islamist movements, it has consistently rejected nefarious intentions, pointing to its role as a mediator and US defense partner. Still, the charges are used as political ammunition in the US and Israel, where key elections will be held over the next two weeks, with some Israelis in particular repeating claims that Qatari funding helped enable Hamasâ Oct. 7 terror attack.
The charges have always been short on evidence. A recent Time investigation uncovered secret correspondence showing that Israel encouraged and coordinated nearly $2 billion in Qatari payments to Gaza over more than a decade. In a 2020 letter, Mossadâs director at the time praised Dohaâs humanitarian efforts for âensuring stability and safety in the region.â
The accusation that Qatar uses university funding to promote antisemitism has also been debunked by a former US ambassador to Qatar who is affiliated with Georgetown, which has a branch in Doha. He noted that 97% of the $6.25 billion Qatar provided to American universities since 2001 went to six institutions, all of which have campuses in the country.

09b1a1053ef7.text:
Gulf states are closely watching as Israelis head to the polls on Tuesday, in the first national election since the Oct. 7, 2023 terror attack. A victory for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would mean an increasingly assertive military posture from Israel; his defeat could âbe an opportunity to move towards a more stable regional order,â Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa Program at Chatham House, told Semafor.
Broadly, a Netanyahu win would mean more of the same for the region, too: The Abraham Accords would hold, and Saudi normalization would stay out of reach without a credible path to Palestinian statehood, Vakil, who is also a lecturer at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, said. A new government wouldnât necessarily shift course on Iran or the Palestinians, but it could âcreate some diplomatic spaceâ for Gulf engagement on Gaza and the West Bank, according to Vakil. âA Netanyahu defeat would be welcomed by most Gulf capitals.â
Polls point to a deadlocked parliament, with the opposition â an anyone-but-Netanyahu bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot â on track to win the most seats, but short of a majority. That means the potential for protracted coalition talks (Netanyahu took 58 days to form a government after the 2022 vote). Eisenkot supports military action to stop Iranâs nuclear program if necessary, but in recent weeks he has called regime change in Tehran militarily unachievable.

e09ff748fe6b.text:
Saudi Arabia reopened Riyadhâs international airport on Sunday even as Yemenâs Houthis vowed to continue attacking the facility, which they had forced to close after deadly strikes two weeks ago. Operations resumed with limited flights by Saudi carriers from half the airport. The capital faced renewed attacks on Sunday, with authorities reporting the interception of Houthi ballistic missiles.
Foreign airlines have not yet resumed flights to Riyadh, and some traffic shifted to Al Qassim airport, more than 350 kilometers from the capital. Riyadh Air, the recently launched Saudi sovereign fund-controlled airline, has moved its entire operations to Al Qassim. The strikes in Riyadh have killed at least 13 people and wounded hundreds â some of the survivors were allowed to speak about their ordeal to Saudi state TV over the weekend.

67ca209a2a2d.text:
Saudi Arabiaâs defense minister and security officials from Pakistan and TÃ¼rkiye are set to meet with Iranian leaders to ease tensions in the region, amid signs that the US-Iran conflict could escalate again. Saudi defense minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistanâs army chief Asim Munir, and the head of TÃ¼rkiyeâs intelligence services, Ibrahim Kalin, will meet with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and national security council secretary Mohsen Rezaei on Monday in Tehran. The talks aim to de-escalate and promote âdialogue and diplomatic solutions,â according to Saudi Arabiaâs deputy minister for public diplomacy.
This is the highest-level contact between Iran and the three members of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement that was signed in August. Washington has pulled non-emergency staff and families from Saudi Arabia and US President Donald Trump said itâs âgetting to be decision timeâ on making a deal with Iran or returning to conflict, suggesting he could resume attacks after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

a5ef8152d41f.text:
Anthropic’s Claude AI chatbot helped a scientist plan potentially risky bird flu experiments.
The researcher relied on Claude to plan studies, analyze data and choose experiments involving highly pathogenic avian influenza, the company reported September 10 in a threat intelligence report. The work sought to identify and introduce mutations that could help bird flu viruses adapt to mammals and transmit more easily between them. Anthropic says that, to its knowledge, no private company had previously publicly shared evidence of potential misuse of its platform for biological weapons development. But the company did not provide enough detail to determine whether Claude simply sped up work the researcher could already do or gave the researcher a new capability, experts say.
Learning how avian influenza viruses might pose a pandemic risk “is absolutely a normal part of virology research,” says influenza researcher Thomas Friedrich of the University of Wisconsin–Madison School of Veterinary Medicine. Such research can help scientists assess whether emerging bird flu viruses pose a greater risk to humans.
But experiments that deliberately aim to boost pathogen traits such as transmissibility or disease severity draw scrutiny, Friedrich says, because of concerns about accidents or misuse.
Though the report comes amid broader debates about the security of AI models, arguments over this “gain-of-function” research predate generative AI. In 2012, studies involving H5N1 bird flu and airborne transmission in ferrets prompted an international debate over whether the scientific benefits outweighed the risks. Some H5N1 transmission experiments were put on hold for a year while researchers and officials worked out how to handle the risks.
In Anthropic’s case, discovered in May 2026, the bird flu researcher accessed Claude from a region where the service was not supported or available. Anthropic says the researcher used workarounds to access Claude anyway. Material shared with Claude suggested the group probably had physical access to relevant virus samples. Anthropic banned the researcher’s account in May for evading restrictions on access.
Anthropic says it could not tell whether the researcher intended harm because legitimate and dangerous biological research can look similar. The company did not respond to questions from Science News about why it considered the case significant, how it assessed Claude’s role in the research or whether any proposed experiments had actually been performed.
Anthropic released too little information to determine the purpose of the work, says biodefense researcher Gregory Koblentz. “There is no evidence that any of this research was connected to the development of biological weapons,” says Koblentz of George Mason University in Fairfax, Va.
The same kind of biological research can serve very different purposes, from civilian science to military defense. Even work done at a military-affiliated institution does not, on its own, show that researchers are developing a biological weapon, Koblentz says.
Anthropic also did not provide enough detail to show exactly how much Claude helped, Friedrich says. The company’s own account suggests the AI model “did not meaningfully add scientific capability,” he says. In other words, it may simply have sped up the researcher’s work, rather than enabling something they could not have done otherwise.
Even if Claude’s role was only to speed up the work, that can make a big difference in a scientist’s workflow, says virologist David O’Connor of the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Systems such as Claude can help researchers find papers, synthesize results and parse data more quickly, he says. “Work or analyses that would have taken me months can now be done in an afternoon.”
As a result, existing scientific information, including about avian flu viruses, may become easier to find and use, O’Connor says. O’Connor says frontier AI models could let scientists tackle questions they might not have attempted before. “The frontier models will change the ambition of research questions that are asked,” he says.
The bird flu research was one of five instances in Anthropic’s report involving uses of Claude that the company says could support biological weapons development. None of the five look technically sophisticated or particularly concerning to biologist Kevin Esvelt of the MIT Media Lab. Esvelt is more suspicious of the researchers’ motives; he says the five cases showed signs of ill intent. But none “represented a competent attempt at weaponization.”
The poor quality of these particular attempts does not show what a more capable user might be able to do with AI-assisted biology, Esvelt says. AI can help with research and analysis, but turning an idea into a biological threat takes additional work, Koblentz says. “Even if AI is used to design a potentially dangerous pathogen, it is not a threat until the organism can be modified in a lab or synthesized.”
That requires facilities, measures for keeping viruses contained, funding, trained personnel and hands-on experience. Those barriers vary depending on who is doing the work, O’Connor says. They would be a major obstacle for an inexperienced person working alone, but less so for scientists with specialized training and access to a well-equipped laboratory.
Regardless, the remaining laboratory steps are substantial, Friedrich writes in an email. “There is a big gap between identifying mutations that could potentially adapt an avian influenza virus to humans and a ‘harmful biological outcome’.”

8080e4eeb536.text:
If Nvidiaâs Jensen Huang is the business worldâs Bugs Bunny, playing every position on the baseball field by himself, Elon Musk is its Forrest Gump, materializing at the center of events both strange and consequential.
In just the past 10 days, Musk has cut a $1 billion check to help the Ellisons build a right-leaning media empire; tested market jitters with a gargantuan SpaceX bond offering; set in motion the largest-ever corporate merger and the largest-ever philanthropic gift; and set a new standard for all corporate demo days with an actual flying car. Further from Wall Street, he reset US foreign policy by cutting Ukraine off from Starlink â a move that says enough about whoâs in charge that President Donald Trump claimed credit for reversing it â and dominated the midterm-elections homestretch with spending that will near $450 million this cycle.
After his post-DOGE meltdown last year, many had thought Musk had been neutered. He lost his lawsuit against OpenAI. SpaceXâs grandiose IPO prospectus drew titters from an investment community generally prone to believe outlandish promises. But like X, Musk has emerged stronger and more central to finance, politics, and culture.

5c9214f86a34.text:
- Published
A nurse has been killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack as they were responding to an Ebola alert in north-eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The two were targeted by local youths who accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the Ebola virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi. The World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the attack.
In an attempt to prevent the virus spreading, neighbouring Uganda has banned all non-essential travel to and from DR Congo and says its citizens returning from there will be quarantined for 21 days.
More than 4,800 people have died and nearly 10,000 been infected in DR Congo since this outbreak began in May.
Reacting to the attack in DR Congo, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said health workers "must be able to carry out their duties in safety and dignity", adding that healthcare personnel should always be protected.
The UN agency also extended its condolences to the family and colleagues of the nurse who was killed and wished the injured worker a swift recovery.
The BBC has contacted the Ebola response team for comment on the circumstances surrounding the attack in DR Congo.
Earlier this month, two countries - Kenya and Nigeria - reported their first cases of Ebola linked to the current outbreak.
The patient in Nigeria was on Monday flown from Abuja to Switzerland for further treatment.
She is the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat who had travelled to the Ugandan capital for a holiday, according to the head of Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Jean Kaseya. She was evacuated alongside her husband, who has shown no symptoms.
Nigeria's health ministry said she was stable, conscious and able to communicate.
Authorities are now trying to establish where she contracted the virus.
The new restrictions announced in Uganda come after questions were raised over her case and that of a Kenyan businessman. Both tested positive for Ebola after travelling through Uganda, even though no cases have been reported there since August.
The Kenyan had arrived from DR Congo where he had business interests.
Only essential travellers, including aid workers, truck drivers and security personnel, will be allowed to cross the border from DR Congo to Uganda, subject to strict health screening, the health ministry announced.
In addition, all travellers entering Uganda, regardless of their country of origin, will be required to complete locator forms to facilitate contact tracing where necessary.
It said returning Ugandans would "undergo 21 days of quarantine at their own cost".
About 60 people who were being monitored after coming into contact with the Kenyan patient have all been discharged, it added.
"All these are measures to ensure that we keep Uganda free of Ebola," Uganda's Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi told the BBC's Newsday programme.
Since the two cases were reported in Kenya and Nigeria this month, Uganda has repeatedly stressed that no cases have been reported within its borders. Uganda recorded 20 Ebola cases and two people died shortly after the outbreak started in DR Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country free of the disease in August.
The two passengers tested positive after passing through Uganda's Entebbe airport on the same day.
Diana Atwine, the health ministry's permanent secretary, said CCTV camera footage showed no physical interaction between the two patients.
The Kenyan businessman died two days after arriving in Nairobi, and the country has since confirmed eight other cases of Ebola. A second woman, related to the businessman died over the weekend.
Ugandan officials had previously said the patient in Nigeria had travelled to eastern DR Congo, only transiting through Uganda. On Sunday, however, the health ministry said Uganda and Nigeria were both working to establish her movements, complete travel history and possible routes of exposure.
The Ugandan health minister said the recent cases meant the risk had not ended and further underscored the need to "remain vigilant".
"We share a border with [DR Congo], where transmission continues, and our communities remain closely connected through trade, travel and family ties," Baryomunsi said.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind this outbreak is relatively rare and there is still no vaccine or specific treatment - though trials are under way.
Additional reporting by Swaibu Ibrahim in Kampala

6957095ef0a2.text:
Lizâs view
How does Wall Street quantify fear? Political boogeymen get names (Red Menace, death panels); financial ones get numbers. The VIX captures the marketâs twitchiness, while credit-default spreads calculate the odds of a company going bust.
When it comes to AI jitters, the price of fear is settling somewhere around 200 basis points.
When SpaceX issued its first corporate bonds â back in the giddy, futuro-optimist days ofâ¦ four months ago â it paid 6.65% for the most expensive piece. The most expensive slice of the $40 billion of private credit borrowing itâs finalized in recent days will cost as much as 8.75%, a person familiar with the matter said, having shot higher since we reported on price talks last week.
Breaking down that gap: At least 25 basis points can be attributed to the Fedâs September rate hike and expectations of another one by the end of the year.
The rest comes down to pure nerves. Those 200 basis points translate into hundreds of millions of dollars of extra borrowing costs that canât be pinned on the Fed or the overdue sobering-up among lenders. It owes squarely to the growing doubts about the ROI of AI and whether borrowers will be good for the money.
Elon Musk touted the deal as a sign of SpaceXâs strength, gliding over its eye-watering cost. âAs of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesnât have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers,â he posted on X Sunday. âWeâre investment grade and have Starlink & launch revenue.â And yet the market is pricing a BBB company like itâs two rungs lower.
Thereâs also, as one executive at an AI infrastructure fund put it to me last week, the âsupply-demand imbalanceâ â finance-speak for AI needs a lot of money and investors need to catch their breath. For now, the AI anxiety appears confined to credit investors, by nature a more dour and pessimistic bunch than stockholders. But fear is contagious, and if it spreads to stockholders, things could get ugly quickly.
Notable
- âThe credit market is getting jammed right now because it hasnât figured out a good way to offloadâ AI-related risks, Citadelâs co-CIO Pablo Salame told Bloomberg. âAIâs rising tide will sink some boats, and itâs a wavy tide.â

9c03aba50baf.text:
The shock reelection in Brazil of leftist incumbent Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva, which polls â and Wall Street prognosticators â had pegged as unlikely, has left markets in disarray. An ETF tracking Brazilian stocks in New York was down 26% pre-market, while a Tokyo-based equivalent dropped 15%. âItâs going to be a tough day. The market will reprice everything,â an analyst told Bloomberg. âEveryone was caught by surprise.â
Investors had largely bet on a win by right-wing opponent FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro, who had promised to shore up the countryâs public finances â under Lula, who has championed welfare and state-led investment, Brazilâs public debt has gone up 10 percentage points to more than 82% of GDP, and the country faces huge fiscal challenges and cooling economic growth. Bolsonaro has already challenged the results, prolonging the political flux and adding fresh pressure to the currency.

c777a30dc762.text:
Meta is issuing new stock for the first time since 2013, announcing a $95 billion offering to fund its AI buildout. About $60 billion will come in the form of new, nonvoting shares that the company created last week, a move that telegraphed its rapacious need for cash and CEO Mark Zuckerbergâs desire to raise it without diluting his control stake (and pay his tax bill).
The offering tops Googleâs $85 billion and Oracleâs $25 billion announced stock sales this year.
All three show how the AI boom is stretching corporate balance sheets: The biggest cash-cow businesses in the world can no longer support it, and borrowing can no longer fill the gap. Hyperscalers are expected to spend $800 billion on AI this year and more than $1 trillion next year. Meta shares are up 2% premarket, suggesting that while credit investors are scared, stockholders are still sanguine.

cec1d59763c9.text: Top Democrats poised for powerful roles next year are demanding that major banks and ports preserve any records they have tied to potential imports or other deals involving Russian diesel . Why it matters: Probing President Trump's agreement with Moscow will be a priority if Democrats regain control of either or both chambers of Congress. The new demand shows that inquiries will extend beyond the White House and into C-suites. Driving the news: "[A]ny importation of Russian diesel into the U.S. raises significant legal questions and may be subject to legal action, as well as congressional investigations," a new letter obtained by Axios states. It's signed by Sens. Chris Coons (D-Del.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.). They're in line to lead the powerful Foreign Relations, Banking, Finance and Judiciary Committees, respectively, if Democrats regain the Senate. Rep. Greg Meeks (D-N.Y.), who's in line for the Foreign Affairs Committee gavel if House control changes, also signed. It's led by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the top Foreign Relations Democrat who is not seeking reelection. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who is also retiring, signed as well. State of play: The Wall Street recipients of Saturday's letter are J.P. Morgan, Bank of America, Citi, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley. The same letter went to port authorities for the ports of Houston, Beaumont, and Corpus Christi, Texas, and New York/New Jersey. Catch up quick: Earlier this month Trump claimed an agreement to bring escalating Russian exports to global and U.S. markets, and the Treasury Department waived sanctions to help enable it. Friction point: The lawmakers and other critics say it runs afoul of a bipartisan 2022 law barring imports of Russian oil, gas, and petroleum products. "The potential arrangement to import Russian diesel also raises significant national security concerns, given that it would finance Russia's brutal and illegal war against Ukraine," the letter states. Yes, but: The Treasury Department has repeatedly claimed the agreement is legal. The big picture: The new letter urges the banks and ports not to enable "purchase, transportation, importation, unloading, storage, financing, or distribution" of Russian diesel in the U.S. It also goes further, urging the parties not to facilitate any transactions for Russian diesel to other markets under the recent sanctions waiver. Zoom in: Citing "anticipation of further congressional oversight," it calls on recipients to preserve a wide range of potential records and communications related to "proposed or actual" transactions. Think contracts, shipping documents, vessel records and plenty more. The demand extends to any communications with suppliers, intermediaries and U.S. government officials. The lawmakers want confirmation by Wednesday that records are being preserved, plus details of any potential or actual Russian diesel transition. What we're watching: It's unclear how much Russian diesel, if any, will reach U.S. shores. Reports Friday in S&P Global , Reuters and elsewhere identify a tanker that initially signaled a New York destination, while the shipping intelligence firm TankerTrackers on Friday said three tankers had signaled U.S. destinations. But ships' planned destinations frequently change for one reason or another. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

A clean-up operation is under way in parts of the UK after Storm Boelo caused flooding and property damage, leaving thousands without power.
The Energy Networks Association (ENA) said around 90,000 properties are still without power as of Monday.
Two men were killed by falling trees during the storm on Sunday - a man in his 20s whose car was hit in north London and a 60-year-old in Mid Kelton, Dumfries and Galloway.
The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for strong winds from 18:00 on Monday to 03:00 on Tuesday across the west coast of England, Wales and Scotland and eastern parts of Northern Ireland.
The Met Office has warned that further power cuts in areas covered by the warning are likely and people should make sure they have essentials prepared, including torches and batteries.
Coastal communities could also be affected by spray or large waves, while travel delays are expected.
Boelo is the second storm to have hit parts of the UK in recent days, following Storm Austen.
Leo Slade, CEO of the ENA said it had been "a tough weekend" and that efforts to reconnect some properties were being hampered by the weather, with sustained winds of 50-85mph across parts of Scotland and northern England.
"Until that weather system passes, we can't safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up, so today is going to be a hive of activity in getting engineers out into the field," Slade told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
He stressed that the UK's power network was very resilient and money was spent to prepare for these sorts of scenarios, but said a debate was needed over how much more investment was required to mitigate for further storms brought by climate change.
Marcus Reed, the operations director at a home fragrance manufacturer, said his factory and shop in Lyndal, Cumbria would be without power until Tuesday evening.
He told the Today programme that he has had to turn away employees and customers.
"To lose two days manufacturing and distribution is going to be really disruptive," he said, adding that it was bad timing as it was "the busiest time of the year" for his business in the lead-up to Christmas.
"This is probably the worst situation I've experienced in my time here; we've had ad hoc issues over weekends where we've lost power, but it's been contained within a 12-hour period. It's the first time anything like this has happened, it's very serious."
Wendy McKinney, whose bathroom shop in the seaside town of Largs in North Ayrshire was flooded on Sunday, told the Today programme the storm had been "devastating to local businesses".
She said the local council only handed out sandbags after flooding had already started:"[They] were just left in the middle of the street yesterday afternoon on pallets just for everybody just to try and help themselves, but it was too little too late."
North Ayrshire Council told the BBC that it had distributed almost 300 sandbags in Largs and Saltcoats and would continue to "respond where it has been safe and appropriate to do so".
A spokesperson said council teams "followed established resilience procedures" but would review flooding reports and "consider any lessons that can be learned".
Disruption to travel has continued on Monday, and some schools in Scotland have been shut either due to lack of power, heating, water or damage.
Another yellow warning of wind, external has been issued by the Met Office, covering much of Scotland, as well as parts of northern England and Northern Ireland from 03:00 to 23:59 on Tuesday.
Monday morning has seen rain in many parts of south-west England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and this is moving north-eastwards reaching central, eastern and northern England, as well as most of Scotland, by around lunchtime.
Winds will also strengthen throughout Monday, and it will turn even windier overnight as the area of low pressure passes close to Northern Ireland and north-west Scotland with gusts peaking on Tuesday.
Additional reporting by Ben Rich, lead weather presenter.

On the face of it, Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva has done the impossible one more time - within three weeks he overturned defeat in first-round voting to gain re-election as Brazil's president.
It was no mean achievement for a man who before his first successful run at the post in 2002 had tried three times unsuccessfully.
When he became president in 2003, he came to office as the first leftist leader of Brazil in nearly half a century.
Now aged 80 and with plenty of experience at governing as large a democracy as Brazil, he has bucked the trend of electoral victory for right-wing leaders in Latin America whose policies mirror that of US President Donald Trump.
Who is Lula and what are his policies?
Lula's first presidential victory in 2002 marked the end of an unprecedented journey from poverty.
The son of a poor, illiterate peasant family, Lula worked as a peanut seller and shoe-shine boy as a child, only learning to read when he was 10 years old.
He went on to train as a metalworker and found work in an industrial city near SÃ£o Paulo, where he lost the little finger of his left hand in an accident in the 1960s.
Lula was not initially interested in politics, but threw himself into trade union activism.
Elected leader of the 100,000-strong Metalworkers' Union in 1975, he transformed trade union activism in Brazil by turning what had mostly been government-friendly organisations into a powerful independent movement.
In 1980, Lula brought together a combination of trade unionists, intellectuals, Trotskyites and Church activists to found the Workers' Party (PT), the first major socialist party in the country's history.
The PT went on to gradually replace its revolutionary commitment to changing the power structure in Brazil with a more pragmatic, social democratic platform.
Lula came to power promising major reforms to the country's political and economic system.
He vowed to eradicate hunger and create a self-confident, caring, outward-looking nation.
In his time in office, Lula pumped billions of dollars into social programmes and can reasonably claim to have helped reverse Brazil's historic inequalities.
By increasing the minimum wage well above the rate of inflation and broadening state help to the most impoverished with a family grant programme, the Bolsa Familia, he helped some 44 million people and cemented his support among the poor.
However, many commentators argue that the programme failed to address the structural problems that underpin poverty, such as a lack of education.
He left office eight years later, after serving two terms as president, enjoying exceptionally high popularity ratings for a retiring Latin American leader - 83% - having raised Brazil's profile on the international scene and presided over the longest period of economic growth in three decades.
Unable to run for a third term, Lula left the presidency and, shortly afterwards, was diagnosed with throat cancer. He even shaved his trademark beard during treatment. Doctors declared him cured of the disease in 2012.
Why was Lula previously jailed?
Under his chosen successor, progress stalled. The economic boom also gave way to recession, and the country's political scene was rocked by a huge investigation into top-level corruption, known as Operation Car Wash.
Lula was among those to get caught up in the scandal. In July 2017, he was convicted of corruption and sentenced to more than nine years in prison for accepting a beachside flat as a bribe from engineering firm OAS - a sentence increased on appeal to 12 years.
Lula was also jailed for 12 years and 11 months for corruption and money laundering for receiving bribes from two construction and engineering firms by way of funding improvements in a country house he and his family used.
He has always maintained his innocence, insisting accusations against him were politically motivated.
In 2019, he was released after having served just over 18 months, after a Supreme Court ruling that the incarceration had been illegal, having come before all appeals had been exhausted.
Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for a third term in 2022, beating right-winger Jair Bolsonaro.
When he re-entered office in 2023, he vowed it would be his last term, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 on Tuesday.
Even backers of the PT will acknowledge that he achieved more in his first two terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - than in his most recent four years in office.
And while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions.
His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism.
Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy.
His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working.
What is Lula's relationship with Trump?
Lula's third term coincided with the return to office of Trump.
The two men represent different ends of the political spectrum and have found it impossible not to voice their differences in public.
Even though the US has a trade surplus with Brazil, Donald Trump imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods in July that year, citing the trial on coup charges of Brazil's right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro as a trigger. The Scene
China is key to global manufacturing across a range of sectors, but foreign capitals â increasingly worried about domestic industry being hollowed out in the face of cheap, high-quality goods from the country â are cracking down.
Few are doing so more aggressively than India, which has set deadlines for local firms to source more of its solar power supply chain domestically, even as it seeks to add a whopping 200 gigawatts of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030.
Beijing is mounting its defense against that strategy: This month, it proposed export controls on several technologies used to make solar equipment, and has reportedly restricted Indian firmsâ access to key parts of the solar supply chain.
âThereâs nowhere else for us to go but to go to China and to get equipment from them that allows us then not to buy the end product from them,â Sumant Sinha, the chairman and CEO of Indian renewables firm ReNew, said in an interview. âOf course, theyâve wised up to this fact.â
Ultimately, though not directly comparable to the Strait of Hormuz crisis, overreliance on China is its own bottleneck, Sinha warned. âWe all talk about increasing electrification â¦ But itâs fully based on dependence on China. And thatâs not a healthy thing.â
So, as a result, countries such as India can only wean themselves off China if China allows them to, he noted. And so, âwhy would they?â
Q&A
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Prashant Rao: Can you describe the kind of broader pressure, either from yourself, your offtakers, whoever, to get off the Chinese supply chain? How much does the Chinese supply chain loom over you?
Sumant Sinha: Itâs more of a sovereign issue than it is an individual company issue. For us, if you tell us to buy from China, we buy from China. Does that increase our dependence on China as a country? Of course it does. I think the sovereign, that is the Indian government, took a view that we did not want to have that reliance. And I donât disagree with that because, why should you have that?
Especially when your own domestic market is big enough. And there are all sorts of geostrategic issues that are going on as well with China.
What theyâve done is actually pretty interesting, which is that they give you a forward notice. And thatâs what they did for solar modules. They said two years from now, theyâre going to stop imports of Chinese modules or any other modules from outside India. So, you have two years to set up capacity.
Lo and behold, at the end of that time period, we now have close to 200 gigawatts of solar module manufacturing. Which is great.
Now theyâve also done the same thing for cells. So that cell restriction is coming into place this December. And from two years from now, theyâre going to do the same thing for wafers and ingots. So theyâre slowly, slowly going further up the value chain. They may do it for polysilicon as well at some point in time, or they may give some other incentives.
I would say that three to four years from now, theyâll have a fully domestic supply chain for solar. And theyâre trying to do similar things for batteries and the battery components and so on as well.
How does that affect your costs?
Obviously our costs are higher than Chinaâs costs. Because letâs say the cost of production in Chinaâs here, our cost of production is slightly higher.
What would you say the ratio is? Like 1.2?
Itâs 20%. But they are selling at a price of 80% to 90%. So, theyâre selling at massive discounts, which they can, by the way, increase if they want to make sure that no Indian manufacturing comes in. And we are selling at whatever is the regular margin to sell at.
So, on a sales price to sales price basis, weâre probably 30% more expensive than that. But that is because Chinese [companies] are making massive losses.
Bottom line is our costs are a little bit higher. But as long as it applies to everybody in the industry, it doesnât matter. Because what that then means is that we just pass on the cost to the end consumer.
Therefore, the end consumer ends up paying that cost. Now, you may argue why should the end consumer pay a higher cost? The end consumer pays a higher cost because ultimately that allows us to localize the supply chain.
How would you characterize your current reliance on Chinese technology?
We are still importing equipment. So, even if we start making cells ourselves, which we are doing right now, we will still have to buy wafers until such time that we start manufacturing wafers in India, which will take us another two years.
A lot of the equipment to manufacture all these items comes from China. And so, we need to import from China. So that reliance is there. Because over the years, whatâs happened is that China not only started making modules and cells and all of these clean tech equipment, but they also started making the capital equipment to make all of these things. And then over time, the R&D to make the capital equipment, and so on.
Theyâve done that very intelligently. Thereâs nowhere else for us to go but to go to China and to get equipment from them that allows us then not to buy the end product from them. Of course, theyâve wised up to this fact.
So, itâs functionally impossible to wean yourself off the Chinese green supply chain?
If they allow us to transfer technology from China, [but] why would they? Thatâs the point. We have to see what to do about it. Itâs not that straightforward.
The thing that I find very surprising is that the rest of the world is fully dependent on China for supply chains in clean tech. Immigration has always been central to Donald Trump's message.
When he famously stepped onto the golden escalator at Trump Tower to announce his candidacy for his first presidential term in 2015, he accused Mexico for of sending drugs and crime north of the border - and it's been a constant rallying cry ever since.
Some of his first-term ambitions to stem the flow of would-be immigrants were constrained by the courts.
But restraints have been weaker in his second term, with a more accommodating Supreme Court and tens of billions of additional enforcement money from Congress.
Who should be allowed to live in the US remains a big issue on the minds of voters in the upcoming midterm elections, which are largely seen as a referendum on the Trump presidency.
He promised a closed border and mass deportations in his successful 2024 campaign - and few can deny that he's delivered on both.
But even among those who voted for a tougher stance, there is a concern that the crackdown has gone too far.
His signature policy has played out in five key ways.
1. A border that is largely closed
Crossings exploded during Joe Biden's presidency, with over 4.5 million migrant "encounters" recorded at the southern border in 2023 and 2024 alone, reflecting the massive numbers of people headed north to the US border.
His administration eventually brought the monthly figures down significantly by restricting asylum claims and removing migrants entering the US illegally without processing.
When Trump returned to office, that stream of migrants became a trickle. Border encounters plummeted.
By the end of Trump's first year in office, the chaotic scenes that had generated headlines around the globe during the Biden administration had largely gone.
On a trip to the border city of El Paso, Texas, in November 2025, for example, the BBC found quiet streets where there had previously been makeshift camps housing thousands of migrants granted parole in the US to await immigration proceedings.
To achieve what he often describes as the "most secure" border in US history, the Trump administration has taken an aggressive, multi-pronged approach.
That has included effectively freezing asylum applications at the border, ending "catch and release" of detainees into the US, deploying troops to the border and pressuring Mexico to clamp down on the flow of migrants headed north.
"President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement on 16 October.
"The results could not be clearer: strong enforcement works."
2. Building of wall speeding up
A vow to build a "big, beautiful wall" at the nearly 2,000-mile (3,218km) US-Mexico border was a signature promise of Trump's 2016 campaign.
Progress on it has speeded up in his second term, boosted by $46.5bn (Â£34.7bn) in new funding from Trump's "One Big Beautiful" spending bill.
According to government figures, external, about 644 miles of "primary wall" - closest to the border - existed before Trump returned to the White House, in addition to 75 miles of "secondary" wall set slightly further inside the US.
Since then, 250 more miles of new wall have been completed, including primary, secondary and waterborne barriers, along with the technology that helps detect illegal crossings. An additional 1,443 miles of barriers are currently under construction.
Experts, however, paint a more complex picture of what has been actually built rather than just improved or updated.
Additionally, the impact the wall is itself having on the broader immigration figures is up for debate.
"Since new wall construction has really begun in earnest, there has been no significant change in the number of people crossing the border," said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, an immigration enforcement expert at the American Immigration Council.
There is no indication the border wall has reduced migrant crossings, he added. The reduction has been more down to Trump's policies and messaging.
Trump, for his part, continues to point to the wall as a successful policy - and continues to claim that Mexico paid for it.
"I'm the King of the Wall," Trump said at a rally in Kentucky on 17 October. "By the way, Mexico did pay for that wall. I charged them tariffs and I charged them costs like they've never paid in history."
3. Detentions and deportations rocketing
Most of the headlines generated by Trump's immigration policies have come from the US interior, where operations by Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to round up people they say are in the US illegally have rocked cities across the country.
During his campaign, Trump promised an immediate start to what he described as the "largest deportation operation in American history", which officials said would begin with people who have committed crimes first.
Arrests - and subsequent detentions in immigration facilities - have shot up significantly since Trump returned to office, including a record of nearly 50,000 in July this year alone, according to data obtained by the Deportation Data Project, external, a repository of US immigration data run out of University of California, Berkeley, and UCLA.
But the same data, external shows that a large chunk of the arrests involve people without criminal convictions. In July 2026, detentions of immigrants with criminal histories reached an all-time low of 27%.
Deportations have also ramped up significantly. By mid-July this year, ICE was removing an average of 1,255 people from the country per day, compared to about 770 in Biden's final months in office - although Biden's own removals had sharply risen in his final year in office.
But the tactics used by ICE in US cities have made many Americans grow uncomfortable, including many of those who supported stricter restrictions broadly. This became increasingly evident following Operation Metro Surge, a two-month large scale enforcement action in Minneapolis in early 202

The October full Moon lit up skies around the world this weekend.
Full Moons throughout the year have traditionally been given names that reflect what is going on in nature.
This particular full moon is known by several names, including the Hunter's Moon, a name rooted in historical traditions in the Northern Hemisphere.
The Hunter's Moon is known to sit in the sky for a particularly long time - similar to the preceding Harvest Moon - giving hunters extra light in the skies.

After a weekend of heavy downpours and severe gales, Storm Boelo is moving away from the UK and the weather is turning calmer.
However, this may not last long as another deep area of low pressure is already approaching from the Atlantic.
As this moves into north-west areas of the UK during Monday and Tuesday it will bring another dose of rain and gales.
Met Office yellow wind warnings have been issued for much of Scotland, northern areas of Northern Ireland, Wales and western England.
However, this latest weather system is unlikely to be as widely disruptive as Storm Boelo - or Storm Austen which came before it - and has not, so far, been named.
The next name on the list for the 2026/2027 season is Chloe.
Rain spreading quickly northwards
Rain to parts of south-west England, Wales and Northern Ireland on Monday morning will move rapidly north-eastwards, reaching central, eastern and northern England, as well as most of Scotland by around lunchtime.
It will also be rather misty and murky over some coasts and hills.
As the rain clears, slightly drier conditions will spread across the UK from the south-west.
While many areas will remain cloudy a few bright or sunny spells are possible, especially in Wales and south-west England.
Southerly winds will bring warmer air than of late, especially in the south where temperatures may peak at 18 or 19C.
Winds strengthening
After a breezy start to Monday, winds will strengthen once again during the day, with widespread gusts of 30-40mph and 50mph gusts likely in many coastal areas and 65mph in some locations.
It will turn even windier overnight and Tuesday as the area of low pressure passes close to Northern Ireland and north-west Scotland, the very strongest gusts could reach 70-85mph in the Hebrides.
Yellow wind warnings are in place covering both of these areas starting from Monday evening into late Tuesday evening.
Check here for the latest information on weather warnings and keep up to date with the forecast for your area via the BBC Weather website and app
The Met Office warning suggests that there is a low risk of significant impacts, with the chance of travel disruption, power cuts, damage to buildings and some flying debris. Some trees are likely to get blown over.
Storm Boelo contained a spell of damaging westerly winds which effectively funnelled through the highly populated Central Lowlands, increasing the likelihood of impacts. In contrast the winds in this system will be southwesterly, with areas of high ground providing a greater degree of protection for the biggest towns and cities.
There is a risk of some localised flooding with more heavy rain forecast. Some coastal flooding is also possible where large waves coincide with high tides.
Calmer from midweek
High pressure will build close to the UK from midweek onwards meaning the weather should gradually calm down.
Showers will continue on Wednesday but most places are expected to be dry by the end of the day.
Under light winds on Thursday morning, mist and fog could cause some travel disruption across some parts of the country. This should largely clear to leave a dry day with sunny spells.
A weather front could bring rain back into western parts on Friday but high pressure is then expected to rebuild with most computer weather models suggesting a drier and calmer spell is likely to develop over the weekend and into next week.

728dfd4618bf.text: President Trump's Board of Peace has appointed Shelley Greenspan, who served as the White House's Jewish community liaison during the Biden administration, to lead its outreach to Congress and the Washington think tank community. Why it matters: Greenspan's selection is part of an effort by the Board of Peace to increase bipartisan support for President Trump's Gaza peace plan. The implementation of the plan is expected to get a renewed push after the midterms and the formation of a new Israeli government. The possibility of Democrats controlling the House or Senate makes the need for bipartisanship on the Gaza plan even more crucial. Driving the news: The plan has been stuck due to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's refusal to take any steps in Gaza before the October 27 elections. In recent months, multiple prominent Democrats have expressed support for Trump's plan. Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton endorsed the plan in June, calling it the most viable proposal. Zoom in: Greenspan, a career civil servant at the State Department, was at the White House National Security Council during Biden's term — both as the American Jewish community liaison and the director for partnerships and elobal engagement. At the Board of Peace she will lead external affairs, putting her in charge of outreach to Congress and Middle East experts. What they're saying: "Shelley brings deep experience working across the aisle, having earned the trust of Democrats and Republicans alike through her service at the White House, National Security Council, and State Department in Democratic and Republican administrations," the Board of Peace told Axios in a statement. "Sustained, bipartisan support from Congress is essential to the work ahead, and Shelley is uniquely capable of leading this effort," the board added. Greenspan told Axios in a statement that she worked in her last State Department role to advance Trump's "vision for peace and prosperity in the Middle East." "I saw how the President's 20-Point Plan can tangibly deliver for the peoples of Gaza and Israel. I look forward to continuing that work with the Board," she said.

bddecd32230e.text: The 2026 midterms have taken a deeply personal turn as campaigns use other people's family tragedies as political ammunition — sometimes over the objections of the families themselves. Why it matters: Some attack ads feature photographs of murdered children and anguished 911 calls, forcing grieving families to relive their worst moments. Georgia governor race: Republican gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson used images of murdered 8-year-old Secoriea Turner and her mother's anguished 911 call to attack Democratic rival Keisha Lance Bottoms, Atlanta's former mayor. Turner's family demanded the ads come down, accusing the campaign of exploiting their grief without permission. Jackson said he would keep airing them . Ohio governor race: Ohio Republican gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign is spending $4 million on an ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton. In the ad, Donna Arthur calls her daughter a liar and disputes her account of childhood homelessness. Acton says her late stepfather — who was married to her mother until his death — sexually abused her as a child, and she hasn't spoken to her mother in decades. Acton's brother corroborated her account , while court records and contemporary news reports support key details. President Trump urged Ramaswamy to keep running his attack on Acton, despite objections from some fellow Republicans. Between the lines: Ramaswamy's campaign said the ad tested well with persuadable voters , even as critics warned it could backfire. Ohio Senate race: A Republican attack ad against former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown featured images of a couple and their 1-year-old son killed in a highway crash to blame Brown's immigration policies. The victims' family demanded its removal , saying nobody sought permission to use their relatives' images or tragedy. North Carolina Senate race: A Republican super PAC featured a grieving father in an attack ad linking the murder of his 23-year-old son to former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper's prison policies. The father said he felt deceived about the ad's purpose. The group disputes his account, while fact-checkers found no connection between the killer and Cooper's prisoner-release agreement. Yes, but: Some survivors willingly share their trauma to challenge politicians' decisions. In Nebraska, Jody Snogren voluntarily appeared in an ad attacking Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts for his 2022 vote to pardon John Arias, who pleaded guilty to raping her. Snogren told The 19th she chose to tell her story to inform voters and had no regrets. Ricketts expressed sympathy for Snogren but defended the pardon , noting Arias had served his full sentence and the pardon came decades after the crime.

d090da3a53f3.text: A tidal wave of litigation is catching up to Meta, leading to $42 billion in recent penalties and settlements , a powerful reminder to AI companies that they could face a court reckoning even when regulation lags. Why it matters : AI companies are racing to build better models and autonomous agents, but they don't enjoy the same legal protections that shielded web platforms for decades. The scale of the penalties Meta is facing offers a preview of potential legal exposure . The big picture : For years, Facebook's parent company navigated a seemingly endless string of scandals — weathering allegations of election interference, privacy lapses and platform harms — and was largely protected from severe litigation penalties due to Section 230. The provision — from a historic 1996 law passed as the internet was just beginning to change modern life — protects tech platforms from being sued over content created by their users. Legal experts say that law doesn't apply to AI. Models create their own content, so companies could face traditional product liability and negligence claims. Catch up quick : The two massive rulings highlight how legal risk for tech giants can extend by a decade, or proceed much faster. Meta was just hit with a $25 billion penalty over the Cambridge Analytica scandal after a jury found the company misled users about Facebook's privacy practices. Many details about that event surfaced nearly 10 years ago. The company said it believes it will win an appeal, and legal experts have said the penalty will likely be reduced. In August, the company agreed to a $17 billion settlement with states related to the impact of Meta products such as Instagram on teen mental health. State of play : A key cog in the Trump administration's regulatory efforts is the threat of litigation. Liability is sure to feature prominently in the risks AI giants such as Anthropic and OpenAI spell out to shareholders as they prepare for massive public listings. Anthropic's IPO is expected before Thanksgiving. The companies face an array of legal threats, including harms caused directly by their models, the potential damage from bad actors who use them and copyright matters that remain far from settled. The potential to be hauled into court isn't limited to AI companies; it could also extend to firms that use AI. Yes, but : Big legal penalties take years to arrive, meaning a product can take off and revolutionize the world long before a court determines whether safeguards are adequate. As recent cases have shown, the AI paper trail is extensive, and records of internal warnings, testing and product decisions will shape the findings by judges and juries. Warnings about catastrophe from AI executives will also be ready at hand, and variations on "I told you so" aren't likely to indemnify CEOs. The bottom line : Meta's recent penalty offers a warning to AI companies: legal exposure can build slowly, then become enormous.

Intense rainfall delayed Iowa’s harvest by nearly three weeks this year, but the combines are finally out in full force. So are top Trump administration officials.
U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin and Vice President J.D. Vance have all traveled to Iowa in the last month, either in their official capacity or to campaign with GOP candidates. President Donald Trump visited Sioux City last Thursday and plans to return to Iowa before Election Day.
Though widespread frustration over affordability could fuel Democratic gains nationwide, Trump’s trade wars, the war in Iran and his support for the oil and gas industry have hit Iowa farmers particularly hard. The state is a leading producer of corn, soybeans and biofuels made from both crops.
With Iowa’s closely watched midterm elections roughly a week away, the Trump administration has rolled out a series of measures aimed at winning over farmers whose livelihoods depend heavily on federal fuel and agricultural policies.
Republicans could lose up to four GOP-held seats in Iowa’s congressional delegation. Democrats hope victories in the state will help them take control of Congress, while Republicans are fighting to preserve their narrow majorities in the House and Senate.
Republican political action committees have recently withdrawn financial support from incumbent Mariannette Miller-Meeks’ campaign in Iowa’s 1st congressional district, signaling little confidence in her ability to defeat Democratic challenger Christina Bohannan, who lost to Miller-Meeks during the 2022 and 2024 election cycles.
In the 3rd congressional district, which includes the more progressive Des Moines metropolitan area as well as reliably conservative Southwest Iowa, incumbent Republican Rep. Zach Nunn must fend off Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott. The Cook Political Report, a non-partisan election analyst, recently shifted predictions for both races from “toss-up” to “lean Democrat.”
The Report calls the U.S. Senate race between current Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek and Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson a toss-up. The race between Republican Joe Mitchell and Democrat Lindsay James in Iowa’s second district is also rated a toss-up, as they vie for the House seat Hinson vacated in her bid for Senate.
The war in Iran and the subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz have exposed how much Iowa farmers rely on fossil fuel imports. Spiking diesel prices have left growers paying almost twice as much per gallon this harvest as last year. That amounts to thousands of dollars of additional costs each day, even on smaller acreages.
Meanwhile, Trump’s tariffs have driven up the price of farm machinery and other essential materials, like fertilizer. Retaliatory tariffs from countries like China are devastating U.S. commodity crop exports and depressing market prices.
U.S. farm debt is projected to hit a record $605 billion this year, raising concerns about a repeat of the farm crisis of the 1980s. Back then, soaring debt, plunging land values and federal policies that encouraged consolidation contributed to widespread foreclosures of family farms.
Last week, Trump announced that the U.S. Department of Agriculture would offer American farmers $8 billion in one-time fuel relief payments.
The National Corn Growers Association welcomed the announcement with cautious optimism.
“We appreciate the administration recognizing how the high cost of inputs, especially diesel fuel prices during harvest time, is adding to the economic pain of America’s farmers,” the organization wrote in a statement. Still, they added, “We urge Washington to focus on durable, bipartisan, long-term solutions that will result in lasting improvements to the farm and national economy.”
“Hail Mary” on Fuel Policies
Throughout the summer, Democratic campaign ads in Iowa criticized Reps. Hinson, Miller-Meeks and Nunn for repeatedly voting against war powers resolutions directing the president to end U.S. military action in Iran.
In September, after voting “no” five times, Miller-Meeks and Nunn broke with most of their party and voted in favor of a resolution. Hinson voted against the Senate version for the sixth time, but days later posted on social media that she wanted to see a “successful and immediate end” to the war.
Votes on these resolutions can signal lawmakers’ views and their awareness of how a war affects their constituents, but the resolutions are still subject to a presidential veto, said James McCormick, a professor emeritus of political science at Iowa State University.
Even if the war ends today, Iowa farmers are unlikely to see an immediate drop in prices, McCormick said. Prices on refined oil products like diesel and gasoline could remain high for a year or more after the conflict ends.
Aaron Lehman, president of the Iowa Farmers Union, described last Monday’s fuel relief announcement as a “Hail Mary pass” by Trump to fix a problem his own policies created. “We need genuine efforts to help farmers now while fixing the real causes of our current situation. We need to conclude the war without sacrificing our farmers’ bottom lines,” Lehman said in a statement.
As farmers face mounting financial pressure, many are looking to biofuels for a potential economic lifeline. Ahead of November’s election, Republican candidates and cabinet members have sought to capitalize on that optimism by courting Iowa’s biofuel industry.
