Press freedom groups are suing the Trump administration over its efforts to block mainstream US news outlets from covering the White House, according to court filings.
The six plaintiffs, which include scholars, advocates and journalists, argue media bans issued by the White House violate the First Amendment of the US Constitution - a critical statute that provides broad protections for the press and freedom of speech.
Their suit comes after CNN, Politico, and MSNOW brought a separate legal challenge over the White House's attempts to revoke or restrict their press access.
The Knight First Amendment Institute and Yale Law School's Media and Information Access Clinic filed the legal case on the plaintiffs' behalf.
The six plaintiffs have asked a New York federal court to declare the White House's selective media bans violate the First Amendment, and to block the administration from continuing to enforce it.
In court filings, the plaintiffs allege they are no longer able to do their work without access to information delivered by the White House press.
The White House policy, they claim, "deprives the public" of reporting, and forces journalists who cover Donald Trump "to account for the possibility that a critical or ill-advised word about the president may result in their access being summarily restricted or revoked".
Such a ban has a "distorting effect" on coverage from the White House, the court filing argues.
The BBC has asked the White House for comment.
The lawsuit did not ask a judge to award financial damages, only to require the defendants to cover their legal fees if they win.
Since Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025, the White House has engaged in a contentious standoff with many longstanding US media outlets, which the president has frequently accused of publishing "fake news".
Last month, it banned reporters from CNN, Politico, and MSNOW from the White House, leading several other media organisations to temporarily suspend their pooled coverage of the president in protest.
The affected news outlets sued, arguing the White House was illegally discriminating against them because of the content of their coverage.
A federal judge later ordered the White House to restore the credentials of the impacted journalists while their lawsuit plays out.
The reporters later said they were allowed back into the White House complex.
The White House has, however, continued to selectively bar journalists, which news organisations in the US argue violates their press freedom protections.
CNN, for instance, has threatened to take further legal action in court as its reporters continue to be denied access aboard Air Force One to cover the president.
And last week, the White House banned a correspondent from The Independent from covering the president's trip to the state of Iowa, after Trump berated the reporter from the UK news outlet during a press conference.
In his second term, Trump has also moved to bring conservative bloggers, influencers and other "new media" figures into the press room, arguing it is necessary to provide diverse perspectives in White House coverage.
In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool - the small group of journalists that has access to the president on any given day - which for more than a century had been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.
The same month, the White House moved to bar Associated Press journalists from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because the outlet used the term "Gulf of Mexico" rather than "Gulf of America".
AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.
Trump last week confirmed he is considering moving the entire press corps from the White House grounds following reports he was contemplating the reconstruction of a swimming pool that sits underneath the James S Brady briefing room.
"I am thinking about moving the press, and putting them in a different location," he wrote on Truth Social. "I will use that location for very badly needed space."

8132e57e8be7.text: By — Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/6-citizens-sue-trump-over-media-ban-saying-it-deprives-them-of-news-as-audience-stakeholders Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 6 citizens sue Trump over media ban, saying it deprives them of news as audience stakeholders Politics Oct 26, 2026 3:36 PM EDT In the increasingly bitter legal standoff between President Donald Trump and media outlets whose reporting he dislikes, a new and crucial third party has emerged: citizens who watch and read the news and need it to do their jobs. A lawsuit filed Monday on behalf of six such citizens — essentially representing the wider public audience — argues that it's not only the rights of news organizations that are violated when Trump bans them from White House premises. Even more fundamentally, the lawsuit argues, such bans violate the public's right to independent reporting about its president and government. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "The ultimate injury here … is to the democratic public," says the suit, filed in federal district court in New York against Trump and three key aides, including the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles. "The First Amendment protects the public's right to know what its government is doing," said Katie Fallow, deputy litigation director at the Knight First Amendment Institute, which filed the lawsuit on behalf of the plaintiffs, along with the Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic at Yale Law School. "The White House cannot decide what information Americans receive by punishing critical reporting," Fallow said in a statement. "When the White House expels reporters because of their coverage and threatens others with expulsion, it isn't just the press that suffers — the public loses access to independent reporting and gets something closer to government propaganda." The Trump administration, asked for comment on the lawsuit, responded in a statement that it attributed to an unidentified White House official: "No person may demand access to the Oval Office." It said media that peddle "misinformation and defamation are completely capable of reporting their manufactured stories from directly outside." The plaintiffs all rely on White House news for their work The six plaintiffs are all people who say they rely on independent and diverse White House reporting for their teaching, journalism or advocacy. They include a noted human rights advocate, a political journalist, a Yale history professor, a high school civics teacher, a legal journalist, and a student journalist at the University of Pennsylvania. The complaint filed Monday recounts how various news organizations that have been targeted by Trump are already battling the administration in the courts. These cases include the current lawsuit by CNN, MS NOW and Politico, whose journalists were banished from the White House in September. A federal judge recently extended an order preventing the White House from enforcing the ban while the case makes its way through the legal system. Still affected, though, is CNN's pool coverage of Trump. The White House has been denying the network its usual slots in the video pool covering the president's activities and travel, and CNN has threatened further action. Also continuing is the legal case involving The Associated Press, whose reporters were barred last year from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some events in retaliation for the outlet's decision not to follow Trump's lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico, which lies partially in Mexican and other waters, to the Gulf of America. The New York Times is also involved in litigation, over a Pentagon policy requiring escorts for journalists on its grounds. And ABC is fighting back against the Trump administration in a dispute over renewal of its broadcast licenses. This lawsuit seeks more wide-ranging relief The new lawsuit filed Monday, though, is different from previous legal action against the president — first, in that the plaintiffs are ordinary citizens, shifting the focus from news gatherers to news consumers, and thus implying a much larger pool of stakeholders. In addition, it seeks more wide-ranging relief. The suit, which names Trump as defendant along with Wiles, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, and Secret Service Director Sean M. Curran, calls not merely for reinstatement of access that has already been impacted, but for a broad injunction that would protect from retaliation every news outlet that covers the White House — now, and in the future. "Defendants' policy of restricting the access of disfavored news organizations deprives the public of the reporting of those organizations," the complaint says. It also "inevitably deprives them of the independent reporting of other news organizations as well, since every journalist who reports from the White House must now account for the possibility that a critical or ill-advised word about the president may result in their access being summarily restricted or revoked." "Plaintiffs ... seek a declaration that the policy is unconstitutional because it imposes restrictions on a limited public forum that are viewpoint-based and unreasonable," the complaint adds. "They also seek an injunction barring defendants from enforcing the policy." Plaintiffs include a human rights advocate, a teacher and a student journalist The plaintiffs are: Kenneth Roth, former longtime executive director of Human Rights Watch and a lecturer at Yale's law school and school of global affairs. Roth "relies on newsgathering and reporting from members of the White House press corps to inform his public writing and commentary," the suit says. Daniel Fro

DoorDash is in exclusive talks to acquire Instacart, according to people familiar with the matter.
A deal is far from certain and the talks could fall apart, the people cautioned. It could not be determined what price was under discussion or how a deal would be structured.
Instacart declined to comment. DoorDash did not immediately return a request for comment. Instacartâs sale process was first reported by the Information. The Information also reported that Uber was interested in a deal for Instacart, but Bloomberg later reported that that interest had cooled.

Discovery and Paramount. The US justice department illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) director James Comey, a federal judge has ruled.
Comey, who lost her job as a federal prosecutor in New York in July 2025, sued the government, arguing she was unlawfully fired because of her father, a critic of US President Donald Trump, and because of her perceived political affiliations.
Judge Jesse Furman ruled on Monday that the Trump administration must reinstate her and that she must be given back pay.
A spokesperson for the justice department said in a statement that it disagreed with the decision and "will appeal in due course".
In his ruling, Judge Furman said Comey's dismissal violated the US Constitution as well as his right to a fair legal process.
He said the US attorney general can fire federal prosecutors but only "in a particular manner and only for certain reasons".
Furman noted that in Comey's role, "she was assigned some of the country's highest profile cases and consistently received the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike".
Comey has worked on cases against the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell, and hip-hop mogul Sean "Diddy" Combs, who was convicted on prostitution-related charges involving his two ex-girlfriends last year.
Furman ordered that Comey to be given back pay from July until December 2025, when she accepted a new job.
In a statement, Comey's lawyers said: "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law".
Comey had previously said the only reason she was told about her firing was that it "came from Washington".
A complaint filed by her lawyers in September 2025 stated that they believed Comey had been fired "solely or substantially because her father is former FBI Director James B Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both".
The justice department said in court filings that the decision was made by former Attorney General Pam Bondi.
The Trump administration has twice brought charges against James Comey, including for allegedly lying to Congress, but that case was dismissed by a judge who said the prosecutor who brought the case was unlawfully appointed.
Earlier this year, the justice department charged Comey with knowingly and wilfully making a threat to take the life of, and to inflict bodily harm, on the president. He has denied any wrongdoing.
The case stems from a 2025 Instagram post shared by Comey, which contained a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47". "Eighty-six" is a slang term for "get rid of", and prosecutors allege it encourages violence against Trump.

Americans have gone all in on "maxxing", making it the 2026 Word of the Year for Dictionary.com.
Short for maximising, the term "can be used on its own or added to the end of any word to convey you're doing something to the fullest or optimizing it as much as possible", Dictionary.com said in a statement.
It's a major departure from two years ago, when the site, after analysing US social media trends, news stories, and search data, chose demure as word of the year. Last year's was "67".
"Maxxing is the linguistic manifestation of a culture increasingly preoccupied with getting the most out of everything," said Steve Johnson, director of lexicography for the Dictionary Media Group.
Digital media used "maxxing" nearly 19 times more in August 2026 compared to the 2025 monthly average, Dictionary.com found. The site also considered affordability, data centre, odyssey, and the shortened form of uncle, "unc", as potential words of the year.
On social media, many people in Generation Z and younger - those under 30 - post extensively about their maxxing efforts to achieve all sorts of perfection.
Influencers focused on fitness and wellness post about "proteinmaxxing" and "fibermaxxing". Those giving their full attention to improving sleep habits say they are "sleepmaxxing".
The influencer Clavicular has gained thousands of followers as he chronicles his extreme "looksmaxxing" - working to meet a set of prescribed criteria for attractiveness, with particular importance given to jawlines, eyes and physique.
"Whatever we're doing, we want to push it further," Johnson said. "But its expanding uses also reveal how people are responding to that impulse. Some embrace it. Some exaggerate it for laughs. Others subvert it entirely to describe stepping back from the relentless pursuit of more."
People were playing with the term - and idea - for decades before Clavicular started posting videos.
In the opening song for the 1990's television show The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, for example, Will Smith raps: "Chillin' out, maxin', relaxin' all cool."

c0c86131b518.text: By — Isabel DeBre, Associated Press Isabel DeBre, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/lula-bucks-regional-shift-to-the-right-and-denies-trump-a-powerful-ally-in-brazil Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Lula bucks regional shift to the right and denies Trump a powerful ally in Brazil World Oct 26, 2026 2:48 PM EDT BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — Brazilian voters have denied Latin America's resurgent right its ultimate prize, snapping a streak of seven straight conservative presidential victories in 18 months. The stunning triumph of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva over Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday, with 51.8% of the vote to 48.2%, limits U.S. President Donald Trump's drive to tighten his grip on the Western Hemisphere and cements Latin America's most populous country and largest economy as a counterweight to Washington. A Bolsonaro victory would have left Mexico's Claudia Sheinbaum as the only progressive president among the region's powerhouses. More broadly, Brazil's vote — held the same day Serbia's opposition scored a stunning win — opened a stretch of high-stakes elections that could reshape global politics, with Israel on Tuesday holding its first national election since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack and the U.S. midterms on Nov. 3. For the Trump administration, which has wielded punishing tariffs, severe sanctions and military force to reassert its dominance in the region, Lula's victory complicates its campaign to enlist Brazil in its military coalition against cartels and to gain preferential access to the country's critical minerals, analysts say. By Monday morning, with his ally Flávio Bolsonaro refusing to concede and calling for the result to be annulled, Trump had yet to publicly acknowledge Lula's reelection, even as congratulations poured in from Brazil's allies and rivals around the world. Yet both sides see reasons to cooperate. Washington wants access to Brazil's vast trove of rare earths to reduce its defense industry's reliance on China. Lula wants foreign investment and tariff relief for Brazilian exporters. "Lula is pragmatic enough to work out some kind of modus operandi with the Trump administration," said Will Freeman, a fellow for Latin America studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, adding that the Bolsonaros' allies in Washington would likely lose sway after the family's second electoral defeat. Flávio's father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, lost to Lula in 2022. "I'm not sure anyone in the Trump administration, beyond a few individuals, will want to keep making the Bolsonaros the central issue in the U.S.-Brazil relationship," he said. Trump's missing piece Across much of Latin America, voters fed up with rising crime have rewarded presidential candidates promising to restore order. From Peru's Keiko Fujimori to Colombia's Abelardo de la Espriella and Chile's José Antonio Kast, newly elected conservatives have courted Trump while taking their cues from El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele, whose sweeping gang crackdown has sharply reduced homicides at the cost of mass arrests and suspended civil liberties. Trump has reinforced that shift with electoral endorsements, financial bailouts and pledges of military aid. "The U.S. is certainly putting its finger on the scale to try to help the more hard-line right-wing elements in the region," said Kenneth Roberts, a professor of government at Cornell University. Brazil would have been Washington's most consequential addition. Bolsonaro had promised to join the U.S.-led security coalition "with great enthusiasm and great honor," making his alliance with Trump part of his pitch to voters. Lula, by contrast, has championed Brazil's long tradition of nonalignment, cultivating ties with competing powers. His government deepened trade ties with China and sought greater global influence through BRICS, a group of emerging economies. Trump's heavy-handed support for the Bolsonaros played into that message. The double-digit tariffs he imposed on a range of Brazilian goods to punish Brazil for prosecuting former President Jair Bolsonaro over a coup plot to oust Lula stirred a nationalist backlash that the leftist leader channeled into the rallying cry "Brazil belongs to Brazilians." "To the extent that the regional superpower becomes a threat to Brazil's democratic institutions, defending Brazilian national sovereignty also becomes a form of defending Brazilian democracy," Roberts said. In his victory speech late Sunday, Lula described the outcome as "a demonstration that this country does not accept being anyone's backyard." Lula's red lines Brazil resisted joining the Shield of the Americas, a U.S.-led military coalition targeting cartels. When Washington in May designated Brazil's two largest criminal factions, the First Capital Command and the Red Command, as terrorist organizations, Lula warned the labels could become a pretext for American intervention. Countries along the main northbound cocaine and migrant routes, many of them heavily dependent on the U.S. market, have been more accommodating. In Ecuador, U.S. troops have joined local police in raids targeting suspected drug networks across the coastal lowlands. Honduras, Guatemala and Colombia have also agreed to joint military operations, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth says, though Guatemala's government has denied it. It's a large country with a very independent history and a military that would not look kindly upon foreign troops in its own territory," said Brian Winter, a veteran Latin America analyst and editor-in-chief of Americas Quarterly, a policy journal. Lieb, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/massachusetts-and-idaho-put-guns-on-the-ballot-one-to-restrict-them-the-other-to-honor-them Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Massachusetts and Idaho put guns on the ballot. One to restrict them, the other to honor them Nation Oct 26, 2026 2:27 PM EDT Parked in his truck along a rural Idaho highway on his way to an elk hunt, Neill Goodfellow pondered a question that will appear on his November ballot: which of six historic firearms to choose as the official state gun? Goodfellow is going to vote for the M1 Garand, a semiautomatic rifle widely carried by U.S. troops in World War II. In Massachusetts, voters are deciding a vastly different ballot question — whether to uphold a 2024 law requiring all firearms to be serialized and registered with the state and broadening a ban on "assault-style" guns. Massachusetts and Idaho are about 2,000 miles (3,200 kilometers) apart — literally and figuratively — in America's gun debate. The November election won't settle the tension between firearm freedoms and restrictions, but the ballot questions will provide a gauge of public opinion. Should voters approve it, Massachusetts Question 9 will continue an array of gun restrictions passed overwhelmingly by the Democratic-led Legislature in a state with one of the nation's lowest gun ownership rates. The question is going to voters because opponents gathered petition signatures forcing a referendum. In Boise, the Republican-led Legislature placed a nonbinding question on the ballot seeking voters' advice on designating "the state gun of Idaho." About 3 in 5 Idaho adults live in households with guns, which ranks among the highest rates nationally, according to an estimate from the RAND Gun Policy in America initiative. Some Republican lawmakers hope the ballot question will encourage more people to vote. Massachusetts gun owners face a registry deadline Residents in Massachusetts face a Wednesday deadline to register their firearms with the state. The referendum on whether to repeal that requirement happens six days later. That sequence has frustrated some gun owners. "It's a total violation of people's rights to require this before they have their chance to vote on it," said Toby Leary, chair of The Civil Rights Coalition, a group formed to lead the effort to repeal the gun law. Normally, when a referendum petition is submitted, a law is placed on hold until an election can occur. But Democratic Gov. Maura Healey signed an emergency provision making the gun law take effect immediately in 2024 — two years ahead of the referendum. Advocates tout the measure as the most comprehensive update in a decade to the state's firearms laws. In addition to establishing a state firearm registry, it bars "ghost guns" that lack serial numbers and devices that convert guns to fire rapidly, and expands a ban on assault-style weapons. It also broadens a "red flag" law to add healthcare providers and school administrators to the list of those who can ask courts to temporarily remove guns from people who pose a risk to themselves or others. "This legislation both preserves a legal pathway to gun ownership while also putting guardrails in place that keep people safe," said Ruth Zakarin, who chairs the campaign committee backing the gun law and is CEO of the Massachusetts Coalition to Prevent Gun Violence. Few states have wide-ranging gun registries A 40-year-old federal law prohibits the U.S. government from establishing a national registry of firearms or their owners. But some states have adopted their own requirements. Massachusetts was the third jurisdiction, behind Hawaii and the District of Columbia, to enact a comprehensive gun registry. Six additional states require registration of some firearms, such as handguns or those defined as assault weapons, according to the Giffords Law Center to Prevent Gun Violence. WATCH: Two doctors offer new ideas to prevent gun violence in America "These laws help law enforcement solve crimes, track down stolen and trafficked guns," said Lindsay Nichols, the center's policy director. "They also discourage illegal gun sales, and they help protect law enforcement by providing them information about what guns might be present when they are responding to an incident." But creating a government database of gun owners also could put people at risk, if the information is hacked and leaked, Leary said. Thieves possessing the addresses of gun owners could monitor their homes, waiting for them to leave for work or vacation to rob them of their firearms, he said. "The criminal element will know exactly who has what, where they live," he said. "It's a wish list for nefarious actors for where they can go get guns." About a dozen states have official firearms Utah and Arizona were the first states, in 2011, to adopt official state firearms. Utah lawmakers chose the Browning M1911 pistol, which was designed by a Utah native. Arizona lawmakers picked the Colt single-action Army revolver, described by the National Rifle Association as "an iconic firearm of the American West." Of the six options presented to Idaho voters, "none of them really have a significant place in the history of Idaho," said Goodfellow, a board member of the Idaho State Rifle & Pistol Association. "My suspicion is a lot of folks are not going to have a clue" which one to choose, he said. Yet for some people, the gun vote is a fun topic to debate. That's primarily the point, said Idaho House Majority Leader Jason Monks, a Republican who sponsored the measure as a means of driving up voter turnout during the midterm elections. It's timed intentionally to coincide with the nation's 250th anniversary. Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra is wading into the political battle which is intensifying over the Rosebank oil field.
He is making a direct appeal to Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to approve the plans to allow production to begin in the North Atlantic.
Environmentalists have long campaigned against the proposals for drilling in the UK's largest untapped oil field, 80 miles north-west of Shetland.
That the debate is now taking place within the Labour Party is a sign of the UK's recent journey on the politics of energy.
When Labour came to power in 2024, it was with a manifesto pledge not to allow any new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea.
A legal challenge thrust the future of the Jackdaw and Rosebank developments into the hands of the then-Energy Secretary, Ed Miliband.
At that point, senior offshore industry figures didn't hold out much hope of getting the go-ahead, given Miliband's deep commitment to renewable energy and his close political ties to Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
All that was before the outbreak of the war between the US, Israel and Iran, which closed the Strait of Hormuz and made an ongoing cost of living crisis even worse.
A new government under Andy Burnham entered 10 Downing Street with greater political freedom on the issue - and a new energy secretary to make the decisions.
Strictly speaking, Jackdaw and Rosebank aren't applications for new drilling licences, just the adjudication of existing ones.
But in political terms, the change of tone within Labour has been clear.
What had been an article of faith on energy has become something much more flexible.
It's a shift that's also plain to see within the SNP, with the Scottish government that once favoured a presumption against new oil and gas drilling now issuing a careful welcome to the Jackdaw announcement.
Last week, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh announced that production could begin on the Jackdaw gas field.
She said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, the project would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add Â£2.9bn to the economy.
Environmentalists said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.
The UK government has always insisted that these decisions are part of a quasi-judicial process, judged on strict environmental criteria, not politics.
But as attention turns to Rosebank, the politics are seeping in.
Within hours of Jackdaw being granted approval, a briefing campaign began suggesting that Fahnbulleh was "minded" to reject Rosebank.
Now, in the week of the Budget, reports have suggested that Chancellor John Healey is in favour of approval.
The timeline of Jackdaw and Rosebank
Neither cabinet minister has given their view publicly, of course.
Fahnbulleh has insisted that the decision is "a regulatory process not a policy process," adding: "It sits heavy for such a big controversial decision because in the end only I can make it."
Even though she isn't looking for advice, the Scottish Labour leader is willing to offer it.
Marra is in Westminster meeting both Healey and Fahnbulleh in the run-up to the Budget on Wednesday.
Marra believes that on jobs and investment, the case for Rosebank is clear.
"I supported Jackdaw and Rosebank because I think they're really crucial for the Scottish economy, for employment, and for the public finances as well," he told me.
"We need to make sure that we're a country that people feel they can invest in.
"You've seen what's happened with Jackdaw in recent days - a real boost to the morale and the investment climate in the north east of Scotland."
He's also arguing for increased levies on banks in the Budget, to contribute towards the cost of help on the cost of living.
That second request looks set to be granted - which is likely why Marra feels able to make it publicly.
On Rosebank, we still can't say for sure how things will go.
But the fact this debate is even being had is itself a symbol of our new energy reality.

Guests attending a wedding on an island in Lower Lough Erne in County Fermanagh ended up stranded after a ferry took on water during Storm Boelo.
At the weekend, the storm brought winds of almost 80mph (129km/h) in some parts of Northern Ireland and caused the cancellation of flights and ferries.
About 12,500 households were left without electricity as a result of the storm, although all have since had power restored, according to Northern Ireland Electricity Networks.
Further strong winds - of up to 65mph (105km/h) - are expected on Monday night, with the Met Office issuing a yellow weather warning for coastal areas in counties Antrim and Down from 18:00 GMT until 03:00 on Tuesday.
Wedding guest ShÃ©a Clarke, who was on Lusty Beg Island, said: "You could see the waves were rough and the wind was going."
A yellow warning for wind along the north coast of counties Antrim and Londonderry takes effect from 03:00 GMT on Tuesday until 21:00 , with gusts of up to 60mph (97km/h) expected.
"Obviously it's too dangerous to cross and the boat can't cross so safety comes first," he added.
Despite the weather, the mood among the wedding guests on the island was good, he said.
"Some people have slept in cars, some people have slept on sofas there's been eight people in one room sleeping on the floor," said Clarke.
"But the spirit has been good the craic is 90... "as long as we don't run out of Guinness or chips."
A boat has since been taking guests off the island.
Olivia Millar, an airline cabin crew worker based in London, was also a guest at the wedding and had planned to be in South Africa on Monday night.
"It hasn't felt like real life but everyone's been amazing and we've just made the most of it," she said.
Michael Cadden, managing director at the Lusty Beg Island Resort and Spa, which hosted the wedding, said the ferocity of the storm was "unlike anything we've experienced on the island before".
"This was a crisis but we've now arranged to transport and are getting all our staff and customers safely home," he said.
Kacper Dymarczyk, a bartender, was locked down with the guests and worked through the storm.
He said there was "no concern" of running out of food or drink as the hotel was "well stocked at all times".
Flights were cancelled at airports across the island of Ireland at the weekend including about 40 at Belfast International Airport and about 30 at Dublin Airport.
On Sunday, the Department for Infrastructure (DfI) said about 470 storm-related incidents had been reported, including fallen trees and flooding.
A spokesperson for Northern Ireland's public transport provider Translink said that some bus services were diverted over the weekend due to fallen debris and rail restrictions were put in place in affected areas.
The Foyle Bridge in Londonderry was closed on Saturday due to high winds but reopened again on Sunday evening.
SDLP assembly member Mark H Durkan said he understood the need to close the bridge during the storm but added that its prolonged closure caused major traffic congestion in the city.
Speaking to BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today, Durkan said redirecting vehicles to the lower deck of the Craigavon Bridge caused a traffic build-up and showed that the city was in desperate need of a third bridge.
"The infrastructural capacity of Derry needs increased," said Durkan.
"I don't think two vehicular bridges for a city of this side and a population of this city is enough."

63d80ce85941.text: By — Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/thune-campaigns-for-republicans-in-marquee-senate-races-in-scramble-to-save-majority Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Thune campaigns for Republicans in marquee Senate races in scramble to save majority Politics Oct 26, 2026 2:06 PM EDT SIOUX CITY, Iowa (AP) — Senate Majority Leader John Thune says he wouldn't be offended if some Republicans didn't want to campaign with him. He knows that he's taken intense criticism from the party's base — and from President Donald Trump — for his chamber's inability to pass voter legislation this year. But Republican candidates in marquee Senate races have welcomed Thune's help as he's traveled around the country in the weeks before the midterm elections, scrambling to save his majority. That includes Rep. Ashley Hinson in this deep red corner of Iowa, a state that Republicans couldn't have envisioned as a tossup race a year ago. Hinson is locked in a tight contest against Democrat Josh Turek to replace retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst. Hinson said she was grateful for Thune's visit as the two spent Friday campaigning together in the northwest part of the state — a luncheon at the Sioux City chamber of commerce, a tour of the Iowa Air National Guard's refueling wing, a roundtable with local business owners and meet-and-greets at a packed high school football game that night. "I'm absolutely convinced that she flat has to win, and if she doesn't, we're not going to be in the majority," Thune said in a joint interview with Hinson between stops, during a brief moment of rest in the back of her campaign bus. He acknowledged the environment for Republicans is tough, but "we have to be able to deliver a message that you have a clear choice in front of you about two very different paths." The stakes for Thune and his party are enormous in Iowa and in several other traditionally Republican states as voters voice frustration with Trump, his war in Iran and high gasoline and grocery prices. Despite a map favoring Republicans, Democrats are hopeful that they can win the Senate. And like several other Democrats running in red states, Turek, a state legislator, is telling Iowa voters that he would be a bipartisan voice in Washington. Hinson acknowledges that voters have concerns. But "there is a lot at stake in this election," she says, "and Iowans are pretty savvy people to understand that this is a six-year term." Thune told voters who showed up to the business roundtable to "do everything you can to help her get there." "We've got to turn out the vote," he said. Thune makes closing argument to save his majority Beyond Iowa, Thune has campaigned with Republican Senate candidates in Nebraska, Georgia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Mississippi, Kentucky, Florida and Minnesota. He's headed to Ohio in the coming days to help Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who is facing a tough challenge from Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown. It wasn't always a given that Thune, elected by his conference to replace Kentucky Sen. Mitch McConnell two years ago, would have so much face time with voters and candidates. Some on the right blame Thune for the failed effort to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require proof of citizenship for voters and mandate voter ID across the country. Thune supports the bill, but it has no chance in the 100-member Senate with the filibuster intact, because Republicans need Democratic support for any piece of legislation to win the necessary 60 votes. Trump has pressed Thune to change the rules of the Senate and ditch the filibuster, but Thune has staunchly refused, citing the need to stop Democratic legislation if and when Republicans lose power again. Tensions between the two men peaked this summer, when Trump appeared to question Thune's leadership. Asked in the Oval Office if the South Dakota Republican was the man for the job, Trump replied that "we're going to find out, and I'll let you know." WATCH: Trump says he ordered suit to block Alaska Senate results if GOP loses Still, Trump has said more than once that he likes Thune personally, and Thune's office released photos earlier this month of the majority leader and his grandchildren at the White House, on a personal tour led by a smiling Trump. Thune is also well-liked among his colleagues and enjoys strong support from within his GOP conference — and from possible future members like Hinson. Thune joked at one of the Iowa events that "I tell all of our candidates, I'll come out for you or against you, whichever helps you the most." Thune navigates Trump, just like GOP candidates Voters in Iowa weren't asking Thune and Hinson about the SAVE America Act. Instead they were mostly focused on issues like childcare and how the economy and farm input costs are affecting their businesses. Like Thune, Hinson has been navigating Trump throughout her campaign — appearing with him at a rally in Sioux City the night before but also speaking out against decisions she disagrees with, like increasing beef imports and a deal with Russia to import diesel fuel. When the president is right about something, "I'm going to be with him, and if he's wrong about something, I'm going to be in his ear telling him," Hinson said. Both are also having to answer for Trump's war in Iran, as they have joined most Republicans in voting against repeated Democratic attempts to stop it. Rising gas prices since the war's inception along with Trump's trade war have hit farmers in the state particularly hard. Despite those votes, Hinson has said on the campaign trail that she wants to see the war come to a "successful and immediate end." “The bright sun was extinguish’d … and the icy earth swung blind and blackening in the moonless air.” These words from Lord Byron’s 1816 poem Darkness evoke a hellish apocalypse. But Byron may have been inspired by the fallout of a real cataclysm — one that happened half a world away.
Mount Tambora, in present-day Indonesia, blew its top in 1815. More than 71,000 people in the vicinity died. And climate-cooling aerosols from the eruption ushered in extreme weather the following years in far-flung places. Cold weather in the summer of 1816, sometimes with frosts and snow, destroyed corn in New England, rice and buckwheat in China and wheat, oats and potatoes in Ireland. In some places, the rising cost of bread sparked protests and riots. The circumstances may have helped spread typhus. Some called 1816 “the year without a summer,” others “the year of the beggars.”
Like Tambora, volcanoes, and the cooling they cause, may be an underappreciated geologic force at times moving behind the scenes of human history.
“These climatic impacts of the Tambora eruption were recorded without any knowledge that this had anything to do with an eruption,” says Clive Oppenheimer, a volcanologist at the University of Cambridge.
While Tambora is the most well-studied eruption in history, others have also rattled the planet. Oppenheimer and his colleagues analyzed 38 large eruptions in the 2026 Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences. Their work pulled together studies linking the geologic events and their effects on climate with their potential societal fallout in food systems, the economy, unrest, culture and religion. The locations and exact timing of the eruptions that spurred some notable cold spurts aren’t known. But understanding how the events impacted the climate, environment and society can offer clues to the past, including how people coped with climate stress.
“Volcanic eruptions, they are kind of this like hammer blow to the climate system,” says Heli Huhtamaa, a climate and environmental historian at the University of Bern in Switzerland. Volcanoes may offer lessons about resilience for modern societies in a warming world, she says.
Volcanic gases create a chilling effect
Volcanoes spew sulfur-containing gases. Over weeks, those gases react in the atmosphere to form particles that block sunlight. The particles can stay aloft for many months, riding jet streams to encircle the globe. Paintings from years after eruptions show bloodred sunsets or landscapes shrouded by hazy skies.
Because no two eruptions are exactly alike, it takes work to grasp each one’s impacts on weather and climate. “If we understand the climate response of one [eruption], that does not mean that we understand the climate response of another,” says Ulf Büntgen, a paleoclimatologist at the University of Cambridge.
Up in the air
A volcano’s explosivity impacts how high it shoots its gases and where they travel. Over time, those gases form particles that block sunlight. The particles can stay aloft for many months, riding jet streams to encircle the globe. In this computer model of a 1991 eruption, colors represent how high particles are in the atmosphere. Red is high and blue is closer to Earth’s surface.
Researchers find the traces of past eruptions in ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica. Scientists try to nail down the date on a sulfur-loaded ice core layer and compare it with tree ring data, a logbook of sorts for summer growing conditions since temperatures impact how trees lay down their wood each year. Scientists can pull together tree ring records from far-flung places and use statistics to work out annual temperatures in a hemisphere.
Cold spells sometimes jump out from tree ring records. For years when cool summers impeded the final stages of wood formation, a chemical method used to estimate temperatures turns wood layers blue. Büntgen and colleagues saw two blue rings around 1345. “And that is very rare. We never saw that two years in a row,” he says. The rings coincided with the timing of the Black Death’s spread in Europe, the team reported in 2025 in Communications Earth & Environment. The researchers traced the connections between chilly summers, poor grain harvests in the Mediterranean and shipping records showing how Italian city states imported flea-ridden grain from the Caucasus.
Oppenheimer, Büntgen and their colleagues broadened the detective work for their 2026 review. The team studied Northern Hemisphere temperature responses to the 38 largest eruptions between A.D. 1 and 1900. On average, each volcano caused about 0.5 degrees Celsius of cooling in the year after the eruption. Recovery to normal temperatures was slower for eruptions that occurred in times that were already colder on average, Büntgen says. In some periods, large or successive eruptions may lead to an elevated amounts of particles in the atmosphere for a long time. The team’s calculations show that high aerosol levels concur with some of the past two millennia’s coldest spells, such as the one preceding the Black Death.
Human agency factors into eruptions’ outcomes
Those cold snaps often had dire consequences. Out of 17 large-scale famines in Europe from 1300 to 1800, 11 followed major eruptions. In addition to faltering crops and famines, the most frequently societal responses described in studies collected by the review authors were disease outbreaks, political turmoil and migration.
The societal circumstances surrounding eruptions are as important as the amount of cooling, Huhtamaa says. She and her colleagues studied crop failures and farmstead desertion in three different volcanic eruptions that impacted Ostrobothnia, in what is now Finland. During the 17th century, Ostrobothnia experienced cooling from three sets of eruptions at different time periods.
Although the latest eruption event, in 1695, was the coldest of all, peasants fared better than they had after eruptions earlier in the century, Huhtamaa and colleagues reporte

1f6edcea35a8.text: By — Julia Frankel, Associated Press Julia Frankel, Associated Press By — Joseph Krauss, Associated Press Joseph Krauss, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/whatever-the-outcome-of-israels-election-netanyahus-policies-toward-palestinians-will-likely-endure Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Whatever the outcome of Israel's election, Netanyahu's policies toward Palestinians will likely endure World Oct 26, 2026 1:34 PM EDT JALUD, West Bank (AP) — Even if Tuesday's pivotal elections in Israel mark the end of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's decades-long political career, his legacy in the Israeli-occupied West Bank — of massive settlement expansion, the displacement of tens of thousands of Palestinians and the empowerment of armed settler extremists — will likely endure. Israelis are deeply divided over Netanyahu's leadership and moral character, but they largely support settlement expansion and are opposed to a Palestinian state. So while Netanyahu's opponents have vowed to crack down on settler violence and remove the most contentious outposts, they are mostly against a two-state solution, seen internationally as the only realistic way to resolve the conflict. "There shouldn't be any illusions," said Mairav Zonszein, senior Israel analyst at the International Crisis Group. "At best, (a new government) would be able to slow down the extremely crazy acceleration that we've seen in the last four years of every aspect of Israel's aggression in the occupied territories and inside Israel itself." The military stands down in the face of settler violence One legacy of Netanyahu's nearly unbroken 17-year rule — the longest of any Israeli leader — is that large groups of armed settlers now routinely defy the Israeli military as they rampage through Palestinian communities, drive people from their homes and seize ever larger swaths of their land. Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack out of Gaza turbocharged the process. Netanyahu's opponents could bring in more troops and authorize stricter measures, but the genie may already be out of the bottle. Netanyahu's government has distributed thousands of firearms to the settlers, who have allies in the military and security forces. Some extremist settlers have become like sheriffs — making arrests, killing Palestinians they say posed a threat, summoning security forces and driving Palestinian families from their homes. The Palestinian Tubasi family was forced out in July after settlers besieged their hilltop home in the West Bank village of Jalud for 19 days. The settlers cut off their water access and their electricity, and threatened to "barbecue" them if they didn't leave, said Mahmoud Tubasi, 60, the patriarch. An Israeli court ordered the military to bring the family back, but that hasn't happened. Troops aborted their latest mission soon after it began, when a mob of over 150 armed settlers quickly assembled, scaled the walls of the home and set a car on fire. Troops threw Tubasi and his family into an armored jeep and drove them away as settlers torched the place. They now live in relatives' houses in the valley below their gutted and blackened home, around which settlers still roam. Israel's military did not respond to a request for comment. "If they wanted to evacuate them, of course, 100%, they can do that," Tubasi said. "This is an army that fights in Lebanon, Gaza and in Iran — they can't control 150 or 200 settlers?" The process is repeated across the West Bank Under Netanyahu, settlers have established over 250 rustic camps across the territory, focusing particularly on areas where Palestinian herding communities have dwelled for decades. The outposts allow the settlers to effectively run Palestinians off vast rural areas by attacking shepherds, taking over water resources and grazing their own herds, all under the eye of Israeli troops. Dror Etkes, a researcher with an Israeli anti-settlement group, says the outposts have allowed the settlers to seize effective control of around a fifth of the West Bank. Israel captured the territory, along with Gaza and east Jerusalem, in the 1967 Mideast war. The Palestinians want all three territories for their future state. READ MORE: Netanyahu denies allegations he's escalating tensions with Iran before Israel's election Since 2023, the strategy has forced at least 127 Palestinian herding communities off their land, according to data gathered by Etkes' organization, known as Kerem Navot, and B'Tselem, another Israeli anti-settlement group. The departures have cleared nearly the entire eastern flank of the West Bank, along the border with Jordan, of Palestinians. The settlers' explicit goal is to prevent the establishment of a viable Palestinian state. Netanyahu's opponents say they will go after the most violent settlers and dismantle outposts — which are illegal under Israeli law. But they will not evacuate the over 100 new settlements Netanyahu's government legalized, including 44 that were formerly outposts. Nor will they remove settlements dating back decades, many of which now resemble fully developed suburbs. Most of the international community views all Israeli settlements as illegal and an obstacle to a two-state solution. Israel views the West Bank as the biblical and historical heartland of the Jewish people and says its future status should be decided by negotiations — which have not been held in over a decade. Even if some outposts are removed, many Palestinians seeking to return would find their homes burned and looted, and would continue to face threats from nearby settlers. "The story is over. There will be no massive dismantlement of settlement," said Etkes. "It's now a full and prouder-than-ever apartheid regime." Amnesty International and other major rights groups accused Israel of the international crime of apartheid even before the Oct. 7 attack and its aftermath. Israel denies the allegation. 035698e30f0b.text: By — Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/netanyahu-denies-allegations-hes-escalating-tensions-with-iran-before-israels-election Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Netanyahu denies allegations he's escalating tensions with Iran before Israel's election World Oct 26, 2026 1:22 PM EDT JERUSALEM (AP) — Israelis entered the final 24 hours of an intense election season on Monday, as reports circulated that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may have clashed with the Israeli military over initiating a possible escalation with Iran immediately before the vote. Tensions flared over reports that Netanyahu and his military chief of staff disagreed over an instruction by the prime minister to carry out an "action" that the army worried could reignite the conflict with Iran. Netanyahu's office denied the report, first published by Israel's Channel 12, as "fake news." Defense Minister Israel Katz also quickly denied the report. "I state unequivocally that there has been no intention by Israel of initiating an attack on Iran before the elections in Israel," Katz wrote on X on Monday, calling reports of rifts between political and military leaders "completely baseless and false." However, he said that Israel would respond forcefully if Iran attacks first. Israel's opposition candidates accused Netanyahu of endangering regional stability for his political preservation. Netanyahu's main rival, former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, warned Netanyahu not to "dare to place your own political interests above the security of the state." He posted on X, "Netanyahu, my eyes are on you." Avigdor Lieberman, head of the hawkish Yisrael Beytenu party which is part of the opposition bloc, sent a letter to Israel's attorney general demanding a criminal investigation into possible treason by Netanyahu's "attempts to drag Israel into a war on the eve of elections, including a willingness to sacrifice (Israeli) soldiers out of fear of losing the election." The election on Tuesday is the first since the Hamas-led attacks in southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which sparked the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza and conflicts across the Middle East. READ MORE: Signs of fraying loyalty emerge in Netanyahu stronghold before Israeli election Israelis are deeply divided heading into what is expected to be a close race, and the veteran Israeli leader's legacy is on the line. Netanyahu's opponents say he should be held accountable for the failures surrounding the Oct. 7 attack. His supporters say that he has led the country back from its toughest moment. The vote also marks another important test for the populist right. Brazil's voters dealt a stunning setback to the movement on Sunday, lifting President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to a surprising victory over Flávio Bolsonaro. The Republican Party of U.S. President Donald Trump, who has endorsed Netanyahu, faces a new test next week in the U.S. midterm election. Although Israelis are breathlessly approaching the election as one of the most crucial in years, people across the Middle East aren't expecting dramatic changes regardless of the victor. Both Netanyahu and his main rivals have similar approaches to Israel's regional security in both Gaza and Iran. In southern Gaza, Jamal Abu Deeb, who was displaced from Khan Younis, said that no matter who is elected, it won't be good news for the Palestinians. "It is all war and destruction," he said, adding that there are still strikes every day that kill people and children across Gaza. "Do you think whoever gets elected will give us a better life? Quite the opposite." Ibrahim Qeshta, who was displaced from Rafah, said that "they all have the same playbook, they have no mercy — death and destruction for everyone." "Eisenkot is like Netanyahu, he will be the same," Qeshta said. "Our people die every day, for nothing." Iran also watched the last-minute electioneering warily. "It makes no difference to us who ultimately takes the helm of a regime whose track record shows that it has brought nothing to our region but violence and bloodshed," Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said in his weekly media briefing on Monday. Wafaa Shurafa contributed to this report from Deir al-Balah, Gaza Strip. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. d93534832e7d.text: A pair of Trump-friendly right-wing populists took a one-two punch Sunday: Brazil rejected a Bolsonaro comeback, and Serbia toppled a strongman's ruling party. The big picture: Brazil denied Trump a close ally at the helm of Latin America's largest economy, snapping a streak of seven straight conservative wins in the region. In Europe, Serbia and Hungary toppled leaders with close Trump ties who had dominated their countries for years. Now, another massively pivotal election looms Tuesday, when Trump ally , Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, will face a battle for political survival . On the eve of the election, Netanyahi touted Trump's endorsement and his "friendship" with the American president. But as the global right has made gains, opposition forces proved this weekend that they still have fuel. Driving the news: In Brazil, leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva staved off a challenge from Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro . The younger Bolsonaro, widely seen as the heir to his father's populist movement, refused to concede and called for the results to be annulled, according to translations . The elder Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence after being convicted of plotting a coup to overturn his 2022 loss . Trump has called the prosecution a "WITCH HUNT." The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment on the race. Between the lines: Brazil's election emerged as a test of Trump's political influence in Latin America, where right-wing and Trump-backed candidates have celebrated an uninterrupted series of wins . Those victories include Trump-endorsed Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia , Nasry "Tito" Asfura in Honduras and José Antonio Kast in Chile . Trump did not formally endorse Flávio Bolsonaro, but he met with him earlier this year and imposed ignificant tariffs on Brazil as he protested the charges against Bolsonaro's father. Lula is a vocal Trump critic. In March, Flávio Bolsonaro told an audience at the Conservative Political Action Conference that America faced a "fork in the road" in the election: "Either you have the most powerful ally in the hemisphere, or an antagonist." Zoom out: Meanwhile, across the Atlantic, a student-led opposition movement toppled the right-wing party of long-serving strongman Aleksandar Vučić, who was seeking to become prime minister. Unlike the Bolsonaros, Vučić conceded defeat Sunday. The Balkan leader had courted Trump's inner circle, including Donald Trump Jr., and described the president as a "kindred spirit." It reflects the shifting tides that also allowed next-door Hungary to oust Trump-allied Viktor Orbán , once one of the Western world's most entrenched populist leaders, in April after 16 years in power. Yes, but: Europe's political upheaval is cutting both ways: While the populist right has fallen in Serbia and Hungary, it's gaining ground in two of the continent's largest economies. In France, far-right presidential frontrunner Marine Le Pen launched her 2027 campaign this weekend, seizing on nationwide unrest to pitch her tough-on-crime, anti-migrant agenda. In Germany, the far-right Alternative for Germany won a record 44% in a state election last month and continues to lead in national polls. What we're watching: Trump's historic move of endorsing Netanyahu in Tuesday's Israeli elections will once again test his influence abroad. Tuesday's election in Israel is set to be tight for Netanyahu, who has sought to elevate Trump's endorsement as he jockeys with former Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot . The 77-year-old Netanyahu has been prime minister for some 19 years in nonconsecutive terms. Analysts see the election as a referendum on the security failure of Oct. 7, 2023, that killed around 1,200 people. Whoever governs Israel could shape Trump's next moves in the Middle East — including whether to escalate the war in Iran. Go deeper: Lula v. Bolsonaro: Brazil election unfolds in Trump's shadow

Sisak, Associated Press By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press By — Alanna Durkin, Associated Press Alanna Durkin, Associated Press By — Larry Neumeister, Associated Press Larry Neumeister, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-doj-illegally-fired-ex-fbi-directors-daughter-maurene-comey-as-a-federal-prosecutor-judge-rules Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump DOJ illegally fired ex-FBI director's daughter, Maurene Comey, as a federal prosecutor, judge rules Politics Oct 26, 2026 1:11 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — The Trump administration last year illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, from her job as a federal prosecutor in New York, a federal judge ruled Monday. Maurene Comey, who was an assistant U.S. attorney for a decade, was illegally fired in July 2025 despite her work on some of the nation's highest-profile cases and consistently receiving "the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike," Judge Jesse M. Furman found. READ MORE: Fired federal prosecutor Maurene Comey sues Trump administration over abrupt dismissal After her firing, Comey sued the Justice Department and others, saying her termination violated the constitutional separation of powers, the First Amendment and the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. She asserted that she was fired because she was the daughter of James Comey, whom President Donald Trump has long viewed as an enemy, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, the judge noted. Furman rejected the government's claim that Comey could be fired because federal prosecutors exercise the president's "conclusive and preclusive" powers. He said the government's claim that Congress is barred from regulating the removal of federal prosecutors "flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent." Furman added: "Indeed, to accept Defendants' argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system." The firing violated the separation of powers, the Administrative Procedure Act and her Fifth Amendment due process and statutory rights, the judge ruled. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Furman reserved judgment on Comey's First Amendment claim pending further arguments to be submitted by each side, though he said he was inclined to dismiss the claim because it was largely moot since she is now in private practice and no longer seeks actual reinstatement. The judge granted Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay from the date of her firing through Dec. 20 to "make her whole" and ensure that she doesn't suffer adverse employment consequences for the "unlawful termination." Comey's lawyers, Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan, lauded the ruling. "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law," they said in a statement. "As the Court correctly held, to accept the government's argument about unlimited executive power 'would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system.' This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law." The Justice Department didn't immediately respond to an email seeking comment. The Justice Department during the Trump administration has fired scores of career employees, including prosecutors and FBI agents, who participated in investigations of President Donald Trump or who were perceived as opposed to the administration's agenda. Some of those firings have also resulted in federal lawsuits. The firing of Maurene Comey was seen as particularly personal, given her father's longtime adversarial relationship with Trump. The president fired James Comey as FBI director in May 2017 as the bureau was investigating ties between Russia and the Republican's successful 2016 campaign for the White House. Trump in the years since has repeatedly called for Comey to be jailed, and his Justice Department has worked with mixed success to make that happen. An earlier criminal case accusing James Comey of having lied to Congress in 2020 was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who filed the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of "86 47," a case he has sought to dismiss that some legal experts have greeted with skepticism. Tucker and Durkin reported from Washington. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Michael R. 69a21532415c.text: TEL AVIV, Israel — Gadi Eisenkot is as low-key as Benjamin Netanyahu is bombastic. He's a political novice up against the longest-serving, most politically savvy prime minister in Israel's history. And yet, on the eve of Tuesday's elections, Eisenkot poses the most serious threat to Netanyahu's hold on power in years. Why it matters: A victory by the Yashar party leader would upend Israeli politics and could reset the country's strained relationships abroad. The intrigue: The contrast between the two top contenders could hardly be sharper. Their roots: Eisenkot, the son of Moroccan Jewish immigrants, grew up in Eilat, Israel's southernmost city. If he wins, Eisenkot will be the first prime minister of Moroccan descent in Israel's history. Their military backgrounds: Netanyahu served in the Israel Defense Forces' elite special forces unit "Sayeret Matkal" and later went into business and politics. Eisenkot joined the IDF Golani infantry brigade and rose through its ranks as a combat commander until becoming IDF chief of staff. He arrived at his rally on Sunday to the tune of the Golani brigade song from 1974. Their ties to America: Netanyahu is better versed in American politics — and more articulate in English — than many American politicians. Eisenkot is not an "American" politician at all, let alone a professional one. He speaks English with a heavy Israeli accent and doesn't deliver catchy soundbites. He does not enjoy being on TV. At his final campaign rally Sunday before about 1,000 supporters, Eisenkot was visibly uncomfortable being in the spotlight, even when the crowd cheered him on. Their trustworthiness: Netanyahu's credibility with the Israeli public has been battered by his long-running corruption trial, his political tactics, his refusal to take responsibility for the failures that led to October 7 and accusations of duplicity in his handling of the Iran war. Eisenkot is seen as a straight shooter, even among many of his opponents. Zoom in: The failure to prevent the October 7 attacks spurred Eisenkot to challenge Netanyahu. Eisenkot, who joined Nƒetanyahu's emergency cabinet shortly after the attacks, lost his son during the war. He later lost two of his nephews in the war. Zoom out: Netanyahu has cultivated a vast network of donors, lobbyists and supporters in American power corridors for the past half-century. Bibi is a household name in America — for better and worse. Eisenkot, on the other hand, is almost anonymous in Washington. Very few people know him personally, even within Jewish organizations. He did spend time in America in the 1990s studying for a master's degree at the U.S. Army War College. Eisenkot's main connection to the U.S. was through the military, particularly his relationship with former Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Gen. Joseph Dunford. After retiring from the IDF in 2019, Eisenkot spent a year as a fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. The numbers: Eisenkot is leading Netanyahu by 8 to 10 points in most pre-election polls. While Netanyahu is toxic among at least half of the voters, polls show Eisenkot enjoys high likability across the board. Netanyahu's efforts to publicly vilify him have been so far unsuccessful. The big picture: Eisenkot ran on a center-right platform. He did not make any sweeping foreign policy pronouncements and took pains to steer clear of any public positions that would allow Netanyahu to paint him as weak. Bibi tried to do it, anyway. Eisenkot has expressed opposition to a Palestinian state under current conditions. He has committed to taking strong steps to crack down on Jewish terrorism against Palestinians in the West Bank. He also pledged to end Hamas' control of Gaza within 18 months of taking office, either through diplomacy or military force. Eisenkot supported the war against Iran and strikes on its nuclear facilities. But he opposed Netanyahu's attempt to use military power to force regime change, calling it unrealistic. Eisenkot supports continuing economic pressure on Iran and building a regional alliance with the Arab world to curb Iranian influence. What to watch: Eisenkot has operated under the assumption that Netanyahu would be endorsed by President Trump. He tried to use his good relationship with GOP mega-donor Miriam Adelson to lobby Trump to stay on the sidelines. When Trump finally endorsed Netanyahu last week and again on Sunday, Eisenkot didn't criticize him, but rather praised the president's support for Israel. "I am convinced President Trump will work in full cooperation with any leader that will be elected by the Israeli people," Eisenkot wrote on X Monday.

Algeria is to send troops to Niger in its first foreign deployment since sending forces to Egypt during the Arab-Israeli war in 1973.
The deployment follows a visit to Algiers by Niger's defence minister, as the country seeks support against armed groups, some of which are linked to al-Qaeda or Islamic State.
Algeria has economic interests in Niger, including a planned gas pipeline that would carry Nigerian gas through Niger to Algeria. The troops are expected to protect energy facilities in northern Niger, near the Libyan border.
The deployment comes as the two neighbours rebuild ties after a diplomatic rift in 2025, when Niger recalled its ambassador to Algiers.
Algeria's upper house of parliament held an emergency session on Sunday to vote on the proposed deployment. According to AFP news agency, 148 of the 174 senators voted in favour. It was later backed by the lower house of parliament.
However, the timing and number of soldiers to be deployed have not been announced.
The move would mark the first use of a 2020 constitutional provision allowing overseas military deployments and a significant shift in Algeria's long-standing policy against sending forces abroad.
"We are not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger, but for a mission to secure economic infrastructure," Algerian senator Belkacem Boulghiti told reporters after the vote.
Algeria's state-owned energy company, Sonatrach, has also signed an agreement with Niger's petroleum ministry to explore for oil in the Kafra region. Two exploration wells are estimated to contain 168 million and 100 million barrels, respectively, Reuters reported.
Relations between Algeria and Niger have not always been smooth in recent years.
Algeria condemned the 2023 coup that ousted Niger's elected President, Mohamed Bazoum, and brought Gen Abdourahamane Tchiani to power.
Tensions rose again in 2025 after Algeria shot down a Malian drone near its border. Niger recalled its ambassador to Algiers in solidarity with Mali, a close ally which is also under military rule.
Relations have since improved. Tchiani visited Algeria in February 2026, and in late August, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune sent fighter jets to Niger to help suppress a coup attempt and also donated four military helicopters.

26a29ec734c8.text: By — Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press By — Bernard Condon, Associated Press Bernard Condon, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/anthropic-files-for-potentially-the-biggest-ipo-ever-as-ceo-warns-of-ais-existential-risk-to-humanity Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Anthropic files for potentially the biggest IPO ever as CEO warns of AI's existential risk to humanity Nation Oct 26, 2026 12:40 PM EDT SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed papers Monday for what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever even as its top executive warns that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity. The filing sets up the San Francisco company for a Wall Street debut next month, potentially eclipsing the SpaceX initial public offering in June that raised a record $86 billion. An Anthropic IPO would also put the company ahead of OpenAI in going public in what is expected to be a pair of blockbuster stock debuts for the rival AI labs. READ MORE: Anthropic and OpenAI sound the alarm on AI safety — and seek to shape how it's controlled The filing comes weeks after CEO Dario Amodei argued in an essay for slowing the development of the most advanced AI models. An IPO could provide Anthropic with enormous resources to accelerate its expansion. The amount the company ultimately raises remains uncertain, as do its final valuation and offering price, but even at lower estimates, it would turn the five-year-old startup into one of the world's most valuable companies and potentially boost the wealth of Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela, by billions of dollars. The 335-page document showed Anthropic's revenue is growing rapidly, but like many other tech companies going public, it has yet to turn a profit. The company behind the chatbot Claude reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, though its losses after taking out certain items were a fraction of that. In the same period a year ago, Anthropic lost $13 billion. Despite the losses, Anthropic, valued earlier this year at $965 billion by private investors, is reportedly set to see that value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established. At $1.5 trillion, Anthropic would rank among the world's most valuable public companies, alongside Tesla. As for money raised, the offering could bring in as much as $100 billion, according to reports, surpassing the current record set by one of Elon Musk's companies, SpaceX, earlier this year. In a regulatory filing, Anthropic said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol "ANT." Risks aplenty, but a big payoff to the founders In the filing, the company said it could use some of that money on acquiring other businesses and technology as well as investing in infrastructure to grow its business to take on rivals. Formed in 2021 by ex-OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company, and the two leaders, Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, are widely seen as bitter rivals. But they have plenty of other competitors, including Google, newer startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX's AI division have all been losing more money than they make because of the huge costs in resources in building AI, fueling concerns of a bubble. The need for cash may explain why Anthropic is rushing to tap public markets this year, and not waiting until next year, as is OpenAI's plan. Adding to the pressure is the possibility demand for AI shares could drop, or even collapse in the coming months. Investors have become increasingly jittery about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently. In addition to helping plug any cash shortfall, the IPO will shower extraordinary wealth on Anthropic's seven founders, including Amodei and his sister. Collectively they own nearly 500 million shares, though it's unclear from the offering document how much that will represent of the company after the IPO. Dario, 43, and 39-year-old Daniela, who is Anthropic's president, are worth $15.5 billion each, according to Forbes, which ranks them as the 176th and 177th richest in the world. Reflecting AI's dangers, the document includes some unusual provisions, including granting those two and their five other co-founders 50.1% of shareholder votes through a special class of shares. Anthropic has also appointed independent, financially disinterested members of a so-called Long-Term Benefit Trust, holding power to appoint directors, that is designed to ensure the company doesn't put financial interests ahead of public safety. READ MORE: AI discovered a software vulnerability that could impact 70% of websites worldwide. The rush is on to patch it Another unusual feature of the filing is its long list of "risk factors," a required disclosure for every public company but in this case one that runs nearly 100 pages — and makes for riveting reading. Among the risks are the quotidian — the possibility it won't be able to retain key staff or navigate regulatory roadblocks — and the horrific. The latter includes the prospect of "malicious actors" using AI models to build chemical weapons, authoritarian rulers turning to the technology to crack down on their citizens and, given the numerous hacking incidents from rogue AI agents recently, the possibility Anthropic's AI models could "pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity." Calls for an AI slowdown The IPO comes as reports emerge about AI's ability to solve problems beyond human capacity for good, but also to carry out harmful, life-threatening tasks while humans lose control. In September, Amodei said the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up.
