107d4d72e2b3.text: In a closely watched election, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated right-wing and Trump-aligned challenger Flávio Bolsonaro. Transport and weather disruptions in parts of Brazil led to a chaotic final stretch at the polls. Bolsonaro is refusing to concede, and President Trump called the outcome "rigged." Stephanie Sy reports. Amna Nawaz: In a closely watched election, Brazil's president, known as Lula, defeated right-wing and Trump-aligned challenger Flavio Bolsonaro last night by nearly 4.5 million votes. Transportation and weather disruptions in parts of Brazil led to a chaotic final stretch at the polls. Bolsonaro is now refusing to concede. And, today, President Trump said the outcome was -- quote -- "rigged." Stephanie Sy reports. Stephanie Sy: On the streets of Rio de Janeiro last night, rejoicing and cheers of relief rang out among Lula supporters. Brazilian voters narrowly reelected the leftist president, Luiz Inacio da Silva, the 80-year-old Lula beating right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro 51 to 48 percent. Lula addressed supporters in Sao Paulo after the win. Luiz Inacio Lula Da Silva, Brazilian President (through interpreter): I want you to know that everything I do, I do with you in mind. All public policies are designed with you in mind. And you have given me the distinction of being the first president of the republic to be elected four times through democratic means. This is a historic achievement that I owe to the Brazilian people. Stephanie Sy: It's historic in more ways than one. Lula was the underdog after he lost the first round of voting earlier this month to Flavio, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted for attempting to stage a coup. Millions of Brazilians who did not vote in the first round came out Sunday, with voters in Rio de Janeiro and the suburbs of Sao Paulo swinging their support to Lula. Ana Candida Cotrim, Lula Supporter (through interpreter): The feeling is that democracy resisted in the midst of authoritarianism, in the midst of the whole world, of the great powers like the United States against Brazil. And we managed to resist with the strength of the people in the streets and on social media. Stephanie Sy: Lula's victory broke a recent right-wing winning streak in Latin America. Now Brazil and Mexico, Latin America's two most populous countries, have bucked the trend. Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum reacted jubilantly today. Claudia Sheinbaum, Mexican President (through interpreter): It shows that, when the people decide to mobilize and defend their rights, they always win. And that is a lesson for Brazil, for Mexico, and for the whole world. Stephanie Sy: Lula's win was a loss for President Trump's influence in the region. And echoing Trump and his father, Flavio Bolsonaro refused to admit defeat last night, saying he planned to request an annulment of the election. Flavio Bolsonaro, Brazilian Presidential Candidate (through interpreter): What happened today was not normal. It was downright unacceptable. A Supreme Court justice for the first time in history, a former lawyer for Lula, with a simple stroke of the pen, at the request of a former partner, changed the rules of the game in the middle of the match. Stephanie Sy: Stormy weather and transportation troubles had led both candidates to request an extension of voting by two hours. But in the end, the country's Supreme Court granted Lula's request shortly before polls were set to close. Supporters of Bolsonaro are crying foul. Jeremias Oliveira, Brasilia, Brazil Resident (through interpreter): Flavio Bolsonaro has already said he will file to annul this election. I hope he manages to, because it's not normal, people. This is wrong. Stephanie Sy: Despite attempts to inject doubt, the results are official. And even right-wing leaders in the region are congratulating Lula. Flavio Bolsonaro will remain in the Senate through the end of his term, however, and with Congress still dominated by Brazil's right-wing. Lula's win, while decisive, is far from a mandate. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Stephanie Sy.

69cda18d8ca1.text:
Environmentalists worldwide are celebrating the re-election of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva as a win for the Amazon’s future and global climate policy.
The three-term incumbent narrowly defeated right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who climate activists warned would have stripped away environmental policies and institutions protecting the world’s largest rainforest if elected.
The victory gives Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, another four years to pursue his pledge to end deforestation by 2030 after the greatest slowdown in forest loss in years. Between August 2025 and March 2026, deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon fell by 36 percent from the previous year.
This comes as nearly one-fifth of the Amazon has already been deforested. Coupled with climate change, the forest is nearing an irreparable tipping point, scientists say, and tree loss could dry out the region and further accelerate climate change.
Carlos Nobre, a professor of climate and sustainability at the University of São Paulo, said preventing the irreversible transformation of vast areas of the Amazon is still possible, but time is running out.
“The reduction in deforestation over recent years has been crucial, but much more needs to be done,” Nobre said in a statement. “The next four years will be decisive for the future of the world’s largest tropical rainforest and for climate stability in Brazil and around the world.”
Despite these warnings, governments across the Amazon, including Lula’s administration, continue to expand oil drilling, mining and industrial agriculture. It’s impacted local communities and environmental defenders.
Lula’s re-election also preserves Brazil’s role in international climate diplomacy after hosting COP30 in Belém in 2025. The government has pledged to implement its Paris Agreement commitments and accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels.
In November 2025, Lula’s administration formally recognized 20 Indigenous territories covering more than 6 million acres, and gave the communities firmer legal grounds to protect the forests on their land from exploitation or seizure.
Climate activists have called for Lula to speed up the recognition of other Indigenous territories, pressure agriculture businesses to stop using illegally deforested land, better protect environmental defenders and cancel oil and road projects that threaten the progress his administration has made.
“The Lula administration has shown that progress is possible, but much more remains to be done,” said Brad Adams, executive director of Climate Rights International.
Lula’s victory doesn’t shield the country from other political challenges, said Maurício Voivodic, the executive director of World Wildlife Fund Brazil. Voters elected Bolsonaro’s far-right Liberal Party to the most seats in both chambers of National Congress.
The newly elected Congress poses a significant risk to the president’s environmental and social agenda, Voivodic said in a statement. An analysis by the Brazilian climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima found that nearly 70 percent of elected lawmakers have low or very low alignment with environmental protection policies.
“This increases the risk of rollbacks in environmental and social legislation, with consequences for forest protection and deforestation,” Voivodic said. “Continued vigilance and public mobilization will be essential to defending the progress achieved.”
Meanwhile, Sen. Bolsonaro is continuing the populist movement built by his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election.
Academic researchers report that Jair Bolsonaro systematically dismantled environmental regulations to enable corporate exploitation of natural resources while targeting Indigenous and traditional peoples, non-governmental organizations, scientists and other environmental defenders across Brazil.
In 2019, the first year of Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency, Brazil’s deforestation numbers spiked to the highest levels since satellite data became available. With Lula’s re-election, Adams said, Brazil’s forests and the people defending them have dodged a bullet.
“Flávio Bolsonaro could have brought back his father’s disastrous policies, which devastated forests and put communities and defenders in danger,” Adams said in a statement. “But the forests and their defenders are still at risk, and Lula should now double down on efforts to protect them.”
About This Story
Perhaps you noticed: This story, like all the news we publish, is free to read. That’s because Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization. We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.
That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. We’ve built bureaus from coast to coast to report local stories, collaborate with local newsrooms and co-publish articles so that this vital work is shared as widely as possible.
Two of us launched ICN in 2007. Six years later we earned a Pulitzer Prize for National Reporting, and now we run the oldest and largest dedicated climate newsroom in the nation. We tell the story in all its complexity. We hold polluters accountable. We expose environmental injustice. We debunk misinformation. We scrutinize solutions and inspire action.
Donations from readers like you fund every aspect of what we do. If you don’t already, will you support our ongoing work, our reporting on the biggest crisis facing our planet, and help us reach even more readers in more places?

e795e7920221.text: Brazil is not the only country to have had dramatic election results this weekend. In Serbia, longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic lost a historic election that brought down his government. William Brangham discussed the results with Heather Conley. Amna Nawaz: Well, and Brazil isn't the only country with dramatic election results this weekend. In Serbia, longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic was defeated after an historic election on Sunday brought down his government. William Brangham joins us now with more. William Brangham: For more on the results from Serbia and how this result is echoing around the world, we turn again to Heather Conley. She served as deputy assistant secretary of state for European affairs during the George W. Bush administration. She's now a nonresident fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and works with an international consulting company. Heather, great to have you back. Help us understand something. Your reaction to this? Because some viewers might think, Serbia is not that big of a nation, under seven million people. They're not in the E.U. They're not in NATO. So how important is this result? Heather Conley, American Enterprise Institute: Well, it's extraordinary because of how it came about and the focus of the concern of the protesters. First and foremost, this was led by students. It's a young persons' -- it's a movement that doesn't have a leader. It's decentralized. It's digitally savvy, and it brought down literally a strongman of Serbia who had all control over the powers, economic, political powers. And the focus of the protest was on corruption, government corruption, and we're seeing that issue become a real global issue. And certainly young people are taking to the streets and really, strongly seeking another solution from government. So I have to say, as a watcher of the Western Balkans, it was like I was watching October 2000, when the people poured out in the streets in Serbia to oust Milosevic. President Vucic was a member of Milosevic's Cabinet, and this was truly people power. And it sort of comes along -- we remember the Hungarian election not too long ago that brought in a new leader who also was fighting corruption. This is also a strike against Russia and China, two countries that were strongly influencing Serbia. And so it's certainly a win for the people of Serbia, but we will see how they govern from here. Big question marks to come. William Brangham: Right, because as you were saying, this wasn't Vucic against another candidate. This was a parliamentary election, and Vucic basically saw that his party was getting drubbed in the polls and conceded this race peacefully. Did that surprise you how quickly he came forward and said, we have clearly lost, time to move on? Heather Conley: Yes, I mean, we always think of the strongman with incredible control over economic powers, that they're not going to go quietly into the night. There was an hour where the Serbian government, the electoral commission, didn't release the results. I think they paused, saw how dramatically large it was, and said, look, we can't fight this now. But if the student-led movement is disorganized, if they cannot form a government, we have all the levers there. We will try to sort of fight this out another day. But I was surprised, and good for them for acknowledging this was a historic win. William Brangham: Did the tenacity of this student movement impress you? I mean, we have seen a lot of protests that have been bubbling up, often youth-driven. But this one lasted quite a while, and as you were saying, seems quite effective. Like, I -- when you look at this, the broad scope of what's happening in Europe, does this feel spiritually, philosophically connected to all these other protests that we're seeing? Heather Conley: Yes, I like to think we're starting to see some dots connected, particularly with youth movement. As you said, this started two years ago when a rail station in Novi Sad, Serbia, it was recently renovated and it collapsed, killing 16 people. It was clearly an example of, again, government corruption that didn't use the right building materials. There was no accountability. So these student protesters began to galvanize around, we want credit -- we want the government to be transparent. We want someone to be held accountable for this. Over time, though, it grew, and it grew about demanding greater things from government, greater accountability, and it and it grew across Belgrade. So there's something that they fought for two years and look at what they achieved. But we're seeing this historically elsewhere. In Albania very recently, students are now growing against a -- what they believe to be a corrupt investment in Albania that has links to President Trump's family. We see... William Brangham: This is the Kushner and his wife's investment in a luxury resort. Heather Conley: Exactly, in Albania. We're seeing that huge pressure on the government, whereas some we have seen in France in these -- in these protests. Now, some of them have become violent, but we're seeing where young people, just high schoolers, were saying, I cannot accept anymore. The fact that I don't have a teacher in my classroom, my classroom isn't working, I want something better. I demand the government take action. And now others are joining in that, unions, as well as the Yellow Vest movement. And even in the Brazil example that you just showed, what appears to be the difference between the first and the second round and the surprising victory by President Lula was a real empowerment, Lula's army of young people, that really were galvanized. So we're seeing young people taking part. Turnout is historically high. But the thing is, they're demanding something different from government, not the same old story. And a lot of this is focused on corruption and that governments are not addressing critical problems. You see that in India with the Cockroach movement over elect -- educatio

a50d5a4a5096.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-administration-charges-former-fbi-director-james-comey-for-the-third-time Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration charges former FBI Director James Comey for the third time Politics Updated on Oct 26, 2026 6:47 PM EDT — Published on Oct 26, 2026 6:01 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is attempting to prosecute James Comey for what it calls a decade-old leak of classified information, an effort the former FBI director's lawyers immediately dismissed as invalid and outside the legal time limit for when the Justice Department can file a criminal indictment. The allegations from the Justice Department were revealed Monday in newly unsealed court documents that shed light on a closed-door fight that represents a clear escalation in the administration's targeting of Comey, a longtime critic and foe of President Donald Trump who has faced two other criminal cases since the Republican returned to the White House last year. The effort to prosecute Comey is also part of a series of politically charged investigative actions the department has undertaken in the run-up to next week's midterm elections. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "Well, they're back — again," Comey said in a video statement released after the documents dropped. "It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice – one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing's changed with me; I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people — and I still believe in an independent federal judiciary." The Justice Department, for its part, said it had filed what's known as a "criminal information" to extend the 10-year statute of limitations for bringing a case. "Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals. This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further," a department spokesperson said. A criminal information is typically filed with a defendant's consent accompanying a plea deal, but Comey's lawyers made clear that they intend to fight the charges as invalid and barred by the statute of limitations. "For the third time in little more than one year, the Department of Justice has attempted to charge Mr. Comey with a federal crime. Mr. Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence," his attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement. The allegation was previously investigated The latest allegation concerns an October 2016 New York Times story related to a secret court order that required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. The story cited two government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity about the order from a judge on the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court that Yahoo was barred from publicly disclosing. Federal authorities, including then-Special Counsel John Durham, began investigating the FBI's Oct. 5, 2016, disclosure to The New York Times in early 2017. Durham wrote a classified memo in December 2018 recommending no criminal charges against anyone in connection with the disclosure, Comey's attorneys said in a recent court filing. In January 2019, the U.S. Attorney's office for the District of Columbia opened a second investigation of the same matter under the code name "Tropical Vortex." But that investigation was closed without any charges filed in February 2020. "Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone. Now, ten years after the article was published, the Government filed an "Information" against Mr. Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury. It purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit," Fitzgerald said. Trump and Comey have a long and uneasy history The first case against Comey was dismissed after the judge found that the prosecutor who brought the indictment was illegally appointed. Comey was charged in a separate case in April over a social media post depicting seashells on the beach that officials said constituted a threat against the president. Comey was the FBI director when Trump took office in 2017, having been appointed by then-President Barack Obama, a Democrat, and serving before that as a senior Justice Department official in President George W. Bush's Republican administration. But the relationship was strained from the start, including after Comey resisted a request by Trump at a private dinner to pledge his personal loyalty to the president -- an overture that so unnerved the FBI director that he documented it in a contemporaneous memorandum. Trump fired Comey in May 2017 amid an FBI investigation into potential ties between Russia and Trump's campaign. That inquiry, later taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller, found that while Russia interfered in the 2016 election and the Trump team welcomed the help, there was insufficient evidence to prove a criminal collaboration. In a letter to the Washington Secretary of State's Office, the Justice Department said it had identified 1,500 votes cast by the over 400 people in prior elections. It asked the state to set aside any ballots the people might cast in next month's midterm until state officials can confirm they are legally eligible to vote. "We are asking the state to set aside those ballots until we can confirm they are legal voters," Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd said in a news conference. Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs was reviewing the administration's demand. His office noted that it had received about 60 subpoenas from the Justice Department since last month seeking information about voters. "We take our responsibility to protect voter information seriously and will only respond to requests that follow due process," Hobbs said in an emailed statement. "We see what's happening in California and don't want Washingtonians to be harassed." The effort is the latest by the administration to identify noncitizen voters, even though noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. President Donald Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine public confidence in elections. The request in Washington is similar to Justice Department attempt to require California to sequester mail ballots from up to 20,000 people the federal government suspects may not be citizens. California has challenged that, and during rare Sunday arguments a panel of federal appellate judges questioned the timing, constitutionality and authority of the Justice Department's demand. The Elections Clause of the U.S. Constitution gives state legislatures the power to set the time, place and manner of congressional elections. Los Angeles County Assistant Registrar-Recorder Monica Flores said in a court filing that her staff went through a sample of 200 records from the Trump administration's list. They found the sample included canceled or inactive registrations, people with no voting history and voters who appeared to have been born in the United States. The Justice Department told Washington it anticipates sending the state an additional list of people it suspects are not citizens prior to Election Day. It also noted that some of the people it suspects registered without citizenship may have since become naturalized. Investigations into prior allegations of noncitizen voters have revealed far fewer instances than the Trump administration has claimed. In Nevada, Trump's administration alleged there were 1,500 potential noncitizen voters on the rolls but subsequent investigation found zero. In Maricopa County, which includes Phoenix, the county Recorder, who is a Trump supporter, announced that there were 207 possible noncitizens on the county's rolls. At last, Army seeing progress in Pacific network
Recent exercises suggest the service and its foreign partners are moving closer to a single-screen data system.
WASHINGTON—After years of frustration, Army leaders are starting to see progress on upgraded networks designed to make it easier to communicate with allies and partners in a Pacific conflict.
“When I arrived at [U.S. Army Pacific Command], we had an exercise in Japan—and I'd only been in command a month. It was a trilateral exercise between the U.S., Japan, and Australia. And we literally couldn't pass voice data to each other. We couldn't create a common operating picture without physically putting icons into this system,” Gen. Ronald Clark, commander of U.S. Army Pacific, told reporters earlier this month.
“It was so frustrating to me because I just left working in the Pentagon where I had literally attended both the signing ceremonies for AUKUS…sharing our most sensitive defense technology. But we are using basically a swivel chair to have a conversation with regard to land forces.”
In recent years, the Army has been building and testing the telecommunications pipelines that allies and partner militaries would rely on in a war with China. U.S. Indo-Pacific Command has a broader Pacific Mission Network, previously known as the INDOPACOM Mission Network, which is used on a more strategic or operational level.
Earlier this year, the U.S., Australia, and Japan used the Pacific Mission Network during the large Balikatan exercise to get a “real-time picture of participating forces across the entire training area,” an Army spokesperson told Defense One.
Months later, the nations reconvened for Yama Sakura 91, an annual military exercise with Japan and Australia that ended Sept. 10.
“Yama Sakura 91 demonstrated the live sharing of simulated information in a command post exercise, while Balikatan 26 demonstrated the live sharing of real-time information across a physical training environment and multiple echelons,” the Army said.
That network, which connects dozens of nations, was the linchpin for USARPAC to test whether it could share and see the same information as allies and partners.
“The [mission partner] enclaves work, so we're able to pass and share data in a way that we had not been before,” Clark said, at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference, calling the network an “important and critical innovation” that addressed years of frustrations.
That means commanders can more easily send “target-quality data” and share a “common operational picture” without needing to swivel between workstations.
For example, Maj. Gen. Bernard Harrington, who leads the Army’s Multi-Domain Command-Pacific and 7th Infantry Division, can gather information on “land-based long-range precision fires, sensors, space capability, [electronic warfare], cyber” and then share it with Pacific Fleet Commander Adm. Stephen Koehler, who led the exercise, and “can then integrate that [data] into a joint context in the fight,” Clark said.
The progress on the Pacific Mission Network comes as the Army looks to add more tech and sources of data—mostly drones—to its forces. That means being able to see, control, and learn from devices and the information they collect will become increasingly important on the battlefield.
Seventh ID recently finished an exercise called Bayonet Quest near Lake Huron, Mich., in which it was able to coordinate high-altitude balloons, and aerial and maritime drones, using a shared data connection, Harrington told reporters.
“We used multiple [unmanned aerial systems], multiple [unmanned surface vessels], long-range, one-way attack, and a high-altitude balloon,” he said. The division also collected and analyzed data from all of those systems using a single data layer.
During the exercise, which ended Oct. 6, the Army was also able to orchestrate the drones and coordinate simulated attacks with an “adaptive and agentic” command-and-control system.
“We were able to pull in a vast amount of data, make sense of it quickly, and then task those systems through a large language model, reducing the need for soldiers on individual ground control stations,” Harrington said in a statement to Defense One.
The exercise showed how unmanned systems could be used in the Pacific, particularly from different locations, which could help keep soldiers safe, he said.
The exercise wrapped earlier this month, but the division plans to keep training with the concept and employ it in future exercises with allies and partners.

755ac944b408.text: By — Sam Mednick, Associated Press Sam Mednick, Associated Press By — Natalie Melzer, Associated Press Natalie Melzer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/tens-of-thousands-of-israelis-living-abroad-are-expected-to-fly-in-for-pivotal-vote Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad are expected to fly in for pivotal vote Politics Oct 26, 2026 5:44 PM EDT TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — For two decades since leaving Israel for Canada, Yael Natra said, she didn't consider returning to vote in her home country's elections. She felt it wasn't right to cast a ballot in a place she no longer lived. But now, after seeing the far right gain power, Natra, 61, said she believed she had no choice. Ahead of Israel's election on Tuesday — the first since the 2023 Hamas-led attacks and ensuing wars in the region — Natra spent thousands of dollars to travel nearly 6,000 miles from Toronto to Tel Aviv to be in the country and vote, she said. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Israeli law generally requires citizens to vote in person in the country, with narrow exceptions for diplomats and certain official emissaries abroad. Natra said she plans to cast her ballot for parties not aligned with the current government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. "The Israel that I grew up in is disappearing," she said in an interview from Toronto, citing an eroding democracy and deeply divided society. "If something won't change this time, I don't know what's going to be." Tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad are expected to fly in for this month's vote, according to AID Coalition, a U.S.-based nonprofit focused on strengthening Israel's democracy. The election is one of the most consequential in Israel in years, widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu's handling of the wars and the hard-right turn Israel has taken both domestically and on the world stage. Israel has more than 7.3 million registered voters, but polling suggests a tight race. Previous elections have turned on thin margins. It's unclear what effect these voters might have, but many liberal Israelis who don't support Netanyahu have left the country in recent years, suggesting that those returning to cast ballots would not support him. "Many Israelis who have left over the years — and especially since Oct. 7 — are exposed to the isolation and animosity toward the country much more palpably than those inside, and as such are likely to want to vote out Netanyahu," said Mairav Zonszein, a senior analyst with the International Crisis Group, a nonprofit think tank. The U.S. tops the list of voters traveling to Israel, one group's estimates show AID Coalition estimates that as many as 67,000 voters are returning to Israel, based on surveys of expatriates and registration data gathered for its "Fly&Vote" initiative. It says about half are flying in from the United States, with others from Europe, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. "It doesn't matter what side of the political spectrum you're on, everyone views these elections as going to be critical," said Jonathan Barsade, AID Coalition's president. Israelis planning to travel from the U.S., United Kingdom and Canada told The Associated Press they felt a sense of obligation to try to preserve Israel's democracy. Hadar Susskind, 53, said he wants a new Israeli government to reverse course in the West Bank and Gaza, halting settlement activity and settler violence in the former and allowing for reconstruction in the latter. He and four relatives who live in the U.S. were flying back to "reaffirm Israel's democracy," he said. "This government is digging the hole deeper every day," he said. "The first thing the new government needs to do is put the shovel down." Dahlia Scheindlin, an American-Israeli political analyst, said the mobilization effort this year is notable, compared with past elections. And while many campaigns have focused on anti-Netanyahu sentiment, she said it's unclear overall how those flying in will vote. "There are also expats coming in to vote for the pro-Netanyahu side," Scheindlin said. Some voters previously supported Netanyahu but say their views changed Netanyahu's main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, is a centrist politician and former military chief of staff who has pledged to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the Oct. 7 attacks and Israel's conduct during the war. Eisenkot says he wants to restore the country's standing with international allies. Natra, who described her politics as center-right, said she voted for Netanyahu in the 1990s. But now, she said, his government's inability to take responsibility for the failures that led to the Oct. 7 attacks and his support for the ultra-Orthodox community have turned her away. Natra's younger sister, 57-year-old Tamar Ichilov, said the "horrible things" Israel is doing in Gaza and the occupied West Bank motivated her to travel to Israel to vote. She said Israel is consumed by a "vendetta" and intent to "destroy" after the Oct. 7 attacks, and she believes its actions have contributed to rising antisemitism. "People don't like us, and I can't blame them," she said in Tel Aviv, shortly after landing at Israel's main international airport. Record numbers of Israelis left in recent years, and some say they hope to return A record number of Israelis have moved away in recent years, a trend that began in 2022 and peaked amid the wars and turmoil following the Oct. 7 attacks, according to Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics. Eti Wissotzky Cohen, 44, said she settled last year in the U.K. with her husband and two children after growing increasingly alarmed by Israel's democratic backsliding and the shrinking space for li

(AP) — Colorado and Washington are reliably Democratic states where elected officials have rejected moves to ban transgender women and girls from female sports competitions. Now activists have gone around lawmakers to put proposed bans on both states' ballots. At a time when some Democratic leaders nationwide are recalibrating their approach to transgender issues, particularly sports, and polls show Americans generally back the bans, supporters are optimistic they will pass and open the door to similar efforts in other places where lawmakers have blocked bans. "What is happening in 2026 is a testing ground for the future," said Chris Melody Fields Figueredo, executive director of the Ballot Initiative Strategy Center, which supports LGBTQ+ rights. READ MORE: Abortion, taxes, trans rights are on the ballot this November. Here's what to know Twenty-seven states — including all where Republicans control both the legislature and governor's office — already have such laws. The efforts are billed as a way to protect women and girls and keep separate spaces for them, tapping into a concern that's gained momentum. President Donald Trump has taken steps to roll back transgender rights. The Supreme Court has upheld state sports bans. A June poll from Quinnipiac University found that about 7 in 10 registered voters think transgender women and girls should not be allowed to play on female sports teams. About one-quarter think they should. Democrats are divided, with about half saying transgender women and girls should be allowed and about half saying they should not. Robert Preuhs, a professor of political science at Metropolitan State University of Denver, said the absence of public polls on Colorado's ballot measure, which also covers college sports, makes it hard to predict whether it will pass. "It's probably going to get more support than some of the Republican candidates that will run," he said. Since transgender restrictions gained traction this decade, states with Democratic-led governors' offices and legislatures generally have rejected proposals such as banning transgender people from the bathrooms that match their gender identity and restricting gender-affirming care. Most Republican-led states have adopted those policies. In addition to the two blue-state questions, a measure in Arizona would broaden an existing ban to include private schools, and one in Nebraska would add an existing state law to the state constitution. The argument has been framed around fairness Let's Go Washington staff member Josh Johnson (left) helps a volunteer while phone banking in Bellevue on Oct. 19 in support of Washington State Initiative 638, which would prohibit transgender girls from competing in girls' sports. Photo by Photo/Lindsey Wasson/AP There's not a clear consensus on whether transgender women and girls have a competitive advantage. Factors include the age of the athlete, the sport, whether the athlete went through male puberty and how long they've received hormone therapy. But the idea that girls are being cheated is personal for some athletes. Ahnaleigh Wilson, a 17-year-old junior at Eastmont High School, about 150 miles (241 kilometers) east of Seattle, has been speaking out against allowing transgender girls to compete in girls' sports since she was in junior high. She said she'd won all her 1,600-meter races in seventh and eighth grade — until she finished second to a transgender athlete in a major meet. "I knew it wasn't right and it wasn't fair," she said. Wilson said three other transgender athletes she's competed against since then placed better in girls races than they would have with the same times against boys. "Women have fought for Title IX and our own categories and it's very important that we keep the dignity of that, and let women have their own sports and their own spaces to be safe and completely fair," she said, referencing the federal law that prohibits discrimination based on sex in education programs and activities, including athletics. Opponents say excluding transgender girls is also unfair. "They will say that they want to protect kids and in particular, young girls," said Nadine Bridges, executive director of One Colorado, which is leading the opposition to the measure there, "but I don't understand how you can protect kids and discriminate against kids at the same time." The number of transgender girls in school sports is believed to be a sliver of the total participants. Neither Colorado nor Washington has an official count. Let's Go Washington, which is behind the measure in that state, says it's counted 16 such athletes and that there could be more. The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association has counted about 101,000 girls in sports that it oversees — a figure that double-counts girls who play in multiple sports. The Vatican press office said the pope's recovery continues to progress in line with favorable assessments from his medical team. It also confirmed the pope is keeping the already ambitious trip program with no announced changes. READ MORE: What is adenocarcinoma? Here's what to know about Pope Leo XIV's form of lung cancer Surgeons on Oct. 13 removed a lobe where the nodule later diagnosed as malignant was located, in the first major health event of Leo's 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. Since returning to the Vatican, Leo has gradually resumed his activities while adjusting his schedule to prioritize recovery and periods of rest, the statement said. The pope's physician, Luigi Carbone, said there's no medical reason preventing Leo's trip to South America, which involves a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes. Leo expressed gratitude for the prayers and support he has received during his recovery and said he was eager to return to a region where he spent important periods of his life. "I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I've experienced so many moments of my life," Leo said Monday. "May this journey be an occasion for us to open our hearts to one another, strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters, and renew our commitment to proclaiming the Gospel with joy." The Vatican said the visit will provide an opportunity for the pope to strengthen ties with local churches, encourage the faithful and promote a message of faith, hope and peace in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. fc5210918beb.text: By — Dyepkazah Shibayan, Associated Press Dyepkazah Shibayan, Associated Press By — Mark Banchereau, Associated Press Mark Banchereau, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/1st-confirmed-ebola-patient-in-nigeria-evacuated-to-switzerland Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 1st confirmed Ebola patient in Nigeria evacuated to Switzerland World Oct 26, 2026 4:46 PM EDT ABUJA, Nigeria (AP) — A Swiss woman being treated for Ebola in Nigeria was medically evacuated to Switzerland with her husband Monday, officials said, as Nigerian authorities continued monitoring 52 people who had been in contact with her. Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Pate said the woman, the country's first case in the current outbreak, left the capital, Abuja, early Monday with his approval. Her condition had improved significantly, and she was stable, conscious and able to communicate, he said. Please check your inbox to confirm. "This does not mean she is not still infectious, hence the strict protocols in place," Pate wrote on X. Her husband, a Swiss diplomat in Nigeria, has shown no symptoms. Switzerland's Federal Office of Public Health said the couple arrived Monday on a medical evacuation flight. The woman was being treated at Geneva University Hospital, while her husband was in isolation at Zurich University Hospital. The agency said both hospitals were equipped to care for them and that there was no risk to the Swiss public. The World Health Organization's regional director for Africa, Mohamed Janabi, said the evacuation was arranged because the couple are Swiss citizens and that Nigerian medical teams had stabilized the woman after treating her through the acute phase of the illness. Nigeria will continue monitoring 52 other contacts, Janabi said. "With the evacuation of the patient and her husband, Nigeria currently has no Ebola cases," he said, stressing that vigilance remained critical. Pate said containment measures remained in place and urged Nigerians to remain vigilant. The woman tested positive after returning to Abuja from Uganda. Nigerian authorities said Friday they had yet to establish how she contracted the virus. Switzerland's foreign ministry told The Associated Press last week that she had not visited Congo and was believed to have been infected while traveling to Uganda with her husband. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the first patients in Nigeria and Kenya had both traveled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport on Oct. 3. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases but later declared itself free of the virus. Kenya has recorded nine cases, including two deaths, since confirming its first case earlier this month. On Monday, Kenya released 20 people from quarantine following their exposure to the virus as contacts of the country's first case, while 98 others were expected to be released starting next Tuesday. "Each of the 20 contacts was assessed against the release criteria, including 21 days without any symptoms since their last exposure," the Kenyan Ministry of Health said in a statement. The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened longstanding fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus. The latest figures from Congo's health ministry show more than 9,900 cases, including more than 4,800 deaths, since the outbreak began in May. The WHO has said the outbreak is the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record and is on track to surpass the death toll of the deadliest: West Africa's 2014-2016 outbreak, which killed 11,000 people. Nigeria was among the countries affected, recording 20 cases before its outbreak was declared over after three months. Banchereau reported from Dakar, Senegal. e8abb19575ec.text: President Trump will campaign with three football stars in Texas on Tuesday, leaning into America's favorite sport as Republicans scramble to turn out voters in the final week before the midterms, Axios has learned. Why it matters: Trump is trying to mobilize the lower-propensity voters who helped return him to the White House in 2024 — but who may be less inclined to vote when he isn't on the ballot. Driving the news: Former college football stars Johnny Manziel and Colt McCoy, along with two-time Super Bowl champion Danny Amendola, will join Trump for campaign appearances in Lubbock and Corpus Christi. The appearances bring some of Texas' biggest football names onto the campaign trail in a state where the sport commands an enormous following. Amendola starred at Texas Tech in Lubbock, Manziel won the Heisman Trophy at Texas A&M, and McCoy was a standout quarterback at the University of Texas. The big picture: Trump has made football a recurring feature of his campaign stops in recent weeks. He attended the Texas-Tennessee game in September and planned to attend the Georgia-Alabama showdown earlier this month before canceling because of a hurricane. Former NFL coach Jon Gruden joined Trump at an Ohio rally this month, while former Georgia and NFL star Todd Gurley accompanied the president on a stop in Georgia. Vice President Vance, a lifelong Cincinnati Bengals fan, visited the team's practice facility last week while campaigning in Ohio. Republicans are also pouring millions into ads during NFL and college football games. What they're saying: "Trump has many bases. And football is one of them, college and pros," said an adviser. "The response is good. And the president loves the atmosphere. So why not?" Between the lines: Football offers Trump a way to reach younger men who helped power his 2024 victory — a constituency Republicans are struggling to energize in the midterms. By the numbers: Polls suggest Republicans face a challenge holding onto Trump's gains among young men. Trump won men under 30 by 14 points in 2024, according to a Tufts University analysis . But a Harvard Youth Poll released last week found Democrats leading Republicans by 26 points among young men who say they will definitely vote in November. Marc Caputo contributed to this report.

a03d5facc91b.text: President Trump and MAGA-world influencers are echoing Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro's claims of a rigged election after the Trump-aligned populist fell to the incumbent president in Sunday's election. The big picture: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's runoff victory has been widely seen as a counterweight to the global right's surge in Latin America. But Bolsonaro, like his father , isn't accepting defeat. What they're saying: "It looked like another rigged election, frankly," Trump told reporters Monday. He added, "Elections have to be indisputable, and it looked very bad to me." The White House referred Axios to Trump's comments when asked to respond. Friction point: Bolsonaro told reporters it was "impossible to recognize the result of this election in the context of how these things have happened," according to a translation . He also vowed to ask for the results to be annulled. Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin's two-hour extension to Sunday's voting has fueled Bolsonaro's claims. Zanin previously served as Lula's lawyer. But both Bolsonaro and Lula's camps requested more time for voters. Lula's team requested the extension because of public transit issues, while Bolsonaro sought additional time in certain states because of weather, Bloomberg reported . The extension was reportedly given as many polling stations were already wrapping up. Multiple outlets noted that the decision risked setting the stage for candidates to dispute the results, despite Brazil's voting system being widely recognized for its reliability. Zoom out: Several prominent voices in the online MAGA movement backed Bolsonaro's refusal to accept the election results, and some urged the Trump administration to act. "The math just ain't mathin'," podcaster Benny Johnson said in a Monday edition of his show where he criticized the election results. He was joined by Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, who argued Brazil looked like "a banana republic." Former Trump White House adviser Steve Bannon urged the administration to sever ties with Brazil on his "War Room" show, adding, "if we don't take action ... it's happening next Tuesday here in this country." Jack Posobiec echoed Bannon's unfounded claims, writing on X, "Look at what the Left is doing in Brazil in broad daylight. Do you really think they wouldn't in the United States?" Andrew Kolvet, who produced "The Charlie Kirk Show," said the U.S. should "quietly pressure them behind the scenes" and not accept the result. He further urged Bolsonaro supporters not to show up for work and "rally in the streets." What we're watching: The attention on Bolsonaro's loss comes as MAGA activists have pushed for Trump to take extraordinary measures, like martial law, if they think the U.S. election is rigged, Axios' Brittany Gibson reports . Trump has continued to stoke the coals of election denialism, while political opponents have accused his administration of trying to intimidate voters and election officials. Meanwhile, the Justice Department has waged an aggressive pre-election offensive, including a preemptive request that could delay certification of Alaska's Senate results and a lawsuit against California over alleged suspected noncitizens receiving ballots. Go deeper: Trump allies fall in two elections as Netanyahu faces next test

27638b3382ab.text: By — Thomas Adamson, Associated Press Thomas Adamson, Associated Press By — Sylvie Corbet, Associated Press Sylvie Corbet, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/france-pledges-new-university-admissions-to-quell-student-anger-but-only-after-macron-leaves-office Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter France pledges new university admissions to quell student anger. But only after Macron leaves office World Oct 26, 2026 4:32 PM EDT PARIS (AP) — France's government pledged on Monday to replace its national online university admissions platform in 2028, seeking to quell student anger after weeks of mass protests over education and living costs. Higher Education Minister Philippe Baptiste announced "substantial change" to the platform for 2027, before its replacement the following year. The concessions target the school grievances that helped ignite the unrest. But the movement has widened to include workers demanding relief from rising living costs, making the government's task broader than resolving a dispute over university admissions. The announcements followed France's worst unrest in years on Oct. 17, when demonstrations over school funding and rising living costs descended into rioting and looting across the country. Groups of protesters set fires, stormed public buildings — including Marseille's City Hall — looted shops and clashed with police. About 2,400 people were arrested over that weekend. READ MORE: From France to Albania, how social unrest is fueling protests across Europe Two high school student groups welcomed some concessions but called for protests to continue. Their representatives spoke after meeting with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu earlier Monday, before the ministers' news conference. Further demonstrations have been planned for Oct. 31, before nationwide strikes and protests called by labor unions for Nov. 5. The 2028 deadline puts a central concession to protesters beyond President Emmanuel Macron's time in office, leaving his successor's government to deliver it. Macron can't seek a third consecutive term in 2027, and far-right leader Marine Le Pen leads polling for the first round of the presidential election on April 18. A second round will be held May 2 if no candidate achieves a majority. The university admissions replacement system still has to be designed, and legal changes may be needed — leaving crucial decisions unresolved even as the government seeks to persuade students to end their protests. The system, called Parcoursup, handles applications to universities and other higher education courses. It has been a focus of the protests, with students criticizing unclear selection criteria and unequal access to their preferred courses. For the 2027 admissions round, institutions would have to publish more detailed selection criteria and explain rejections when applicants request reasons. The government also promised 15,000 additional places in higher education, introduced across 2027 and 2028, and increases in student grants linked to inflation from the start of the 2027 academic year. Another round of nationwide demonstrations on Saturday saw less violence. Authorities estimated turnout at more than 400,000, while organizers put it at nearly 800,000. Rapper Jay-Z will perform at the Super Bowl half-time show in February, the NFL has announced.
Jay-Z's company Roc Nation has produced the half-time show since 2019, and he plays a key role in selecting each year's performer but he has not performed before at the NFL championship game.
"Anticipation as to who Jay-Z might have guest star at halftime for the big game will now kick off," the NFL said in a statement. "Of course, his wife, BeyoncÃ©, will be atop the list."
Next year's Super Bowl LXI will take place on 14 February near Los Angeles.
The hip-hop star will follow in the footsteps of other recent half-time performers including Bad Bunny, Kendrick Lamar, Usher, Rihanna and The Weeknd.
The musical performance draws global attention while the sport is watched by tens of millions of people in the US.
Kendrick Lamar's 2025 performance was the most watched Super Bowl half-time show in history and won the Emmy award for outstanding music direction.
The announcement was made after Jay-Z, whose real name is Shawn Carter, performed two shows last weekend at the Los Angeles stadium where the Super Bowl will be played.
The LA shows were part of a tour to celebrate the 30th anniversary of his debut album Reasonable Doubt.
"From 'Reasonable Doubt' to standing on the Super Bowl halftime stage, this has been a journey," said Jay-Z, whose real name is Shawn Carter.
"Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world's biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true."
NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said he "couldn't be more excited for fans around the world to experience the artistry, creativity and cultural impact he will bring".
"When we first reached an agreement with Roc Nation to produce the show, I had just one request: that Jay-Z take the stage himself one day, whenever the moment felt right to him," Goodell said.
The star's accolades include being the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame, 25 Grammy awards and being inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.

The Duchess of Sussex has been confirmed as a co-host of the new season of Junior MasterChef Australia.
Meghan will join the 2027 series as a "special guest" with fellow host Poh Ling Yeow, according to Australia's Channel 10.
The duchess said she "can't wait" to take part in the programme after an appearance as a guest judge on MasterChef Australia last year. It was the show's largest Sunday audience since 2023, according to the statement from Paramount ANZ.
The announcement comes as Meghan faces increased scrutiny due to her father Thomas Markle being accused of child sexual abuse. He denies the allegations.
The BBC understands Meghan broke contact with her father last year, telling him she and authorities knew he had abused young girls.
Markle has strongly rejected the accusations as "lies" which are being used to destroy his reputation.
Meghan's return to Australia follows a four-day tour of the country she and Prince Harry undertook in April.
Meghan's MasterChef debut was announced on the second day of the tour, a Wednesday on which the duchess had been notably absent from public-facing appearances. That evening, it was revealed she had been filming an episode of the programme.
It is understood she was not paid for her appearance. Australia's Network 10, which airs the series as part of Paramount ANZ, did not respond to a question from the BBC about whether Meghan would be paid for co-hosting the Junior MasterChef season.
"I love cooking with my own kids, so seeing what these young stars create in the kitchen is going to be a lot of fun," Meghan said in a statement.
In August, the Sussexes announced they were moving back to the UK from California. The couple left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties in early 2020, before settling in California in March that year.
They embarked on media careers which included a high-profile interview with Oprah Winfrey and a deal with Netflix and Spotify.
Meghan's lifestyle and cookery show on Netflix, With Love, Meghan, ran for two series and a Christmas special but did not perform well with audiences.
She also launched lifestyle brand As Ever, which includes a food range, but in March it ended its partnership with the streaming platform.
Last year her trademark was registered in more than a dozen product categories in Australia, including cookware and table linen.

Jordan has struck what its military says were "terrorist organisations" in Syria in retaliation for an attack on a Christian funeral last week that killed nine people.
Syrian health officials told state media five people, including women, children and an elderly man, were killed in the strike on a village in the southern Daraa province. Jordan said its fighter jets had killed and wounded "several terrorists", without giving further details.
Jordan said it had co-ordinated with the Syrian government. Syria said it had not been notified of Monday's attack.
It comes after a nine people were killed and 34 injured in a shooting at a funeral in a Greek Orthodox church in Karak on Friday.
In response to the strike, Syria said it had closed a border crossing with Jordan.
"The decision includes the complete suspension of passenger and commercial traffic in both directions, to ensure the safety of travellers and workers at the crossing," Syrian authorities said in a statement carried by state media.
It added that it had "opened direct channels of communication" with Jordanian officials and had launched "comprehensive investigations to establish the full circumstances of the targeting".
Nassib is the only passenger and commercial border crossing between Jordan and Syria.
Earlier on Monday, senior government security officials said Jordanian security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law over the church attack.
The Public Security Directorate (PSD) said the unnamed "terrorists" were found hiding in an abandoned house in Karak before dawn.
Jordan's Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told state-affiliated TV the attackers were all Jordanians and "had been holed up in a building in one of the villages near the site of the attack".

Driving down roads lined with jubilant supporters from the western state of Lara to the capital Caracas, Maria Corina Machado's return to Venezuela could hardly have been more different to her exit 10 months earlier.
Colourful, loud, open and defiant, it stood in stark contrast to the way the Venezuelan opposition leader slipped out of the country in the dead of night in December last year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo.
She had been unable to make it back to her homeland until now, thwarted on several occasions by the Venezuelan government - and by the Trump administration, which insisted the "time wasn't right" for her return.
Now, it appears, it is.
"Maria Corina is the indisputable leader of Venezuela," says 20-year-old Gregory Noriega, wearing a sweatshirt emblazoned with the logo of the opposition movement Vente Venezuela. "Her return represents hope."
"This is a step forward in the electoral process which we've been waiting for since last year," echoes 18-year-old Hilary, who turned out on to the streets of the capital hoping to catch a glimpse of the opposition leader on her victory lap.
"She's returned after the double earthquakes when Venezuela needs her," adds her friend, Manuel. "The whole country is behind her to show that now Venezuela isn't scared."
Much has changed since Machado left Venezuelan soil to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
Then-President NicolÃ¡s Maduro is no longer at the top of the Venezuelan government.
Maduro was forcibly removed from power by US troops on 3 January, and whisked to New York where he faces drugs, weapons and torture charges â to which he's pleaded not guilty.
He was replaced by his former vice-president, Delcy RodrÃguez, who has turned the page with Washington in ways few could have imagined.
The bilateral relationship is today unrecognisable from the years of mutual animosity during the reigns of President Hugo ChÃ¡vez and then his handpicked successor, Maduro.
The new circumstances throw up some interesting conundrums for both sides.
When Machado left Venezuela, she had long been considered Washington's favoured alternative to Maduro. She returns to find the Trump administration perfectly happy with the one they've got â at least for the time being.
The Trump administration recently signed a major oil deal with Venezuela which gave the US a 100-year concession over a staggering 65bn barrels of Venezuelan crude oil.
The deal was reached in conjunction with a Venezuelan private company called North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) run by a businessman with a chequered past, Alejandro Betancourt.
Machado has openly criticised the deal which the RodrÃguez government reached with the US, albeit careful to direct her criticism at Caracas and at Betancourt rather than President Trump, to whom she gave her peace prize and whose trust and support she craves to move forward.
President Trump has repeatedly said how satisfied he is with Delcy RodrÃguez, calling her "wonderful" and "a terrific person". This was the vice-president of an administration he previously described as made up of "narco-communists".
But the outpouring of jubilation for Machado's caravan into the capital shows she can still count on significant support on the streets, says Venezuelan political analyst Beningno Alarcon.
"The return of Maria Corina Machado, in my personal view, is the most significant [political] event since 3rd January," says Alarcon. "It means the most important political leader in Venezuela is back in the country."
"The reception for her return shows that her ability to mobilise her support remains intact, which means the opposition in Venezuela now has something very solid: a leadership which is present on the ground as opposed to solely in exile," he says.
Alarcon provides some evidence that the opposition â and the public at large â feel more emboldened since 3 January, a situation he believes will become only more pronounced with Machado's reappearance.
For instance, a joint study by the political think tanks Polis and Nexo suggests that Venezuela saw three times as many street protests in the first nine months of this year as in all of 2025, with demonstrations spanning a range of issues, from politics and working conditions to water supply.
Furthermore, there's evidence that the repression of such protests has reduced by more than half.
In such an environment, the return of a figurehead like Machado can galvanise an electorate that has spent years fearful of the consequences of speaking out.
Her return also needs to be seen within the context of the wider talks brokered by Washington between the Venezuelan government and the opposition towards a negotiated political solution.
Certainly, the US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, was quick to say her "safe return" to Venezuela was "the direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks".
The Nobel Peace Prize winner still faces charges in Venezuela ranging from treason to conspiracy of insurrection. For years, she and her supporters have dismissed the charges as politically motivated and baseless.
Having made at least eight attempts to return to Venezuela by air and by sea before the Trump administration gave her the green light, Machado now knows she has Trump's blessing to be back on home soil â a position Delcy RodrÃguez is both unwilling and unlikely to challenge.
She called Machado's return a "show" and the entire cross-country event, which was livestreamed by her supporters over the weekend, was studiously ignored by state television outlets.
But RodrÃguez, too, needs a harmonious relationship with Washington if she is to avoid a fate similar to that of her predecessor and indicated she might be prepared to hold talks with Machado.
For as much as Trump has complimented RodrÃguez, he has also made it clear that Washington expects nothing less than her full submission and malleability on key issues like energy.

a005a3319fb0.text: A day after Venezuela's exiled opposition leader returned to Caracas with great fanfare, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a veiled warning against interfering with the country's fragile democratic transition pushed by the Trump administration. "You're not going to street-protest your way into a democracy," Rubio told reporters Monday without explicitly mentioning María Corina Machado . Why it matters: Machado's demands for elections next year — and her criticism of a massive U.S. oil deal struck with the current Caracas regime — have put administration officials on edge after her surprise return. "Rubio is on a political edge," said a White House source familiar with his thinking. "Venezuela is the top foreign policy achievement of this administration, and if the progress we made gets undone and Machado is a spoiler, nobody wins." A Machado spokesperson didn't return messages seeking comment. Zoom in: Machado and U.S. officials agree that Venezuela needs to hold elections. But she has demanded they be held in 2027, while U.S. officials aren't sure. They want three things to happen first: Reform Venezuela's Supreme Court. It's stocked with loyalists of Nicolas Maduro, who was seized Jan. 3 by the U.S. and spirited to New York City to face narcotrafficking charges. The State Department hopes a new court is picked by year's end. Reform Venezuela's National Electoral Council. It's also filled with Maduro's people, and with the Supreme Court it helped him steal his last two elections as president. The State Department hopes a new council will be in place by early next year. Fix Venezuela's debt. Venezuela has one of the world's largest sovereign debt problems — $300 billion, more than its gross domestic product. The hoped-for timeline regarding this hurdle is less clear, and Rubio didn't explicitly discuss it Monday. Between the lines: As Axios first reported in September, Trump discussed all three of those issues with Rodriguez when he also told her privately that elections need to happen one day. In a transcript of Rubio's briefing, a senior State Department official added another possible issue: reforming the security services, which also could take time. "If you want a democratically elected government to succeed, you don't want them to inherit an economic apocalypse that brings it down," the official said, according to the transcript. "What happens when the security forces that are not loyal to the system decide they're not gonna follow orders from — no matter who got elected? They're not gonna follow their orders; they're not gonna follow through. Now Caracas once again becomes the murder capital of the Western Hemisphere, maybe the world." Rubio did not specify any timelines. He told reporters he wouldn't allow Venezuela's current government, run by former Vice President Delcy Rodriguez, to stall out Trump's administration, which ends in January 2029. "What if they just try to wait us out for two years? That's not going to happen," Rubio said. "I mean, we have timelines that are agreed to, and so far they've met every one of the timelines." To call for a new election, Rodriguez would have to declare a vacancy in the presidency. That would trigger an election six months later, State Department officials said. So under the most optimistic timeline, Rodriguez could call for an election for next June. Trump administration officials emphasized to Axios that no date for an election is clear, and that it could take place next year or in 2028. Rubio also said he wants to stay on the job as long as possible: "Best-case scenario, I'm in this job for two more years and two months. So I clearly intend to see this thing well in advance of the time I leave" the administration. The intrigue: Rodriguez and Machado (whom Maduro banned from running in 2024) have made clear their mutual opposition to each other. Without naming her rival, Rodriguez told reporters Monday that Machado should feel remorse or regret for supporting the "external onslaught, that external military-style aggression against Venezuela." That's code for the U.S. seizing of Maduro, but Rubio told reporters he's paying attention to Rodriguez's actions and not her words. So far, he said, she's delivered on eliminating Iranian and Cuban influence in the country and extraditing former Maduro ally Alex Saab, a cooperating witness against him. "If at the end of the day we have a new [Supreme Court], a new [Electoral Council], a new election, and a new ... system of government, that's what we want," Rubio said. "And no matter what people say along the way, as long as it happens, this is a results-based process." The bottom line: Rubio said Venezuela has "got to change the infrastructure of the elections. Not in 10 years. Not in five years. Not in two years. It needs to happen quickly under the timelines that we've established." "But if anybody tries to derail that process, they're doing great harm to Venezuela."

The Vatican has confirmed that Pope Leo will go on his South American tour as planned, following his surgery for lung cancer.
He was diagnosed with lung cancer and underwent successful surgery in Rome on 13 October to remove a tumour on the lower part of his right lung.
The 71-year-old is scheduled to travel to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on 6-17 November, the Vatican said, adding that the he was looking forward to it "with great joy and enthusiasm".
The Pope will follow the same programme as planned, visiting 10 cities on the tour.
"I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I've experienced so many moments of my life," Pope Leo said.
The Pope's trip will begin in Uruguay on 8 November, where he will visit the capital Montevideo, as well as other key cities.
He will then travel to Argentina from November 11-17, visiting a number of places including the capital Buenos Aires.
After that he will spend six days in Peru, where roughly 76% of the population are Catholic, and will include stops in Lima, Chiclayo, Cuzco and Pucallpa.
Peru's Cardinal Castillo, the Archbishop of Lima, has said the trip would involve young people, women who help run community kitchens and members of the country's indigenous communities, according to Vatican News.
The archbishop highlighted the Pope's close ties with the people of Chiclayo, where he lived for several years. The Pope has Peruvian citizenship.
The Catholic Church sent him to Peru as a missionary in 1985, when he was 30 years old.
He joined the Augustinian mission in Chulucanas, in the Peruvian department of Piura, and the following year, joined the mission in the city of Trujillo.
For almost three decades, he worked between the US and Peru.
Leo announced the news of his lung operation himself to the world on 11 October during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung.
He reassured pilgrims that the growth was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage" but that his doctors had advised him to have it removed.
The surgery lasted for 90 minutes, and he was discharged from Rome's Gemelli hospital on 17 October.
The Pope's surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, said he was in an "absolutely satisfactory clinical condition", and said there were "no clinical reasons" why the trip should not go ahead.
Tests showed the cancer was "localised".
Since his operation, the pope has been resting and gradually resuming his work. He has been "adjusting his daily schedule in consultation with his doctors to prioritise his recovery while continuing to fulfill the responsibilities of his ministry," the Vatican said.
Leo was "deeply grateful for the prayers and affection he has received from throughout the world," the Vatican said.
The Vatican said Friday that Leo would cancel a planned trip to Assisi on October 27th, on the recommendation of his doctors.

A pineapple-sized fungus has quietly grown undetected in the forests of southwestern China – until now. The massive mushroom may set a size record for a major branch of the fungal family tree.
The fungus — named Dianjunus rex — may also represent a previously unknown family, researchers report September 28 in Frontiers in Fungal Biology. Fittingly, D. rex is part of a lineage that split off from other fungi right after the dinosaurs — like T. rex — went extinct.
In 2024, researchers in China were conducting a survey of fungal diversity in a tropical rainforest in Yunnan Province when local farmers tipped them off to an unusual fungus in the area. The farmers included photos, says Indunil Chinthani Senanayake, a mycologist at the Kunming Institute of Botany in China. Some of the farmers who’d made the discovery took a bite of the mystery fungus, Senanayake says, and the tipster “wanted to confirm whether it was edible or not.”
When Senanayake and her colleagues went to the location, they found strange, yellowish, tentacle-like and spatula-like mushrooms growing out of decaying tree roots. These were some kind of ascomycete, or “sac fungi”. Sac fungi like morels, truffles and molds make their spores in microscopic bladderlike receptacles, unlike the bowling pin-shaped reproductive structures in club fungi, the group that includes most culinary mushrooms.
The mushrooms we see growing out of the ground are called fruiting bodies and make the spore-producing cells for the often hidden or subterranean fungus. Most sac fungi have relatively small fruiting bodies. But the mushrooms growing off these mysterious Yunnan fungi were enormous, with some reaching 50 centimeters tall. The team took samples of the fungi back to the lab for further study and found that they weighed up to 2.2 kilograms. By their estimates, these are the largest spore-making fruiting bodies among all sac fungi.
Torda Varga — a mycologist at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew in Richmond, England who was not involved with the research — notes that some truffle species are known to get close to the bulk. D. rex appears to be the largest sac fungal fruiting body he’s aware of. “What I find particularly remarkable is that a fungus with such an enormous fruiting body appears to have remained scientifically undocumented until now,” says Varga, though he adds his experience has mostly been within Europe.
The researchers compared samples of the fungus’s DNA with those from other fungi to determine its evolutionary relationships. They found that it was a relative of species like candlesnuff fungus and dead-man’s-fingers, which make fruiting bodies only a few centimeters tall, but that it was probably in its own, unique family. The team gave the new species the name Dianjunus rex, referencing both the Latin “rex” for “king” and the ancient Dian kingdom of the region.
The team’s genetic analysis suggests D. rex’s family first evolved in the aftermath of the mass extinction at the end of the Cretaceous Period that wiped out the dinosaurs, some 65 million years ago. “During the dark, cold, postimpact years after the mass extinction, fungi that decompose dead organic matter could keep functioning better than light-dependent photosynthesizers,” Senanayake says.
Varga wonders if searching databases for bits of DNA shed into the environment could help uncover other members of D. rex’s royal family in the absence of physical specimens.
“Some of these [genetic] sequences might belong to previously undocumented relatives of Dianjunus rex,” he says. Finding these hidden species could tell researchers more about the biology and evolutionary history of this king of the sac fungi.
