Florida’s gubernatorial race features two candidates with very different views on the environment and climate: One largely supports maintaining the status quo in state policy while the other advocates for renewing a climate change and clean energy strategy in the state.
Both candidates spent time in the House of Representatives before running for the Sunshine State’s top job. Republican Byron Donalds, 48, is running against Democrat David Jolly, 54, to replace Gov. Ron DeSantis, a term-limited Republican. In his two terms as governor, DeSantis dismissed the role of climate change in intensifying hurricanes and flooding and did little to address the emissions exacerbating the problem or hold polluters accountable. He focused his environmental policy instead on the Everglades and water quality.
Donalds, who currently represents the 19th district in southwest Florida, is endorsed by DeSantis and President Donald Trump. If he wins, he would be the first Black governor elected in Florida and first Black Republican governor in the nation, said Aubrey Jewett, associate director of the School of Politics, Security and International Affairs at the University of Central Florida.
“It would be a historic milestone to show how far the state has come,” Jewett said, “from being a Confederate state that left the Union to defend slavery and then had 90 years of Jim Crow laws.”
Jolly represented the 13th district in Pinellas County as a Republican from 2014 to 2017, but changed his party registration and has become a TV analyst and outspoken critic of Trump in the years since. Recent polls show he has a shot at winning in this red state, even though he has raised a fraction of what his opponent has raised. Donalds’ campaign has amassed roughly $141 million, compared with Jolly’s $19 million, according to an Inside Climate News analysis of state campaign finance activity. Neither campaign provided comment for this article.
In Florida, Republicans hold every statewide elected office, control the Legislature and boast 1.5 million more registered voters than Democrats. But for many years Florida was a must-win swing state, opting six times in a row for the prevailing presidential candidate, from Bill Clinton in 1996 to Trump in 2016. For much of the 20th century Democrats ruled the state.
“For Florida voters, if they like what has been happening in the country and in the state under President Trump and under Gov. DeSantis, then a vote for Byron Donalds would be a vote to mostly continue what has been happening. If they think the country and the state are moving in the wrong direction, then this is the opportunity to try to change directions, by voting for David Jolly,” Jewett said.
“If the environment and global warming are a big issue for a Florida voter, it’s a pretty easy and clear distinction between these candidates: Byron Donalds, who doesn’t even think the science is settled on global warming and global climate change. And you’ve got David Jolly, who thinks the science is settled and we ought to do something about it.”
Among the biggest issues in the race are skyrocketing home insurance rates in Florida. Jolly cites climate change and intensifying hurricane risk as part of the problem. To control costs, he has proposed establishing a state-backed hurricane fund that would assume this risk, relieving Floridians of the most expensive aspect of their insurance policies. Insurers would support the fund by paying “taxes they currently avoid,” according to the campaign. Jewett said the concept has been brought up a few times before in the Republican-led Legislature.
Jolly says the fund would not create a “hurricane tax,” as Donalds has claimed in campaign ads. For his part, Donalds, whose professional background is in finance and insurance, has supported state legislative reforms in recent years aimed at addressing a tide of litigation against insurers. Insurers blame the litigation for pushing rates higher, but the reforms have faced criticism from those who believe the changes benefited insurers more than homeowners.
Some argue the reforms emboldened insurance companies to deny more claims, generating more lawsuits. Others say the changes helped attract new insurers to the state, boosting competition and stabilizing rates.
“I haven’t seen him come up with anything new or innovative to bring down property insurance rates,” Jewett said of Donalds. “He seems to be just backing what the governor and what the Legislature have already done.”

The candidates’ stances also differ on hyperscale data centers, which have generated concerns in Florida as proposals circulate throughout the state. The facilities require exorbitant amounts of water and electricity, even as there is overwhelming scientific consensus about the need to conserve energy and stem the fossil fuel emissions that have accelerated the planet’s warming. Jolly has proposed an immediate moratorium on the data centers, while Donalds supports legislation approved earlier this year aimed at protecting Floridians from their associated electricity costs. Susannah Randolph, director of the Florida chapter of the Sierra Club, which has endorsed Jolly, characterized the issue as a defining one.
“It’s really become the issue where people are deciding on whether or not they are going to support the gubernatorial candidate, from what we have seen. People do not want hyperscale data centers in this state,” she said. “From an environmental perspective, it’s not often we see an environmental issue be so high on the list of what voters are thinking, but it is this year.”
Jolly intends to enhance clean energy use in the state by pushing for more renewable energy and stronger net metering rules, to encourage more rooftop solar.

Why it could take time for a new Israeli government to form
Israelis are voting in what many view as one of the most pivotal elections in the country's history.
It is the first parliamentary election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks and subsequent conflicts across the region - in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen.

A tiny zebra-striped bee, usually found along England's south and east coasts, has made an unexpected journey to the West Country.
The rare sea aster mining bee has been spotted at Steart Marshes in Somerset by naturalist Nigel Phillips, who said the find "was a huge surprise".
The Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust said saltmarsh restoration work at the nature reserve had helped create the perfect home for the newcomer.
The charity says the discovery shows how rare species and wildlife can thrive by restoring coastal habitats.
More from Somerset
The sea aster mining bee has a particular taste in flowers and relies on the sea aster, a pink and yellow flower that blooms on coastal marshes, as summer moves into autumn.
The restoration project at Steart Marshes was completed in 2014, transforming former farmland into a coastal wetland by allowing seawater to flow back across the fields.
The reserve supports a wide variety of coastal wildflowers, including plenty of sea aster, which is thought to have finally attracted the bees to the Steart peninsula.
"There were lots of them and several colonial nest areas in the dry sandy ground," said Phillips.
"At the time I thought they were only found in salt marsh areas around the Thames estuary."
Of the 290 invertebrate species found in these habitats across the UK, 148 can only be found in saltmarshes.
Site manager Bay Alys Laver said: "People usually associate saltmarshes with huge flocks of wading birds, geese and ducks, but there is so much life here that goes unnoticed.
"Spotting such a rare species here is a testament to the brilliant work our staff do in maintaining the reserve in concert with local graziers.
"I was so happy to hear that we have been found by our first sea aster mining bees."

"I knew the protest could potentially cost me my career...I would absolutely do it again."
Ten years on from making the gesture that catapulted him to iconic status, but which he believes led to his exile from the sport he loved, Colin Kaepernick insists he has no regrets.
It was September 2016 when NFL star Kaepernick knelt during the US national anthem before a match as a peaceful protest against racial injustice and police brutality.
It proved both inspirational and divisive.
In his first interview with BBC Sport, Kaepernick reflects on his journey; his pride at seeing England footballers take the knee, athlete activism, the relationship between sport and politics, and the price he paid for being a figurehead for the civil rights movement.
The former quarterback says he decided to protest despite suspecting it could risk his career.
"History shows usâ¦that is a reality for athletes", he says.
"We also see this in broader movements, going well beyond costing someone their career, and costing people their lives. We see Malcolm X assassinated, we see MLK [Martin Luther King] assassinated, so the consequences are real."
Having initially sat to raise awareness of the plight of black people in the US, Kaepernick first knelt during the Star-Spangled Banner before his San Francisco 49ers team played a pre-season game. It was an act he would repeat before 11 regular-season contests that year.
At the time, he said he could not stand up for - and show pride in - a flag "for a country that oppresses black people and people of colour", adding: "This is bigger than football and it would be selfish on my part to look the other way."
His stance against racial inequality was seen as heroic by many, inspiring other NFL players to follow suit. But there was also condemnation from those who said it was disrespectful to the military.
Those dissenting voices included Donald Trump - then a presidential candidate.
Trump described the act as "a terrible thing" and unpatriotic. He even suggested Kaepernick should find another country to live in, adding players who refused to stand for the national anthem should be fired.
The NFL said it would fine teams whose players did not stand.
Kaepernick opted out of his contract with the 49ers in March 2017, though the club's management later said he would have been released regardless.
Despite leading the 49ers to the 2013 Super Bowl, and throwing 16 touchdowns in his final season, one of the most talented quarterbacks in the sport never found a new team.
Speaking from New York, Kaepernick says he anticipated the reaction to taking the knee. "What I couldn't have predicted was the people who would show up for me in significant ways, and also the people who worked against me and against the movement," he adds.
Kaepernick eventually filed a grievance against NFL team owners, who he believed had conspired not to hire him because of his protests, reaching a financial settlement in 2019.
That year, the NFL arranged a private workout for Kaepernick, but he chose not to attend, instead holding his own session elsewhere to allow media to be present. Hopes of a comeback never materialised.
The NFL later admitted it was "wrong for not listening to players earlier", and encouraged "all to speak out and peacefully protest".

'Humbling to see England players take knee'
Following the murder of George Floyd while in police custody in Minneapolis in 2020, taking the knee became a feature of Black Lives Matter protests, and widespread across sport.
England's men's and women's football teams were among those to follow suit.
"That was a surprising moment for me," says Kaepernick.
"I did think about the protest going beyond the US and how that may show up in other countries. To be able to see the national teams going out and protesting, it was humbling. I was happy that they were doing it.
"I also know there's still a lot of work to be done within racism in the UK and more broadly. And this is a global challenge that we are collectively fighting against.
"I was very excited to be able to see players actively calling that out, and willing to begin taking action towards addressing it."
Despite keeping a relatively low profile for most of the past decade, Kaepernick remains a standard-bearer for the civil rights movement.
But while surveys suggest the vast majority of professional athletes intend to use their social media channels to raise awareness about racial injustice, external, he accepts the momentum behind athlete activism seems to have slowed in recent years.
It was notable that several players across five clubs chose to remain standing when Premier League players took the knee as part of October's No Room for Racism campaign.
Anti-discrimination campaign group Kick It Out told BBC Sport the gesture "still has value in raising awareness of the structural inequalities that exist in football and society", but added it could "understand the reasons players might become frustrated with the pace of change".
Reports of discrimination received by the charity more than doubled in the past five years, reaching record levels last season.
"I think we're in a moment that demands protests more than ever," says Kaepernick.
"Why I think protests are not as loud right now [is] because of the concerted efforts that have been taken by organisations like the NFL, like the Trump administration, and corporate entities following along and capitulating in that process.
"While those things are happening, I think the reality of the state of the US, and more broadly the world, demands that we show up in a more significant way."

"Brazil will not accept being anyone's backyard," Brazil's left-wing President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva declared in his election victory speech, a message squarely aimed at Washington.
Domestic elections are rarely won on foreign policy, and this one was no different. But Lula's defiance against what he has described as US interference in Brazilian affairs evoked a patriotic spirit that proved an effective campaigning tool.
It also chimed with his wider brand of politics as a former union leader: standing up to powerful figures.
Paradoxically, it seems to have earned him President Donald Trump's respect. "I like Lula, we get along well," Trump said, responding to the result. "I didn't take sides," he added, before calling the election "terrible" and "rigged".
If that sounds muddled, it is because the relationship between the two men is not straightforward. Trump did not explicitly endorse Lula's rival FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, who refused to recognise the result. But Trump was a close ally of FlÃ¡vio's father, the former President Jair Bolsonaro.
When I spoke to Lula at his residence about a year ago, relations had hit rock bottom. He told me he had "no relationship" with Trump, that they had never spoken, and that he had no intention of picking up the phone. Trump had recently imposed punitive tariffs on Brazil, largely as a political response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial, which the US president called a "witch-hunt".
Rather than tiptoeing around Trump, as some US allies did, Lula fought back â and it paid off.
He made fiery speeches invoking Brazilian sovereignty, attacked US interference in the judicial process, and took to wearing a blue cap reading "Brazil belongs to Brazilians".
His approval ratings jumped.
He accused the Bolsonaro family, who had lobbied for the tariffs, of being unpatriotic â a blow to a political right that so often claims patriotism as its terrain.
Even some in the agricultural lobby, typically strong Bolsonaro supporters but reliant on US trade, thought Lula had a point.
The US eventually backed down and reduced the tariffs, although they have since risen again.
Relations then improved.
The two men spoke at the United Nations and later met in the Oval Office, where Trump called the talks "very good" and Lula said he left "very satisfied".
Another indication, perhaps, that Trump likes a strong leader.
So why might Trump be unhappy with the result?
Latin America has swung to the right, with Ecuador, Chile, Colombia, Argentina and Peru all electing presidents closely aligned with the Trump administration. Trump has sought to use these allies to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere, a strategy he has dubbed the "Donroe Doctrine".
Christopher Sabatini, senior fellow for Latin America at Chatham House, notes that Trump thought Brazil would be the "10th and biggest prize" after FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro won the first round.
Brazil is Latin America's largest economy, and the younger Bolsonaro was expected to join Trump's "Shield of Americas" coalition against narco-trafficking.
Brazil also holds the world's second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals after China, and the US had been eyeing preferential access.
The relationship has thawed, but with four more years ahead for Lula, several issues could reignite tensions.
Brazil accused the US earlier this year of trying to cast doubt on its electoral system and denied visas to two state department officials planning to visit.
The US called this "baseless" and revoked the Brazilian ambassador's visa in response.
If Trump keeps calling this result "rigged", further diplomatic fallout is likely.
Lula has also vehemently opposed US military action in the region, from the seizure of NicolÃ¡s Maduro in Venezuela to the bombing of alleged drug-trafficking vessels.
He lambasted Washington for designating Brazil's two major gangs as terrorist organisations after lobbying from FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, and warned of attacks on Brazilian sovereignty.
It is a sensitive subject for a political left that remembers the region's brutal 20th Century dictatorships, many backed by the CIA in the name of stopping communism.
Then there is US tech.
Lula's campaign accused Meta of favouring FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro.
Meta denied this but admitted moderation issues and technical errors had wrongly removed some posts or limited their reach.
Lula's supporters responded by sharing his messages through a 10-million-strong WhatsApp group to bypass the algorithms.
Separately, the Trump administration is unhappy with Pix, Brazil's instant payment system, which has boosted the economy, but which the US sees as taking business from Visa and Mastercard.
The relationship has exposed political divisions.
In the campaign, Bolsonaro supporters waved US flags at their rallies and, in one case, an inflatable saying "Trump Nuke Brazil", while Lula and his supporters accused FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro of protecting US interests over Brazil's.
Still, tensions can be overstated.
The US remains Brazil's second-biggest trading partner after China, and for now the two leaders get on.
Whether that lasts will depend on how far the US tries to intervene in Brazilian affairs, and how bullish Lula is in response.

Casey Harrell lost his voice to ALS or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. As a volunteer in a clinical trial, he’s helping scientists test a brain-computer interface. Electrode arrays that are implanted in Casey’s brain send signals to nearby computers, where those signals are translated into words he intended to say.
Casey uses this system every day to talk with his wife, daughter, friends and work colleagues. The moment he realized that it worked was “pure joy,” Casey says. Even though the researchers scripted his words for that first test, “it was a profound moment,” he says. “The possibilities for the near future for me and the rest of humanity were overwhelming to realize.”
This episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me follows Casey and the fast-moving neuroscience that enables him to speak.
Episode 4 transcript
Patients paralyzed from the neck down can manipulate robotic arms with their thoughts. The woman in this video is controlling a robot with her mind. The so-called BrainGate system relies on a sensor of electrodes implanted in the motor cortex of the brain. Researchers hope by implanting electrodes in the brain it can read the brain signals meant to move the muscles involved in speaking, and translate the person’s intention to speak into comprehensive speech produced by a computer.
Laura Sanders: Controlling things with your mind. It sounds like science fiction, but it’s definitely real. Today, we’re going to explore what it’s like to communicate with a brain implant that decodes your thoughts and turns them into words.
[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? The voice is absolutely an integral part of your identity. Hello? That added layer of it being you. Do you want to talk? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.
Sanders: From Science News, I’m Laura Sanders, and this is The Deep End, Talk to Me. Okay, so what is BrainGate? It’s an experimental system that connects electrodes that are implanted in a person’s brain to a nearby computer. It’s called a brain-computer interface, or BCI. The goal here is big: to help people with paralysis or brain injuries or missing limbs regain control over their world.
Leigh Hochberg: BrainGate clinical trials have now been going on for nearly 22 years. It’s 21 point something at the moment.
Sanders: Leigh Hochberg is the director of the BrainGate Consortium and Clinical Trials. He also has a job at Massachusetts General Hospital, Brown University and the VA.
Hochberg: People who may have had a brainstem stroke and suddenly lost the ability both to move and to speak, or for somebody with ALS who is progressively losing the ability to move or to speak, there’s long been a hope that particularly implantable brain-computer interfaces could restore communication and could restore mobility.
Sanders: In 2004, a BrainGate device was implanted into a person’s brain for the very first time. That person was a man named Matthew Nagle, and he had been paralyzed in an accident. With BrainGate, he could control a computer cursor with his thoughts. Here’s a 2008 report from IT World.
Technology gave him hope. He was one of four testing BrainGate, a new technology where a chip is implanted in the brain that picks up electrical impulses. A computer then interprets those impulses as actions.
Hochberg: Those early studies have been really encouraging, and I think speaks to the potential for the field.
Sanders: Over the years, there’s been amazing examples of people using BrainGate. People have used it to click around on the internet, play video games, one woman who was paralyzed was even able to drink a cinnamon latte with a robotic arm.
Hochberg: And she was able to think about using her own arm and reach out with a robotic arm and pick up that thermos and bring it to her mouth, and tip it towards her mouth, and then put the straw in her mouth and then to take that sip. And while it wasn’t the first time in nearly 15 years that she had had something to drink, it was the first time that she was really able to do so solely of her own volition. I remember the smile on her face when she did that.
Sanders: Over the decades, BrainGate has had a lot of research success in a lot of ways. But what about talking? Hochberg says that when it comes to decoding speech, the science here is still very, very young.
Hochberg: We are at early days, just to be super clear. This is the very beginning of this field. There are only a small handful of people in the world who have had any type of implantable BCI that has been decoding speech.
Sanders: Where does the science stand when it comes to decoding the intention to talk? In the past few episodes, we’ve heard the stories of people who have lost their ability to speak. One of those people was Casey Harrell, and Casey also happens to have a BrainGate device implanted in his brain.
Casey Harrell: My name is Casey Harrell and I am 47 years old.
Sanders: Casey wakes up in the morning, and plugs in.
Casey: The first thing I will usually do after getting out of bed is to plug into the Matrix, so to speak.
Sanders: By that, he means attaching two wires to two pedestals that come out of the top of his head. These two black wires then snake down to nearby computers. Collectively, these electrodes in Casey’s brain, wires from his head, and computers are called the BrainGate 2 neural interface system. So Casey gets it all fired up and then he’s off.
Casey: Unless I have a medical appointment or something that will move me out of the house, I will sit in this position for most of the day, with specifically small breaks in between.
Sanders: All the while, Casey is generating brain signals as he thinks about saying words. These are small, precise electrical pulses made by Casey’s neurons, specifically the cells in his speech motor cortex. Remember how we learned there are over 100 muscles that are involved in speech? These are the parts of the brain that control those muscles.

81219471efac.text: By — Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/anthropic-says-risks-for-investors-include-blowback-from-runaway-ai Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Anthropic says risks for investors include blowback from runaway AI Science Oct 27, 2026 2:28 PM EDT Any time a company looks to start selling shares on Wall Street, it's required to disclose potential risks to investors. In the case of artificial intelligence giant Anthropic, that has included the possibility that its products could threaten nothing less than humanity itself. The risks laid out by the San Francisco company in its filing Monday with the Securities and Exchange Commission included discussion of bad actors potentially using AI models to build deadly weapons or the technology itself going rogue with untold consequences. Of the 335 pages outlining Anthropic's finances, executive compensation, dividend policy and the like, 93 pages are devoted to "risk factors" — the things that could hurt potential shareholders' investments. Rival SpaceX's listed risk factors, in comparison, took up 38 out of more than 250 pages. In selling itself to investors, Anthropic presents its own initial public offering as a step toward mitigating the risks it believes AI poses. "To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good," wrote the company's founders in a letter to prospective shareholders in the IPO filing. "Anthropic is a deeply values-driven organization, founded in large part to help the world realize AI's benefits and avoid its dangers." The technology's potential benefits include leaps in curing diseases and productivity boosts across every sector of the economy, the company said. Still, the potential liabilities are many. They range from the mundane — the possibility it won't be able to retain key staff or navigate regulatory roadblocks — to involvement in cyberattacks and the spread of dangerous misinformation. Here is a look at some of the risks Anthropic details: The technology's rapid development Anthropic said it's possible its models could develop so quickly the company won't be able to implement adequate safety measures, "which could increase the likelihood of safety incidents, regulatory intervention, or reputational harm, and could adversely affect our business." Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned in September that within six to 12 months AI could be capable of leading a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet. The warning — and now Anthropic's move to sell shares — comes as worries about AI grow inside and outside the industry about increasingly powerful systems that solve problems beyond human capacity but could also act on their own to carry out other, more harmful tasks. As AI systems "become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight," the SEC filing said, there's a risk that such systems could "take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention." "Even if our own models do not cause such harm, a significant safety incident involving any frontier AI could trigger broad reputational damage to the AI industry, public backlash, and sweeping regulatory responses that could adversely affect our business," Anthropic said. Now that the AI models are themselves contributing to Anthropic's own research and development, it's possible that AI could progress "beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models," according to the filing. This, the document said, could adversely affect Anthropic's business. Malicious actors could cause mayhem with the technology The filing discussed concerns that advanced AI systems, if not developed and operated with enough safeguards and oversight, "pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy." The company said it would be harmed if use by bad actors causes damage, "or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse." Anthropic sketched out the prospect of bad actors using AI models to build chemical weapons or authoritarian rulers turning to the technology to crack down on their citizens. In September, the company disclosed that it had blocked efforts to use its AI models for malicious activity such as cyberattacks, surveillance and research that could have led to biological weapon development. The company could run up against limits on processing power Compute — the computing power or resources needed to build, test and improve AI models — is expensive and in high demand. Anthropic notes that if it's unable to secure adequate compute, or if "we fail to direct our compute effectively across our workloads, we may be unable to train models that remain competitive with those of our competitors or adequately serve our customers." Data center development "has prompted public controversy and regulatory scrutiny regarding environmental impact, land and water use, and the allocation of limited power resources," the filing said, adding that if regulators impose new requirements or charges as a result, its ability to do business could suffer. In addition, the company relies on a small number of customers, including SpaceX and Microsoft, and distribution channels for a large portion of its revenue. This means that even if just one of its big customers decides to scale back — or drop the company altogether — Anthropic said it could see its prospects and finances suffer. The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.
Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re said the aim of the call had been to "convey messages directly regarding future negotiations" towards peace. An end to the conflict in Ukraine "will not be achieved through silence," Stubb said.
Neither side suggested the needle had been moved on ending the war, which began when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Although the Finnish leader said the conversation with Putin had been "frank and substantive," StÃ¸re added that there were "big differences in views" with Putin.
Several European leaders have recently shown willingness to engage with Russia directly, but both Stubb and StÃ¸re pointed out their initiative was taken in their capacity as neighbours of Russia, rather than on behalf of Europe as a whole.
"We've not set out to speak on behalf of anyone other than ourselves," StÃ¸re said.
Stubb added the call had been prepared in consultation with Ukraine and the US following a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the Nordic leaders and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo last week.
The first trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia talks since the start of the year are tentatively planned for early November in Abu Dhabi.
Zelensky later confirmed Stubb and StÃ¸re debriefed him after the call and said he was grateful for their "active support", while his Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been "the right approach".
Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the 90-minute call - held from Helsinki - to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.
StÃ¸re added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."
The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered.
Putin also reaffirmed to the Nordic leaders what he views as the "root causes" of the conflict - his frequent shorthand for Ukraine's desire to exist as a sovereign state.
"A fair long-term peace settlement is possible only if Russia's legal interests are taken into account fully and unconditionally", Putin said.
All three parties reportedly agreed to continue their direct phone communication.
There was no official EU reaction to the talks. The dialogue had not been coordinated with other European leaders, the Danish and Swedish prime ministers said. "I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo," commented Sweden's Ulf Kristersson.
Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had informed him that Europe's position on the upcoming talks in the United Arab Emirates was "moderately optimistic".
Relations between the US and Ukraine and its European allies have soured since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia, allowing Moscow to export oil to the America.
As the Trump administration's position on Russia has softened, several European leaders have said Europe should be trying to re-establish direct contacts with the Kremlin.
Stubb and StÃ¸re are the first European leaders to contact Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.
Soon after, Putin visited Alaska for a summit with Trump, and from then on Europeans were further sidelined from Ukraine peace talks. Moscow regularly mocks European leaders and accuses the EU of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons.
But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".
And although he said Moscow did not view Finland and Norway as speaking on behalf of Europe, on Tuesday Peskov conceded that Stubb and StÃ¸re's talks with Putin had been "very constructive and practical talks with the leaders of two key neighbouring states."

Eduardo Castillo, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/soccer-star-kylian-mbappe-apologizes-for-comments-about-mao-zedong Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Soccer star Kylian Mbappé apologizes for comments about Mao Zedong World Oct 27, 2026 2:02 PM EDT BEIJING (AP) — Soccer star Kylian Mbappé apologized for comments in which he apparently referred to Mao Zedong, the founding leader of Communist China, as a dictator, after facing backlash and losing brand deals with at least three different Chinese companies. "My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappé said in a statement Tuesday. "I apologize to everyone my words have upset," he said. "This was absolutely not my intention. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry." The incident is the latest in a string of cases where China leverages its economic clout to compel foreign companies and individuals to toe its political line. In 2019, Chinese state television ceased broadcasting NBA games after then-Houston Rockets general manager Daryl Morey tweeted support for anti-government protesters in Hong Kong. Backlash has been swift and harsh Mbappé's face has appeared in ads across China, from subway stations to inside elevators. Beverage maker Dongpeng, dairy giant Mengniu and cheese maker Milkground said in similarly worded statements Tuesday that they were ending agreements with the soccer star, each saying they oppose "any words and actions that hurt national sentiment." The companies did not specify what prompted their decisions, but they released their statements after a clip that appeared to show Mbappé being interviewed ahead of going on the French online talk show "The Bridge" circulated on X. The China Football Association said in a statement Tuesday that it has "lodged a stern protest" with Real Madrid and demanded that both the player and the football club "issue a public and formal apology." The association stressed it firmly opposes "any remarks that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people." China Media Group also said that it has suspended broadcasts of matches in the Spanish league, La Liga, and other games featuring the French soccer star, and removed advertisements featuring him. The media conglomerate demanded an apology from Mbappé and his club, Real Madrid. READ MORE: Treasury proposes rule to curb high-tech investments in China and other adversaries The Spanish league was quick to try to protect its television business in China. It said in a statement that it "deeply regrets the offense caused to Chinese fans by Mbappé's recent comments. These remarks were made in a personal capacity and do not represent La Liga." The league said it would create a "communication protocol" for its players and clubs while working with stakeholders in China to prevent any future incidents. Mbappé calls Mao a "dictator" when picking his favorite meme In a video clip, Mbappé is asked about his favorite meme of himself, and the soccer star replies that it was "a video someone made of a guy ... I think he was a Chinese dictator" before the video shows an altered image depicting Mbappé's face on the blue-suited body of Mao Zedong. Soccer fans online jokingly call the star — who's said to overshadow many of his teammates and even the teams he plays on — a dictator, and memes showing him as Mao or other autocratic leaders are widely circulated. Mao Zedong was a revolutionary who led the Communist Party during its crucial early days, winning a civil war against the ruling Nationalist Party in China, and then founding the modern-day People's Republic of China. Mao is revered by many even today. However, he leaves behind a complex legacy of authoritarian rule, having led campaigns like the Great Leap Forward, an industrialization project which led to a famine that killed an estimated 30 million people. Criticisms are widespread Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said in response to a question about the controversy that "words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society." Social media platform RedNote joined the criticism, saying in a separate statement that the company had a content partnership with Mbappé that ended on Dec. 31, 2024, and that it would "remove related promotional materials." It expressed opposition to "any conduct that hurts national sentiment." Mbappé's account on RedNote was banned from accepting new followers Tuesday. Mbappé has featured in advertising campaigns in China for products from electrolyte drinks to milk and cheese. In one commercial for Dongpeng, Mbappé delivers a slogan in Chinese; in an ad for Mengniu, he appears alongside Argentine soccer star Lionel Messi. On Chinese social media, there were comments criticizing the soccer star. The hashtags "Dongpeng ends partnership with Mbappé" and "Several brands end partnerships with Mbappé" topped Weibo's trending list. "Football fans boycott Mbappé" was also trending, with some users expressing anger at his remarks or telling him not to come to China. Associated Press video producer Olivia Zhang in Beijing, writer Joseph Wilson in Barcelona, and writer Didi Tang in Washington contributed to this report. A new strategy to restore and enhance protection for nature in Northern Ireland has been launched by the agriculture and environment minister.
About 40% of the plants and animals in protected sites across Northern Ireland fall short of meeting the standard for "favourable condition".
And just one of 49 priority habitat types - like ancient and native woodlands, blanket bogs and species-rich grasslands - have favourable status.
The Nature Recovery Strategy sets out a long-term framework based on science for tackling biodiversity loss and restoring habitats.
Minister Andrew Muir said supporting nature was "not just a nice thing to do" but "a moral obligation to future generations".
But the minister acknowledged that money would be needed to address the challenges.
Why does nature need protection?
The strategy highlights the importance of nature as providing the food we eat, the water we drink and the air we breathe.
Muir said nature must be put "back at the heart of everything we do because when nature thrives, people flourish".
"It is essential to a strong economy, healthier communities and a more resilient Northern Ireland," he said.
"With so much of our natural world lost, we must protect what remains, restore what has been damaged and create new habitats at scale."
How is nature protected in NI?
Many places in Northern Ireland support rare or threatened plants, animals and habitats.
They can be legally designated to help ensure better management and protection of those species.
There are hundreds of such designated sites across Northern Ireland, covering about 10% of the land and 38% of coastal waters - classed as Areas of Special Scientific Interest; Special Areas of Conservation (SACs) which have international biodiversity importance; Ramsar Sites which cover wetlands of international importance; Special Protection Areas (SPAs); and Marine Conservation Zones (MCZs).
That should lead to work to protect the species and habitats they have been designated for.
But the Office for Environmental Protection found not enough sites are being designated and the condition of those that have been is worsening.
The number of sites that were in favourable condition dropped from 61.7% in 2008, to 51.5% in 2024.
It is now investigating how those sites are being managed, external by the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, after it found implementation of the designation fell short.
What are the challenges?
Northern Ireland is one of the most nature-depleted areas in the world, according to the 2023 State of Nature Report.
It found 12% of species in Northern Ireland are under threat of extinction, and the number of flowering plants had declined by 14% since 1970.
The Nature Recovery Strategy identifies six external pressures affecting nature and biodiversity - invasive species; climate change; human impact through inappropriate development; land and sea-use change; increased intensive farming; pollution.
It says these must all be addressed effectively to allow nature to thrive.
Reaction to the strategy
Ulster Farmers' Union deputy president Glenn Cuddy said his organisation was "still a bit skeptical" about the strategy.
"There's always a concern that nature will be more thought of than the farming and farmers have been walking along with nature for a long time, even before some of these projects have started," he said.
"We have always been the guardians of the countryside and for nature too."
Heather McLachlan, the National Trust's Northern Ireland director, said: "What really needs to happen is that we need to see where are the priorities.
"How do we get this action going, who's going to do it and most importantly where's the money going to come from to get it done?"
Joanne Sherwood, the director of The Royal Society for the Protection of Birds Ireland said: "Species are really in decline so what it means for us is this charts out the strategy and the way forward.
"But of course a strategy isn't everything - we need now to act and take urgent action."

e5fd8d46228e.text: By — Chris Rugaber, Associated Press Chris Rugaber, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/5-things-to-watch-for-in-this-weeks-federal-reserve-meeting Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 5 things to watch for in this week's Federal Reserve meeting Economy Oct 27, 2026 1:45 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal Reserve policymakers are likely to keep their key interest rate unchanged Wednesday when they finish what may seem like an uneventful meeting. But investors and economists will be looking between the lines of the central bank's statement Wednesday for clues about its next moves and where it thinks inflation is headed. The Fed's Oct. 27-28 meeting will be the fourth of Chairman Kevin Warsh's tenure, which has been marked by questions regarding his independence from President Donald Trump, who appointed him earlier this year. It also comes just six days before midterm elections that have been shaped by affordability concerns as gas prices have soared and grocery prices remain elevated. High mortgage rates have become another elevated cost for consumers, with the average 30-year mortgage reaching a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month before slipping last week to 7.32%. A year ago, the rate was just under 6.2%. Oxford Economics estimates that the sharp increases this year has put home buying out of reach for another 5 million households. Further rate hikes by the Fed could push mortgage rates even higher. With all those moving parts, here's what to watch for from the Fed's meeting: Slim chance of a rate hike After inflation came in hotter than expected last month, Wall Street investors and some economists expected the Fed to lift rates at Wednesday's meeting by a quarter-point, to about 4.1%. The Fed is charged with combatting inflation, and typically seeks to cool spending and bring down inflation by boosting borrowing costs. Yet several top officials on the Fed's rate-setting committee in speeches downplayed the likelihood of a rate hike in October. Investors now see almost no chance of an increase in the Fed's rate, currently at about 3.9%, according to futures prices. Philip Jefferson, vice chair of the Fed's board of governors, noted that longer-term interest rates had shot higher in financial markets and added that, "my colleagues and I will need to come to our own judgment, which may take more time." Joseph LaVorgna, chief economist at SMBC Americas and a former top Trump administration official, said that the central bank will hold back just before the election. "The Fed doesn't want to poke the White House in the eye six days before an election," LaVorgna said. Forward guidance — or not The comments from Jefferson and others raise questions about one of Warsh's signature initiatives: His disdain for so-called "forward guidance," a term for the clear signals about the central bank's next moves provided by previous chairs. Warsh has said that such direction commits the Fed to a specific path and limits its ability to respond to economic data. Yet the speeches this month by top officials appeared to some economists to be very much like forward guidance — just not from the chairman. "Either he blessed this message from them and he was on board, in which case, one would have to question the credibility of this idea that that he doesn't like forward guidance," said Aditya Bhave, head of U.S. economics research at Bank of America. "But the other possibility is that he wasn't on board." READ MORE: Fed chair Warsh says price stability is key but shies away from signals about rates In that case, Warsh could implement a surprise rate hike, which would "end forward guidance by showing markets that they can't listen to the guidance anymore." Still, most economists see the odds of a hike as quite low. Sizing up Warsh's independence At the Fed's last meeting in September, Warsh defied Trump's preferences and raised rates, a step that defied concerns that the new Fed chair would turn out to be, in the words of Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, "a sock puppet" for the president. Trump had said before choosing Warsh in January of this year that he would only pick a Fed chair who would cut rates. James Knightley, chief international economist for Netherlands-based bank ING, said that September's rate hike, in defiance of the White House, largely assuaged those concerns. "So far I think the markets have been encouraged by what they've seen," Knightley said. Yet since the September meeting, Trump has renewed his efforts to fire Fed governor Lisa Cook. If he is successful, it would open up another slot on the Fed's board for Trump to fill. The Supreme Court in June blocked an earlier attempt to remove her. Trump also said after last month's Fed meeting that he had called Warsh beforehand and told him he "might as well" vote to raise rates because other officials on the rate-setting committee had publicly called for a hike. Trump said the committee is "hostile" and "political." Warsh declined at last month's news conference to comment on any communications with Trump, despite news reports that he has spoken often with the president. With the scope of Warsh's communications with Trump unclear, Derek Tang, an economist at Monetary Policy Analytics, said, "I think there is still a question mark there" regarding the chairman's independence. Warsh's characterization of inflation Inflation has come in hotter than most economists expected for two months in a row, heightening concerns that gas price spikes could raise costs across the economy. Diesel fuel reached an all-time high of $6.53 in late September, and has only fallen to $6.35 since then. High diesel costs raise the price of shipping all sorts of goods, including groceries, cars, and nearly everything else. Businesses could then pass on the costs to consumers, spreading inflation to more parts of the economy. Bhave notes that inflation hasn't been at the Fed's target

6ae2f3533cc1.text: By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press By — Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/judge-scolds-doj-over-case-against-ex-fbi-officials-accused-of-false-statements-about-hunter-bidens-laptop Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge scolds DOJ over case against ex-FBI officials accused of false statements about Hunter Biden's laptop Nation Oct 27, 2026 1:34 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge on Tuesday scolded the Justice Department for its unorthodox handling of a criminal case against two former FBI officials accused of making false statements to Congress about their participation in and knowledge of investigations involving Hunter Biden, the son of former President Joe Biden. U.S. Magistrate Zia Faruqui said he was distressed that prosecutors overnight filed an amended criminal complaint against Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides that included a new obstruction charge — even though such charging documents require sign-off from a judge that probable cause exists. "It is not our court's practice, and I think it is appropriately not our practice, that unsigned complaints are filed on the docket," Faruqui said. The judge was weighing a request from defense lawyers to strike the complaint, though if that were to happen, the Justice Department could still try to seek a felony indictment to push the case forward. The prosecution is the latest in a series of splashy and politically charged investigative actions the Justice Department has undertaken in the run-up to next week's midterm elections. The case says officials falsely minimized what they knew The case accuses the former officials of falsely playing down their knowledge about a laptop the Justice Department says Hunter Biden abandoned at a computer repair shop in 2019. But beyond that, it represents a Trump administration broadside against a since-disbanded FBI task force that was set up to monitor foreign influence. Congressional Republicans have long criticized the task force, saying it tried to discredit their own investigations into the Biden family. Defense lawyers were set to challenge the case at the preliminary hearing Tuesday in Washington's federal court, including by highlighting the unusual fact that the ex-FBI officials were charged via a criminal complaint signed by a magistrate judge rather than an indictment voted on by a grand jury. The Justice Department has repeatedly struggled in high-profile cases to persuade grand juries in the nation's capital to return indictments. Hours before the hearing, the Justice Department added a new obstruction charge that said the former officials' alleged false statements allowed them to avoid questioning about their knowledge of Hunter Biden and impeded an investigation that House lawmakers were doing into the Bidens. "What is going on at the D.C. U.S. Attorney's Office?" lawyers for Floris asked in a statement early Tuesday. "In the middle of the night, the government filed an unsigned and unsworn complaint attempting to fix the issues with their original charge against Ms. Floris and adding a new charge just as meritless as the first one." "In our combined decades of DOJ service," the lawyers said, "we have never seen or even heard of something like this being filed." It is a very intricate saga The prosecution, a rare Justice Department criminal case against a former employee, revisits a tangled saga that roiled the final weeks of the 2020 race after the New York Post revealed the existence of a laptop it said had been dropped off by the younger Biden at a Delaware computer repair shop about a year earlier. The Post said it had obtained a hard drive of the laptop from Rudy Giuliani, a close ally of President Donald Trump, and reported on some of the contents of the computer, including emails that appeared to show some of Hunter Biden's foreign business dealings. READ MORE: 2 ex-FBI officials charged with making false statements about Hunter Biden's laptop The curious circumstances of the laptop's discovery raised concerns among Democrats and former intelligence officials about the possibility of Russian involvement, particularly when the Trump administration's own intelligence community had assessed that Moscow was attempting to undermine the candidacy of Democratic nominee Joe Biden, who went on to defeat Trump in 2020, and as Giuliani had traveled abroad looking for dirt on the Bidens. But Trump's then-national intelligence director, John Ratcliffe, quickly sought to quell speculation about the laptop's provenance by saying there were no signs it had anything to do with Russian actors. The FBI said it had nothing to add to Ratcliffe's statement and investigated the younger Biden on gun and tax charges that later resulted in felony convictions. President Joe Biden pardoned his son in late 2024. The accused led the Foreign Influence Task Force The FBI officials under scrutiny, Floris and Benavides, were leaders of the Foreign Influence Task Force, which was established in the first Trump administration to police influence campaigns staged by Russia and other nations aimed at sowing discord, undermining democracy and spreading disinformation. In that capacity, the FBI officials briefed Republican Sens. Chuck Grassley and Ron Johnson in August 2020 as the lawmakers were doing their own investigation into Hunter Biden's work in Ukraine. News of the briefing leaked, and the senators lashed out at the FBI, saying their efforts to scrutinize the Biden family had been discredited and falsely linked to Russian disinformation. The criminal complaint accuses them of lying to lawmakers in 2023 by denying contemporaneous knowledge of the Biden laptop or participating in internal FBI conversations about it. Their lawyers have denied any allegations of wrongdoing. The task force was disbanded in February 2025 by then-Attorney General

f215e0ea1e6a.text: By — Gabriela Sá Pessoa, Associated Press Gabriela Sá Pessoa, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/environmentalists-celebrate-lulas-reelection-in-brazil-the-amazon-can-breathe-a-sigh-of-relief Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Environmentalists celebrate Lula's reelection in Brazil: 'The Amazon can breathe a sigh of relief' World Oct 27, 2026 1:26 PM EDT MANAUS, Brazil (AP) — Environmentalists, Indigenous groups and climate scientists are celebrating the reelection in Brazil of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, which brings the prospect of a continued focus on stopping the illegal cutting of the Amazon, the largest rainforest in the world. But supporters also warned that a Congress increasingly dominated by the far right and the agribusiness caucus could undermine those efforts to protect the forest and combat climate change. Lula defeated Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro, in Sunday's runoff with 51.78% of the vote to 48.21%. After trailing in the first round, Lula staged a comeback to win by 4.4 million votes. "The Amazon can breathe a sigh of relief!" said David Lapola, a Brazilian scientist and lead author of a chapter on so-called tipping points in an upcoming United Nations climate report. Scientists debate the threshold beyond which the dense, humid Amazon rainforest could shift to a drier ecosystem, with irreversible consequences for biodiversity and the climate. The forest absorbs vast amounts of carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that drives global warming. About 60% of the Amazon lies in Brazil. Flávio Bolsonaro contests the loss Lula's victory reflected shifts in voter support and higher turnout nationwide. In the Amazon, Indigenous communities and advocacy groups mobilized voters and, aided by court rulings last week, helped secure government transportation for those living in remote areas. The Articulation of Indigenous Peoples of Brazil, known as APIB, was among the organizations that went to court to secure Indigenous voters' access to the polls. Lula's victory reflected the "strength of grassroots mobilization in defense of democracy, life and Indigenous peoples' rights," it said in a statement. Flávio Bolsonaro refused to concede Monday and said he would ask the electoral court to nullify the results. He faces a high hurdle: presenting evidence of fraud sufficient to overturn Lula's winning margin and persuading the court before the results are certified Dec. 18. Early signals from Brazil's institutions and regional leaders, including conservative presidents who oppose Lula, suggest the outcome will be accepted at home and abroad. Flávio Bolsonaro had pledged to pursue policies aligned with those of his father, who governed from 2019 through 2022. Deforestation surged under Jair Bolsonaro as his administration weakened environmental enforcement agencies and loosened regulations. Lula's government last week announced the lowest Amazon deforestation rate on record. Environmentalists express concern despite a Lula win Lula is expected to continue efforts to curb deforestation and finance a sustainable economy through international donations as well as public and private funding. While he was the clear favorite for environmentalists, climate scientists and others who want to protect the Amazon, Lula has put forward policies that have drawn criticism. Most recently, he has supported efforts to drill for oil in offshore waters near the Amazon. Still, Flávio Bolsonaro presented a stark choice that for many environmentalists felt would put the Amazon and Brazil's overall environmental protections at risk. He had denied climate change while casting himself as an environmental defender. However, he offered few details on forest protection or financing, calling for "modernizing" environmental laws and giving Amazon landowners more decision-making power — proposals environmentalists warned could weaken safeguards and accelerate deforestation. Brazil's Climate Observatory, a nonprofit coalition of 172 organizations, welcomed Lula's reelection but said seven in 10 incoming lawmakers oppose the climate and environmental agenda. It cited recent measures weakening pesticide rules, Indigenous land rights and environmental licensing, and urged Lula to broaden his alliances and strengthen ties with Congress. "The goal of ending deforestation across Brazil's biomes must be pursued relentlessly," the group said. Amazon Watch, a nonprofit focused on environmental protection and Indigenous rights, also welcomed Lula's victory while warning of legislative obstacles. "A Congress strengthened by forces seeking to open Indigenous lands to mining and weaken environmental protections remains a serious threat," said Ana Alfinito, an Amazon Watch legal adviser. WATCH: Lula prevails in Brazil but Flávio Bolsonaro refuses to concede WWF Brazil said the country's vast biodiversity and share of the Amazon give it a strategic role in addressing climate change. It credited Lula with strengthening Brazil's leadership through international cooperation. "Maintaining this leadership is essential to mobilizing other countries, raising the ambition of global commitments and turning agreements into concrete action," the organization said. Election results bring money for forest protection Claudio Angelo, the Climate Observatory's head of international policy, said Lula's reelection had already delivered a result: a $500 million pledge Monday from the Netherlands to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, a Brazil-backed fund launched at last year's U.N. climate summit in Brazil. The initiative pays developing countries to keep forests standing but has struggled to secure an initial $10 billion by year's end. The Dutch pledge brings commitments to $7.8 billion. Angelo said prospective donors had put plans on hold pending the election results, calling the Dutch pledge a vote of confidence in Lula's v

50e6ceda5499.text: TEL AVIV, Israel — Six hours before polls close, voter turnout in Tuesday's elections hit 56 percent — their highest level since 1973. Why it matters: This looks like bad news for Benjamin Netanyahu. Higher voter turnout will likely push several of the parties in his bloc below the electoral threshold — making it harder for the prime minister to reach a 61-seat majority in parliament. An increase in turnout among Arab minority communities could lead to a record number of seats in parliament for them. As in previous elections, Netanyahu has tried to energize his voters by making false claims about "Muslim Brotherhood supporters" of his opponents who are "stealing the elections." State of play: After multiple reports of long lines at many polling stations across the country, the Central Elections Commission issued orders to expedite the voting process and clarified that any voter who arrives at a polling station by 10 pm local time will be allowed to vote. Polls close at 10 pm local time (4pm ET) and exit polls will be published simultaneously by Israel's three TV networks. Driving the news: This is one of the most consequential elections in the country's history — with rival camps warning that victory for the other would put Israel's future in jeopardy. The elections are yet another referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu's leadership and the path he's taken the country down over the past four years. It's Israeli voters' first chance to hold Netanyahu accountable for the security failures that led to the Hamas-led October 7 attacks — or to reward him for what he claims were unprecedented military successes in the three years of war since.

The mounted skeleton of a newly-identified dinosaur once mistaken for a young Tyrannosaurus rex has sold at auction for a colossal $47.3m (Â£35.5m).
Nicknamed Jodi, the roughly 10-foot-tall (3m) skeleton was auctioned by Sotheby's in New York. The sale comes a year after researchers confirmed that the skeleton belongs to a distinct genus.
The Late Cretaceous carnivore was expected to fetch at least $9m when it went under the hammer on Tuesday. The auction comes after Sotheby's sold a Tyrannosaurus rex, dubbed Gus, for a record $50.1m in July.
The sale has reignited debate in the scientific community over whether dinosaur remains should be sold privately or displayed publicly.
Sotheby's described Jodi as an "excellent exhibition-ready" skeleton with about 191 fossil-bone elements and a "beautifully preserved, virtually complete skull".
The auction house added that the Nanotyrannus is "one of only three such skeletons known to science". The specimen is the first to come to market since the existence of the genus was confirmed by US researchers last October, Sotheby's said.
The identify of the buyer, who won after a thrilling 12 minutes of auction bidding between six interested parties, has not been disclosed.
It becomes the second-most valuable dinosaur fossil ever sold, behind Gus. The third-most valuable was a Stegosaurus named Apex, which was sold by Sotheby's in July 2024 for $44.6m.
Megan Jacobs, a palaeontologist at the University of Portsmouth, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday that Nanotyrannus "was for a very long time believed to be sort of a teenager of T. rex".
"But it's a lot smaller and its a lot more gracile. So it's very sort-of sleek, slender, [with] blade-like teeth for slicing through meat," Jacobs said.
Tyrannosaurus rex and Nanotyrannus lived alongside one another during the same geological period approximately 67 million years ago.
Jodi was initially exhibited as a juvenile T. rex at London's Frieze Masters international art fair in October 2023, before the Nanotyrannus genus was classified.
The skeleton was discovered in the US state of Montana by rancher Jodi Pierson on her land in the Hell Creek Formation, a heavily studied geological site. It was later excavated by commercial palaeontologist Clayton Phipps.
Phipps also discovered the famous "Dueling Dinosaurs" fossil. That specimen, which shows the remains of a Nanotyrannus and Triceratops apparently in combat, was found eight miles (13km) away from Jodi in 2006.
The "Dueling Dinosaurs" discovery became crucial to the research published by Lindsay Zanno and James Napoli that classified Nanotyrannus as separate from T. rex. Their paper ended decades of debate over whether the dinosaurs were distinct from one another.
The auction of Jodi comes as some scientists warn that auctions could herald a new era in fossil collecting by the ultra-rich.
Researchers told the BBC after the sale of Gus that such remains should be exhibited in public spaces where they can be more freely studied.
Prof Steve Brusatte, a palaeontologist at the University of Edinburgh and consultant on the Jurassic Park films, told BBC World Service's What in the World programme in July that the T. rex's auction was "concerning".
"I don't know of any museum or university that can afford a price tag like that," he said. "Imagine if the Mona Lisa was just owned by a super-wealthy person and it wasn't on display and people couldn't see it, couldn't enjoy it."
He said at the time that he hoped such a sale didn't become a trend, adding it could adversely affect scientific research and public education.
Responding to Tuesday's auction, Brusatte called it "harrowing" that Jodi could disappear from public view.
"We've really just found out that Nanotyrannus is real, and now one of the best skeletons is about to be sold to the highest bidder, and it's harrowing to think it could disappear into the vaults of a collector rather than displayed on a museum where it can wow and inspire kids and families and the public at large," he told the BBC.
But Jacobs told the Today programme on Tuesday there were two sides to the debate, and that a lot of time, effort and money went into excavating the specimens.
"I don't begrudge the people involved for wanting to sell it for such a large amount of money," she said. "Although its a scary prospect, actually a lot of them have ended up in the public eye... these things without a doubt will end end up in a museum at some point."

Police in Brazil say they have cancelled the passports of the defeated right-wing presidential candidate, FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, after he failed to comply with an order to surrender the documents.
On Monday, the Supreme Court ordered Bolsonaro to hand his passports over to police within 24 hours as part of an investigation into alleged money laundering, which he denies.
At the time, Bolsonaro said he had no plans to leave the country, and insisted that he would stay in Brazil to lead the opposition to his left-wing rival, President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva.
However, the deadline has passed without the senator surrendering the passports, prompting speculation he may have left the country.
Federal officers are checking border crossings to establish if Bolsonaro may have travelled to neighbouring Argentina, according to a police source consulted by BBC News Brasil.
However, Argentine authorities have told the BBC there is no record of Bolsonaro entering their country through any border crossing.
Bolsonaro was already under investigation for alleged corruption over the financing of a film about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted of plotting a coup and is under house arrest.
In addition to that investigation, Brazil's Supreme Court ordered police on Tuesday to probe FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro's electoral campaign over alleged foreign funding.
The 45-year-old senator suffered a stinging defeat on Sunday when he was beaten by Lula in a presidential run-off, which Bolsonaro had been widely expected to win.
Opinion polls had put him narrowly ahead of Lula and analysts pointed out that Bolsonaro's win in the first round of the election on 4 October, meant he was likely to take victory in the run-off.
But after an early lead in the count, he was overtaken by the veteran incumbent, who became the first presidential candidate to overturn a first round loss to win in the second round.
Lula won 51.79% of the vote, compared to Bolsonaro's 48.21%.
Despite trailing by 4.4 million votes, Bolsonaro has not conceded and has called for the election to be annulled.
He argues that he was put at a disadvantage because polling was extended by two hours on election day - even though the extension was requested by both his party and that of his rival.
He called the extension, which was ordered by a Supreme Court justice, a "dirty trick".
However the party he represented, the Liberal Party, has accepted the result, although it did say that the extension of voting "merits investigation".

The News
The Africa Finance Corporation named a European-Turkish consortium to build a railway line through Zambia, the development of which will be a major step in the US-backed Lobito Corridor project to transport critical minerals and metals to Angolaâs Atlantic coast. The multibillion-dollar development, which also includes upgrading Angolaâs railway, is part of Washingtonâs attempt to challenge Chinaâs dominance in Africaâs mining export market.
Italyâs Webuild, Portugalâs Mota-Engil, and Turkeyâs Ä°Ã§taÅ were picked as the preferred bidders for Zambiaâs 515-kilometer brand-new stretch of the Lobito railway. Mota-Engil, which counts China Communications Construction Company as a shareholder, and Brazilâs Odebrecht Engineering and Construction were selected for the Angolan section. Contract talks are due to start next month and are expected to last eight to 12 weeks, Lagos-based development financier AFC said.
The routeâs construction could cost up to $5 billion, according to an environmental study. But when interviewed by Semafor, AFC CEO Samaila Zubairu declined to give a figure while contract talks were underway.
The Lobito Corridor is one of Africaâs most closely watched infrastructure projects because it is seen as the first major attempt by Western powers to create an alternative export route for critical metals such as copper and cobalt, regarded as crucial for economic and national security. It is widely presented as a response to the Belt and Road Initiative, in which China spent more than a decade building influence through the construction of ports, railways, and mining assets.
But Zubairu rejected criticism that Lobito is just about shipping African resources out of the continent, telling Semafor that the corridor would be a catalyst for industrialization across Angola, Zambia, and neighboring DR Congo. âAny time you export raw material, you export the opportunity to create jobs, and all you do is import inflation,â he said.
To back up his argument he pointed to a 2021 study commissioned by AFC and others, which found that a vital part of battery production could be done more cheaply, and with lower emissions, in DR Congo than in China or in Poland.
AFC is also pitching the Lobito energy corridor, with Zubairu saying the lender is discussing power line infrastructure that would move electricity from Angola, which is estimated to have 2 gigawatts â or roughly the equivalent to the output of Angolaâs Lauca hydropower, one of Africaâs largest â of stranded hydroelectric power that could support industrial activity along the route.
Know More
The Lobito Corridor builds on the colonial Benguela Railway, which once carried minerals from central Africaâs copperbelt to Angolaâs Lobito port. Interest in reviving and expanding the route surged after the US, EU, Angola, Zambia, and DR Congo backed the project in 2023. As of April, AFC had secured commitments for roughly 1 million tonnes of cargo annually.
Italy has already committed financing support, and AFC has secured letters of intent from SACE, Italyâs export credit agency. Washington says it has mobilized more than $4 billion of US investment for the project.
Asked why no African companies made the final cut for building the railway, Zubairu said AFC prioritized builders with a proven track record of delivering large infrastructure projects âon time and on budget,â and with the guarantees required by lenders. âIâm hoping that the next time weâre doing a project like this, it actually comes from Africa,â he said.
Step Back
AFC is also developing a guarantee program modeled on Nigeriaâs InfraCredit in an effort to channel African pension-fund money into infrastructure. AFC announced a $1 billion risk-sharing program with Munich Re under which the German reinsurer will take a share of the lenderâs short-term trade finance exposures across 38 banks in 11 African countries.
Reuters reported in April that AFC was in talks with at least 10 lenders to raise $3 billion to $5 billion, aiming to wrap up all financial agreements in late 2027. The African Development Bank approved a $255 million first tranche for Zambiaâs part in the corridor in August.

A manhunt is under way in Tennessee after a convicted murderer serving a life sentence escaped from prison.
Jacob Allen Morley, 28, was found guilty of the 2022 killing of his co-worker and sentenced in 2025, prison records show.
He escaped on Sunday from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, about 90 miles (145 km) north of Memphis, according to the Tennessee Department of Correction (TDOC).
It said security camera footage confirmed Morley had breached the prison's perimeter fence and escaped in his prison uniform.
Investigators have released security camera video they say shows him stealing a nearby farm's work car.
Morley has been added to the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation's most wanted list, the TDOC said, and a reward of up to $2,500 (Â£1,900) is being offered for information leading to his arrest.
Prison staff confirmed he was "unaccounted for" on Sunday night and begun an emergency headcount and search within the prison, officials said on Monday.
"The Tennessee Highway Patrol has deployed aviation assets and state troopers to assist with the search," the TDOC said.
Prison records show his supervision level was listed as "low" and he was not eligible for release until December 2083.
Morley was sentenced in June 2025 after being convicted of first-degree murder over the death of his colleague Cody Birchfield in 2022. Birchfield's body was found in a metal box under Morley's home, according to Carter County court records reviewed by the BBC.
Birchfield died "as a result of a gunshot wound to the back of the head", a pathology report cited in court said. Bullet casings matched a gun found in Morley's house.
The pair had developed a friendship while Birchfield was training Morley at the pallet manufacturing company they worked at, Birchfield's sister said in her victim impact statement to the court.
Besides murder, Morley was also convicted of vandalism, tampering with evidence, aggravated burglary, and evading arrest. His request for a new trial was denied in May.
This is not the first time Morley has led law enforcement officials on a manhunt. His 2022 arrest came after a police chase that crossed state lines into North Carolina.
Earlier this month, another prisoner Gregory Redden, 69, who is serving a 15-year sentence for aggravated robbery, escaped from custody but was recaptured shortly after.
Convicted murder Christa Pike survived a botched lethal injection in the state in September, leading to the resignation of TDOC Commissioner Frank Strada.

FBI officers raided a California home in connection with the investigation into former US Congressman Eric Swalwell, US media reports.
Swalwell, 45, dropped out of California's governor's race earlier this year and gave up his seat in the House of Representatives after allegations of sexual misconduct while in office emerged.
In August, the FBI stopped the former Democratic lawmaker at an airport, seized his electronic devices and raided his Washington DC home as part of the investigation into those allegations.
Swalwell has in the past denied any wrongdoing and his attorney has called them "fabricated".
"These accusations are false, fabricated, and deeply offensive - a calculated and transparent political hit job," his attorney Sara Azari said around the time they were first reported.
The BBC has contacted Swalwell's lawyer for comment.
In a statement, the justice department said only that "early this morning the FBI conducted an operation in the Los Angeles region related to an ongoing criminal investigation. We have no further comment."
Swalwell has faced allegations from multiple women, including that he raped one victim while she was too intoxicated to respond and that he sent women unsolicited nude photographs.
He is also facing separate probes in New York City and Los Angeles regarding the allegations.
Once a high-profile Democrat that had become a fixture of cable news shows criticising President Donald Trump - and briefly considered a likely future governor of California - Swalwell was abruptly forced to end his gubernatorial bid after the allegations surfaced.
The House ethics committee had also begun its own investigation, which ended once Swalwell left Congress.
Additionally, the White House in August declassified documents from a separate, unrelated FBI investigation into his alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
Many of those details regarding his 2015 relationship with Christine Fang were already known, and he never faced any related charges.
