ac7df6c28a05.text: Senate leaders could be guessing who will control the chamber well into November, thanks to a slew of tight races and state-specific voting rules. Why it matters: A GOP majority would ease the pressure on Senate Majority Leader John Thune to move quickly on nominations, while a Democratic majority would give Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer more leverage in the lame-duck session. If the chamber splits 50/50, leaders will have to start negotiating their power-sharing agreement. Zoom in: Four states could leave the majority in limbo. Alaska: Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) is trying to fend off former Rep. Mary Peltola (D). Alaska election results have taken weeks to finalize because of the vast state's transportation challenges, mail ballots and ranked-choice tabulation. The Trump Justice Department is preemptively trying to block results from being finalized if Sullivan narrowly loses. Maine's ranked-choice voting could lengthen the vote tallying if neither Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) nor Democratic nominee Troy Jackson gets more than 50% in the first round. Kansas' three-day grace period for mail-in ballots could delay results in the race between Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton and Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.). It is far closer than expected. In Texas, a dragged-out recount could be coming. A candidate can request one if the margin is less than 10% of the winner's vote total — which is likely to happen between state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) and state Rep. James Talarico (D). The candidate who requests it has to pay. The clock: Congress currently plans to leave for the holidays on Dec. 18. But if Republicans lose both the House and Senate , Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) wants senators to stay in town through the holidays (yes, Thanksgiving and Christmas) to work on a massive GOP reconciliation package they can pass without Democratic support. The big picture: Congress has a long to-do list either way, including funding the government past Dec. 11, passing emergency defense spending and potentially raising the debt ceiling. It needs to pass the National Defense Authorization Act, Farm Bill and permitting reform, reauthorize the warrantless wiretap authority under FISA Section 702 and confirm nominations before they expire at the end of the year. The bottom line: "I'm guessing that's a possibility this year," Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.) told reporters today about working in D.C. through the holiday recess.

fc3ee73e15dd.text: Israelis turned out in record numbers for their first election since the Oct. 7 attacks and the war in Gaza. Projections show opposition parties won more seats than the coalition led by Prime Minister Netanyahu, potentially setting the stage for a change in government. But Netanyahu’s opponents do not have enough seats to form a majority, leading to weeks of negotiations. Nick Schifrin reports. Geoff Bennett: Israelis turned out in record numbers for their first election since the October 7 terrorist attacks that launched the war in Gaza. Amna Nawaz: And, according to projections, opposition parties have won more seats in Parliament than the coalition led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, potentially setting the stage for a change in government. Nick Schifrin is live for us in Tel Aviv tonight -- Nick. Nick Schifrin: Amna, this is the headquarters for Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition coalition. His party and his supporters are emphasizing that they, along with the Arab parties, won many more seats than Netanyahu's coalition. And Netanyahu's coalition lost many seats. But, Amna, the bottom line is that this coalition does not appear to have a path toward forming a majority government after what many Israelis call one of the country's most consequential elections. Tonight in Tel Aviv, the party that wants to unseat Israel's longest-serving prime minister says they have a mandate to change the country. But 40 miles up the road in Jerusalem, Netanyahu's party is saying it won the most votes and there's no path to an opposition government. There are 120 seats in the Israeli Parliament, which means a coalition needs 61 to form a majority government. Netanyahu's coalition is estimated to have won 50 seats. Eisenkot's coalition is estimated to have won more, 53, but not enough to secure a majority. Arab parties, who are anti-Netanyahu, have an estimated record 17, but it's unlikely that Eisenkot's coalition allies will agree to work with them. We have been traveling through the country in the lead-up to the election, and there is a widespread perception that this moment is historically fractious and the election existential. Jonathan Barsade: Doesn't matter what side of the political spectrum you're on. Israel is at a crossroads. Nick Schifrin: Jonathan Barsade is a dual American-Israeli citizen and the president of the nonpartisan America-Israel Democracy Coalition. Jonathan Barsade: These elections are going to determine what direction Israel is going to go and how Israel is going to look for the next 40, 50 years. That's a sentiment everyone -- they feel it. Nick Schifrin: He's helped lead the largest ever effort to bring Israeli expats back to the country to vote since Israel has no mail-in voting. Some 70,000 have returned. Including Ruth Mekel, who's wise enough not to give her age. She flew here from New York to vote against Netanyahu. Ruthie Mekel, Israeli Voter: These are really critical, critical elections, historic elections, in order to prevent this government from ending the democracy and starting an orthodox religious way of life. Nick Schifrin: A few miles to the south, voting's a family affair for 3-year-old Michael... Avshalom Seri, Rishon LeZion, Israel, Resident: He's a good citizen. Nick Schifrin: ... who helped his grandfather also vote against Netanyahu; 75-year-old Avshalom Seri says new leadership could bring peace. Avshalom Seri: I hope that we will come with different leaders, leaders that -- thinking for peace. We have children. We have grandchildren, and we think about them, the new generation. We fight so much. That's enough. The time for peace. Nick Schifrin: But Netanyahu and his supporters believe Israel's peace comes from his strength. Woman: This is the work of a genius. Nick Schifrin: And like a chess player, they argue only he has the strategy to take on Israel's enemies, and only he has the relationship with President Trump to finish the job in Iran. Maor Vaknin, Likud Adviser (through interpreter): With the help of God, in the next four years, Bibi will continue to do more things with Trump in the two years that Trump has left. We will solve this problem, which is called Hamas, Hezbollah, Lebanon, Syria, Iran, and then we succeed in cutting off the head of the snake, as Bibi promised. Nick Schifrin: Forty-four-old Shimi Elias also brought his son Omri to vote. He usually votes for Netanyahu, but this year voted for Netanyahu ally, right-wing Minister of Finance Bezalel Smotrich. Shimi Elias, Israeli Voter: The government since the war, I'm happy with what they achieved. Nick Schifrin: Tonight, those divides remain, and a country hoping for a decisive decision once again faces uncertainty. Amna Nawaz: And Nick is back with us now from Tel Aviv. So, Nick, without either side winning a majority here, what happens now, and specifically what does that mean for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu? Nick Schifrin: So, as you know, Amna, there will be a lot of horse-trading over the next few days and the next few weeks and perhaps even the next few months. Perhaps the most likely outcome from the Eisenkot campaign, or at least the best outcome from them, would be what's known as a minority government. They would form a government with fewer than 61 seats. But, as we laid out in the piece, that would require collaborating with the Arab parties. And inside of Eisenkot's coalition, that's already been rejected. Now, of course, in Israeli politics, a lot of things can be said before the election, and that changes after the election, but right now there's not a lot of popularity or support for the idea of getting Arab support to create that government. Now, President Trump and his aides would like to see some kind of unity government, Netanyahu and Eisenkot working together. Eisenkot and every single one of the leading opposition party, the leading -- the leaders of the opposition parties, have absolutely refused that scenario. So if there is no minority gove

85f1976054cd.text: White evangelical Christians have been among President Trump’s most loyal supporters for more than a decade, and our new PBS News/NPR/Marist poll shows that most still approve of him. But signs of slippage are emerging ahead of the midterms. Stephanie Sy reports on the overlap of politics and faith. Geoff Bennett: White evangelical Christians have been among President Trump's most loyal supporters for more than a decade now. And while our new PBS News/NPR/Marist poll shows that most still approve of the president, there are signs that support may be slipping as the midterms approach. Here's Stephanie Sy. Stephanie Sy: On a Wednesday night at Village Church in Blythewood, South Carolina, Pastor Erik Estep is preaching from his pre-midterm election sermon, the Bible and politics. Pastor Erik Estep, Village Church: I believe the church is the bulwark of truth for our nation. And it will take people like you and churches like this church to protect this nation spiritually and morally. Stephanie Sy: White evangelical Christians have been the bedrock of Donald Trump's support for more than a decade, and they largely still are. In the latest PBS News/NPR/Marist poll, 66 percent say they approve of the job Trump is doing as president, 26 points higher than the number of Americans overall who say the same. As Trump rallies his base ahead of the midterm elections, nearly three-quarters of white evangelicals also plan to back Republicans for Congress. For Trump, it's a bond that once seemed unlikely. In 2016, candidate Trump rocketed to the top of the Republican primary, a thrice-married New York real estate mogul caught on tape bragging about groping women and accused of relationships with more than one porn star. President Donald Trump: I stand before you today to fulfill one of my highest and most important duties under the United States Constitution, the nomination of a Supreme Court justice. Stephanie Sy: But, as president, he accomplished what has long driven many Christians at the polls, his appointment of three conservative Supreme Court justices, which led to the historic overturning of Roe v. Wade and a rollback of abortion protections for millions of American women. Estep acknowledges his congregants don't all vote alike, but making abortion illegal is one issue where they are mostly aligned. Pastor Erik Estep: To vote according to what our faith prescribes us to vote. Some people have different perspectives, but there's not much of a different perspective when it comes to issues of abortion and life. I think the Bible's pretty clear. Stephanie Sy: But even among evangelicals, Trump's support has slipped, reflecting an overall fraying of his coalition. His approval rating among those that voted for him has dropped 12 points since the start of his second term. That falloff is particularly steep among Latinos and young voters in other recent polling. Even at Village Church in South Carolina, some are wavering. Cynthia Carroll, South Carolina Voter: I was a Republican. I voted Donald Trump into -- as president. And now I'm more on the fence between conservative and a Democrat. Stephanie Sy: Until recently, that loyalty had survived some striking moments, like when conservative Charlie Kirk was assassinated last year and his widow, Erika, chose to forgive his killer. Erika Kirk, CEO, Turning Point USA: I forgive him because it was what Christ did and is what Charlie would do. Stephanie Sy: President Trump took a different stance. President Donald Trump: That's where I disagreed with Charlie. I hate my opponent. Stephanie Sy: And this spring, the president posted an AI image of himself appearing as a Christ-like healer. President Donald Trump: I did post it. Stephanie Sy: After Christian leaders labeled it blasphemous, Trump deleted it, explaining he thought the image portrayed him as a doctor, which he also is not. Robert Jones, CEO, Public Religion Research Institute: I think part of it is really about a vision of the country that he has promised them. Stephanie Sy: Robert Jones, president of the Public Religion Research Institute, says the evangelical support Trump does still enjoy is rooted in a certain vision of America. Robert Jones: The message is, we're a white Christian country. We're losing that identity. But if you stick with me, I'm going to make sure that we keep that identity. Stephanie Sy: But voters who identify as Christian may have more options this election. Christian faith leaders are running for the Senate as Democrats in Kansas and Texas. In reliably red South Carolina, where the Senate race is unusually tight. Republicans are trying to energize evangelical support for Darline Graham by focusing on transgender issues. President Donald Trump: The Democrat who Darline is running to defeat is a far left political hack who supports transgender for everybody and believes in telling confused children they're trapped in the wrong body. Stephanie Sy: During a recent campaign rally in the state, Trump painted Democrats as enemies of conservative values. Robert Jones: So when you have, like, that willingness to like literally demonize your political opponents, and then you have got a group that has been attached to you by party and religion, it sets up a kind of toxic environment. Stephanie Sy: For his part, Pastor Erik Estep does not endorse specific candidates or a party in his sermon. Pastor Erik Estep: We think that it falls on pastors. If you want people to respond and to get out and to be to be heard, well, there has to be some sort of motivation. Stephanie Sy: What motivates his congregants this year may well be critical on Election Day. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Stephanie Sy.

887a84ce72f8.text: Indonesia is battling its worst wildfires in more than a decade, made worse by El Niño. Many were deliberately set to clear land for farming, including palm oil plantations. More than 12,000 schools across Indonesia have closed because of the toxic haze. Nathaniel Undas, a school principal and photographer, has been documenting the fires on social media. Amna Nawaz: Indonesia is battling its worst wildfires in more than a decade, made worse by El Nino weather patterns. Many of these fires were deliberately set to clear land for farming, including palm oil plantations. Rain this week brought some relief, but the rainy season isn't expected until next month. More than 12,000 schools across Indonesia have closed because of the toxic haze, which has also spread to neighboring countries. In Central Kalimantan, where children have been out of class for weeks, one school principal and photographer has been documenting the fires on social media. He spoke to us from an empty classroom at the Golden Christian Middle School. Natanael Undas, Photographer: My name is Natanael Undas. I'm a school principal Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan. It is a kind of rain forest and then a lot of native trees. We got a lot of fruits. We got a lot of tree for timber. But now the sky, it turns yellow. It turns like hell. The last time I saw the blue sky was in August '20. The haze come to our city. And then the fire goes closer, closer, closer and closer. And then, like the last week, it was a really huge fire in the city. I'm really sad, because my student lost a lot of school hour and learning experience. If you go outside in a school hour, probably at 8:00, 9:00 a.m. in the morning, they go outside, they play with other friends without a mask and thinking it's just like a school holiday in the middle of yellow sky. This fire is not natural disaster at all. It is manmade disaster. We're hoping the rain will come soon. Last night, there was a huge rain, even only for 17 to 25 minutes. We're longing to inhale the smell of rain, the smell of air, the smell of wet leaves, the smell of wet land. Last night, when it was raining, I open a little bit of my door, and I try to smell the rain. It's like a smelling the perfume that's mixed with smoke. It's still poisoned, so I need to close it. Not many people knows about what really happening right now, what we are experiencing, especially what we are inhaling. A lot of children are suffering because of respiratory issue. I don't want my daughter having the same experience. I don't want to lose this generation. We still can save this.

5060f9921bf8.text: This year, the 26th president's legacy received a remarkable new tribute: the opening of the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in the Badlands of North Dakota, a landscape that helped shape his lifelong commitment to conservation. Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown recently paid a visit for our arts and culture series, CANVAS. Geoff Bennett: Finally tonight, a birthday salute to Theodore Roosevelt. The nation's 26th president one of its most consequential was born on this day back in 1858. And, this year, his legacy received a remarkable new tribute, the opening of the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in the Badlands of North Dakota, a landscape that helped shape his lifelong commitment to conservation. Our senior arts correspondent, Jeffrey Brown, paid a visit for our arts and culture series, Canvas. Jeffrey Brown: It's a spectacular setting nestled in the rugged Badlands of Western North Dakota, a breathtaking tribute to the life and legacy of Theodore Roosevelt. It's a landscape that deeply impacted T.R., who once said he'd never have become president if not for his time here. And it continues to inspire and move people today. Craig Dykers: We wanted it to feel that it belonged, so that it didn't feel that it just dropped out of the sky. Jeffrey Brown: Yes. Craig Dykers: At the same time, we wanted it to feel fresh and new and different from anything anybody had seen before. Jeffrey Brown: Craig Dykers, co-founder of the international architecture firm Snohetta, helped design the new 93,000-square-foot Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library. Craig Dykers: There's a sensation of what the landscape means that you learn when you move through it. Jeffrey Brown: After settling on this remote location, Dykers camped alone for 12 days in the Badlands searching for inspiration. Craig Dykers: In the wilderness here, the more you go into it, the more you're able to experience what he called lonesome freedom, or lonely freedom. And that's an interesting idea, that you're alone, but you feel free. Normally, we think of being alone as a scary thing, especially in a place that's wild. Jeffrey Brown: Beautiful, but potentially very scary out there, right, if you're alone. Craig Dykers: Yes, if you're alone, but, at a certain point, you and the context around you become one. Jeffrey Brown: The son of wealthy and prominent New Yorkers, Teddy Roosevelt first came to the small town of Medora to hunt bison in 1883. He returned the following year as a heartbroken 25-year-old after writing in his diary: "The light has gone out of my life." Edward O'Keefe: The Women Who Created a President": Theodore Roosevelt came to North Dakota at a time of incredible stress and distress in his life. He had lost his wife and his mother on the same day of different causes in the same house. He healed and he recovered in the Badlands of North Dakota. Jeffrey Brown: Edward O'Keefe is the CEO of the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library Foundation, a nonprofit that raised more than $500 million to complete the project. O'Keefe, author of a biography of T.R. and who now leads public broadcasting's WNET Group in New York City, says Roosevelt's time in North Dakota would shape the rest of his life. Edward O'Keefe: He found resilience in nature. He mourned, and he was depressed when he was in Dakota. And he finally got to live that life that he'd only read about in books. Theodore Roosevelt felt that North Dakota saved his life. Jeffrey Brown: So far, large crowds have poured in since the library opened July 4, offering visitors a chance to learn about a president who left an indelible, if complicated, impression on American life. A champion of conservation and protector of public lands, Roosevelt was also a champion of military might and expansion abroad. Edward O'Keefe: Theodore Roosevelt is like a Rorschach test. What you see in him says more about you than it does about him. Republicans, Democrats, independents, everyone loves T.R., right? That's the beauty of Theodore Roosevelt. He brings people together. Jeffrey Brown: And while it's a presidential library in name only, Roosevelt's personal papers are mostly scattered elsewhere, some of his most famous speeches light up the walls, and visitors can see photos and artifacts from every part of his life, from his student days at Harvard, to a hat and single-action Colt revolver from his time as a New York City police commissioner. Edward O'Keefe: Theodore Roosevelt later said, it's better to wear out than to rust out. And he did it every day of his life. He lived only to 60 years old, and those were very, very packed 60 years. Jeffrey Brown: Other highlights include his custom-tailored Rough Rider uniform worn during the Spanish-American war. AI ACTOR: I wanted every guest to feel the worth of their talents. Jeffrey Brown: And there's even an AI hologram of Roosevelt designed by Microsoft that takes questions. Mr. President, what do you hope people visiting your library take away from it? AI ACTOR: I hope visitors leave knowing a single thing. We have power to protect wild places just as I did. Edward O'Keefe: Theodore Roosevelt wrote a letter in 1918, a year before he died. He said: "If I could keep one memory of my entire life, it would be my experiences as a rancher and a cowboy in Dakota." Jeffrey Brown: Using heavy timber, rammed earth walls, and Many materials native to the region, Dyker says the library was designed to give visitors a chance to reflect, all while taking in the surrounding natural beauty, from a walkable roof above, to rocking chairs below. Craig Dykers: If you look at the shape, it has a shape that's characteristic of the low-lying Badlands in the distance. It's not the same, but it has the feeling of something you might find out here. Narrator: Here we have a group of beings who are not able to protect themselves. Jeffrey Brown: The library also uses educational videos like this one to address some of Roosevelt's troubling legacies

What we know about Ukraine-Russia truce in Oleshky, brokered by Melania Trump
Fighting in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has stopped after a truce, which the White House said was secured by US First Lady.
The truce is meant to allow aid deliveries and a civilian evacuation on Friday.
But residents have told the BBC they were weary of the ceasefire as the evacuation routes could potentially take them through Crimea and Russia.
BBC's Ukraine correspondent, Dan Johnson, has more details.

4f7b97b509b5.text: Some Democrats are making a play for segments of the "Make America Healthy Again" base, hoping pitches about food safety and environmental health will attract voters disillusioned with the Trump administration's lack of progress on those fronts. Why it matters: Policies around cleaning up the food supply and agricultural practices helped forge a coalition that's credited with helping President Trump win a second term. But disagreements over issues like pesticide use are fueling speculation that MAHA voters may not show up in force to help Republicans in the midterm elections — and may be persuaded to put their faith in Democrats instead. Driving the news: Some Democrats say they're the party better positioned to take on established interests through regulation and are honing messaging with an eye toward the 2028 presidential race. The Center for American Progress, an influential progressive think tank, recently released a proposal focused on healthier foods and reducing harmful chemicals alongside polling showing Democrats are poised to claim the agenda as their own. "I do think the MAHA grassroots movement has raised the salience of some issues where Democrats have an opportunity to align, particularly on chemicals and pesticides," said Topher Spiro, an author of the CAP report. "I think that these are issues that have been percolating for a long time, and that, frankly, Democrats haven't done a great job of prioritizing." "If you're looking at who are the swing voters in this electoral environment, they overlap very highly with voters who care about these issues," added Becca Siegel, chief insights officer at CAP. Though affordability concerns have dominated the midterm elections, some Democratic lawmakers and candidates have already backed legislation or policy agendas that overlap with MAHA themes. Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed last month released a proposal titled "Building a Healthier America" that included calls for banning certain pesticides — a key unrealized MAHA goal — and healthier school meals. House Democrats' health care working group included a section in its policy agenda called "Reclaiming MAHA and Protecting American Families." Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) — a potential 2028 presidential candidate — has publicly supported some food policies advanced by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and pushed legislation increasing the liability of companies for potential harm from pesticides. By the numbers: CAP's polling found that 37% of Trump voters are open to voting for a Democratic candidate running on a platform that addresses core MAHA issues, and that Democrats are more trusted than Republicans on health, food and environmental issues. Nonpartisan polling from the Annenberg Public Policy Center found that much higher percentages of the public support MAHA-aligned policies than identify as MAHA supporters. 80% of respondents said they support labeling ultra-processed foods, 79% support removing ultra-processed foods from school lunches and 76% support removing artificial dyes from food. That's even though only a quarter said they are MAHA supporters. Yes, but: One prominent MAHA faction is built around medical freedom and questioning the safety of certain vaccines — a nonstarter for many Democrats who've been sharply critical of Kennedy's health policies. But the Annenberg polling found that MAHA vaccine priorities are much less popular than its food agenda, and that even among the faithful, some vaccine agenda items barely have majority support. State of play: The latest blow to the MAHA coalition came last week, when Trump health adviser and MAHA advocate Calley Means resigned from his post, reportedly over the slow pace of food-related policy changes. Means insisted on X that there's been unprecedented policy and cultural change since the start of the second Trump administration and that the "movement is just getting started." But other MAHA leaders have publicly shared their frustration. "To be clear, [Kennedy] is a hero but his commitments to our movement are being stalled by corporate capture and special interests at the very top of the White House," Vani Hari, an influencer also known as Food Babe, posted on X . "The progress he is trying to make is getting killed by the corporations poisoning us," she added. What they're saying: "The Trump administration has already secured extensive victories for the MAHA Agenda, including overhauling the dietary guidelines for Americans, axing artificial ingredients in our food supply and investing in regenerative farming," said White House spokesperson Allison Schuster. "The MAHA coalition has never been stronger or more empowered, and President Trump and Secretary Kennedy will continue to take decisive action to deliver more wins for the American people," Schuster added. "Secretary Kennedy is driving a historic overhaul of federal food and health policy under President Trump's MAHA agenda: strengthening oversight of food ingredients, advancing the first federal definition of ultra-processed foods, and making chronic disease prevention a department-wide priority," said HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard, adding that Democratic lawmakers have "repeatedly opposed or challenged key elements of this agenda." What we're watching: Whatever the outcome of next week's elections, these issues likely aren't going away. Alignment on healthy food policy and pesticides could spark interesting bipartisan collaborations in a split Congress next year. But the run-up to the presidential election could also feature a fight over who would best champion these issues on the left.

fc6b8b4a67d4.text:
Alexisâs view
The longstanding debate over whether African nations should view gas as a âtransition fuelâ in the shift to renewable energy has gone quiet. Western institutions in recent years refused to invest in gas infrastructure, arguing countries would be locked into fossil fuel dependence. Many African policymakers responded that advanced economies built their wealth on coal and oil, adding that Africa accounts for less than 4% of global carbon emissions. But the energy shock caused by the Iran war has silenced the debate.
Put simply, the world needs gas to generate electricity and power heavy industry. The Gulfâs state-owned companies are looking for stakes in gas projects after being targeted in strikes, said Andrew Farrand, director of Middle East and North Africa at consultancy Horizon Engage. âWeâre now in a world where producers have to diversify,â he said. Efforts by European nations to reduce their dependence on Russian gas were already underway. And the Trump administration has pushed the World Bank to end its prohibition on financing upstream gas projects.
Nigeria, which has the worldâs ninth-largest proven reserves of natural gas, stands out as a major beneficiary. Rising demand for its liquefied natural gas has been accompanied by a flurry of investment announcements, including for discoveries that lay moribund for decades.
Timi Soleye, president of Lagos-headquartered energy company CRYO Gas & Power, said he has fielded a sudden wave of inquiries from investors in recent months because the risk calculus for large gas projects in Nigeria had âchanged substantially.â The Gulf of Guinea, which carries gas from Nigeria and Equatorial Guinea, has no choke points, so blockading it would take âa full navy,â Soleye said.
A new debate is taking shape. Policymakers in countries with sizable gas reserves â such as Mozambique, Senegal, and Tanzania â will have to balance the benefits of exporting gas against retaining some for electricity generation. Both approaches require costly infrastructure, but while exports could quickly fill government coffers, using gas to fuel industrialization has the potential to deliver a larger long-term payoff.
Notable
- Tanzania made its first major natural gas discovery in more than a decade, its energy minister said, as the country advances plans for a $42 billion LNG project, one of East Africaâs largest proposed energy developments.

de3775aca318.text: Some of the biggest vulnerabilities in election security are lying in plain sight. Why it matters: There's no credible evidence that voting-system vulnerabilities have been exploited to change election results. But researchers have found isolated flaws that threaten ballot secrecy, accurate vote recording and independent verification of results. The big picture: Voter-marked paper ballots and rigorous audits are the gold standard for trustworthy elections, election-security researchers and activists tell Axios. Researchers have challenged unfounded claims that elections were stolen through hacking while also warning against dismissing real vulnerabilities in voting systems. "A vulnerability is not an exploit," Philip Stark, a retired UC Berkeley statistics professor who developed an audit protocol for checking paper ballots, said at a recent conference. "You can leave a key under your doormat, and that doesn't mean someone takes the key and opens your door." Zoom in: Election security experts interviewed by Axios found these vulnerabilities in parts of the U.S.: 1. Paperless voting: Louisiana is the last remaining state to use paperless voting machines statewide on Election Day. Voters press buttons to select their candidates, and the machines record their votes electronically without producing a paper ballot. That leaves no independent record to check whether votes were counted correctly. Most other states retired the machines after researchers exposed their vulnerabilities to hacking and the inability to independently audit their results. Election security expert and computer scientist J. Alex Halderman, of the University of Michigan, called Louisiana "the dinosaur of American elections." Louisiana's secretary of state's office declined an interview request, but in a press release said the state is expected to award a new election equipment contract at the end of the year. 2. Ballot-marking devices (BMDs) let voters select candidates on a touchscreen before printing a paper ballot. Researchers warn the machines are vulnerable to hacking and errors, and studies show voters often fail to catch mistakes on the printout. A demonstration at the hacktivist conference Def Con in 2025 showed how a machine from Georgia — which an Auburn professor got through court-sanctioned access — could be manipulated by altering what the voter sees and the choices they mark or by changing the vote tally. "That's the kind of thing that our chief information officer and his team does track," said Blake Evans, executive director for Georgia's secretary of state office, when asked broadly about vulnerabilities exposed at Def Con. "[W]e do have the physical security with the fields and the counties that store their equipment securely in secure places." Roughly 23% of U.S. registered voters live in jurisdictions that exclusively use BMDs for in-person voting, according to the nonprofit Verified Voting . BMDs are an essential accessibility tool for voters who can't mark a paper ballot on their own, but security researchers favor offering them alongside hand-marked paper ballots. 3. A software flaw in Georgia's vote-counting system could be used to expose how individual voters cast their ballots, according to research from Princeton University. Researcher Max Springer used public voter records and roughly $20 in AI credits to reconstruct the order in which nearly all in-person ballots were cast in the Georgia counties he studied. With an additional public record, Springer was able to match individual voters to their ballots, as he demonstrated with two counties and 2,200 votes in his study. He wrote that the method could be applied to other counties. Researchers first exposed the bug in 2022 , and Dominion Voting Systems (now Liberty Vote) released a patch the following year. At the time, about 21 states were using the software. There's no centralized database that tracks when these software updates are implemented around the country. The Georgia secretary of state's office said "there haven't been any significant software updates since 2019." State of play: Georgia's secretary of state's office said it has shared guidance with counties to address the ballot secrecy issue, and it plans to limit the exposure by not making all of its election data public in November. Liberty Vote declined to comment. In a post on its website, the company says every "Liberty Vote system is tested, certified, and verified to meet the highest standards of election security and reliability in accordance with all applicable state and federal requirements." The bottom line: Stark says voters should be aware of two things that can be simultaneously true: "The systems are garbage from a software and cybersecurity point of view. There's lots of ways that they can fail." "And there is no direct evidence that anything has happened on a large scale that changed the outcome of say the presidential election or federal election."

11c337564821.text: The cybersecurity world braced for catastrophe after AI uncovered critical flaws in the web's foundational code , but the anticipated wave of automated attacks has surprisingly struggled to get off the ground. Why it matters: Millions of hacking attempts have so far yielded few successful attacks, an apparent lucky break due to the degree of difficulty of building attacks on the bugs. The defense work at many companies to address the issue also appears to have helped. The last week has unfolded in ways that remind some researchers of the Y2K phenomenon, a software problem in 1999 where warnings of armageddon helped rally companies to engineer a solution in time. Driving the news: Security researchers say the PHP vulnerabilities that prompted widespread panic last week have proven unusually difficult to exploit, despite a flood of attempts to develop working attack code. Yet the difficulty of exploiting PHP shouldn't be mistaken for evidence that AI-powered hacking isn't a serious threat, Samantha Lewis, head of threat intelligence at Armadin, told Axios. "We don't have to wait another two years before this happens (again)," she said. "It could be three hours from now that the next one of these launches." Between the lines : The sheer volume of AI-discovered bugs means the next era of cybersecurity will be defined by resilience—how quickly a company can detect an intruder, contain the damage, and recover. "This is the worst outlook I've ever had, and it also is the most interesting thing I've ever seen in my life," ExtraHop CEO Greg Clark told Axios. "This stuff actually works, it's going to change everything." Rubrik CEO Bipul Sinha warned that the world is in an "era of cyber tsunami," noting that "it will wash over everybody, nobody will be 100% safe." Zoom in: The shift to building resilience doesn't require throwing out the security playbook. Instead, companies should double down on basic cyber principles, such as using multi-factor authentication, Justin Timothy, threat intelligence consultant at GuidePoint Security, told Axios. Rubrik's Sinha also recommended that organizations start preparing by identifying the most critical services that they need to keep up and running and develop a plan to restore those first after an attack. ExtraHop's Clark suggested companies should get their own AI tools up to speed on what's precious in their systems and how best to protect them at machine speed. Samantha Lewis, head of threat intelligence at Armadin, told Axios that companies should proactively test their own systems for exploitable weaknesses so they're not caught flat-footed when the next major vulnerability disclosure arrives. Catch up quick: Experts have dubbed this month " Black October " after a chaotic week of AI-discovered software flaws and attacks on the platforms powering the AI boom. OpenAI's agents discovered critical flaws in PHP , software used by roughly 70% of websites, and Brotli , a widely used data compression library. Breaches at AI coding agent OpenCode , developer platform Railway and AI gateway LiteLLM put customers' API keys and other credentials at risk. Rob Joyce, former head of the NSA's cyber division, warned on X last week that the "transition from vulpocalypse to breachpocalypse is here." What to watch: AI is already making it easier to find and exploit longstanding security weaknesses, even if these particular vulnerabilities have proven challenging to target. The bottom line : Y2K was averted through massive, coordinate effort, not luck. The companies that survive the AI cyber era will be the ones using this current grace period to nail down the basics and prepare for when the alarms finally go off.

823033d5a824.text: Rival satellite companies are jockeying to loosen Elon Musk's grip on battlefield communications after his company's restrictions on Ukraine's Starlink service shook officials in Europe and the U.S. Why it matters: The episode, which temporarily disrupted Ukraine's drone usage, shows how vulnerable a military can be to the whims of a single company or market dominator. State of play: Musk's SpaceX, which is the parent company of Starlink, is by far the world's leader in space-based connectivity with more than 11,000 satellites, per the American Enterprise Institute's data . Eutelsat, a France-based SATCOM firm, is behind them with more than 600 satellites in its OneWeb network. This summer, Starlink announced it hit 12 million customers across more than 160 countries and territories. SpaceX's massive lead has made it difficult for European countries that want to establish independence from the Musk-led company. Driving the news: Now, non-U.S. firms seeking to compete with SpaceX are pitching their services with more urgency. Last week, Finnish firms ICEYE and Nokia announced an agreement with Ukraine's defense ministry to explore "sovereign satellite communications." The duo's initial satellites are "expected to launch in 2028," an ICEYE spokesperson told Axios, adding the need for reliable satellite communications has been "evident for years, especially in Europe." "Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in the ICEYE-and-Nokia announcement. "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control." Zoom in: The Wall Street Journal reported last week that Musk ordered the slowdown of Ukraine's Starlink service. Other outlets have said the White House was involved, which President Trump denied. Musk responded on Oct. 24 that Ukraine "violated Starlink terms of service" by using it for offensive drone strikes. That "loophole," he added, was recently "closed." Follow the money: After Starlink's connection was throttled, shares in Eutelsat spiked . In an interview on French TV last week, Eutelsat CEO Jean-François Fallacher said the company's service is already available in Ukraine and its service can be used for drones. "If one day we wanted to decide to cut off a country or to no longer offer services in a country, it is not a decision made by the CEO alone. It is a decision made by our board of directors with a traditional governance system that we find in Europe," Fallacher said, according to a translation. Threat level: Rebecca Wasser, the defense lead at Bloomberg Economics, said the Starlink incident shows a "loss of faith" not only in the U.S. security commitment, but also in a U.S. company's ability to provide key services. "I think we are going to see more of this push towards European sovereign capability when it comes down to space-based communications," Wasser told Axios . Our thought bubble: This is the latest development in battlefield networking and coordination, without which troops can fight but cannot win. The bottom line: "Satellite communications are no longer simply a support function," Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) wrote in a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last week. "The events in Ukraine show how a single point of control can be turned against the forces that depend on it."

015e7b14686f.text:
If you tell parents in Ghana that their child is using AI at school, theyâre likely to be delighted, says Shabnam Aggarwal, chief technology officer of Sierra Leone-based Rising Academies. Unlike American parents who often bristle about AI in elementary grades, across Africa, many see AI as a way to âgive their kids a leg up,â she said.Rising Academies created an AI tool called Rori that generates math and other lessons for students on WhatsApp, adapting the difficulty level based on their responses. It writes in natural language and is built to work in areas with low connectivity.
Rori is designed to supplement classroom learning, which has taken a hit from Africaâs severe teacher shortage. âTeachers are trying really hard, but theyâre just not getting the support and training they need,â Aggarwal says.
The pitch would be controversial in other parts of the world. Four in ten US adults say they expect AI to have a negative impact on society, according to a February survey from the Pew Research Center, and two of the largest US school districts have recently restricted studentsâ use of AI.
But students across Africa who used Rori for two 30-minute sessions a week outscored a control group by a margin roughly equivalent to an extra year of study, according to an eight-month study of 500 students conducted in 2023 by Oxford and J-PAL researchers.
Rori is now expanding to government schools in Sierra Leone, Liberia, Rwanda, and Ghana. And similar experiments are playing out in other locales, including in Nigeria, where a 2025 study found access to Microsoft Copilot helped students learn English.

5a28d3dfa3ba.text:
Chinaâs largest online delivery service, Taobao Instant Commerce, handles 40 million orders a day. But to coordinate a final handoff, couriers often call customers on the phone to meet up â a hurdle for workers who are deaf or hard of hearing.
The issue has a real economic impact: Researchers at the University of Toronto, UC Santa Barbara, and Zhejiang University found that deaf and hard-of-hearing couriers earned 10% less per hour than other colleagues. They also received more negative customer ratings and were more likely to make late deliveries.
In an effort to close that pay gap, three engineers at Taobao worked in their off hours to build a simple accessibility feature that allows workers to select preset messages (or write their own), and use the AI tool to call the customer and read out the message.
Researchers estimated that the tool closed roughly a third of the hourly pay gap. Late deliveries and bad ratings also declined, with workers who had more severe hearing loss benefiting the most.
The feature is part of a broader accessibility push in China, where businesses are required to reserve at least 1.5% of job opportunities for people with disabilities. After Taobao rolled out its AI calling feature, rival Meituan followed suit.

e2c86cd51703.text:
Indiaâs courts are drowning in documents âÂ and even recording witness testimony can create a bottleneck. âItâs writing, writing, writing, all day,â says Kerala judge Suresh Babu in the annual report of nonprofit Adalat AI. That type of inefficiency matters: In 2024, nearly three-in-four people in prison in India were being held without a conviction as they awaited processing.
Adalat AI builds speech-recognition software trained on Indiaâs legal system, alongside AI tools to manage cases and court documents. Co-founder and CEO Utkarsh Saxena calls his team the âplumbers of the court systemâ, the ones who fix and unclog the pipes.
For example, when a witness answers a question, the judge can now dictate what should be recorded by Adalat. Then, both parties check the text on screen before moving on. Those transcripts are then submitted as the courtâs official record of the testimony. âWe arenât automating decision-making, weâre automating the administrative processes to give judges back time to do the things that actually matter,â Saxena says.
The test will be whether faster paperwork leads to shorter cases. In internal studies, Adalat has seen major improvements in the number of witnesses heard and orders issued at courts that use its tools, which have reached more than 6,000 courtrooms across 11 states. A randomized evaluation with research center J-PAL is currently underway.
Some jurisdictions now mandate the use of Adalat AI technology for recording witness testimony. A similar push is happening in Singapore, where courts introduced AI-powered transcription tools in December 2023.

fe6c062c9f8e.text:
Drug-resistant infections kill more than a million people each year. But big pharmaceutical companies have largely abandoned the quest for new antibiotics, because the research and development needed to discover them is time-consuming and expensive.
Autumn Arnold, a PhD student in the Stokes Lab at McMaster University in Canada, came up with a fix: an AI model that predicts which chemical compounds might kill dangerous bacteria.
The model, called ESKAPE, is free to use: Researchers upload a list of compounds and get a prediction of their antibacterial activity. âAll you need is an internet connection,â said Jonathan Stokes, a microbiologist who runs the lab. Researchers retain ownership of their discoveries, and donât have to share the compounds they submit.
âWe have this perfect storm with rising resistance, a really lean antibiotic pipeline, and enormous economic headwinds,â Stokes said. âItâs going to cost you $1 billion to make a new drug, and youâre never going to make your money back.â
So far, researchers have screened more than 12 million molecules using the ESKAPE model. In total, the model can screen more than 40,000 compounds a day, which has the potential to dramatically speed up drug discovery.
Another approach, developed by researchers at MIT and Swedenâs Karolinska Institutet, is using âgenerative deep learningâ to create entirely new molecules to target antibiotic resistance.
âThis is a global problem,â Stokes says. âWe need everybody helping out.â

ed7ff12fbedd.text:
After a hurricane, drones can capture detailed images of damaged homes and roads. But getting those images to emergency responders is harder: The files are huge, and connectivity in the wake of a storm is often spotty.
CLARKE, developed at Texas A&M University with funding from the National Science Foundationâs AI Institute for Societal Decision Making, is designed to speed up the process. After a drone lands, the CLARKE system can analyze images without an internet connection, and teams can then send compact reports detailing building damage and road conditions, rather than huge image files.
The work is part of a broader effort to use AI in emergency response efforts. After Myanmar experienced a major earthquake in March 2025, Microsoftâs AI for Good Lab analyzed satellite imagery to help aid groups identify damaged buildings.
By reducing delays in transferring and interpreting images, researchers estimate CLARKE could help emergency managers make decisions roughly a day earlier. This, in turn, allows them to focus on the hardest-hit areas first. In a serious crisis, that could save lives.
âThe information exists for emergency managers to make decisions, but it exists in a place where they canât get to it,â Texas A&M researcher Tom Manzini said.
Manzini says CLARKE can assess 2,000 homes in seven minutes. Emergency responders used the system after hurricanes Debby and Helene in 2024. It is now part of the standard operating procedure for Floridaâs disaster drone team, FL-UAS1. In total, Manzini and his team have trained 125 emergency responders on using the CLARKE system.

Hospital Beds for the Nation’s Sickest Kids Are Disappearing
Hospital units dedicated to treating the nation’s sickest kids are disappearing nationwide. In the past year alone, hospitals have closed pediatric intensive care units for critically ill kids in Montana, Oregon, and Missouri. Overnight hospital wings for kids have also shuttered in Illinois and California.
Depending on the hospital, pediatric units — which are separate from neonatal intensive care units — can serve patients ranging from a few weeks old to well into their teens or early adulthood. As hospitals look to cut costs, many are converting those beds into more services for newborns or adults. As a result, pediatric intensive care has become centralized in medical hubs, requiring critically ill children to travel farther for lifesaving care.
“You can’t expect that people will be fine if the next-closest children’s hospital is a flight away or an eight-hour drive,” said Elizabeth Mack, a pediatric critical care doctor and spokesperson for the American Academy of Pediatrics.
Hospitals cutting pediatric care tend to cite low patient volumes; it’s relatively rare for a child to need intensive care. It’s also hard to find doctors to treat those rare cases because the nation is short on pediatric subspecialists, who earn less than those focused on adults. Meanwhile, hospitals are often paid less to treat children than adults, and buying gear tailored to kids adds extra costs.
The gap in care is acute in rural places. Cutbacks are happening across community hospitals, whether owned by small nonprofits or massive private equity companies.
A recent analysis of pediatric inpatient units, hospital wings that provide overnight care, found they decreased by nearly 30% from 2008 to 2022 — down from 1,749 hospitals to 1,226. That left three-quarters of the hospitals without any pediatric inpatient services.
Medical researchers and organizations warn such gaps will widen due to cuts in federal Medicaid spending. The Trump administration has added administrative hurdles to access the low-cost health coverage and whittled down who qualifies. While those changes focus on adults, about half of the nation’s kids are covered by Medicaid or its related Children’s Health Insurance Program. Public aid researchers have said that when caretakers get tangled in paperwork, children can lose coverage.
Fewer people enrolled in Medicaid — adults or kids — means hospitals are about to see a financial hit.
Mack, who also works as a hospital consultant on patient quality, said cutting kids’ services for most hospitals is “a spreadsheet issue.”
“This is a very pricey endeavor, and it’s not sustainable,” Mack said. “There’s not a great answer here.”
‘It’s About Quality’
Even without recent closures, many sick kids already travel long distances to obtain care.
When Darby Waldbillig’s toddler struggled to wake up one morning in 2022, Missoula was the Montana family’s closest pediatric critical care option — a 100-mile emergency flight from their home at the time in Helena, the state capital.
“Her face was swollen. She was drifting in and out of consciousness,” Waldbillig said.
Her nearly 2-year-old daughter, Siobhan, had bacterial meningitis, a life-threatening infection that swells tissue around the brain and spinal cord. Local emergency room workers started antibiotics before transferring her to Missoula’s Community Medical Center, where Siobhan spent more than a week in the pediatric intensive care unit — the same unit that closed this month.
“I firmly believe it’s because of those doctors that she lived,” Waldbillig said.
Whether Community Medical Center can still take cases like Siobhan’s depends on how sick a child becomes.
Greg Cook, the hospital’s CEO, said most kids who come in the door will still be able to stay for treatment. The difference is that the sickest kids — those in critical care who, for example, need a ventilator or continuous monitoring for a seizure — would be stabilized, then sent elsewhere.
“We made the decision to take care of the kids that we could absolutely take care of,” Cook said. “It’s about quality more than it is about the dollars.”
In a later email, hospital spokesperson Megan Condra said the decision was driven by low patient volumes and long-standing staffing challenges. “Our decision was not driven by concerns about the quality of care currently being provided,” she said.
Cook said the hospital hasn’t been able to recruit pediatric critical care doctors to live in Missoula since its last local pediatric critical care doctor retired eight years ago. Instead, specialists have been flying in on rotations. Cook said, on average, the hospital saw approximately two kids a month who needed intensive care when the decision to close the unit was made.
Cook estimated the unit’s closure will affect roughly 25 patients a year. The next-closest option in the state is Kalispell — a pediatric intensive care unit about 150 miles north of Missoula.
Hubs for Pediatric Care
Not all hospitals are hurting in the same way.
Community Medical Center in Missoula is owned by for-profit Lifepoint Health, whose revenue is more than $10 billion a year, according to its website.
Cook said hospital leaders downgraded the unit after consulting with Lifepoint Health. “Asking Lifepoint to float the program” wouldn’t have solved its main issue, he said.
St. Vincent Medical Center, a Portland, Oregon, hospital that closed its pediatric intensive care unit last November, is part of Providence, a nonprofit health system operating across seven states. The latest financial records filed with the federal government show Providence Oregon had a more than $15 million shortfall as of 2024.
But St. Vincent, like Community Medical Center in Missoula, cited too few patients, not money, as the main reason for the unit’s closure. The four-bed unit was often empty, said St. Vincent Medical Center spokesperson Lisa Helderop.
Raj Basu is division chief of critical care

In California and Other States, Dads Are Now Even With Moms in Paid Leave Claims
Karlo Campana is usually outnumbered these days. He has three young kids under age 4. On a recent Saturday, he played a mini game of basketball with his two older kids in their Southern California home, shooting a ball into a hoop on the door, while his baby boy watched from his bouncy chair.
Campana took paid time off in May after the birth of his son — just as he did for his daughters.
“You need that adjustment period,” he said. Campana, who works at an ad agency, said having the time off not to think about work — or worry about losing income during that time — was crucial for him and his family during a sleep-deprived period.
“My wife isn’t doing it on her own,” he said. “She doesn’t feel like she’s alone on this journey. She feels like she has support.” He jokes that by kid No. 3 he thought he had nailed diaper changes without getting peed on — but he was wrong.
“The benefits are I get to spend time with each of them when they were in the infant stage, the baby stage, and I get to hold them and, you know, change the poopy diapers,” he said. “ It’s like the funny moments of, like, being a parent, like, ‘This is it right here, you’re in the thick of it.’”
Campana is among a growing number of fathers who take leave to bond with a new child in states that offer paid family leave programs — and are part of a larger cultural shift that has seen dads handling more caregiving duties. In California — as in several other states — men make up about half of bonding claim applications. Last year, men even surpassed women — as in Colorado and Washington — for the first time in the state’s history. This trend comes at a time when the federal government has said it wants Americans to have more babies, and families report affordability is an obstacle to raising them.
No federal law guarantees paid parental leave, but California is one of 14 states, plus Washington, D.C., that have passed legislation to enact paid family leave programs — and in many of those places, more dads are opting in.
“We’re in a very different place in terms of our understanding of gender roles, of paternity leave, of dads’ roles than we were 20-plus years ago,” said Molly Weston Williamson, policy director at Paid Leave for All, an organization that advocates for paid family leave policies.
California’s program offers, within a year, up to eight weeks of paid bonding leave for parents after a birth or adoption. That’s on top of six to eight weeks of paid disability leave that moms get to recover after birth.
Research has shown that paternity leave confers benefits beyond allowing a father extra time to bond with a new child: It has positive effects on the whole family, including better health outcomes for both parents. Paid parental leave has also been linked to lower odds of postpartum depression and a decrease in infant mortality rates.
In California, men accounted for 51% of bonding claims filed in 2025. It’s a massive shift from when the state program started in 2004, and men made up about 18% of claim applications.
States fund paid family and medical leave with different combinations of employer and employee contributions; California is among six states where family leave is entirely funded by employee payroll deductions.
In addition to changing gender norms, Weston Williamson said, other factors likely contribute to the increase in claims by men in the state: greater awareness about the program and recent changes to the benefit.
In 2025, the state boosted the amount of income a worker can recoup while on family leave. Now, in California and other states, the leave benefit can be as high as 90% of their regular salary.
“That makes it a realistic option for a lot more families, and I think we’re seeing dads and moms responding to that change,” Weston Williamson said. Still, she said, there’s a lot the new data about dads isn’t telling us.
“We’re getting one particular vantage point into this data, which is useful and valuable, but it’s only telling us sort of part of the story, and we’d need other kinds of information to better understand the full picture,” Weston Williamson said. “Is it that more dads are working and therefore are potentially eligible for these benefits? Is it that women are deciding not to take leave?”
While private employers can offer their own paid leave as a benefit, this data reflects only people who took leave through the state.
A spokesperson for the California Employment Development Department, which administers the state family leave program, said the department couldn’t provide definitive reasons for the increase in bonding claims by men.
One thing is clear: The growth in these states comes as more parents are feeling strained economically. President Donald Trump has said, “We want more babies,” and has promoted policy initiatives like expanding access to in vitro fertilization and offering investment accounts for newborns.
“People really are very worried about the affordability of kids,” said Jeremy Pope, a professor of political science at Brigham Young University.
In 2025, 7 in 10 Americans said raising children had become unaffordable, according to the American Family Survey out of Brigham Young University. It was the biggest single-year jump since the survey started more than a decade ago.
“I don’t think they want government involved in the decision to have kids,” Pope said. “But they worry a lot about how much it costs and they would like to see ways of making those costs smaller or getting help with those costs.”
The Pew Research Center found in a recent survey that among full-time working parents who are not self-employed, 84% said paid parental, family, or medical leave would be “extremely or very helpful” to them, but only half said it was available to them.
Dad-of-three Campana said he initially wasn’t sure if he should take paternity leave because of lingering gender stereotypes.

Plans are advancing on the Gulf Coast of Texas for an enormous seawater desalination plant which, if built, would be part of one of the largest water infrastructure developments in the country.
Unlike other projects, this one wouldn’t belong to the public, but to a private, foreign water supplier.
IDE Technologies, an Israeli water treatment giant that operates some of the largest seawater desalination plants in the world, was awarded the contract for the landmark Harbor Island project on Corpus Christi Bay this summer by the Nueces River Authority, a small state water agency.
“For our company, globally, this is Project One,” IDE regional sales director Mark Ellison told the NRA board of directors at its September meeting. “Our top priority.”
A 60-year-old, formerly state-owned firm, IDE has built more than 400 desalination plants in 40 countries, according to the company.
In Texas, rapid growth and intensifying droughts have stretched present water supplies to their limits. Generations of state leaders have touted the promise of seawater desalination plants, which would produce freshwater from the salty Gulf of Mexico. But Texas still awaits its first such facility.
Today, IDE’s Harbor Island project is the largest of five seawater desalination plants planned in the state.
The development of seawater desalination in Texas would mark a breakthrough for the state, unlocking a new, abundant source of water from the ocean. But it would come at a high cost to consumers, and would mark a dramatic transfer of the public water supply to private ownership.
“We’ve been here for a decade getting ready to get this started,” said Ellison, a former state water official during a presentation last month to officials in Corpus Christi, a major industrial port and the nation’s largest export hub for crude oil. “We’re moving very actively to get going.”
It would be the largest desalination plant in the Western Hemisphere, according to IDE, eventually producing up to 100 million gallons per day of freshwater. It would include nearly seven miles of two-story-tall sub-sea tunnels, plus a vast system of pipelines and pump stations running more than 200 miles inland to the booming towns and cities of south Central Texas.
IDE plans to finance and build the plant while the NRA develops the pipelines, with a combined estimated price tag of $6.4 billion.
In cost and complexity, it would rival the iconic aqueducts, pipelines and dams of the American West.
“It would be one of the more ambitious projects in U.S. history,” said Drew Molly, a former chair of the American Waterworks Association and chief water officer for the city of Houston.
On Sept. 23, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality approved its final permit for the Harbor Island plant.
Elsewhere on the coast, IDE announced plans in April for another desalination plant near Brownsville that would produce 50 million gallons per day. Nearby, a small public utility, the Laguna Madre Water District, is also developing its own 5 million gallon per day plant.
A Canadian company, EPCOR, announced plans last year for a 27 MGD desalination plant near Houston. A plastics manufacturing complex, CC Polymers, plans to boot up a 9 MGD plant early next year and, like IDE’s Harbor Island facility, wants to begin selling water to the city of Corpus Christi, which has tried for more than a decade, to no avail, to build its own desalination plant.
“The private sector realizes that water is a scarce resource,” Molly said. “And the private sector wants to capitalize.”
It goes beyond desalination. Across the state, private and investor-owned water projects have cropped up in recent years, aiming to pump large volumes of groundwater and sell it to booming cities and subdivisions, too.
That bucks the traditional model in Texas, where water supplies are typically owned by public agencies like cities, towns, river authorities or utility districts.
“Water infrastructure should be owned by the community, not the property of a private company that is making a profit,” Molly said.
Officials in the city of Corpus Christi, where Molly previously served as head of the water department, ultimately rejected plans to build a municipally owned desalination plant, put off by its surging cost estimates.
Now, Corpus Christi plans to start buying water next year from the desalination plant at CC Polymers, the plastics manufacturing complex, which is jointly owned by companies from Taiwan, Indonesia and Mexico.
Corpus Christi also plans to buy water at an undetermined price from IDE’s plant at Harbor Island.
“I’m quite reluctant to move in that direction,” said Roland Barrera, a member of Corpus Christi City Council. “It’s better that the public agency owns the system.”
High Price of Private Water
IDE plans to announce a price of water from its Harbor Island plant in January. After that, Corpus Christi will decide whether or not to sign a long-term purchase contract, which would require the city to pay for water whether it uses it or not.
Barrera, the council member and owner of an insurance business in downtown Corpus Christi, worries what will happen when the city’s contract expires in 20 or 30 years. Communities may have to pay whatever new prices the companies set.
“It’s too much uncertainty,” Barrera said. “It’s going to be very expensive.”
Desalinated seawater is already the priciest water supply option that exists. The law requires public utilities to provide water at the cost of service, while private projects seek to maximize profits.
A private project wouldn’t be eligible for the low-interest government loans that typically finance the public sector. Costs to borrow money in private equity markets are nearly twice as high. Ashleyâs view
Britain wants to pour another Â£120 million â roughly $160 million â into a government lab that tests the worldâs most powerful AI models, an infusion of cash that alone is more than 10 times the annual budget of its US counterpart.
That money is part of a new AI package that UK Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey previewed ahead of his budget presentation to Parliament on Wednesday.
The UKâs governmentâs decision to devote resources to AI security and research is a response to heightening concerns about AI capabilities and related cybersecurity risks. It contrasts sharply with the approach in the US, where federal efforts to evaluate AI are receiving far less cash and are shared by different parts of government.
In addition to the Â£120 million infusion, the UK also plans to dole out Â£60 million to a sovereign AI fund to help boost domestic AI companies, and Â£18 million to boost homegrown chip design. And the government will devote Â£10 million per year to research on how AI is shaping employment.
âWe are incredibly well-placed to succeed â Britain has the only trillion-dollar tech sector in the Western world outside of the United States, the UKâs AI Security Institute is a global leader in frontier model testing, and we have the capital market depth to help companies scale and grow,â a senior UK government spokesperson told Semafor.
âThe new funding commitments in this budget, alongside investments from US firms like OpenAI and Anthropic, demonstrate that the UK is a global destination for AI firms to do business,â the spokesperson said.
The UKâs AISI, formed in 2023, has more than 100 staffers, including alumni from labs like OpenAI and Googleâs DeepMind, as well as from British intelligence agencies and universities.
Healey called the package âa distinctively British approach to AI,â predicting it is unlikely to face trouble in Parliament, where his Labour party holds a large majority.
The View From Washington
In the US, the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence â recently renamed to reflect President Donald Trumpâs choice description for AI â operates on a budget of about $10-$15 million a year within the Commerce Departmentâs National Institute for Science and Technology.
CAISSI, which was formed the same year as its UK counterpart under the Biden administration, has undergone major changes since Trump took office for a second time. It does not currently have a permanent director; the last one, Chris Fall, resigned in July. It was originally called the US AI Safety Institute, but the Trump administration removed âsafetyâ from its name in 2025 to make clear its desire to embrace AI acceleration.
â[The UKâs] AISI is an extremely impressive organization, in large part because the UK has invested a great deal in it,â Arthur Tellis, a senior technology fellow at the Institute for Progress, a technology think tank in Washington, told Semafor.
âWhile resource improvements are critical, it is also important that CAISSI [has] empowered technically competent leadership, a direct line to the White House, and a business model that allows it to track and shape frontier AI development,â Tellis said. âRight now, CAISSI is simply too small and distant to do this effectively.â
The US entity has ongoing agreements with top AI labs to vet their models before release and describes itself as âindustryâs primary point of contactâ within the US government. The work that the private sector does with it and its British counterpart is voluntary and not required by law.
Some in Washington are clamoring for CAISSI to get more resources. That includes members of Congress, along with White House Office of Science and Technology Director Michael Kratsios. A White House spokesperson told Semafor that President Trump asked for $27 million in funding for CAISSI in his FY2027 budget request, a 145% increase over the current budget.
âOur allies and our adversaries recognize that now is the time to build the expertise to understand and oversee frontier AI,â Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., told Semafor. âThe United States canât afford to fall behind. Paltry funding for CAISSI limits its ability to recruit top talent, support the durable guardrails Congress is working to pass, and help America lead on global standards for this fast-moving technology.â
The bipartisan bill Trahan proposed alongside Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., earlier this year would allocate $100 million for CAISSI annually through 2029.
Room for Disagreement
There are some who will argue that the US government is putting sufficient resources towards AI development â even if that funding isnât focused on safety and security.
The Energy Departmentâs Genesis Mission, for example, just announced $159 million in awards for work on AI-enabled quantum, science, and energy projects.
Trump himself has sought to address safety concerns by convening AI executives at the White House to sign a nonbinding âAccord on Super Intelligenceâ and establishing a new task force on AI led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.
âAmerican SI models are the most powerful models in the world, and President Trump will ensure that America continues to lead in SI innovation,â a White House official told Semafor in a statement.
âCAISSI will continue to play a role in both pre-deployment testing and the Super Intelligence Force. To ensure all components of the SI Force are under one roof, senior CAISSI officials will collaborate with relevant colleagues from the White House,â the official continued. âThe SI Force will work together to accelerate innovation, ensure the safe and responsible deployment of new models, and protect the American people.â

- The New York Times profiled the UKâs AI Institute in May.

Fewer Americans than ever think that their representative in Congress deserves to be reelected ahead of a midterm election, according to new Gallup polling, a warning sign for incumbents from both parties battling for their seats next week.
Forty-three percent of US adults say their own representatives deserve another term, while just 15% â also a record pre-midterm low â say most members have earned reelection.
Independents are the least impressed by current representation in Washington; only 36% say their representative should be reelected, while 9% say most should be.
Congress is also struggling with low favorability scores: 14% of Americans approve of the way Congress is handling its job.
Notably, Republican votersâ approval of Congress has dropped from 53% shortly after the GOP assumed control of Washington to 29% today.

The cryptocurrency industryâs leading network of super PACs is yet again spending huge sums against Sherrod Brown in Ohio, despite doubts that the investment will pay off.
The network known as Fairshake spent $40 million in 2024 to unseat Brown, then the Senate Banking Committee chair; after Brown lost, crypto antagonist-in-chief Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts replaced him as the panelâs top Democrat.
Now, Fairshake is spending $55 million to keep Brown off the Hill, even though Senate rules bar him from reclaiming his Banking seniority if he wins.
As Brown pulls ahead in polls, skepticism is mounting that Fairshakeâs latest Ohio play will help keep the Senate red â though President Donald Trump will travel there today to help the cause.
âThat $40 million that Fairshake spent [in 2024] moved the needle zero â¦ and theyâre doing it again,â one financial services lobbyist said.
Some of Fairshakeâs most vocal critics questioned whether its backers are getting a clear picture of the battleground landscape. The Ohio Senate race is the second-most expensive this cycle, with spending topping $500 million this week.
âA lot of the tech people backing Fairshake really donât believeâ that Democrats can take back the Senate, a crypto executive aligned with the party told Semafor. âTheyâre not hearing the alternative views anymore.â
This executive pointed to Fairshakeâs decision to stay out of the Maine Senate race as an example of its spending priorities being disconnected from its legislative goals. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, opposed the latest crypto bill but isnât facing any critical spending from Fairshake.
âThereâs no 4D chess being played here,â a person close to Fairshake responded. âFairshakeâs showing everyone â supporters and opponents in both parties â that they show up for champions in good times and bad.â
But if Brown loses his bid to return to the Senate, it would further isolate the Democrats who are already warning that Fairshakeâs play for Ohio makes future progress on crypto legislation harder to picture.
And if he wins, the Democratic caucus could decide to make an exception by restoring his seniority. Heâs so far stayed mum on whether he even wants to return to the Banking Committee, which may prove less politically advantageous than other panels. Another option: The Senate Agriculture Committee, which could give Brown the opportunity to pass a farm bill before he faces voters again in two years.
A spokesperson for Brown did not return a request for comment.
