In the final stretch of their midterm drive to gain control of Congress, Democratic candidates are talking mostly about the pain of high energy costs, not the risks of climate change.
But advocates of climate action view the Nov. 3 elections as a crucial moment for the movement. U.S. voters will decide whether to upend the compliant Republican-led Congress that stood by as President Donald Trump’s administration took unprecedented steps to bolster fossil fuels and choke off support for alternatives.
Environmentalists argue that it is especially urgent to put a check on the president in order to tackle the monumental new challenges posed by the rise of artificial intelligence and data centers. The world is close to overshooting the Paris Agreement’s 1.5-degree Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warming threshold, increasing the risk of large-scale and potentially irreversible change.
“These elections are … starting to set the groundwork for 2028,” environmental author and activist Bill McKibben said in a recent interview with Democracy Now. “And that’s going to be, at least in climate terms, probably, maybe the last election that happens in a timeframe when we still really have an opportunity to affect some of the outcomes of these things.”
McKibben has been traveling across the country to mobilize voters with Third Act, the senior citizen-led group he founded. He does so, he has said, with an understanding that the Trump White House will have the power to quash any attempts at new climate action by Congress. Even if Democrats manage to flip four seats in the House and four seats in the Senate to gain control of both chambers, there are not enough seats in play to give them veto-proof majorities.
Nevertheless, even a bare majority in the House for the Democrats—and some projections show them gaining 15 seats or more—would give them power to seize back some of the control the Trump administration has assumed over government pursestrings. Gaining an edge in the Senate—a more difficult goal, but achievable—would give Democrats power to vote down presidential appointees, including Supreme Court justices, or prevent them from getting to the floor for a vote.
History is on the side of the challengers; the president’s party has lost ground in the House in 20 of the past 22 midterm elections. The only exceptions—1998 and 2002—were years when presidential approval rates were exceptionally high. Trump’s approval rate this month hit a record low of 33 percent.
Still, Republicans are pouring money into Senate races. The GOP has an overwhelming cash advantage, fueled in part by the one-sided giving of the fossil fuel industry. The oil and gas industry so far has spent $172.8 million on candidates or partisan political committees in the midterm elections, with 97 percent going to Republicans or conservative groups, according to a tally provided to Inside Climate News by the nonprofit group OpenSecrets. The tech industry, including cryptocurrency, online betting and artificial intelligence firms are together investing even more money in electing anti-regulation candidates, mainly Republicans, according to several analyses, including by Reuters and the watchdog group Public Citizen. The world’s richest man, Elon Musk, has become one of the biggest political donors in history, directing a reported $276 million toward helping struggling Republicans like Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in his bid for U.S. Senate.
The environmental movement can’t hope to match the combined spending of the industry groups supporting Republicans, but they have sought to muster an historic effort. The LCV Victory Fund, the super PAC of the League of Conservation Voters, last week announced it was more than doubling its planned investment in the midterm elections to $110 million, a figure that includes spending by 30 affiliate organizations across the country to elect pro-environment governors and state legislatures. That places it among the largest outside issues groups supporting Democratic candidates.
LCV Action Fund, a separate group that coordinates with candidates to get out the vote, has invested $3.5 million in its longstanding GreenRoots volunteer member mobilization program and a new paid canvass program, Clean Energy Corps. In addition, nearly $27 million in donations have gone from environment-focused voters directly to candidates’ campaigns through GiveGreen, a bundling platform sponsored by LCV Victory Fund and NRDC Action Votes. The political affiliates of Environmental Defense Fund have a goal of spending a combined $18.2 million on independent ads run by the EDF Action Votes and in grassroots mobilization efforts coordinated with candidates through EDF Action PAC.
Climate: Hushed or Hidden?
In the midterm elections of Trump’s first term in office, the drive for action on climate change was a galvanizing force that helped flip the House to the Democrats. With the Green New Deal as a rallying cry, young voter turnout surged nearly 80 percent that year compared to the prior midterm election. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York was just one of a slew of climate action champions elected to Congress in the so-called “Class of 2018.”
In 2026, however, climate advocates are focusing on high energy costs and the threats of data centers. A recent Inside Climate News analysis showed mentions of climate change have plummeted over the past year in press releases issued by Democrats in the House and Senate. The trend indicates there’s been at least some embrace of the advice offered earlier this year by the Searchlight Institute, a think tank founded by centrist Democratic strategist Adam Jentleson: “The first rule about solving climate change: don’t say ‘climate change.’”

Over the course of two weeks in October, Maine’s incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins and her Democrat challenger, former state Senate President Troy Jackson, met for four debates. Each debate focused heavily on energy affordability, and each exchange followed roughly the same script: When Jackson brought up the high costs of heating a home with oil, Collins volleyed back by talking about the high costs of powering it with electricity, and vice versa.
With Jackson trying to link Collins to the Iran War that has caused heating oil prices to skyrocket, and Collins in turn blaming state policies enacted under Jackson’s Senate majority leadership for rising electricity rates, experts say it’s unclear whether either gained a major advantage on this issue during the debates.
“We don’t have a whole lot of indication the debates have moved anyone,” said Mark Brewer, chair of the Political Science Department at the University of Maine.
In addition to trading blame for a phenomenon that, at least on the power side, analysts say has multiple overlapping causes, the candidates revealed a stark contrast in their proposals for getting costs under control.
Collins emphasized more U.S. drilling and imports of fossil fuels, while Jackson said he would prioritize large clean energy projects and ongoing electrification. The implications for fighting climate change are significant.
The race, deemed crucial to Senate control, has been most recently rated a “toss-up” by the New York Times. Jackson leads by two points in most polls, reflecting a statistical tie.
Heating Fuel and the Iran War
Mainers already contending with a a host of affordability challenges were walloped with a new one when they went to fill their heating fuel tanks ahead of winter: The cost of heating fuel is up over 80 percent from just a year ago, which will put the average cost of heating a home with fuel this winter, as about half of Maine does, at over $4,000.
The high cost of fuel and gasoline has been directly linked to blockages of the Strait of Hormuz following the U.S.-Israel initiation of war with Iran in February. It’s a war Collins initially backed before opposing it beginning in late April and that has claimed the lives of dozens of Americans and likely thousands of Iranian civilians.
Jackson unrelentingly linked Collins to the war during the debates, pointing to her five votes against resolutions to bring troops home in the first months of the war. Collins explained these votes in the debates by saying the 1973 War Powers Resolution recognizes the president’s wide discretion during the first 60 days of overseas conflicts, which is largely true, but ignores that that same law leaves Congress the avenue Democrats tried to use to end hostilities.
Collins also pointed to her nine votes since April in favor of ending the war and criticized Trump in the third debate. “The President did not have a good plan. He should have anticipated the closure of the Strait of Hormuz,” she said.
Collins emphasized how she has tried to blunt rising costs for consumers: pushing for the early distribution of financial support for low-income Mainers to buy heating fuel and the release of national reserves. The low-income heating assistance program is one that Trump has tried to end.
Trump’s signature 2025 budget law ended consumer tax credits for electric vehicles and heat pumps that could have helped more households afford to transition off fossil fuels. Heat pumps continue to offer a much more affordable way to heat a home in Maine than oil, propane or kerosene, despite rising electricity costs.
Collins helped advance that “One Big Beautiful Bill” on a procedural vote before voting against it. Collins’s campaign did not return multiple requests for comment.
Jackson also blamed high electricity prices on the Iran War, even though the increases predate the war by several years. Jackson’s campaign did not respond to questions on this point.
Electricity Costs and State Policies
If the war’s not primarily behind high power bills, what is?
“If you look at the policies that have driven up the cost of living in Maine, you have to look at Augusta,” Collins argued. She pointed specifically to a program that requires utilities to buy power from rooftop and community solar arrays at guaranteed prices.
That program is a piece of the puzzle—but a relatively small one, according to Maine’s Office of the Public Advocate, an official appointed to represent the interests of ratepayers.
State Republicans have criticized the program, known as net energy billing, in recent years, saying it cuts power costs for largely well-to-do households who can afford to install solar panels, while increasing them for everyone else. Maine Democrats have defended it as making it easier for anyone who wants to save money by going solar.
Collins specifically pointed to Jackson’s leadership when the program was expanded greatly in 2019 and his vote against eliminating the program entirely in 2023, a move the Public Advocate said would save the average household $275 per year.
Instead, the legislature modified the program by ending new applications for larger projects and effectively reducing the compensation for some existing ones. Jackson defended this compromise.
“It did cost more than it should have, but we reformed it twice,” he said in one debate.
According to an analysis prepared for the state Public Utilities Commission, the program cost Maine’s ratepayers $193 million on net in 2025.
Maine’s current public advocate, Heather Sanborn, found those costs explain about 14 percent of the increase in electric bills since 2020—a number dwarfed by the impacts of rising electricity supply costs (45 percent) and costs to build electric poles and wires and repair them after storms (27 percent).
Sanborn, who voted for the 2019 law as a state senator, explained in an interview that the recent reforms should limit the costs of net energy billing going forward, though not eliminate them.

A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world said it suspended operations due to extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia.
The US-based operator of Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and "temporary living arrangements".
It is unclear how many were on board but the nearly 200m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a "continuous voyage around the world".
Global fuel prices have soared since the Iran war started earlier this year. The ship's operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 (Â£6,000) from $1,800.
The company said it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port". But those measures turned out to be insufficient to "offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs".
"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," it said.
The company would spend the next 60 days on "restructuring and recapitalisation", though "no outcome is assured", it said.
There were reportedly around 200 passengers on board when they were ordered to disembark in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, a once sleepy beach town that has gained global notoriety in recent years as a hub for scam centres.
The Villa Vie Odyssey's voyage was expected to span 3.5 years and cover nearly 150 countries, according to its website.
Its departure had faced delays as the ship underwent repairs, leaving passengers stranded in Belfast for months and costing the company millions of pounds.
The ship was more than 750 days into its circumnavigation before announcing its suspension of its journey on Tuesday - which means its passengers would now be stranded in Cambodia.
"It was not on my bingo card of places where I'd be spending a lot of time," one passenger, Holly Hennessey, told the BBC from Cambodia.
"We're all in different hotels; there are a number of shipmates in the hotel that I'm in. We're just waiting."
The Villa Vie Odyssey is equipped with several bars and restaurants, a pool deck and a pickleball court, according to its website.
Permanent residencies in its cabins range from $120,000 to $440,000. These cabins are also also available for rent from $3,500 a month.
Last year, the company launched a lifetime residence programme for people to spend their retirement years at sea.
In 2024, days after US President Donald Trump won his second term, Villa Vie Residences announced a four-year "Skip Forward" package. Its CEO told Fox Business at the time that it was the "perfect product for those who said they'd leave the country if 'XYZ' wins the election".
Hennessey said the ship's residents had earlier been asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as global prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed". Some people decided to disembark and travel on land, she said.
But some, like Hennessey, have decided to stick around in Cambodia in the hopes that the Villa Vie Odyssey will set sail again soon.
"Until they say we are done - done done - I am not giving up. I could never duplicate this lifestyle. The idea of going home? It would be so trite," she said.
"Cambodia's not the worst place to hang out."

With results still trickling in, it currently appears that Israel's veteran Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has done better than was widely predicted with his Likud emerging as the largest single party.
His existing bloc with ultra-nationalist and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties appear to be just short of a 61-seat majority in the 120-seat parliament. However, analysts caution that this is subject to change because the early count was skewed towards areas known to have strong right-wing support.
A dramatic deadlock had been widely forecast as Israelis surged to the polls â with turnout reaching more than 77%.
In Israel's fragmented political system, the signs are that Netanyahu's main rival, the former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, would struggle to command a parliamentary majority without parties led by Israel's Arab minority. According to partial results, they have equalled or gained on their previous record number of seats.
On the campaign trail, most Jewish opposition parties pledged not to work with Arab-majority lists, citing a lack of shared values.
However, Israel's Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers if others were prepared to join forces with them. In this election, Arab Israelis â who often identify as Palestinian citizens of Israel and represent one-fifth of the population â appeared to turn out in unprecedented numbers.
Many saw this as a make-or-break election to defeat Israel's most right-wing-ever government, accusing it of stoking racism and hatred.
A huge caveat in all of the current analysis is that the high number of as-yet-uncounted absentee ballots â mostly representing the votes of Israeli soldiers â mean that we are not expecting to have a clear idea of the final results for another day or two.
Overnight, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot addressed their supporters, pledging to form the next government.
"The right-wing bloc has a clear, decisive majority among the Zionist public, among the Jewish public and all those who support the Jewish state. That is what has become clear. A decisive majority," the PM told his celebrating supporters â although he stopped short of declaring victory.
"We must form a strong, national, right-wing government. That is what must be done," he added.
"The public has chosen change," Eisenkot told his Yashar party after exit polls came out â most of which were initially more favourable to the opposition. "The coalition of failure has lost the people's trust. The Israeli public voted against Benjamin Netanyahu continuing as prime minister."
"I will work with my partners to ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government: stable and good for all of Israeli's citizens. And quickly â because that is what this moment demands, and because the country needs to be brought back together."
There are deep divisions in Israeli society which have been underscored by this and previous elections. They have served not just as referenda on Netanyahu's leadership â as he faces a corruption trial on charges he denies â but also as votes on what kind of country Israel should be.
The PM and his current coalition partners have taken the country on a hardline religious, nationalist trajectory over the past four years. There were mass protests over their plan for a judicial overhaul prior to the unprecedented Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023 which triggered a series of wars â in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Many Israelis want to see their country more firmly anchored in liberal and secular values.
Remarkably, the past four turbulent years do not appear to have significantly changed voting patterns.
"We see in the polls, that the relative weight of the two main sides: pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu is about the same," Professor Tamar Hermann, a pollster at the Israeli Democracy Institute told me, just prior to the election. "People expected that after October 7th, Netanyahu will be down the drain or even toppled but it didn't happen."
Already, overnight, the main Israeli parties will have begun their intense political wrangling to try to form a new coalition government.
"Each side will try to pull over defectors, or will try to see if they can make a minority government and will try all these different political kinds of wizardry," is how veteran Israeli journalist and author, Yaakov Katz described the process to me. "But it might not work, and it could take weeks or months to see if someone is actually capable of forming a government."
The leaders of the bigger parties typically try to win over smaller ones with promises of cabinet positions, budgets or specific policies.
It is key now to see if those in the main opposition "change bloc" are ready to break a taboo by seeking a political deal with the Arab parties.
On the campaign trail, one of the bloc's leaders, right-wing politician Avigdor Lieberman, went as far as to say that he would not sit in a minority government that relied on their support. It was a sign of the increased mistrust and hostility towards Arab citizens since the 7 October assault.
When I recently met Mansour Abbas, head of Ra'am â the smaller of the two Arab lists â he told me that having been part of the diverse coalition that temporarily unseated Netanyahu between 2021 and 2022, he wanted to join the next government. He believed that potential partners would be more open to an alliance after the election.
"These are familiar and well-known party-political considerations. All politicians in Israel say one thing before elections and speak a different language after elections," he said. "We have experienced this before, and it does not concern us."
Meanwhile, Netanyahu and his allies have already begun an intense campaign of delegitimising the Arab parties â casting their fellow citizens as a threat from within.

King Charles III has begun his tour of the Caribbean by acknowledging the "great suffering of the past" as he faced calls for slavery reparations.
Speaking an event in the Bahamas celebrating local youth, the King said the country's culture was "born out of darkness", and it was "only right" to acknowledge historic injustices.
His nine-day tour will culminate in the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), where the King has confirmed leaders will discuss the region's legacy of slavery.
The visit, his first as monarch, comes in the wake of renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit.
Prior to the trip, Buckingham Palace said the King would not shy away from "colonial legacy" and the impact of the slave trade during his visit but, in line with the UK government position, he will not apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade or offer reparations.
Upon his arrival on Tuesday, the King met Governor General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and its Prime Minister Philip Edward Davis, before speaking with members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as he inspected a guard of honour.
King Charles, wearing sunglasses and a grey suit, was then met with cheers as he arrived for his first engagement at a youth rally at Clifford Park - where he attended independence celebrations for the Bahamas as Prince of Wales in 1973.
The young people in the crowd had been given time off school for the event. "It's my first time seeing him in person out of TikTok so he's out there, it's cool," one student told the BBC.
A small group of protestors gathered close to the rally shouting "pay us what you owe us" and "return artefacts you've stolen."
The group of around a dozen protestors was kept outside the main venue as they called on the King to help change the UK government's position on apologising and offering reparations.
"He's a man of influence. The Crown still has influence. And if they do not do it then we will become a republic and we will turn our backs on England if you do not show respect to the former colonies," said one protestor, Sharon Purcer-Cooper.
During his speech in Nassau, the King acknowledged his 50-year-long commitment to fighting climate change and highlighted the challenges faced by low-lying Caribbean islands, saying that "our world cries out for healing".
He went on to call on young people at the rally to "take up the sacred task to play your part" as "in years to come, this will be surely be the measure of every person - how they answered the call to care for planet earth - the source of our life, our prosperity and our security".
The King resumes engagements in the Bahamas on Wednesday, where he will hear how vulnerable the low lying islands of the Caribbean are to climate change.
He will also learn more about the Bahamian tradition of Junkanoo - a cultural festival and street parade.
Buckingham Palace said opportunities for the King to reflect on the legacy of the slave trade will be built into the schedule of his nine-day tour of three Caribbean countries with visits planned to memorials and other places of reflection and remembrance.
A spokesperson for the palace told the BBC that the King's programme on the tour "will primarily focus on shining a light on the many modern partnerships and opportunities for the future", specifically those which are "having a transformative effect on the region".
For the King, the spokesperson added, the "tour is both a new journey but also the continuance of a lifelong one, in which he has sought to engage, understand and educate about the most shameful aspects of our past".
Those themes will be reflected by the King through the nine-day visit, the palace said.
The visit has been planned alongside the governments of the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda with an emphasis on honouring the past but also looking forward to the ambition and possibility for future generations.
The King will move to Guyana later this week where his engagements will focus on the environment and biodiversity.
He will then visit Antigua and Barbuda, where he will be joined by Queen Camilla, for the CHOGM and his keynote speech as leader of the Commonwealth.
The biennial summit will bring together leaders of 56 Commonwealth countries to address shared challenges and advance cooperation.

The port-call situation is wearing out Navy warships
Diego Garcia is the only safe place for ships fighting Iran, but the remote atoll can’t provide the maintenance they need.
A few years ago, a port call in the Middle East might mean bottomless-mojito brunches in Bahrain, hitting the indoor ski slopes in a Dubai megamall, or a desert safari in Qatar. But since Operation Epic Fury began eight months ago, U.S. warships in the theater have basically had just one option: Diego Garcia, some 2,500 miles away.
It’s not great for morale, but the consequences go beyond disgruntled sailors who tire of fishing off the British island in the Indian Ocean. The remote coral atoll lacks the pierside infrastructure that many Gulf, Mediterranean, and Pacific ports can offer. As the Navy stretches its fleet with longer deployments and fewer port calls, warships are losing the ability to do crucial mid-cruise maintenance.
“When a ship is deployed overseas for longer than the nominal seven-month deployment period, that increases the amount of time for equipment on the ship to break, get worn down, or worn out. As a result, when the ship finally does make it back to the United States, it might need more maintenance and repair work than it would have needed if the deployment had not exceeded seven months,” said Ron O’Rourke, who retired this year after more than 40 years as a naval analyst for the Congressional Research Service.
“That can increase the time and cost to do the maintenance and repair work, and an increased time needed to do the work could prevent other ships from entering maintenance and overhaul as scheduled. This can lead to a cascading effect in delaying maintenance on other ships.”
A Navy officer with expertise in maritime security agreed, noting that “even deployed ships need time alongside”—that is, moored directly to a pier or tender vessel for what’s called voyage repair availability—“to fix broken things, remediate rust, paint, etc. If these ships are kept out for 10 to 12 months, they’ll be missing other scheduled maintenance events and be much more broken than they should be when they get home.”
The Navy itself nodded to the problem in a recent press release about the aircraft carrier Abraham Lincoln, which is changing homeports to receive overdue depot-level maintenance after a nearly 11-month deployment.
“Regularly scheduled depot-level maintenance maximizes the lifespan of our Navy vessels and keeps our fleets lethal, modern, and ready to defend the nation.”
The Lincoln’s 321-day deployment—and the carrier Gerald R. Ford’s 326-day deployment before it—set records for consecutive days at sea and length of deployment, respectively. But a few Arleigh Burke-class guided missile destroyers are on track to far surpass those numbers. And Navy officials recently told families in Yokosuka, Japan, that for the foreseeable future they should expect all ships to deploy for 10 to 12 months.
A Navy spokesperson said they would “not discuss specific readiness rates, operational requirements, force-allocation deliberations, or future force movements. However, we remain committed to regular maintenance to maximize the lifespan of our Navy vessels and keep our fleets lethal and ready to defend our nation.”
‘It’s empty’
Instead of the luxury hotels and hundreds of restaurants sailors can visit in ports like Dubai and Bahrain, Diego Garcia has a military supply base and a small town with a handful of restaurants. And since virtually every ship deployed in the region is using the island for port calls and resupply, store shelves don’t always stay stocked.
The guided-missile destroyer John Finn, which left Japan in January, pulled into Diego Garcia after months at sea.
“Everybody’s going to the ship store and it’s empty,” a sailor’s spouse told Defense One. “You can find ice cream, but you’re not going to find your necessities that you need to function.”
The ship had pulled in because it was “empty,” the spouse said, after having spent all of its weapons in the campaign against Iran. “So they had to spend that week resupplying.”
The spouse of a sailor on the Mustin, another guided-missile destroyer, said her husband was able to get socks but not shoe polish at the exchange on base during the only port call the ship has made since leaving Japan in April.
“He got off like, preparing to be able to get the stuff that he needed right now, and he goes, ‘They don’t have shit,’” she said. “They didn’t have anything.”
For the Mustin crew, the port call seemed like a welcome respite from their months at sea, until they were told just before getting off the ship that they would not return in August as originally planned, but stay deployed until April 2027, the spouse told Defense One.
“The sad part is, they were actually in good spirits,” she said. “And then I know things went really rowdy in Diego Garcia because they were given the bad news literally the day before they pulled in. … There was one of the nights in Diego Garcia that two sailors ended up in the ER with alcohol poisoning. And so then they lost their last night of liberty because of it.”
O’Rourke said the British island “can provide an opportunity to be on land for a while, and to engage in certain R&R activities. But the options for doing R&R things at Diego Garcia are a lot more limited than they are at other ports, such as Singapore or somewhere in the Mediterranean.”
Ralph Cossa, chairman of the Pacific Forum, was less diplomatic.
“Please shoot me if that’s the only R&R I’m going to get in 10 months,” he said.
Mail delays
Sailors have asked their families and friends to send them supplies, but mail is taking three to six months to reach the destroyers, the spouses said.
The Mustin spouse sent her husband six boxes at the end of June; he received one in September and the rest in October. The John Finn spouse said it took four months for a few packages to reach her sailor, and some that “took even longer than six months to get out there.”

Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said.
Official data released in the last week, external show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%.
The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole.
The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say.
China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children.
The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population.
At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under.
No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy.
The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said.
"It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying.
The demographic shift is "symbolic" and could suggest more public spending will move from families and schools to pensions and healthcare, said Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.
It may also pose a challenge to the country's ambitions, as it could limit its economic growth as well as people's spending power, said National University of Singapore sociology lecturer Mu Zheng.
China's ageing population has been driven by a mix of factors, including rapid urbanisation and the effects of the controversial one-child policy, which was in place from 1980 to the end of 2015.
The strategy, designed to keep China's rapid population growth under control, is estimated by the country's government to have prevented about 400 million births since it began, though this number has been contested.
The policy played a key role in shrinking the population and means there are fewer younger people to support a growing number of elderly relatives, Mu said.
But despite easing restrictions on the size of families, Beijing has struggled to persuade couples to have more children, with birth rates hitting historic lows.
Other contributing factors include changing gender roles, rising living costs and higher education levels that have put pressure on fertility rates, Mu said.
Beijing made further support for older people a part of the measures in its five-year economic blueprint that was announced earlier this year.
Financial help for pensioners has been a growing part of Chinese government spending. More than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior citizen allowances and subsidies by the end of 2025, according to official figures.
The Global Times noted that many people entering old age who were born between the 1950s and the 1970s have generally higher incomes compared to previous generations, stronger purchasing power and are healthier.
The dependency ratio is widely-used to measure ageing populations but it has also been questioned by some experts who argue that its scope is too limited.
Gietel-Basten said the use of the statistics risks "taking agency away" from older people - many of whom he says have been misrepresented as dependants.
It also does not take into account improvements to healthcare, he added.

9707f03ffdf3.text: By — Susan Montoya Bryan, Associated Press Susan Montoya Bryan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/dolores-huerta-labor-and-civil-rights-icon-dies-at-96 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Dolores Huerta, labor and civil rights icon, dies at 96 Nation Oct 28, 2026 12:36 PM EDT Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers union to improve working conditions in the nation's fruit and vegetable fields and coined the phrase "Sí, se puede!" that became a widespread rallying cry, has died. She was 96. Huerta's family said in a statement through her foundation that she died Wednesday at home. READ MORE: For feminists, the deaths of Parton and Steinem days apart deliver a double dose of grief She kept a busy schedule well into her 90s, marching in protests and speaking in cities across the country about race, poverty, LGBTQ+ and women's rights on behalf of her Bakersfield, California-based foundation. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Huerta's resolve cemented her place in history as one of the nation's most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists. Her three-word Spanish-language slogan — which translates to "Yes, it can be done" — was grounded in the belief that people could affect change. WATCH: Still an Activist at 82, Dolores Huerta Calls Herself 'a Born-Again Feminist' Her work over the decades earned her a number of accolades, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor. When then-President Barack Obama presented the award in 2012, he praised Huerta as a tenacious leader and joked that he had stolen her slogan for his 2008 campaign. This year, Huerta sent shockwaves through the Latino community when she revealed that she was sexually abused in the 1960s by the farmworker movement's co-founder, César Chavez, leading to the birth of two children, a secret she kept for 60 years and long after he died. Dolores Huerta of the United Farmworkers joins Dick Gregory, National Organization of Women President Patricia Ireland, the Rev. Jesse Jackson and actor Danny Glover during the 1996 "Fight the Right March" organized by NOW. Photo by Lou Dematteis/Reuters From the early 1970s on, Huerta's life partner was Richard Chavez, César's brother, and together they had four kids. She also had seven children from two earlier marriages. Huerta said she had kept silent for so long because she feared that coming forward would compromise her life's work and unravel all the progress made for workers. When asked during a 2026 interview with the news organization Latino USA about keeping the secret, Huerta said: "It was my personal pain, it was my personal problem and, you know, I think it was worth it because it was my cross to bear. I'll say it that way." Homegrown activism Huerta was born Dolores Clara Fernandez in 1930 in Dawson, New Mexico. Her father was a miner and union activist who went on to win a seat in the state Legislature. Her parents divorced when she was 3, and her mother took her and her brothers to California. Immersed in a melting pot of Mexican, Filipino, African American, Japanese and Chinese working families, Huerta learned from her mother — who owned a restaurant and hotel — about independence, compassion and activism. Huerta was a young, energetic elementary school teacher in the farm-rich San Joaquin Valley when she decided to answer another calling after growing frustrated by her students' poor living conditions. READ MORE: Labor rights leader Dolores Huerta says she was sexually abused by César Chavez "I couldn't stand seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes," she said in a 2017 PBS Independent Lens documentary on her life. "I thought I could do more by organizing farmworkers than by trying to teach their hungry children." Huerta's early work with a civil rights group in Stockton resulted in her meeting Chavez. The two wanted to focus more on the plight of farmworkers, so in 1962 they started the National Farm Workers Association, which became United Farm Workers of America a few years later. She was a key leader and negotiator for the union for years. She was among those who joined Filipino grape pickers on the picket line in what became the five-year "Delano Grape Strike." With Chavez, she negotiated collective bargaining agreements and contracts with big growers, winning the first health and benefit plans for farmworkers. WATCH: Communities rebrand César Chavez Day as abuse allegations taint his legacy Chavez, who died in 1993, once described her as fearless, committed to the cause and tough when it came to negotiations. On the campaign trail She met Sen. Robert Kennedy of Massachusetts during his visit to Delano in 1968 and became a volunteer on his presidential campaign, registering Mexican Americans in California to vote. Huerta was on stage with Kennedy after he won the California primary and he publicly thanked her moments before he was shot. The assassination devastated Huerta, but she kept organizing for farmworkers' rights. Huerta was jailed 22 times for union demonstrating. In 1988, she was seriously injured while protesting Republican presidential candidate George H.W. Bush's opposition to the UFW grape boycott during his visit to San Francisco. Caught in a crowd, she was struck by a police officer's baton, suffered three broken ribs and a pulverized spleen, and required more than a dozen blood transfusions. She reached a settlement with the city to resolve her claims. After a long recovery, Huerta shifted focus and hit the road to campaign for women's rights and encourage Latinas to run for office. She also campaigned for Democratic Presidents Bill Clinton, Obama and Joe Biden. California Gov. Gavin Newsom considered

The Scoop
PsiQuantum is building its first product. It isnât a quantum computer, but it could become a superpower for AI data centers.
The company has been working for a decade on building quantum computers that use photons as âbitsâ of information and has built its own optical chips that control light particles with extreme precision. That ability to manipulate light could turn out to be a marketable tool in the next phase of the AI race, where data centers, bottlenecked by the limits of copper wiring, are switching to using fiber optics instead.
PsiQuantum says it has been showing potential customers a prototype of a new âoptical circuit switchâ that could be used to route optical signals from GPUs across data centers much more efficiently.
Know More
The AI boom wouldnât have happened without the ability to network hundreds of thousands of AI processors together. But all that networking is also the data centerâs weakest link. While GPUs can crunch numbers at blazing speeds, they are bottlenecked by the comparatively slow copper that carries the output of that math from GPU to GPU.
Thatâs especially true during the training process of increasingly large AI models that require the most coordination between large numbers of GPUs.
The next generation of data center racks are more often using optical cables to carry the data between GPUs. But optical information must be converted into an electrical signal in order to be routed to its destination, then converted back into light, before itâs converted once again when it reaches its destination.
All those conversions happening billions of times per second in the largest data centers require optical switches that generate heat, energy and bulk.
PsiQuantum says its new device can do that without ever having to convert the photons into electrical signals. It could be used to create speed-of-light connections between server racks in AI data centers that generate almost no heat and consume negligible energy.
The only major hyperscaler currently using purely optical circuit switching in an AI data center today is Google, which built a system that uses tiny mirrors, known as MEMS, to direct the light signal.
Robert Soderbery, executive vice president of PsiQuantum, said in an interview with Semafor that separate data center racks will effectively behave as one, using PsiQuantumâs device. Data could flow between GPUs in separate server racks at the same speed and latency as they would between GPUs interconnected inside a single rack. That would be a huge advantage because today server racks are reaching the limit of compute density, size and energy efficiency.
PsiQuantum isnât alone. The battle to convert data center networking to photonics has been raging since the ChatGPT moment kicked off the AI race. Earlier this year, photonic computing company Lightmatter helped launch an initiative to standardize optics in the data center space. Nvidia has been spending billions on investments in optics computing companies like Lumentum and Coherent.
For now, the GPU reigns supreme but data centers are seeing a lot more of the light.

- Published
US civil rights leader Dolores Huerta has died at the age of 96, her family has announced.
Huerta campaigned alongside fellow labour leader Cesar Chavez for farm workers' rights in the 1960s and 1970s, founding the United Farm Workers Union (UFW) with him.
Through her foundation, Huerta had continued her activism work addressing immigration and voting issues.
"As you can imagine, this is an incredibly difficult time for us, and we ask for privacy as we grieve this incredible loss to our family," family spokesman Erik Olvera said on Wednesday.
Earlier this year, Huerta said Chavez, who died in 1993, had "manipulated and pressured" her into having sex and on another occasion forced her in the 1960s.
That was after the New York Times published an investigation detailing allegations from Huerta and two other women, who said Chavez groomed and sexually abused girls involved in the labour movement.
Huerta said the two encounters with Chavez resulted in pregnancies that she chose to keep these secret, arranging for the children to be raised by other families.
Chavez's family said in a statement at the time that they were "devastated" by the reports and praised the women's "courage to come forward".

9c882b45720e.text:
Davidâs view
The day Jeffrey Epstein died, I was at the Iowa State Fair hearing from presidential candidates, and he was not exactly on their minds.
When left-wing podcasters asked 2020 hopefuls if theyâd probe the circumstances of the convicted sex offenderâs death, a few looked rattled. Theyâd prepped for so many questions, but not this. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn. was an exception, questioning how a man on suicide watch could hang himself. She also had to explain, for some reporters, what she was talking about: âThis was a sex trafficking scheme.â
Voters no longer need refreshers on Epstein. Democrats have run hundreds of ads this cycle linking their opponents to the disgraced financier, worth tens of millions of dollars. Iâm not the first take-slinger to ask whether this is the âEpstein election.â
Iâm here to answer with the reason why the message is working. This is the most expensive midterm election ever. Weâve witnessed the biggest donation in American history by one man (Elon Musk) to help one candidate (Ken Paxton). For the first time, off-year elections have attracted more cash than was spent to win the presidential race two years earlier.
The very wealthy can spend unlimited sums on campaigns, and while plenty of candidates denounce this â âoverturn Citizens Unitedâ will thrill the audience at any Democratic town hall â thereâs no serious effort to pass a constitutional amendment that would shrink that voice. Thatâs where Epstein comes in.
Many Americans are predisposed to think that wealthy people earned their money and that itâs churlish to try to take it away from them. But itâs easier than ever to argue that some ultra-wealthy people are strange, selfish, and even evil. Democrats, the GOP pollster Patrick Ruffini wrote this week, exploited the âconspiratorial, anti-system tendencies in the electorateâ and found a much sharper weapon to swing at Republicans.
If this pays off for Democrats, serious credit will be due to California Rep. Ro Khanna. As a co-chair of the 2020 Bernie Sanders campaign, he saw how clarifying it could be for audiences to hear that billionaires were hoarding wealth while most people struggled. After President Donald Trump promised to release Epstein case files but didnât, Khanna and Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., found the votes to force it last year.
The files didnât take down the Trump presidency. But Khanna found a framework for anti-billionaire populism in battling the âEpstein class.â
âThe Epstein class has become a symbol [of] how the wealthy and powerful rig the system to avoid accountability and enrich themselves,â Khanna told me as he campaigned for the Democratic challenger in a Wisconsin seat Trump won by 5 points.
This theme aligned with what Democrats wanted to do anyway: run against Republicans as pawns of the ultra-wealthy. Why wouldnât the GOP slow data center construction? Billionaires. Why wasnât Congress bringing down costs for regular people? Billionaires.
When Trump was on the ballot, it helped Republicans that he was perceived as so wealthy that other billionaires couldnât influence him. Democrats struggled to land the anti-plutocrat attacks that worked against Mitt Romney because prominent billionaires and corporate leaders refused to support Trump.
That changed after Trump returned to power last year, and Democrats got comfortable again with populism. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, who picked up the âEpstein classâ term from Khanna, pointed to its presence at Trumpâs inauguration: âThey are the elites they pretend to hate.â
If Democrats have a good Tuesday, their willingness to run against vast wealth and suggest that thereâs something evil about it will have proven essential. âIf youâre a billionaire, Ohio looks picture-perfect,â Ohioâs Amy Acton says in one of her final ads â one of several, from her allies, that go after GOP gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy for the crime of flying a private jet.
And when former President Barack Obama headlined a Michigan rally with Abdul El-Sayed, an attendee shouted affirmation back at him: âObamaâs not on the Epstein files, either!â
El-Sayed pointed and smiled at the man. He let the applause ring out.
Room for Disagreement
Republicans have some substantive rebuttals to this line of attack. Hadnât the president jawboned other billionaires into funding child investment accounts? Wasnât everyone invested in tech stocks getting richer?
Not as rich as the people who had money already. In fact, the best counter to the anti-billionaire line has proven to be â¦ turning it on Democrats.
In Wisconsin, and other places where LinkedIn founder Reid Hoffman has funded Democratic PACs, Republicans attacked Hoffmanâs friendship with Epstein and asked why Democrats werenât giving back his money. When Abdul El-Sayed fundraised with members of the Soros family, Republicans said his campaign trail rhetoric about money in politics was a ruse.
Notable
- Katie Phang, a journalist whoâs sued DOJ over redactions in Epstein file releases, wrote in the Guardian about their impact on the elections.
- Politicoâs Playbook looked at whether you could call this the âEpstein election,â with Democratic strategists very happy that candidates adopted their âcorruptionâ framing.

ec0d7a6134fe.text:
The Scoop
Even with the political wind at their backs for this midterm, Democrats still arenât sparking enthusiasm among low-propensity voters. So when doorknockers for the countryâs largest hospitality union fan out in swing states, they donât start by mentioning the party.
UNITE HERE, which boasts more than 300,000 members across the country, tells its organizers to zero in on votersâ personal financial situations before seeking support for Democratic candidates. In Texas, a doorknocker for the union might reference last yearâs Hilton Americas-Houston hotel strike before pivoting to telling a voter that Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico and gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa supported workersâ drive for a higher wage.
âThatâs more what we find effective, because there is an apathy about Democrats in general,â Gwen Mills, UNITE HEREâs president, told Semafor. âWe talk about the agency that workers and working-class people have to change their lives through their union, and then through voting. Thatâs a different angle into having a conversation about the election.â
Itâs a sign that Democrats still have work to do nationally to rebuild their brand, and it also reveals the messages voters are hearing right before Election Day on pocketbook issues that are dominating the national mood.
UNITE HERE is well-known for its heft in Nevada, where the hospitality union has played a massive role in Democratsâ turnout machine over the past two decades. Itâs still playing in the Silver State, working to flip back the governorâs office from GOP control and hold the stateâs three battleground House districts.
The union is also working to bring its economic message to more than a million households across a broader array of races in Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Maine, Michigan, Mississippi, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Texas. UNITE HERE has focused its persuasion project on reaching low-propensity voters â the bloc that often swings elections â by talking about workersâ issues.
Low-propensity voters, pollsters have found, often think the system is âriggedâ against them and are highly skeptical of both parties.
âWeâre talking to people who really feel left behind by the political system,â Mills said. âTheyâre working-class voters. And I think they see, whether they voted for Trump or Biden, right, or for Democrats or Republicans, theyâre like: âThis system is failing us.ââ
The campaign is taking UNITE HERE to unusual places, like Floridaâs 27th District, which GOP Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar won by 20 points in 2024. The union is running a Spanish-language canvass there in support of Democrat Eliott Rodriguez, a tough slog in South Florida where the Republican brand is still strong.
But though the union wants to win that race and other battleground seats, its work in Florida isnât just about the midterms. Mills described a hope to get out ahead of larger demographic shifts already underway in American politics.
âWhen the Census happens in 2030, youâre going to have a shift in the electoral college â¦ [moving] seats in Congress out of states like New York and California, into states like Florida and Texas, and really across the Sun Belt,â Mills said. âWeâre certainly focused on building the infrastructure in those places.â
Room for Disagreement
The hospitality union is not explicitly partisan and said that it could support pro-union Republicans in a future election. But not this year.
âIn the past, we certainly supported Republicans, and we could in the future,â Mills said. âBut thereâs a particular moment here, and folks who arenât standing up to the brutality of these policies that are being passed donât get excused.â
Burgessâs view
Millions of dollars of ad buys can only do so much to reach voters. Itâs doorknockers like those working for UNITE HERE â and conservative organizations like Americans for Prosperity â that are doing the hard work behind the scenes to persuade voters.
No one factor will be decisive, but if thereâs an archetype of this yearâs swing voter, itâs the folks this union is trying to reach: low-propensity voters who hate both parties.
Notable
- UNITE HERE and state AFL-CIOs and their affiliates are targeting swing voters in several states with the âContract with Working Americans,â a populist economic platform they devised independently of the national AFL-CIO, Semaforâs Brendan Ruberry reports.

9a35ccd40e0b.text: By — Cara Anna, Associated Press Cara Anna, Associated Press By — Areej Hazboun, Associated Press Areej Hazboun, Associated Press By — Audrey Horowitz, Associated Press Audrey Horowitz, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/israelis-await-final-election-results-as-netanyahu-rivals-weigh-joining-forces-with-arab-parties Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Israelis await final election results as Netanyahu rivals weigh joining forces with Arab parties World Oct 28, 2026 11:58 AM EDT JERUSALEM (AP) — Anxious Israelis watched election results near completion Wednesday after the highest voter turnout in over a quarter-century, as no clear winner emerged and weeks of negotiating could lie ahead for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and an array of opposition parties trying to unseat him. READ MORE: No clear winner in Israeli election, exit polls indicate, as Netanyahu's fate hangs in the balance Arab-led parties made a historic showing, but it's not clear if other opponents of Netanyahu's far-right government would form a coalition with them for a majority of seats in parliament. Issues around the Palestinians and their descendants remain incredibly sensitive in Israel. Netanyahu seeks to remain the country's longest-serving prime minister. In defiant comments after the vote — which showed his Likud party losing ground since the 2022 election — he dismissed as treasonous the idea of partnering with Arab parties. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. On Wednesday, Netanyahu warned against a "dangerous government" that might include them. He won't work with the Arab-led parties, whose constituents make up 20% of Israel's population, and they have also ruled out any partnership with him. READ MORE: Why it could be weeks or months before Israel's election winner is known His top challenger, centrist former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has left the door open to partnering with Arab parties under certain conditions, including their recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and of Hamas as an extremist group. But it's not clear whether some of Eisenkot's likely partners who have ruled out such an alliance will change their minds to force Netanyahu from office. Israeli voters choose parties, not individuals. With 85% of votes counted, Netanyahu's Likud party has 20.8% and Eisenkot's Yashar party has 16.1%. The official count does not indicate how many seats each will have in parliament, the 120-seat Knesset. Emerging results indicated that neither Netanyahu's nor Eisenkot's coalition blocs would reach the 61 seats needed for a majority; local media projected 53 seats for Likud and allied parties, 48 for Yashar and allied parties and 19 for Arab-led parties. Netanyahu faces a setback but not outright defeat Nearly 78% of eligible voters turned out, the highest since 1999. Final results are expected by the end of the week, and will capture about a half-million absentee ballots yet to be counted from military personnel and diplomats. Voting reflected unease over Netanyahu's alliance with the far-right and anger in a war-weary nation over military draft exemptions for the significant ultra-Orthodox Jewish population; the Likud party's share of the vote declined from 23.4% in 2022. But results suggest opponents were unable to capitalize on the grief caused by the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack to decisively push him from office. WATCH: Projections show no clear winner in Israel's election One far-right partner losing support was national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. For many Israelis, he represented the worst strain of Netanyahu's government, openly taunting Palestinian detainees and asserting that many in Gaza are "not even people." Vote-counting suggested Likud would remain the largest party and best placed to be tapped to form a government by Israel's president, Isaac Herzog. The president, however, isn't required to task the leader of the party holding the most seats. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections," Herzog said Wednesday. The most obvious path to a parliamentary majority could involve Eisenkot partnering with Arab-led parties — which have 14.9% of the votes counted — but that's politically challenging. In a speech early Wednesday that focused on national unity, Eisenkot pledged to form a government and promised "a new era — an era of hope." If no one can put together a majority coalition, new elections could be held early next year. Israel held five elections between April 2019 and November 2022 because of a similar stalemate. It is unclear whether thousands of Israelis living abroad would again fly back home to vote, and whether Arab voters would again surge to the polls. Minority governments also are possible, but they must rely on cooperation from parties outside the government to pass legislation. Arab-led parties could hold the key Confronted with Arab parties' strong election showing, Israelis have renewed a debate about identity. "We have no future here if we do not stop being afraid," said Yair Golan, whose Democrats party supports bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition. "We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes." Israel's Arab citizens are descendants of Palestinians who remained in the state after its creation in 1948. They often face discrimination and are viewed with wariness because of their solidarity with the Palestinian cause. That suspicion intensified after Oct. 7, even though Arab citizens were also among those killed and abducted. dd6746a93cf3.text: Dolores Huerta , the pioneering labor organizer who co-founded the United Farm Workers and coined the rallying cry "Sí, se puede," died Wednesday at 96, her family announced on her Instagram account. Why it matters: The civil rights legend helped lead strikes and boycotts, fought to expand rights for Hispanic Americans and became a powerful kingmaker in politics. What they're saying: "We are deeply saddened to announce that our beloved mother, Dolores Huerta, has passed away today at the age of 96," her family wrote in a statement posted on Instagram . "As you can imagine, this is an incredibly difficult time for us, and we ask for privacy as we grieve this incredible loss to our family. We know that many of you around the world share in our mourning, and we will be following up on plans to recognize and celebrate her incredible life and legacy." This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

32901d0fcf13.text: By — Joseph Wilson, Associated Press Joseph Wilson, Associated Press By — Iain Sullivan, Associated Press Iain Sullivan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/dozens-dead-in-spain-after-high-speed-train-slams-into-another-stopped-on-tracks Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Dozens dead in Spain after high-speed train slams into another stopped on tracks World Oct 28, 2026 11:41 AM EDT URDA, Spain (AP) — One high-speed Spanish train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks Wednesday, killing at least 68 people and shredding carriages in the country's second deadly rail collision this year. The regional government for Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people needed medical treatment in hospital. Rescue workers continue to search in the wreckage for survivors and bodies. READ MORE: Barcelona commuter train crash kills 1, days after deadly train collision in Spain The accident comes with memories still fresh of another crash between high-speed trains in southern Spain in January involving trains from the same two companies. Spain's rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo, involving two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain. One train, run by the state-owned RENFE company, ran into the tail of the other train owned by private company IRYO that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track in a rural area between two villages. READ MORE: What to know about Spain's housing protests sparked by an 87-year-old woman's eviction David Gómez, a construction worker, was working with his brother and another colleague nearby when they heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El País. "People were trying to get out through the windows ... We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought," until emergency services arrived, he said. "As I was trying to pull a young woman out, there was a piece of a leg." Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia. Until this year, there had been no fatal crash on Spain's dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992. It was a source of national pride. Transport minister says crash was due to 'inexplicable' decision Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said that the accident was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command center for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame. Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped IRYO train at 8:53 a.m. Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed. Puente said they were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph (124 mph) for that stretch of the track. "I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts," Puente said. Everything went flying when the trains collided, a passenger said The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left one car torn into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope. Spanish Health Minister Mónica García said that emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and bodies from the two most damaged train cars. She said that the injured are being sent to different hospitals in the area. "It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said. Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO. "We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact," he said. "The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook." Another passenger recounted to Cadena Ser radio how she felt the train slam on the brakes and was thrown forward in her seat, breaking the small table in front of her. She said she saw body parts and trapped people covered in blood. Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train. IRYO, an Italian-owned company, said in a statement that it has "activated its security protocols and is closely working with authorities." The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, said civil protection authorities had asked his officials to prepare a sports pavilion to receive injured passengers. A military emergency brigade was deployed to help emergency services, firefighters and police. Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while unscathed survivors were put on buses. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez canceled his agenda to focus on the crash. He wrote on X that he was "dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo." "Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers," wrote Sánchez, who faces a national election next month. "All my thoughts are with the victims and their families." Spain's King Felipe VI visited the crash site. He and Queen Letizia said in a short statement on X that they were following news of the accident. Two trains have collided in Spain just south of the capital Madrid on Wednesday morning.
Rail operator Adif says the incident occurred between a Renfe train and another of the Iryo company, which covers the Madrid to Seville route.
So far at least 68 people are confirmed to have died in the incident.
Here is what we know about the crash so far.
Where and when did the crash happen?
The two trains collided just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) between municipalities Mora and Orgaz, and about 140km (100 miles) south of Madrid.
The accident happened when a high-speed train travelling from Madrid to the south of the country collided with another train that was apparently stationary. The crash caused at least two carriages to fall down an embankment.
Broadcaster RTVE, quoting the transport ministry, said a Renfe train rear-ended an Iryo train.
Renfe is Spain's national state-owned railway company while Iryo is a private high-speed railway operator.
All train traffic on this line has been stopped at stations along the route, Adif said.
Renfe said services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia remain suspended.
A passenger on board one of the trains told local media there was a heavy impact about 40 minutes into the journey.
What caused the crash?
Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by a Renfe train "due to causes that are still unknown.
Transport minister Oscar Puente has said a computer failure led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
"In the event of a system failure, the control centre takes over," he said, adding it was the control centre which decided to allow the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.
That decision, Puente said, was made "under inexplicable circumstances". It resulted in the Renfe train crashing into the Iryo train, which was stationary on the tracks further ahead.
How many passengers were on board?
More than 500 people were believed to be on board both trains.
Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the government of Castilla-La Mancha region, told TVE that one of the trains - managed by the Iryo company - was carrying 146 passengers plus one baby, while the Renfe-managed train had 397 passengers on board.
A former government minister was also among those reported missing.
The Spanish Confederation of Business Organizations (CEOE) posted on X that, FÃ¡tima BÃ¡Ã±ez - who heads the organization's foundation - was on board one of the trains involved in the crash.
The Castilla La Mancha regional government said 64 people are now confirmed to have died.
Speaking separately to Spanish media, he warned the death toll could increase further.
Eighty people are being treated for injuries, according to authorities, with 50 of the casualties said to be in a serious condition, and 15 more in a critical condition.
How have the authorities responded?
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has said "the whole of Spain is grieving" and that "lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart".
"The pain is immense," he said on a visit to the crash site.
The government was "trying to determine what was the origin of this tragedy, of this terrible accident," he added.
"We will get to the bottom of this, and if there has been any negligence, it will come to light.
"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."
SÃ¡nchez and other Spanish politicians have cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday, including campaigning for next month's parliamentary elections.
Spain's royal family posted on X that it was "shocked and concerned" and expressed condolences for the relatives of the deceased and those affected by the crash.
A spokesperson for the EU said the bloc was ready to help Spain if needed.
A huge emergency response is under way with fire crews and helicopters at the scene.
Hospitals in the area have suspended planned surgeries as they deal with an influx of patients from the crash, Spanish media have reported.
A blood transfusion centre in Madrid has also appealed for "urgent" donations. In a post on X, Centro de TransfusiÃ³n said it made the request "in the face of a possible sudden increase in care needs".
It reported that facilities in Toledo, Ciudad Real and AlcÃ¡zar de San Juan have cancelled procedures as casualties from the crash begin to arrive.
This is the second high-speed rail tragedy in Spain this year.
In January a high-speed train derailed in southern Spain, its rear carriages going into the path of a state-run Renfe train, claiming the lives of 46 people.
