An estimated three-quarters of NFL players who died in a 16-year period had the devastating neurogenerative disease called CTE.
Back in 2017, researchers reported that an estimated 99 percent of former NFL players developed CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, from an analysis of donated brains. But the families who provided the donations may have done so because their football-playing relatives had symptoms related to CTE, which could skew the results. A new study, which accounts for this potential bias, estimates that nearly 75 percent of former NFL players have CTE at death. It’s the first population-level estimate for NFL players, researchers report October 28 in JAMA Network Open.
The development of CTE is linked to repeated blows to the head over time. The disease can occur in people who play contact sports, experience intimate partner violence or engage in military combat. A study of American football players suggests that the longer the duration of repeated head trauma, the higher the risk of CTE and the more severe the condition. During life, people who are later diagnosed with CTE can experience symptoms including memory issues, difficulty concentrating, depression and poor impulse control.
A brain protein called tau, which usually helps nerve cells communicate and performs other jobs, goes awry in CTE. Brains with the disease are snarled with irregular, damaging clumps of the protein. The condition is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy, and has been identified most frequently among American football players.
The new study, by a Boston University research team, included all previous NFL players who passed away from January 2008 through December 2023. The more than 2,300 players included almost 400 with samples in the university’s UNITE Brain Bank, with the remainder identified from records in the U.S. National Death Index. The research team determined that families of NFL players who had CTE-related symptoms in life were five times more likely to donate their relative’s brain than families whose relative did not experience symptoms. Taking that into consideration, the team landed on a population-level CTE estimate for NFL players of 74.5 percent.
The research team notes that determining the true prevalence of CTE is important to understanding the public health impact of the disease.

b4907d52bf2a.text: TEL AVIV, Israel — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's electoral coalition opened a sizable lead over Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc with 85 percent of the vote counted. But while Netanyahu outperformed exit polls, which had Eisenkot's opposition coalition ahead, neither bloc will clear a 61-seat majority. That sets the stage for weeks of wrangling over the country's next government. Why it matters: Netanyahu will emerge from the election down but not out. His bloc is on pace to secure 53 seats — 11 fewer than he currently commands. But Eisenkot's bloc trails with 48 seats, leaving both men without a clear mandate to lead a government. While Eisenkot could theoretically swear in a government with the support of Arab parties — which are on track to secure a record-breaking 19 seats — such a scenario is highly unlikely. The intrigue: The actual vote count significantly boosted Netanyahu's standing compared to initial exit polls, which showed Eisenkot's bloc ahead. President Trump told Axios in a brief interview Wednesday that at first he received "horror reports" about Netanyahu's prospects. But "he's in pretty good shape now," Trump said. "I heard my endorsement made a big difference for Bibi," he added. Asked whether he is going to get involved in an effort to form a Netanyahu-led unity government, Trump said he hadn't thought about it. "I will take a look," he said. State of play: There are 500,000 votes left to be counted, from soldiers, diplomats, prisoners and others who voted outside their designated area. These votes could slightly shift the blocs' seat totals or the allotment of seats within each bloc. But they are unlikely to change the overall balance of power. Driving the news: Israeli President Isaac Herzog will begin consulting next week with the different parties before issuing a mandate to either Netanyahu or Eisenkot to form a government. "We must do everything possible, especially after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to arrive with an open mind," Herzog said on Wednesday. If neither side can assemble a majority, a new round of elections would be scheduled as early as April. Between the lines: Herzog could try to persuade Netanyahu and Eisenkot to form a unity government, but Netanyahu doesn't seem interested in that. On Tuesday night, he called for a "strong right-wing government." Netanyahu will likely try to convince one of the opposition leaders to cross over to him. All of them, however, committed publicly before the election not to do that. Under another scenario, Eisenkot could try to form a minority government with outside support from the Arab parties. But such a government could collapse quickly and lead to a Netanyahu victory in the next elections. On the other hand, allowing Netanyahu to remain on as a caretaker prime minister until the next elections could also lead to defeat for the opposition bloc in the next elections. It would give Netanyahu's bloc more time to organize and ease its divisions. For Netanyahu, staying as caretaker prime minister until new elections are held could be the best option. It would leave him with almost full powers to direct Israel's national security and foreign policy and move forward with renewed war against Iran. What to watch: The opposition will likely take over key positions in the Knesset after the new parliament is sworn in next week. That would allow Eisenkot and his partners to install a Knesset speaker, control the legislative agenda and pass laws they agree on — such as forming a national commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to the October 7 attacks.

9787c344d78d.text: With less than a week until a potentially historic midterm election , the political discourse is being dominated not by war or seismic shifts in technology, but by the Cheesecake Factory . The big picture: Culture wars regularly swarm American political discussions, especially when the jibes are personal. Former President Obama's passing joke over the weekend about Cheesecake Factory decor did just that — by criticizing President Trump 's personal taste and style. "He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory," Obama said, poking fun at the president's controversial White House renovations . Zoom in: John Murphy, professor emeritus at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign who studies political rhetoric, tells Axios that the first time he heard Obama's comment, he "really did think, 'this is going to go somewhere.'" That's both because of the messenger and the butt of the joke: Obama "can get under Trump's skin like no one else in the world can," he says. Obama knows all too well how seemingly trivial moments can blow up; in 2014, he wore a tan suit instead of a black one to discuss foreign policy, and years later his sartorial choices remain a political talking point. The tan suit has its own Wikipedia page , and still nets pop culture references . State of play: Days after Obama's quip, the news cycle and social media are still serving up the joke, and the White House posted "Lo-fi" beats accompanied by a cartoon image of Trump in front of a Cheesecake Factory. Conservative critics used the jab to paint Obama as elitist. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , a multimillionaire, criticized Obama outside a Cheesecake Factory, saying he "had a great meal, and I would tell the Martha's Vineyard set to give it a try." Murphy notes that framing comes from a classic red v. blue playbook to paint Democrats as "elitist." "It's a conscious strategy, I think, on the part of conservative media to gin up culture-war arguments," he says. The other side: Trump's pushback, however, has centered less on the class divide seized by some members of conservative media — and more on his White House renovations. "We have to explain to Obama that the White House is a symbol of America," Trump told reporters Monday. He continued, "Guys like Obama don't see it ... he doesn't see filth. He doesn't see broken ornaments on a building," later adding, "for you to say it's a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president." The White House referred Axios to Trump's previous comments when asked for comment. The bottom line: The fight has also drawn in the restaurant chain itself: Rick McCormack, its former longtime vice president of design, lamented "the pettiness of politics" and told CNN he was disappointed to see the company caught in the dispute. Go deeper: How the Cheesecake Factory got dragged into a midterms food fight

b280382f69ff.text: By — Daniel Kozin, Associated Press Daniel Kozin, Associated Press By — Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/watch-defeated-brazilian-candidate-flavio-bolsonaro-arrives-in-u-s-amid-investigation Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Defeated Brazilian candidate Flávio Bolsonaro arrives in U.S. amid investigation World Oct 28, 2026 10:54 AM EDT MIAMI (AP) — Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and his family landed in Miami on Wednesday after fleeing Brazil. Watch Bolsonaro's arrival in the U.S. in the video player above. The stunning move came after 48 hours in which Bolsonaro refused to concede to Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and then threatened to attempt to annul the election result. READ MORE: Brazil's Flávio Bolsonaro and his family will get U.S. visas after presidential election loss Bolsonaro's father, Jair Bolsonaro, also fled to Florida after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula before returning to Brazil three months later. On Monday, the U.S. said that it would grant visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family. Bolsonaro, a Trump ally, visited the White House in May. Bolsonaro first fled from Brazil to Argentina and then Ecuador alongside his wife and two daughters, Argentina's migration authority said Wednesday — a day after the 45-year-old senator and his family were granted United States visas by the Trump administration. Bolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil's Supreme Court for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in two cases. The court had ordered Bolsonaro to hand over his regular and diplomatic passports by noon Tuesday — two days after he lost the vote to Lula. It remained unclear whether he had complied, but allies said late Tuesday he also has an Italian passport. WATCH: Lula prevails in Brazil but Flávio Bolsonaro refuses to concede Argentina's migration authority said Bolsonaro, his wife Fernanda Antunes Figueira Bolsonaro, and his daughters Carolina Figueira Bolsonaro and Luiza Figueira Bolsonaro crossed into the country at 10:50 p.m. Tuesday. They entered via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, a primary border checkpoint linking Brazil to Argentina's northeastern province of Misiones. "Those who did so possessed valid travel documentation and faced no legal impediments to entering the country," the Argentine migration authority said on X. The authority said that at 11:30 p.m. local time, shortly after clearing immigration control, the four boarded a private charter flight operated by aviation company Baires Fly S.A. According to the filed flight plan, the aircraft departed for Guayaquil, Ecuador. The move is almost certain to cause a big diplomatic rift between Lula and Argentine President Javier Milei, a Trump ally who traveled to Brazil to take part in Bolsonaro's campaign. Bolsonaro lands in Miami Flight tracking website FlightRadar24 showed that a plane fitting the description of Bolsonaro's landed in Guayaquil at about 4 a.m. local time, before taking off minutes later for Miami-Opa locka Executive Airport. The plane carrying Bolsonaro and his family landed in Miami at around 9:30 a.m. EST. Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, told several dozen supporters outside the presidential residence in Brasilia before the plane landed that he didn't have precise information about Bolsonaro's whereabouts, but said he had left Brazil. READ MORE: Lula bucks regional shift to the right and denies Trump a powerful ally in Brazil "I regret that he left Brazil, because he could have stayed here and proven that the accusations are not true," Lula said. "This act of leaving Brazil is shameful." Paulo Figueiredo, a close Bolsonaro ally who lives in the U.S., said in a short statement that he can't confirm information from foreign authorities, but added "Flávio Bolsonaro is well, in security and resting with his family." Figueiredo also said there would be a press conference Thursday in Miami to discuss the case. Representatives of Brazil's government didn't immediately respond to requests for comment from The Associated Press. President Donald Trump said early Wednesday that he would approve of Bolsonaro coming to the U.S., calling him and his family "fine people." "The election was really strange, and I thought it was terrible," Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, after returning from campaigning in Texas on Tuesday. He did not elaborate, but stressed that he didn't endorse the election results. Leaders all over the world and the Organization of American States, or OAS, endorsed the result and congratulated Lula, who was reelected by a margin of about 4.4 million votes in the second and final round. On Tuesday, Milei's administration spokesman Adrián Ravier said "there is no asylum request (from Bolsonaro) and there is nothing more to add." Bolsonaro visited his father, who is under house arrest, before leaving Brazil The defeated candidate was served with a Supreme Court order to surrender his Brazilian passports Monday. In a video, he said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula. After that defeat, Jair Bolsonaro fled Brazil for Florida. He returned three months later. Flávio Bolsonaro said on Monday in a video that he was attempting to organize opposition among his congressional colleagues to the election results. His eight-year term as a senator expires Jan. 31, 2027, which will also cause him to lose special jurisdiction at the country's Supreme Court. Brazil's Supreme Court

55100058e3e5.text: If Democrats gain full control of Congress next week, as many polls and prediction markets suggest they will, private equity could once again find itself in the political crosshairs. The big picture: Private equity has become a rhetorical punching bag for a number of Democratic House and Senate candidates, including in debates and on the stump, as an affordability bête noire. Most of this has related to housing, both single-family and mobile homes, but also has extended to health care. What they're saying: "It's no doubt that housing is way out of control and a big part of that is because private equity has come into Maine," said Troy Jackson in an Oct. 6 debate with Sen. Susan Collins. "I do think we have to go after private equity, make it so that they can't buy these things and charge outrageous prices." Chris Pappas, running for an open Senate seat in New Hampshire, said during a campaign stop at a mobile home community: "We need to... address the housing crisis that we're seeing, including addressing the corporate private equity influence that we're seeing in housing that's making it less affordable and is causing a lot of consternation here at this park." Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) decried PE ownership of residential care facilities during a public event, saying: "Those people know nothing about health care." State of play: Congress passed a bipartisan bill this past summer to restrict PE ownership of single-family homes, with the Treasury Department last week issuing related regulations . The legislation became law despite not being signed by President Trump, who supported it but was in a snit over the Senate not passing his voter identification bill. Zoom in: A Democratic sweep would likely result in Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) taking the Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee gavel, which means she'd go from writing strongly worded letters to holding hearings and guiding legislation. "Americans are sick and tired of private equity's playbook of rolling through industry after industry, jacking up prices and leaving local businesses and workers in the dust," she tells Axios. "After we passed a bipartisan law this year to ban private equity from buying up homes, candidates everywhere are campaigning on reining in private equity in the next Congress, whether in hospitals, mobile home communities, residential care facilities, or other industries." It's also worth noting that Warren has Republican allies when it comes to some of these issues, having worked with Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) on a stalled health bill that has been more endorsed by Senate candidate James Talarico. The bottom line: Private equity has a very successful track record in beating back federal legislation that could hurt its bottom line. What to watch is if past proves to be precedent.

Israel looks to be in political deadlock.
With 85% of votes counted after Tuesday's election, neither the incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition, nor the bloc of his key challenger Gadi Eisenkot look set to have a majority.
In order to form a government, it looks likely one of the leading parties would have to break their campaign promises - meaning the most probable outcome may well be new elections.
Here are four possible scenarios.
National unity government led by Netanyahu
Could Netanyahu persuade Eisenkot to join him in a national unity government?
Eisenkot would have to abandon his key platform to do so. He's framed himself as the only alternative to Netanyahu, and built his campaign on ousting him from power.
Just last night, he took to the stage at his campaign HQ and called on Netanyahu to "announce his retirement from political life today," telling the crowd that Israelis are fed up with Netanyahu's "culture of lies", "division and incitement".
But that was before one of the main exit polls - which had initially projected a lead for Eisenkot's bloc - was revised, and he was overtaken by Netanyahu.
Netanyahu could try to persuade Eisenkot's Yashar Party to join his Likud Party in a unity government by ditching the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties he is currently in coalition with. But last night at Likud HQ he thanked his "loyal partners" and called for a "strong right-wing government"- remarks some have interpreted as meaning he intends to preserve his alliance with them.
One thing that could make a unity government more likely is a renewed conflict with Iran, which could place serious pressure on party leaders to put aside their political differences and work together. In the days prior to the election, Israeli and US media reported that Netanyahu was pushing for fresh strikes on the country, and had pressed Donald Trump to approve US involvement.
This would no-doubt be framed by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to save his own political skin by entering another regional conflict.
Eisenkot-led coalition with Arab parties
This would be a seismic shift for Israeli politics. Only one independent Arab party has ever formally been part of a coalition, in 2021, and it didn't last long.
Eisenkot and every other Jewish party in his bloc bar one have already ruled out entering government with them. But right now, it's the opposition's only path to a majority.
The Arab parties were the story of election night. They look to have defied expectations and could gain a record 19 seats - helped by an unprecedented turnout from Israel's Arab population, who account for about one-fifth of the country and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.
For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout last night, inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, has shaken things up.
The United Arab list, who are currently projected to win around 7 seats, have said they'd join an opposition government, while The Joint List, who are projected to win 12 seats, have said they'd support one from outside.
However, the only Jewish leader advocating this scenario right now is The Democrats' Yair Golan. And a coalition like this would be very fragile, especially on issues like Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
The fact there is such a unified front from the Jewish parties against Arab participation points to Israel's deep divisions.
Netanyahu-led majority, with right-wingers from opposition
Could Netanyahu persuade the right-wing parties in Eisenkot's bloc to break away and join his coalition?
The two most likely candidates for this are Naftali Bennett - joint-leader of the Beyachad political alliance - and Avigdor Lieberman, leader of the Yisrael Beiteinu party. They are both right-wingers who are hardline on security, and share some political ground with Netanyahu.
But both campaigned explicitly to oust him, and to extend military conscription to the ultra-Orthodox - bringing them into direct conflict with the two ultra-Orthodox parties already part of Netanyahu's government. So it's difficult to see them joining forces.
Some have suggested Bennett and Lieberman's parties could replace the ultra-Orthodox parties, but current electoral math suggests that grouping may not have the seats needed for a majority.
New elections
If none of the above scenarios can be negotiated, the default outcome would be new elections.
Many would see this as a tacit win for Netanyahu, who would remain as caretaker PM until the new elections take place - which he may believe he has a better chance of winning.
Some analysts think the high Arab turnout would not be replicated again - especially if their record representation in parliament led to no change - and it could also mobilise more right-wing voters in a second poll. Netanyahu may also bet that the estimated 70,000 Israelis who flew home from abroad to vote, and are thought to skew against him, wouldn't do so again.
Additionally, several right-wing parties who failed to pass the electoral threshold of 3.25% may attract fewer votes or may not even run, thereby bringing more votes to Likud and its allies.
Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five separate elections as Netanyahu and his rivals struggled time and again to co-operate.

006e44426030.text: By — Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/watch-live-fed-chair-warsh-holds-briefing-after-latest-interest-rate-decision Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Fed chair Warsh holds briefing after latest interest rate decision Economy Oct 28, 2026 10:14 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The Federal Reserve is expected to stand pat on interest rates Wednesday even though inflation has accelerated in the past couple of months as the Iran war has caused spikes in oil and gas prices. Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh is expected to hold a news conference at 2:30 p.m. EDT. Watch live in our video player above. The Fed's latest policy meeting concludes less than a week before the midterm elections, which have focused heavily on concerns about the cost of living and affordability. Consumers have generally soured on an economy weighed down by more expensive gas, groceries, and clothing, among other items. READ MORE: Trump promised to stop inflation. Now Republicans may pay the price in the midterm elections The Fed, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, wants to return inflation to its 2% target, which it typically does by raising its short-term interest rate. Higher borrowing costs, over time, can cool spending and slow inflation. The Fed raised its key rate last month for the first time in three years, from about 3.6% to 3.9%, in what many investors and economists perceived was a first step toward a renewed effort to bring down inflation. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Yet Warsh faces a host of challenges in achieving that goal. President Donald Trump slammed the Fed for raising its key rate last month, though he largely blamed the central bank's rate-setting committee, rather than Warsh, whom he appointed. And some of the forces driving inflation — specifically the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure and higher energy prices — won't easily be tamed by higher interest rates. At the same time, other parts of the economy are already being hit by higher rates, which were lifted by market forces, even before the Fed hiked last month. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month, though it has since slipped a bit. Higher mortgage rates have made buying a home unaffordable for 5 million more Americans since the beginning of the year, according to Oxford Economics, a consulting firm. Over time, Fed rate hikes can make mortgages, auto loans, and credit card borrowing more expensive, adding to Americans' sense that things like homes and cars are getting pricier. READ MORE: How much longer will consumers be willing to muscle through higher prices? After the Fed announces its rate decision, Warsh will speak at a news conference, where his remarks will be closely watched for hints about the Fed's next steps. He will likely repeat the Fed's desire for a "timelier" return of inflation to the 2% target. Some may view that as a sign the Fed will boost its key rate at its next meeting, in December, a move already widely expected by Wall Street investors. If the Fed keeps rates on hold, Warsh will be pushed to explain why the central bank hiked in September but not this month. Inflation picked up in September, when consumer prices rose 3.7% compared with a year earlier. The increase was much bigger than the 2.4% rate in February, just before the Iran war. And on a monthly basis, the consumer price index — the most widely-followed inflation gauge — rose 0.3% in both August and September. At that pace over a full year, inflation would rise much more quickly than the Fed's 2% target. On Thursday, a separate inflation measure more closely followed by the Fed, the personal consumption expenditures price index, is forecast to have jumped 3.6% in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August. Core prices, which exclude the food and energy categories, are forecast to have risen 3.1%, up from 3% the previous month. Aditya Bhave, head of U.S. economics at Bank of America, said economists and the Fed have gotten too complacent about above-target inflation. Higher oil and gas prices will likely keep inflation elevated for several more months, he said, and rising diesel costs will elevate shipping prices for nearly every type of good, which could spread inflation more broadly through the economy. "Unless the Fed takes this problem more seriously and stops essentially making excuses about inflation, I think we're not going to get back to 2% until the next recession," Bhave said. Warsh will likely seek to keep the Wednesday press conference relatively short. It was about 30 minutes last month. Warsh's predecessor, Jerome Powell, often held news conferences for about 45 minutes. The Fed's policy meeting is part of a busy week for central banks around the world. The Bank of Canada will also meet Wednesday and is forecast to lift its key rate a quarter point, to 2.5%. Policymakers at the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan are both scheduled to meet Thursday and are expected to keep their key rates unchanged. For Warsh and the Fed, another key consideration is that the U.S. economy is growing at a healthy pace and unemployment remains low, at 4.2%, even if hiring is also sluggish. The government will report Thursday on growth for the July-September quarter, which is expected to reach 3%, according to a forecast by data provider FactSet. That would be up from 2.2% in the April-June quarter. Many economists argue that solid growth is evidence that interest rates aren't particularly high and the economy could withstand higher rates to combat inflation. All eyes would normally be on Riyadh this time of year, when the titans of finance make their annual pilgrimage to FII, pontificate on the global economy, and meet one of their most important clients: the Saudi monarchy. Then come the less buzzy stops in Abu Dhabi, Kuwait, sometimes Dubai, and Doha, all important sources of fees and capital, but reluctant to take the shine off Saudiâs annual investment jamboree.
This year, Houthi attacks forced the postponement of FII, but executives â including Apolloâs Marc Rowan, BlackRockâs Larry Fink, Blackstoneâs Stephen Schwarzman, and KKRâs Scott Nuttall â made the trip to the region anyway.
They were seen in Abu Dhabi and Kuwait this week. Rowan and Schwarzman spoke to The National, the newspaper owned by the UAEâs vice president, about opportunities in the region, some of which are driven by the war: Rowan estimates Gulf states will spend $1 trillion hardening infrastructure and building alternative transport routes, and Schwarzman expects a âvery substantial construction boomâ as countries move vulnerable infrastructure underground.

e854025dd5cd.text:
Bahrain-based Investcorp has joined a group of Saudi investors to acquire industrial fire safety and security business REDA Gulf as it prepares for an initial public offering in the next few years. The deal was one of the first involving a foreign investor into the kingdom since the war with Iranian-backed Houthi militias escalated in recent weeks. The buyout was led by Thara Future Investments, founded by former Public Investment Fund executive Hisham Attar, and Saudi family office AlTouq Group.
âREDA is a leading company in a highly regulated industry, and stands to benefit from a greater focus on safety and security,â Attar told Semafor. âWe believe that investors in the kingdom supporting the themes of economic diversification and resilience will be rewarded in due course.â
The deal is also a bet on a recovery in Saudi Arabiaâs IPO market, where recent listings slumped immediately after their debut and a new set of regulations could deter investment banks from underwriting deals.
The investment is the second for Thara, which is backed by some of the kingdomâs most prominent private investors and family offices. The firm aims to source deals in Saudi Arabia, syndicate locally, and partner with international investors, rather than raise a typical private equity fund, Attar said. Investcorp participated through its $500 million Saudi Pre-IPO fund.

5810113f8680.text:
Even as the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz rankles supply chains, the UAE is still pitching itself as a trade gateway connecting Asia, Africa, and Europe. Its trade pact with Canada, signed Tuesday, is expected to boost exports to the emirates in aerospace, cereals, machinery, and vehicles. UAE Foreign Trade Minister Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi told Semafor that the UAEâs âstrategic location and our growing network of [Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement] partners offer Canadian exporters and investors a pro-business platform for seamless access to some of the worldâs fastest-growing economies.â
Bilateral non-oil trade rose about 20% in 2025 to $4.2 billion, and the UAE pledged to invest $50 billion in Canada last November. UAE money is already widely evident: Nova Chemicals in Calgary is now part of Borouge International, co-owned by Abu Dhabiâs XRG, and DP World operates terminals in the Port of Vancouver. The pact could foster ânew industrial capabilities â¦ and new infrastructure projects,â Al Zeyoudi said. Canada has been an eager commercial partner under Prime Minister Mark Carney, who is looking to offset a beleaguered trade relationship with the US.

Executives spend so much time these days worrying about the businesses AI might destroy that we can overlook the new businesses it will create. Hereâs one from Hasbro: Mr. Potato Head, voiced by the late Don Rickles, answering your customer-service calls.
The toy and game giant is building a business to license AI versions of its iconic characters, CEO Chris Cocks said on Semaforâs Compound Interest. Hasbro launched its Sixth Wall AI studio in June to mine its 166-year history of IP. Cocks said the company is negotiating with a major cellphone carrier to have a Trivial Pursuit quiz show, voiced by an AI-generated LeVar Burton, replace customer-support hold music.
âWeâll serve as the kind of talent agents and creative directors for what the characters do,â Cocks said. âThen itâs up to another platform to express it.â (Liz wants a Megatron option for Alexa; Cocks noted the âTransformersâ character is already serving as the AI-powered, and occasionally judgmental, deejay at Hasbroâs Rhode Island headquarters.)
Cocks compared the proliferation of AI tools to the early days of the internet, when IP rightsholders found themselves on the losing end of a cultural battle over user-generated content.
âRather than trying to fight the dispersion of a really powerful and innovative new technology, weâre choosing to embrace it,â he said. âItâs an opportunity for us to make a bit of money, our partners to make a bit of money, and then the voice talent and creatives behind these characters that people love to also be able to participate economically.â
Guardrails, Cocks is quick to point out, are key: Mr. Potato Head, whose voice will be based on recordings from the Toy Story actor and insult comicâs estate, âwonât express certain things that Mr. Potato Head shouldnât be offering an opinion on.â

9f79e29d9162.text:
The rare Voatsiperifery pepper, native to Madagascar and coveted by international chefs, is facing the depletion of its wild habitat through irresponsible harvesting, bush fires, and charcoal production. Madagascarâs natural forests shrank 27% between 1990 and 2025, according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization, meaning the vines on which the pepper grows have nowhere to climb.
In France, the pepperâs main export market, it sells for $167-$222 per kilogram, while at home it has been considered medicinal by the Malagasy people for generations. French-Malagasy entrepreneur Olivier Ramaherison told AFP that he is now experimenting with domesticating the plant to see if the horizontal branches of the vine can mass-produce the pepper closer to the ground.

90cda26cdc9d.text:
Hollywood actor Idris Elba launched a filmmaking program for African creatives using artificial intelligence, in the latest stage of his efforts to boost the continentâs movie industry. Backed by $1 million from Google, the starâs Akuna Group opened applications for a one-year training and production course for filmmakers living in Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, or South Africa.
While there may be skepticism in parts of Hollywood about the technology, the initiative taps into a growing interest in using AI for media and entertainment in Africa, both to expand creative possibilities and also overcome cost disadvantages where funding constraints can frustrate projects. Participants in Elbaâs program will fully own their films, but are expected to have reliable internet and consistent power to enrol. The British actor, whose parents hailed from Ghana and Sierra Leone, is behind a number of programs aimed at developing creative industries across the continent.
Infrastructure issues, such as poor broadband and electricity access, still pose a challenge for African creators who want to use AI in filmmaking. An AI-generated Yoruba-language film released this month failed to live up to expectations after its hostâs servers were overwhelmed during a premiere.

aeafd8fba4a2.text:
Russia is shifting its recruitment focus for its war in Ukraine to people from countries including Burundi and Zimbabwe, as it seeks to replace soldiers lost in the fighting, according to Ukrainian intelligence findings reported by Bloomberg. The move follows efforts by Kenya and South Africa to stop their citizens from joining the Russian army.
Almost 700 Burundians have reportedly signed contracts with the Russian military, along with 530 Zimbabweans. Overall, the Ukrainian research identified more than 5,400 Africans who had joined the army, with recruitment also rising in Cameroon, DR Congo, Sierra Leone, and Sudan. A new UN report found that Russian authorities trafficked men from 29 countries into their army through deception and coercion.
The news came on the eve of a Russia-Africa summit in Moscow, with President Vladimir Putin seeking to expand trade and investment across the continent. Putinâs government has repeatedly denied illegally recruiting Africans, but the allegations have caused friction with African governments, and experts say the war in Ukraine is straining Russiaâs resources and limiting what it can deliver economically.

83903d1a2829.text:
General Motorsâ decision to up and move its stock listing from the NYSE to the Nasdaq â a bid for inclusion in the latterâs tech-heavy index, which would bring new investors to its stock â doesnât mean itâs a tech company.
The carmaker famously failed in its foray into self-driving cars with Cruise, into which it poured more than $10 billion with little to show. GMâs on-again, off-again relationship with electric vehicles has left customers, investors, and its own employees confused about the companyâs strategy. On Tuesday, hours after repositioning itself as a tech company, Reuters reported that the carmaker plans to, yet again, retool some of its factories to introduce new hybrid versions of its popular three-row SUVs.
Yes, GM is pushing out AI features, including an assistant that can control vehicle functions, answer questions, and help plan routes. But Wall Street remains skeptical: Despite the 5% share pop on Tuesday, GM still trades at a legacy automaker valuation rather than a Big Tech multiple. Walmart made the switch from NYSE to Nasdaq last year, a move meant to deliver $19 billion of index-fund money into its shares. Hilton, too, announced its move to Nasdaq last week.

86f0f48fd8a1.text:
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu asked lawmakers to approve a $22 billion borrowing plan to fund infrastructure projects to be undertaken if he secures a second term in Januaryâs election. The request came as the president and his chief rivals stepped up campaigning in major Nigerian cities.
Tinubu has backed ambitious infrastructure projects since taking office in 2023, including a 750km coastal highway to connect Lagos to eastern commercial cities. But the $11 billion project, which is under construction, has been beset by controversy after the government floated a plan to divert it into an existing road.
Previous administrations have been plagued by poor accountability on large-ticket projects, a problem the presidentâs critics say remains the case under Tinubu.

The Dangote refineryâs $1.6 billion share sale drew investors from across the continent, Africaâs richest man said, in a rare demonstration that Africaâs savings can move across borders at the scale needed to fund its biggest companies without passing through London or Johannesburg. The continentâs largest ever initial public offering, aimed at funding a $14 billion-plus plan to expand the capacity of the giant refinery in Lagos State, closed on Tuesday.
The share sale, which values the company founded by Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote at nearly $50 billion, is widely seen as a test case for whether the continentâs domestic savings, estimated by multilateral lender Africa Finance Corporation at $4 trillion, can help deepen its capital markets.
But the deal also poses a challenge to Johannesburg, which has long traded on its status as Africaâs most liquid capital market â larger than the rest of the continentâs bourses combined â because the IPO largely bypassed it. The Johannesburg Stock Exchange, which said in August that Dangote had âstrong intentâ to pursue a South African listing, told Semafor that local banks were âexploring JSE-listed instrumentsâ offering exposure to Dangote.

31ac2a0fade8.text:
On a family trip to Atlanta, Víctor Ortega Jiménez spent time taking pictures and videos of flamingos as they fed in their pond. It wasn’t to admire their long legs or flamboyant pink color. Instead, he noticed the “beautiful” ripples spreading across the water as the birds ate under the surface. But he didn’t know why the waves were happening.
It took “more than four years to answer that question,” says Ortega Jiménez, of the University of California, Berkeley. “But I think the answer was fascinating.”
Ortega Jiménez’s focus is biomechanics, or the study of how mechanics applies to animal movement and structure. His goal is to understand how animal behaviors might lead to human-made engineering feats.
He discovered that, by retracting their heads, flamingos produce vortexlike traps with water to scoop up algae. They stomp around — or dance, if you will — amplifying the vortex. The series of motions brings the food to their crooked beaks. The beaks then filter in food, releasing silt and mud.
The impressive process can weed out particles the size of a single cell. This kind of self-cleaning filter for extremely small particles can be applied to remove microplastics and so-called forever chemicals called PFAS from water, Ortega Jiménez says.
“Nature is always full of secrets,” he says. “And I think that’s the riddle that keeps me going, trying to understand nature. That’s my way to see science: by observation and trying to be inspired and trying to solve a problem.”

0f96502f645a.text:
The News
A Nigerian entrepreneur who co-founded two billion-dollar African startups and was a founding investor in a third is making another bold bet: that African software engineers will fill the rising global demand for AI talent.
Iyinoluwa Aboyeji has started Talent Nation to supply developers to multinationals, providing the human input that remains relevant to making usable AI products. The new venture mirrors Andela, a company he launched in 2014 and which â with the backing of investors like Mark Zuckerberg, Serena Williams, and former US Vice President Al Gore â trained a generation of software engineers in six African countries. The dizzying levels of capital being raised by AI companies in Silicon Valley, underscored by the buzz around Anthropicâs march to a potentially historic IPO, point to a market opportunity that could surpass his previous endeavors.
âWeâve got a goal of a million AI engineers over the next 10 years,â Aboyeji, who also co-founded Flutterwave and was one of the first checks into Moove, told Semafor in an interview. Most developers from his new companyâs training programs will be African, though âI donât know that we are going to constrain ourselves,â he said. Andela, which Aboyeji left in 2016, eventually moved beyond training only African software developers in 2021.
Talent Nation is taking off with seed money from African investor Enza Capital and London-headquartered fund LocalGlobe, Aboyeji said, but declined to say how much. The startupâs inaugural program, Learn2Earn, has received 63,000 applications, from which less than 3% were selected and are currently in training in multiple campuses. It does not charge fees for tuition.
âDeveloping talent at scale is an extraordinarily complex undertaking,â Kesiah Valkin, the companyâs CEO and Talent Nationâs co-founder, said. âIt is easy for us to say that Africa has enormous talent but whatâs really hard is building the infrastructure to actually find that talent and develop them to globally competitive standards.â
Know More
Africaâs AI scene is not recording anything close to the flood of money pouring into the frontier model companies from tech giants such as Microsoft, Google, and Nvidia. Compared to the rush to build data centers in the US, high-level AI conversations in Africaâs leading technology ecosystems often focus on governance concerns and national policy documents, like those published by Nigeria and Kenya over the last two years.
Substantial infrastructural moves are being made, too. A company owned by Zimbabwean tech billionaire Strive Masiyiwa opened its first AI factory â composed of data centers and chips that process large language models â in Cape Town, South Africa this year and plans to build another in Johannesburg. But beyond the need for data centers and capital investment into companies building AI-enabled services, the supply of human talent is the largest global gap in AI development and one that Africa is positioned to fill, Talent Nationâs founders say. Africa has only 62,000 AI specialists, accounting for 5% of the global AI workforce, according to the Boston Consulting Group.
With the AI investment arms race has come a war for talent that involves the offer of multimillion-dollar pay packages. In the US, base salaries for AI engineers are now much higher than the mean for other jobs in the US, according to online learning platform Coursera. âWhen you see compensation behaving like that, it usually means supply is constrained,â Valkin said.
Some of the startupâs plans are yet to be finalized. For example, Aboyeji said he has not made a decision whether Talent Nationâs trained engineers will be the companyâs full time employees or freelancers. But a key pillar of his calculation is that AI engineers can become world-class for less than $5,000 over a two-year training period, without paid instructors but based on a peer learning system.
âWe donât need $300,000 AI engineers. Thatâs not how this technology is going to find its way to mom and pop shops around the world,â Aboyeji said.

South Korean chip giant SK Hynix reported a sevenfold increase in third-quarter profits from a year ago, the latest sign of a tech boom driving nationwide economic growth. The earnings, which were powered by surging demand from the AI infrastructure buildout, come after official data showed South Koreaâs GDP growth beat analystsâ expectations. Goldman Sachs upped its forecasts for expansion this year and next as a result.
Yet there were calls for caution: Private consumption fell, fueling expertsâ concerns of a growth imbalance that could hurt other parts of the economy; South Koreaâs central bank warned this year of âsemiconductor Dutch disease,â referencing a 1960s gas boom in the Netherlands that strengthened the currency, crimping demand for other sectorsâ goods.

Democrats in the US Congress are already planning how they would use their power if they win a majority in the House or Senate in next week's midterm elections.
Success is by no means guaranteed, even if midterms can sometimes be brutal for the incumbent party that holds the White House.
Control of the chamber, however, would give the party power to issue subpoenas - summons to testify or produce documents - as well as additional funding to launch investigations early next year.
Democrats are weighing whether to investigate senior figures in the Trump administration - and possibly the president himself. Staffers have begun assembling a list of possible investigations and witnesses, according to people familiar with the discussions.
Here are a few potential Democratic targets if the party emerges victorious on 3 November.
1. Trump's family and finances
Democrats have made it clear that lucrative deals brokered by the Trump family's vast business empire will be primary targets of any initial investigations.
"We want to make sure that [American] taxpayer dollars are being used wisely and not being stolen or pocketed because of corruption," Virginia Democratic Representative Suhas Subramanyam, a member of the House Oversight Committee, told the BBC.
Items under consideration for investigation include ties between the administration and corporate entities - particularly cryptocurrency firms - as well as the international business dealings of the president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.
Other topics could include the $400m (Â£301m) aircraft gifted by Qatar to serve as Air Force One and multimillion-dollar defence contracts awarded to firms linked to the Trump family.
"What's shocking to me is not only that this administration, cabinet officials and even the president and his family have been corrupt and self-dealing, but they've been so brazen and open about it," Subramanyam said.
The White House has repeatedly denied any allegations of wrongdoing.
"President Trump is focused on retaining Republican majorities in Congress and doubling down on the progress he has made to lower costs for families," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said.
"Democrats have no agenda to improve the lives of the American people, just plans to obstruct and baselessly target President Trump's commonsense agenda," she added.
A White House official said the administration is "always prepared" to respond to oversight requests regardless of who is in Congress.
2. Hegseth and the Pentagon
Democratic lawmakers have vowed to look into Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's handling of the war with Iran that began in February - including the number of civilian casualties, munitions shortfalls, spending and claims of poorly prepared troops and facilities.
Other topics, according to a source familiar with the discussions, could include boat strikes in the Caribbean that the administration says are aimed at stopping the flow of drugs into the US.
In April, a group of House Democrats filed rare articles of impeachment against Hegseth. They cited the war in Iran and accused him of "high crimes and misdemeanours".
Impeachment requires only a simple majority in the House, but conviction - and removal from office - would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate. No cabinet official has ever been removed this way.
Some experts believe that the negative publicity that would come from congressional hearings could ultimately lead to Hegseth being fired or resigning from the position.
"[If] it looks bad for the White House, and it's a drag on their media attention, President Trump might be likely to cut loose those officials, because he doesn't want that bad press," said David Miller, a political science professor and expert on the presidency at American University in Washington DC. "In a sense that could be a win for the Democrats."
Richard Painter, the former chief White House ethics lawyer under George W Bush, told the BBC that the decision to launch the war should come under scrutiny.
"The bigger issue is this: this war was never authorised by the United States Congress, and I don't care who the secretary of defence is," he said.
"The constitution says that Congress declares war," he said, and lawmakers should "haul these folks in" to answer questions.
In a statement, Pentagon Press Secretary Kingsley Wilson defended Hegseth's record, calling him a "transformative leader" who has "slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters".
"By every measurable metric, the Department of War is better under Secretary Hegseth's leadership than before," she said, using the administration's preferred name for the defence department.
3. Immigration and ICE raids
Senior Democrats - including Robert Garcia, the California Democrat tapped to lead the House Oversight Committee should the party take back the chamber - have identified immigration enforcement as a key priority for potential congressional investigations.
These could examine allegations of misconduct by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents during immigration raids across the country.
But these investigations may prove difficult and politically tricky.
In 2024, Trump campaigned on a promise of mass deportations of undocumented migrants - a message that resonated with many of his supporters.
But recent polls suggest many Americans, including those who backed Trump in that election, are uncomfortable with some of the tactics used by ICE in American cities so far this year.
It means Democrats will have to walk a fine line between opposing ICE tactics and appearing to dismiss broader immigration concerns, Painter told the BBC.
4. A third Trump impeachment
Democrats are split on the possibility of attempting to impeach Trump for a third time.
Some, such as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, have expressed support for an impeachment, citing what they view as an unauthorised war with Iran and other alleged impeachable offences.

The Finnish and Norwegian leaders broke a Western European taboo and held talks with Russiaâs president, sparking division on the continent as it pushes to strengthen backing for Ukraine. The 90-minute telephone conversation was met alternatingly with anger and acceptance in Europe, which has largely sought to make Moscow a pariah since its 2022 invasion.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahuâs coalition took a slight lead in a tight election race, defying exit poll projections, though he remained short of the numbers required to form another government.

Tanzania announced its first gas discovery in more than a decade, a finding that comes as African nations race to boost their energy independence. The continent, which imports the majority of the fuels it uses, has been badly exposed by the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, which have pushed up prices and sown political instability.

- Published
Tanzania has announced a significant discovery of natural gas in the Mnazi Bay area in the south of the country - the first such find in a decade.
Energy Minister Juma Homera attended a ceremony at the Kasa-1X ST2 well, which is jointly owned by state-owned Tanzania Petroleum Development Corporation (TPDC) and French oil firm Maurel & Prom, to mark the occasion.
He said the estimated 223 billion cubic feet (6.3 billion cubic metres) discovery was a "major milestone" in the development of the small oil and gas sector in the East African nation.
The new well is expected to start production early next month and is intended to boost domestic supplies.
Tanzania has existing natural gas reserves of 57.54 trillion cubic feet.
"The discovery is important in ensuring the country has reliable, clean and safe energy at affordable costs, particularly at a time when demand is increasing due to industrial growth and other economic activities," Homera said.
Natural gas accounted for nearly 80% of Tanzania's sources of electricity generation, according to government statistics for 2024.
In recent years, the country has also encouraged the use of compressed natural gas to power vehicles, with natural gas plants and filling stations set up mostly in the largest city, Dar es Salaam.
Some Tanzanians have been converting their vehicles to a dual-fuel system - with the locally available natural gas allowing for cheaper prices than petrol.
Tanzania made its first natural gas discovery in 1974 on the Songo Songo Island in the south-east Lindi region, followed by a second discovery at Mnazi Bay in neighbouring region of Mtwara in 1982.
The commercialisation of these discoveries began in 2004. This propelled further gas exploration both onshore and offshore, with the largest single discovery of 2.7 trillion cubic feet of natural gas in 2016.

- Published
Serbian police shot dead a young man outside the Israeli embassy in Belgrade in the early hours of Wednesday after what authorities called a "terrorist attack".
The country's interior minister, Ivica Dacic, said the attacker had rushed at a police officer with two knives while shouting the phrase "Allahu Akbar". The officer sustained a minor knife wound to the face and shot the attacker.
Dacic said the suspect has not been identified, but he was a minor and Serbian citizen who was being monitored by security services as he was "known to be a supporter of the Islamic State".
Speaking to reporters outside the embassy, Dacic said an investigation is ongoing, but security services said the suspect had posted a picture of the Islamic State flag on his Instagram.
Dacic raised the country's terrorism threat level to "red alert" - the highest threat level â meaning stricter security checks and increased police presence at places like infrastructure facilities and areas where large crowds gather.
The interior minister said he had visited the injured police officer, who was reportedly doing well and did not need hospital care for his wounds.
Armed security personnel were seen standing guard outside the Israeli embassy on Wednesday morning.
Israel's foreign ministry confirmed in a social media post that no embassy personnel were injured and the mission was closed at the time of the incident.
This is the second such attack on Belgrade's Israeli embassy in less than three years; in June 2024, a man shot a police officer in the neck with a crossbow.
The officer who was shot survived the attack and shot dead the assailant, identified as a Serbian man who had converted to Islam.
Wednesday's attack comes just one day after elections in Israel.

4a79d84e9fe6.text:
The chemical building blocks that gave rise to life on Earth probably didn’t come from comets.
Most comets would have been traveling too fast and at too steep an angle to Earth for prebiotic compounds to survive impact with the planet, researchers contend October 28 in Scientific Reports. While the study doesn’t completely rule out the possibility that comets brought these molecules to Earth, it contradicts the long-standing idea that comets seeded Earth with the chemicals necessary for life to arise.
“Even though we see that comets contain all of these molecules in really high concentrations, it’s not straightforward to go from there to saying we’re going to have all of these available for prebiotic chemistry on the surface of the Earth,” says Richard Anslow, a planetary scientist at the Met Office, the national meteorological service for the United Kingdom in Exeter.
Comets carry carbon- and nitrogen-containing molecules left over from early in the solar system’s formation. These molecules can react to form biologically important compounds like sugars and DNA. Scientists have long thought that comets could have delivered these building blocks to Earth when they collided with the planet during its first billion years.
But it’s important to revisit these ideas as our understanding of both comets and the early solar system improves, says Nicolle Zellner, a physicist at Albion College in Michigan who was not involved in the study.
In the new work, Anslow and colleagues used computer simulations to predict the likelihood that a chemical called hydrogen cyanide would survive a comet’s journey through Earth’s present atmosphere and its impact with the planet’s surface. The early Earth’s atmosphere was probably much denser, so would have been even more destructive.
The strong chemical bond between the carbon and nitrogen atoms in hydrogen cyanide can release energy that drives later chemical reactions necessary for life. It also makes the molecule particularly stable compared to other carbon-based chemicals.
“It’s probably one of the more robust molecules to surviving impacts,” Anslow says. “So if things look bad for hydrogen cyanide, then we think it’s going to be much harder for other, more complicated molecules that are more likely to be broken down during these impacts.”
Based on the simulations, a comet impact that kept hydrogen cyanide intact would be extremely unlikely, the team found. On average, the simulations suggest that only one impact would have been able to deliver a meaningful amount of hydrogen cyanide to the planet’s surface over more than a billion years. For hydrogen cyanide to survive the crash, the comet would have to be larger than 100 meters across, slow moving and traveling at an oblique angle to Earth.
A comet that met those narrow criteria would also have had to crash into land, rather than an ocean, to kick off any biologically useful chemistry. If the comet landed in the ocean, any hydrogen cyanide that survived would be diluted too quickly to trigger those reactions.
While still improbable, comets may have been more likely to deliver carbon-based molecules to Mars than to Earth, the simulations showed. Mars’ thinner atmosphere and smaller size meant that comets would impact at lower speeds. That could mean that more compounds could survive the collision.
If Earth’s carbon-based chemicals didn’t come from comets, they may have come from carbon-rich asteroids called carbonaceous chondrites, says Gordon Osinski, a planetary geologist at Western University in London, Canada, who was not involved in the study. Other sources might have included volcanoes and hydrothermal vents.
The study “definitely will make people think twice about comets being the originator for the delivery of organics,” Osinski says. “I hope other people will try to reproduce these results [and] then potentially try something similar with carbonaceous chondrites as well.”

The rapid decline of Antarctic sea ice since 2016 has triggered a dramatic shift in a crucial part of Earth’s climate system, scientists say.
In a paper published Wednesday, researchers documented a sharp salinity increase in a vast layer of the Southern Ocean, extending from 2,300 to 4,000 feet deep and encircling Antarctica. The shift reverses decades of freshening and echoes ocean changes usually associated with major global climate shifts over millennia but is now happening in just a few years.
The switch from a decades-long trend of freshening water to increasing salinity has implications that could extend beyond Antarctica. The layer, known as Antarctic Intermediate Water, spreads northward into the Indian, Pacific and Atlantic oceans, transporting heat, carbon, oxygen and nutrients toward the tropics, and even across the equator, said co-author Bishakhdatta Gayen, a researcher and professor at the University of Melbourne and at the Centre for Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences in Bengaluru, India.
Gayen said the study combined six independent datasets to track changes in the Southern Ocean from 2004 to 2024. The data came from Argo floats, which drift through the ocean and periodically descend to different depths to measure water properties such as density and salinity, then resurface to transmit the readings. A 2025 study also detected increasing surface salinity linked to declining sea ice, he added.
Antarctic sea ice reached its highest extent in the satellite record in 2014 and suddenly dropped to a record low just two years later. The sea ice remained well below the 2014 extent and reached another low point in 2023, when it measured about 1 million square miles below the 1981 to 2010 average, with an area of ice about four times the size of Texas gone. As the ice dwindles, there’s less freshwater available during the melt season, making the Antarctic Intermediate Water saltier.
Changes to the density, thickness and salinity of the layer influence how heat moves between the surface of the ocean and deeper waters, which “could affect how the ocean stores and redistributes heat,” Gayen said. More monitoring is needed to track the changes, he added, because impacts are potentially “knocking on your door” within five years.
Those impacts, he said, could include increased storm frequency and ocean heat loss identified by a 2024 study. Earlier this year, a far-reaching scientific review concluded that changes in Antarctic sea ice cover “influence the global distribution of atmospheric heat and moisture, as well as atmospheric variability.” The “speed and persistence” of the sea ice decline suggests the ocean around Antarctica may be moving into a new state that is likely to affect not only Antarctic ecosystems, but the entire global climate system, the review found.
Michael Meredith, an oceanographer with the British Antarctic Survey who led the BAS Polar Ocean for years, said the new research shows that dramatic Antarctic sea-ice loss since 2016 is already affecting the properties and circulation of deep ocean waters.
“The Southern Ocean is the key juncture for all the world’s oceans,” he said. “It’s the major site where old waters are reprocessed into new, so this could have global consequences.”
The Southern Ocean also plays a “massive role” in drawing down human carbon dioxide emissions, which moderates the rate of climate change where people live, he said. Anything that disrupts key ocean cycles demands our attention, he added.
Meredith said it’s not yet clear whether the shift is permanent because it’s based on a relatively short observational record. But, he said, global climate models used to guide policy still struggle to accurately reflect recent sea ice losses, which shows that more research and monitoring is needed.
“Our climate models need to catch up,” he said. “But if the low sea-ice state persists, these changes will keep spreading through the world’s oceans, and the effects will ripple out across our climate and ecosystems.”
Related research in recent years found that deep circulation in the Southern Ocean has slowed, reducing the rate at which new waters flood and cool the deepest areas. The new study makes it clear that the upper part is rapidly changing in response to changes in sea ice, he said. “That matters,” he added, “because the upper circulation can affect our climate within years to decades, not centuries.”

The family of a Kenyan woman allegedly murdered by a former British soldier 14 years ago has expressed outrage after being told an extradition hearing for the accused had been postponed until May 2027.
Relatives of Agnes Wanjiru, whose body was found in a septic tank near a British army training camp in Kenya in 2012, described the delay as "completely unacceptable" and have accused the authorities of failing to keep them informed.
Robert James Purkiss was arrested in the UK last November and is fighting extradition to Kenya to face trial for the murder of the 21-year-old mother.
He denies the allegation. His hearing was due to be held in London next month.
Wanjiru's niece, Esther Njoki, told the BBC that the family had learnt of the postponement through the UK embassy and had received no official explanation.
"We have exercised patience and endured uncertainty for years, but our patience is now being taken advantage of," she said in a statement.
"Agnes deserves justice. Her daughter Stacy deserves answers about what happened. And as a family, we deserve to be treated with dignity and kept informed about proceedings that profoundly affect our lives."
The family said it had already raised money and made arrangements to travel to the UK for the hearing, which was due to take place in three weeks.
It is now calling on the authorities to expedite the proceedings, warning that the latest postponement means the case will enter its 15th year without a trial.
The family said a UK court was expected next week to give the reasons for the hearing delay.
Wanjiru disappeared in March 2012 after spending an evening at a hotel in Nanyuki, about 200km (124 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi, where British soldiers were stationed for training.
Her body was found nearly three months later in a septic tank at the hotel. She had suffered stab wounds to her chest and abdomen and left behind a five-month-old daughter.
A Kenyan inquest concluded in 2019 that she had been unlawfully killed by one or two British soldiers.
In September 2025, a Kenyan High Court issued an arrest warrant for a British national after prosecutors presented evidence they said justified bringing murder charges.
Purkiss' lawyers said he intended to contest his extradition to Kenya.
He appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court in February via video link, where he was further remanded in custody.
Last year, the then British Defence Secretary John Healey met Wanjiru's family during a visit to Kenya and pledged his government's support for efforts to secure justice.
The UK government has previously said it remains committed to helping the family, but would not comment on ongoing legal proceedings.

News that Jalen Hurts played a game hours after being diagnosed with a blood clot had already shocked the NFL world.
The Philadelphia Eagles then said their star quarterback will probably miss the rest of the season after multiple blood clots were found in his lungs - a life-threatening condition if not treated quickly.
It raised questions over the NFL's handling of the matter and its general approach to player health and safety, partly because the game in question was part of the league's international series.
Hurts' initial diagnosis was in London, before the Eagles played at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on 11 October, and he flew back with the team that evening.
What do we know about what happened? Why was Hurts allowed to play and then fly home straight after? And what does it mean for him, the Eagles and the NFL?
What happened?
Sunday, 4 October: Another player stepped on Hurts' left calf during Philadelphia's defeat by the Los Angeles Rams, although he completed the game.
Thursday, 8 October: Hurts first reported an issue to the team. He trained in full all week and had treatment on Thursday and Friday.
Saturday, 10 October: The Eagles arrived in London in the morning and Hurts visited the Cleveland Clinic that evening. An ultrasound showed he had a superficial blood clot (vein thrombosis) in his calf but he was cleared to play on Sunday.
Sunday, 11 October: Hurts returned to the team hotel at about 3am before playing the full game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. A follow-up ultrasound was recommended within 72 hours and Hurts was cleared for the flight home.
Wednesday, 14 October: After receiving daily treatment, Hurts had another ultrasound, which showed the clot had moved, and he was ruled out of the next game.
Monday, 19 October: Joint statement by the Eagles and Hurts' agent said further tests showed he now has deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli (multiple blood clots in both lungs).
His treatment will involve blood-thinning medicine and he should make a full recovery but is expected to miss the rest of the season.
What has the NFL said?
Some of the initial reports said that Hurts did not sleep for 36 hours before playing in London, but his agent later confirmed that he slept after returning to the hotel and also at the stadium.
Dr Allen Sills, the NFL's chief medical officer, was in London that weekend and arranged for Hurts to be evaluated at the Cleveland Clinic, an American-owned private hospital which is an official supplier of sports medicine services for the NFL's London games.
The NFL has protocols in place for concussions, emergency preparedness and extreme heat, for games in the US and overseas.
But, speaking at a news conference last Tuesday, Sills explained the league does not have a protocol for situations such as this.
Nevertheless, Sills said that those who dealt with Hurts were "incredibly conservative" and that he had "complete confidence" in how the Eagles handled the situation.
Later that day, the NFL Players Association (NFLPA) called for a full investigation, adding that the NFL "previously informed the union that it did not plan to review the care [Hurts] received".
However, on Sunday the league and NFLPA released a joint statement saying they are "working together to review the matter".
Was anything done wrong?
The NFL's next international game is in Madrid on 8 November and the local medical co-ordinator is Real Madrid's chief medical officer, Dr Niko Mihic.
Dr Mihic told BBC Sport that blood clots among athletes are "not that common" and remembers in a previous role it took three visits for a baseball player to be diagnosed with a blood clot, because it is not something immediately associated with sports injuries.
Medical advice on whether to sleep and/or stay active is decided case by case. The same goes for whether it is safe to board a long-haul flight with a blood clot, as Hurts was allowed to do.
"It's not as simple as some people think," said Dr Mihic. "There's an amount of judgement that goes into this. It's like you're stuck between a rock and a hard place, but then you make your call."
As he and the NFL finalise their medical preparations for the Madrid game, Dr Mihic expects them to discuss scenarios such as that involving Hurts.
Asked what the NFL can learn from Hurts ultimately getting blood clots in his lungs, the league's Dr Sills replied: "I don't think you can take that outcome and say there was something flawed about the process.
"Sometimes in medicine we do all the right things and other things develop... but we have a committee that looks at all these cases."
What does it mean?
Whatever the outcome of the NFL's joint review with the NFLPA, the league will face greater scrutiny over how they handle players around games played overseas.
Players had a 16-hour flight for Australia's first NFL game in September, while the NFLPA's executive director JC Tretter expressed safety concerns over the quality of the field for the game in Brazil.
There are a record nine international games this year and, although the NFL ultimately wants 16 per season, Tretter added that "the goal has to be growing the game while maintaining the standards our players deserve".
Only Hurts knows how he feels about the way he was treated by his team and the NFL's doctors, but even before this issue there had been talk of the 2025 Super Bowl MVP leaving the Eagles.
Even if he does make a full recovery and returns to action, the 28-year-old will always have to bear blood clots in mind.
"The worst risk factor for recurrent embolisms is having had one previously," said Dr Mihic.
As for Philadelphia, they do not have an experienced quarterback in reserve and back-up Tanner McKee could not prevent them suffering a fifth straight defeat on Monday.
They were beaten 38-21 at home by the Dallas Cowboys to extend their longest losing streak under coach Nick Sirianni, so this could be a long season for the injury-hit Eagles.
Or with the trade deadline
