Investors and journalists have now spent two days parsing Anthropicâs IPO filing â its risk factors, its $80 billion headline net loss, and its unusual governance structure â but thereâs one number Silicon Valley prizes above all.
The company reported an 85% gross profit margin on the core work of running its existing AI models â as The Information wrote, itâs âa reality checkâ for skeptics who thought the consumption-based, pay-as-you-go pricing wouldnât be profitable.
It could also be a good sign for Anthropicâs rival, OpenAI, which runs a similar business model, even though itâs considered less efficient in part because of its massive non-paying user base.
Anthropic is still losing a lot of money overall, and its margin excludes the cost of training new models. But the number on its core product puts it in the same camp as Metaâs ad machine, which runs at roughly 81-82% gross margin, and above analystsâ estimates for Google Search ads (75â80%) and the iPhone (mid-40s).

4721e0563119.text: By — Will Weissert, Associated Press Will Weissert, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-trump-rallies-voters-in-ohio-after-divisive-ramaswamy-campaign-ad Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Trump rallies voters in Ohio after divisive Ramaswamy campaign ad Politics Oct 28, 2026 1:22 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump likes to play make-believe with his supporters. Trump is expected to speak at a rally in Ohio at 7 p.m. EDT. Watch live in our video player above. "Just close your eyes," he tells them, "and pretend I'm on the ballot." WATCH: Poll gauges voter enthusiasm for both parties a week before election It's a typically self-involved appeal from someone who has been the center of the nation's political gravity for more than a decade. Now, he's finishing the midterms with a cross-country blitz of campaign rallies that allow him to bask in applause when he's otherwise profoundly unpopular. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. In a year marked by the war with Iran, fears about artificial intelligence, redistricting fights, high energy prices and increasing concerns about the cost of living, Trump's deeply personal approach might be the election cycle's biggest gamble. WATCH: Democrats put economy and affordability at center of final campaign push Republicans still love the president, who remains dominant even as he approaches the back half of his second term. But his approval ratings are low enough to potentially sink his party and its bid to maintain control of Congress. "I don't think there's anybody that wants Donald Trump out there at these rallies more than Democratic candidates," said Jessica Mackler, president of EMILY's List, which focuses on electing Democratic women who support abortion rights. READ MORE: Inside Georgia's push to rebuild trust in elections after Trump's false claims Every time there's another Trump event, she said, "we look at that as a win." White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said Trump is "the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party." "The choice has never been more clear," he said in a statement. "Doubling down on President Trump's winning, commonsense agenda, or the Democrats' extreme liberal policies and obstruction." Trump thinks the way to win elections is more Trump It goes far beyond a whirlwind rally schedule. The president organized even small details of the first-ever Republican midterm convention last month in Dallas, speaking both nights. He also was depicted there as the Marlboro Man, a cowboy on horseback and with a white Stetson who could ride to the rescue, on everything from baseball caps to beer cozies. WATCH: Why Trump's coalition of evangelical voters could be fraying Trump even has a personal spin on his blockbuster attempt to win over voters by pledging big checks if Republicans hold Congress, saying "I'll give you $5,000" even though the improbable idea would likely need lawmaker approval. Political groups associated with the president have spent at least around $277 million since Sept. 1 to help Republicans — a staggering sum that nonetheless didn't completely drain the $416 million that Trump's flagship Super PAC, MAGA Inc., had in the bank to start last month. READ MORE: What our final poll before Election Day says about midterms and Trump But that wasn't enough for Trump. He used taxpayer funding to run television ads celebrating himself, including one nearly identical to a spot from 2024 — the last time he really was on the ballot. It's consistent with a self-centered, second-term approach From expanding executive power, to turning the presidency into a profit center for his family, to molding the White House in his own gilded image, Trump's self regard has escalated since he won back the White House. "I can do stuff that is unbelievable," he bragged at a rally in Kentucky. WATCH: Campaigns spend big to sway voters with increasingly personal attack ads Trump crammed the Oval Office with gold flourishes, demolished the East Wing to build a sprawling ballroom and converted the Rose Garden into a patio space reminiscent of his Mar-a-Lago estate. There's also a new helipad that he showed off to Xi Jinping, China's communist leader, during a recent visit. The president is focused on reshaping Washington as well, dispatching National Guard troops to the streets, closing the Kennedy Center after failed attempts to add his name to the building, planning a towering arch just outside the city and pushing to revamp a century-old public golf course. Trump has wielded his iron grip on the Republican Party in ways that could hurt its chances in some races. He helped Ken Paxton, who has a history of legal and ethical problems, defeat incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Texas primary, making the general election campaign against Democrat James Talarico more competitive. WATCH: Candidates enter final week of campaigning with control of Congress at stake Trump also clashed with North Carolina Sen. Tom Tillis, prompting him to retire, and pushed Michael Whatley to run. Now Republicans are bracing to lose the seat to former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper. Trump is 'the dividing line' in the midterms The Trump-centric approach backfired during his first term in 2018, when a similar presidential rally barrage didn't stop Democrats from retaking House control. This time, many of the issues that helped Trump win reelection in 2024, such as his handling of the economy, could prove to be liabilities for Republicans. Just 17% of U.S. adults approve of Trump's handling of the cost of living, as the Iran war keeps fuel prices high and stokes inflation fears, according to an AP-NORC poll conducted in late September. 79decea20b9a.text: Republicans fear that Vivek Ramaswamy 's explosive attack ad featuring his opponent's estranged mother could cost them the Ohio governor's race, based on new internal polling that shows him falling further behind, Axios has learned. Why it matters: The poll's findings underscore Republicans' anxiety over Ramaswamy's decision to air the deeply personal attack on Democrat Amy Acton despite warnings from some fellow Republicans that it crossed a line. Driving the news: The private poll, commissioned by a Republican group and obtained by Axios, found Acton leading Ramaswamy by eight points — up from a two-point lead in the same poll earlier this month, before the ad began circulating on Oct. 19. The ad "is having a significant effect on the gubernatorial race," a memo attached to the poll states. Catch up quick: The ad at the center of the controversy features Donna Arthur, Acton's estranged mother, who accuses her daughter of lying about her childhood and urges Ohioans not to vote for her. Acton has said she was sexually abused by her stepfather when she was 12 and that her mother sided with her abuser. The stepfather was charged with sexual assault but fled to Pennsylvania, where he died in 2004 as a fugitive. Acton and her brother were removed from their mother's custody. Acton has said she hasn't seen her mother since 1978. Zoom out: As Axios first reported , Ramaswamy's campaign treated the ad as a game-changer in the campaign for governor, committing $4 million to airing the commercial statewide despite warnings from other Republicans that it could backfire. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R), who worked closely with Acton when she was the state's health director, said that airing the ad was wrong and urged Ramaswamy to take it down. But President Trump and Vice President Vance backed Ramaswamy. Vance told the bipartisan critics of the ad to "stop whining." The intrigue: The new poll done for Republicans indicates that the ad was indeed a game-changer — just not the type Ramaswamy's campaign hoped it would be. A memo attached to the poll said that 86% of the survey's 800 respondents said they had seen, read or heard something about the ad. By a 2-to-1 ratio, those who said they were familiar with it said it made them more likely to vote for Acton. Between the lines: National Republican operatives fear the backlash against Ramaswamy over the ad could also hurt U.S. Sen. Ohio Jon Husted's reelection bid in a state that could be key in determining control of the Senate. Husted has said he wouldn't have run the ad. "Vivek's ad put the whole Republican ticket on defense. He better hope Ohio doesn't decide the Senate majority," said a GOP operative who has been briefed on polling in the race. The ad was shot months ago , a source familiar with the situation said, but there was internal resistance to running it — with one huge exception. "The candidate is the one pushing for it," a source close to the campaign said. The ad initially was published online because the campaign was testing to see its effectiveness. The ad was sent it to poll respondents to watch on their computers and smartphones to rate, according to the source. "This was not planned. But Vivek got what he wanted," according to the source. "I probably wouldn't have run it." Yes, but: A separate Suffolk University poll showed a narrower deficit for Ramaswamy — four points, an improvement over Suffolk's previous findings in late September, which found Acton up by nine points. The other side: Ramaswamy has defended the ad, arguing that Acton has misrepresented her past and avoided addressing substantive issues facing Ohio voters. What they're saying: A Ramaswamy campaign representative declined to comment. What's next: Trump is scheduled to campaign in Chillicothe, Ohio, with Ramaswamy and Husted on Wednesday evening. Axios' Marc Caputo contributed reporting. The Republican group's internal survey of 800 likely Ohio voters was conducted Oct. 23–26 and found Ramaswamy's support had fallen from 45% earlier this month to 42%, while Acton's climbed from 47% to 50%. The survey had a margin of error for each candidate's result of +/- 3.46 percentage points.

Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public.
The leak includes names, work addresses and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work they do for each agency.
Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks that a government agency has been targeted by leaks or hacks.
A DHS spokesperson said the agency is "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively."
"We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected," the spokesperson added.
"We will update the public when more information is available."
The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was made public online. A group called the Department of Peace accessed the information from DHS, while journalist and cybersecurity researcher maia crimew alongside the website Distributed Denial of Secrets put it online.
The information was put in a database named Icepick.
Most of the agents included, more than 21,000 of them, work for CBP, according to the data. Nearly 6,600 work for ICE.
Other records show agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and even people working for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.
The leaked information also included dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents that led and worked on those operations, and some of the technology they used in their work, including tech provided by Cellbrite and Palantir.
The groups wrote in an online statement that the the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets.
"The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in it's simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added.
BlueLeaks refers to a massive leak of US police data in 2020, data from which DDoSecrets also hosted.
A spokesperson for the Department of Peace pointed directly at actions by ICE agents for the groups work to hack DHS records.
"On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat'. This is what happens to ICE when you do that," the spokesperson wrote on Wednesday.
Mullin in March became Secretary of Homeland Security.
The Department of Peace said it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta.
Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them.
A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised."
Last month, the FBI was hacked by a group called ShinyHunters, which took personal information about thousands of agents.
In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt.
Public backlash to US immigration enforcement has been building as the Trump Administration has pushed a huge increase in arrests and deportations of people suspected of being in the country illegally.
Immigration operations this year have repeatedly turned violent, external, with ICE agents shooting at more than two dozen people and killing at least nine people.
Those killings include the high profile deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, both of whom were shot and killed by ICE agents this year in Minnesota, despite not being the targets of arrests.
Often, ICE agents carry out enforcement actions while their faces are covered by masks and sunglasses. Immigration agents rarely identify themselves, despite being required by law to do so, and US politicians have publicly demanded, external DHS enforces the requirement.
Since President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, the US has enacted nearly 1 million deportations, external, according to data from the Migration Policy Institute. More than 70% of the deportations have been of people with no criminal record.

f4a1f886251c.text: By — Danica Kirka, Associated Press Danica Kirka, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/king-charles-iii-cant-escape-britains-role-in-slavery-as-he-tours-caribbean-nations Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter King Charles III can't escape Britain's role in slavery as he tours Caribbean nations World Oct 28, 2026 7:49 PM EDT LONDON (AP) — For Britain's royal family, slavery is the issue that won't go away. As King Charles III tours the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda over the next nine days, he will be repeatedly reminded that he is the inheritor of a throne that presided over the enslavement of millions of Africans who were shipped to the Caribbean and North America, where they worked for the profit of their owners and, ultimately, the British Empire. Facing demands that Britain apologize and pay reparations, palace officials say Charles will reiterate previous comments that slavery was an "atrocity that forever stains our history," while stopping short of an apology. READ MORE: UN calls for reparations to remedy the historical wrongs of trafficking enslaved Africans "It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past," the king said Tuesday at a youth rally in Nassau, the Bahamian capital. But the language suggested by the palace won't silence the monarchy's critics, said Brooke Newman, the author of "The Crown's Silence: The Hidden History of the British Monarchy and Slavery in the Americas." "That is hollow," Newman said, referring to Charles' expected comments. "It doesn't create dialogue. It doesn't allow for any kind of conversation with descendants, and it absolutely does not move this issue forward. And so people are frustrated because they're being essentially told by the government and by the king that this matter is off the table." Monarchy's links to slavery date to 1563 In 464 heavily footnoted pages, Newman, a professor of history at Virginia Commonwealth University, details the monarchy's links to slavery from the late 1500s through the abolition of the slave trade in 1807 and the abolition of slavery in the British Empire 26 years later. British monarchs did more than just preside over an empire where enslaved Africans were shipped across the Atlantic Ocean to labor in the sugar, tobacco and cotton fields of the New World, Newman argues in her book. As early as 1563, more than 40 years before England established its first colony in North America, Queen Elizabeth I supported sea captain John Hawkins' plan to raid Portuguese ports on the coast of West Africa and transport captured Africans to Spanish colonies of the Caribbean. In return for lending Hawkins a Royal Navy warship, the queen received a share of the profits. "His daring slave-trading venture enriched the royal coffers, securing Elizabeth I's historical legacy as the first English monarch to profit directly from the transatlantic slave trade," Newman wrote. Africa trade started with gold and ivory, expanded to humans But Elizabeth I wasn't the last. Almost 100 years later, King Charles II gave the Company of Royal Adventurers into Africa, later known simply as the Royal African Company, exclusive trading rights to the west African coast. The company quickly expanded from commodities such as gold, hides and ivory into the trade in enslaved Africans. The king and his brother, the Duke of York, who later became King James II, were among the company's investors. Pressure for Britain — along with the United States, Portugal, Spain and others who profited from slavery — to pay reparations has increased in recent years as Caribbean and African nations united behind the issue. A person in the crowd holds up a sign reading "Pay us what you owe us" as Britain's King Charles (not pictured) watches a Junkanoo parade in Parliament Square in Nassau, The Bahamas, Oct. 28, 2026. Photo by Ben Stansall/Pool via Reuters The United Nations General Assembly in March approved a resolution calling for reparatory justice, including a full apology and compensation both for the period of enslavement and for continuing harms such as reduced economic opportunity, lower income levels and shorter life expectancy for Black people in the Caribbean and the Americas. The U.K. abstained from the vote. The king is constrained by government policy Charles won't apologize during his Caribbean tour because he speaks on behalf of the elected government, not for himself, said Craig Prescott, an expert on constitutional law and the monarchy at Royal Holloway, University of London. "It's not a matter for the king, in that sense," he said. "And it is the longstanding policy of the government to, yes, note that slavery happened and that it is a stain on British history, but that reparations are not payable." Reparations could potentially cost the U.K. hundreds of billions of pounds, so the issue is particularly sensitive for the current government, which is struggling to pay for popular social programs as the rising cost of living squeezes taxpayers. But Charles must also think about how his comments will be received in the Caribbean and throughout the Commonwealth, which he heads. The Commonwealth is an association of 56 independent nations, many of which are in Africa, Asia and the Caribbean and were once part of the British Empire. The British monarch remains the head of state for 14 Commonwealth countries other than the U.K. The last four days of the king's Caribbean tour will be in Antigua and Barbuda, which is hosting a biannual meeting of Commonwealth leaders. Caribbean leader appeals to Charles as a man, not the king Hilary Beckles, the chair of the Caribbean Community's reparations commission, called on Charles to respond to the demands of Caribbean people as a human being, not as the head of the Commonwealth or the monarch of the United Kingdom. "I'm appealing to Charles Windsor, a parent, a grandparent, a man today who refle

9e86bcd6549c.text: By — Jill Lawless, Associated Press Jill Lawless, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/russell-brand-denies-all-charges-as-he-testifies-at-his-rape-and-sex-assault-trial Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Russell Brand denies all charges as he testifies at his rape and sex assault trial World Oct 28, 2026 7:35 PM EDT LONDON (AP) — Russell Brand acknowledged in a London court on Wednesday that he had been obsessed with sex as a younger man, but denied multiple charges of rape and sexual assault, saying the claims have had a "devastating" impact on his life. The British actor-comedian entered Southwark Crown Court alongside his wife, Laura Gallacher, to testify in his own defense, telling reporters that "today is the day for truth and justice." READ MORE: Russell Brand pleads not guilty to charges of rape and sexual assault Brand, 51, stood in the witness box and took the oath, then gave his full name: Russell Edward Brand. He answered "no" to each charge as his lawyer, Ian Winter, asked whether he was guilty of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault. Brand denied forcing any of the six alleged victims to do anything against their will. "Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary, and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself," Brand said. Brand said the allegations had had a "devastating" impact, with friends and colleagues abandoning him. He said no one with relevant evidence had been willing to testify in court on his behalf. "My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations," he said, adding later that dealing with the "traumatic" allegations had come "at the expense of my marriage, my children and health." Brand said he even was barred from staying with his baby son in hospital after anonymous allegations of sexual misconduct were made against him in a newspaper and a TV documentary in 2023. "The reason given by Great Ormond Street Hospital when my son was receiving open heart surgery and subsequent treatment was due to the material published," he said. Six women accuse Brand of misconduct Over the past two weeks of the trial, prosecutors set out their case and the jury heard from six women who accuse Brand of sexual misconduct between 1999 and 2009. Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones told jurors that Brand was "ruthless, he was calculating, he was manipulative. And, the prosecution say, he was a sexual predator." Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including "Forgetting Sarah Marshall" and "Get Him to the Greek" and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry. In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion. The allegations cover a decade when Brand went from rising stand-up comedian to major celebrity in the U.K. The first victim alleges that Brand raped her in a hotel room during the Labour Party's annual conference in the seaside town of Bournemouth in 1999. Another woman alleges that in 2001 Brand tried to drag her into the men's bathroom at the London office of music channel MTV, where she worked. A third woman alleges that Brand orally raped her in 2004 in the toilet of a London bar, and a fourth says Brand kissed and groped her at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005. Another complainant says Brand anally raped her at his home after she met him at one of his shows in 2009, while the sixth says the comedian demanded a massage and pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an advertisement in 2009. Prosecutors say the women don't know one another and separately went to police after the TV documentary was broadcast in 2023. The Associated Press doesn't name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life. Brand says all encounters were consensual Under cross-examination by Karmy-Jones, Brand acknowledged he had dedicated a lot of his earlier life to "beyond reckless philandering." "As I became more successful and famous I was very comfortable allowing that to facilitate sexual access, which I agree with you was wrong," he said. He said "yes" when asked if he had been obsessed with sex when he was younger, but "no" when the prosecutor asked: "Do you accept that you were desperate for it and sometimes couldn't function without it?" As he completed a day on the stand, Brand was asked again whether he had committed the crimes he is accused of. "Not guilty is my plea in every single case," he said. The Scoop
Kalshi has hired one of former President Barack Obamaâs top advisers, political strategist Eric Schultz, a person familiar with the matter told Semafor â the latest sign of companies anticipating Democratic victories in Tuesdayâs midterms.
Schultz signed  a short-term contract to serve as an out-of-house adviser to Kalshi, a second person familiar with the matter said. His hiring comes as Kalshi users forecast a 91% chance that Democrats win a majority in the House and a 65% chance of a Democratic Senate majority. 
No matter how well Democrats perform, prediction markets may find themselves facing tougher scrutiny in the next Congress, since lawmakers in both parties have expressed skepticism of the Trump administrationâs favorable regulatory approach.
Kalshi did not provide a comment. Schultz, who has maintained his own consulting firm since Obama left office, did not return a request for comment.
Schultz, who previously served as Obamaâs deputy White House press secretary, is one of several Democrats the firm has brought on this year. It has also tapped another Obama aide, Stephanie Cutter, as well as former Biden administration official John Bivona.
Businesses in adjacent industries are also stockpiling Democratic lobbyists â and occasionally phasing out Republican hands â in preparation for 2027. Veteran GOP adviser Joel Kaplan recently announced his departure as Metaâs global policy chief, while OpenAI recently hired Jessica Schumer, daughter of the Senate Democratic leader, to focus on the Northeast.
Kalshiâs Democratic firepower extends to its legal team: Neal Katyal, the attorney who convinced the Supreme Court to strike down President Donald Trumpâs tariffs, is representing the prediction market in its legal battle against states and tribes. The Kalshi-backed Coalition for Prediction Markets is represented by the Biden administrationâs solicitor general, Elizabeth Prelogar, and helmed by a former House Democrat, Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney of New York.
Some of the industryâs new hires could get pulled back into politics next year if Democrats choose to dig into the Trump administrationâs involvement with prediction markets. Maloney, who twice voted to impeach Trump, at the time called for Kalshi and Polymarket investor Donald Trump Jr. to testify before Congress.
Notable
- Kaplanâs selection as global policy chief in early 2025 left Meta âwell-placed for a Republican-dominated Washington,â Semafor reported at the time.
- Trumpâs top prediction market regulator told Semafor that heâs weighing further legal action against states that try to regulate the industry.

9dd75e159c91.text: By — Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Becky Bohrer, Associated Press By — Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-calls-for-prosecution-of-alaska-senate-candidate-peltola-over-sullivan-name-controversy Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump calls for prosecution of Alaska Senate candidate Peltola over Sullivan name controversy Politics Oct 28, 2026 7:29 PM EDT JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — President Donald Trump called for the criminal prosecution of the Democratic candidate running for Senate in Alaska on Wednesday after revelations that her campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan. WATCH: Trump calls for Peltola to drop out after report her campaign helped recruit 2nd Dan Sullivan The race is among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber. Trump had previously directed his Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race should Democrat Mary Peltola defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. "I think they should be prosecuted," the Republican president said about Peltola and the other Sullivan, responding to questions about a report in The New York Times. He earlier had posted on social media that "Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done." The newspaper obtained text messages between members of Peltola's campaign discussing recruiting other people with the same name as the two-term Republican. They eventually landed on a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg named Dan J. Sullivan. He made it through the state's August open primary and is one of four candidates on the ranked vote ballot for next Tuesday's general election. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats' behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola's campaign: "Zero, none, zilch," he said in June after announcing his run. He did not respond to a message seeking comment Wednesday from The Associated Press. Peltola's campaign, in a statement, said: "Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any DC politician will keep her away from that fight." A top state elections official earlier this year ruled Dan J. Sullivan ineligible for the primary ballot, concluding that his declaration of candidacy was filed "with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot's fairness or neutrality." The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. Alaska Republican U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, who has endorsed Sullivan and is a longtime friend of Peltola, said in a statement that Alaskans "deserve the honest truth from Mary and her campaign — what has been revealed is a pattern of lies and coverups and a culture of deception that belongs nowhere in our elections or among our elected officials." Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan's campaign, said: "Mary Peltola, her campaign and her senior advisers colluded with the DSCC, national Democrat lawyers and Alaska Democrat operatives to recruit candidates to deliberately confuse and deceive voters." Peltola's campaign, in a statement Wednesday, said it "has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign." They issued a similar statement in June after Sen. Sullivan questioned the other Sullivan's candidacy. Democrats, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick. "The DSCC is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan," the organization said in a statement Wednesday. The Times report said DSCC staffers were on texts with the Peltola campaign discussing the second Sullivan. Legal experts said the report about Democrats appearing to recruit Dan J. Sullivan as a way to potentially confuse voters will have no impact on a lawsuit filed recently by the U.S. Department of Justice. President Donald Trump directed the department to file the lawsuit, which seeks to halt certification of a possible Peltola win, citing the presence of the second Dan Sullivan on the ballot. "It's a dirty campaign trick, and it's good reason the Alaska Supreme Court should have permitted the candidate to have been removed from the ballot," said Derek Muller, a Notre Dame law professor. "But now it's in the hands of the voters, not litigation." It's not the first time a candidate's appearance on the Alaska ballot has been questioned. In 2024, the state Democratic Party sued to keep off the U.S. House ballot a man with no apparent ties to the state who is serving time in a federal prison in New York. A divided state Supreme Court allowed him to remain on the ballot. The man is running again this year, also in the House race, and is on the Nov. 3 ranked vote general election ballot. The Times story about the recruitment of Dan J. Sullivan is based partly on interviews with Peltola's former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired in August amid a campaign shake-up. The newspaper said she tried to retract her comments last week. Efforts by the AP to reach Rios were not immediately successful. As of Monday, 46,204 ballots had already been cast in Alaska, according to AP data. Sen. Sullivan is listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent. The other Sullivan is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation. Riccardi reported from Denver. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 52d049e2e35e.text: The most-aired ad in the closing stretch of Mississippi's Senate race features a Jeffrey Epstein survivor attacking GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith for voting against releasing files related to the convicted human trafficker. Why it matters: In the past week, Hyde-Smith has been outgunned on the airwaves. AdImpact data shows that only one of the eight most-aired spots portrays her positively. Five of the ads either positively portray her Democratic challenger, Scott Colom , or attack Hyde-Smith for her Senate record, largely painting her as an out-of-touch senator who cares more about her rich donors. The other two ads are for down-ballot races. Zoom out: The Epstein survivor ad has aired more than 1,200 times over the last week, costing the left-leaning New Deal for All super PAC over $329K, per AdImpact. In the ad, Jena-Lisa Jones condemns Hyde-Smith for her vote on the Epstein files and urges Mississippians to vote against her to protect their children. That vote, which passed 51-49 last year, indefinitely postponed an amendment that would have required the full release of the Epstein files by then-Attorney General Pam Bondi. "I do want transparency, and I support releasing information that can legally be released while protecting Epstein's victims. But a procedural vote on one amendment is not the same thing as saying the Epstein files should remain secret," Hyde-Smith said in a statement to the Mississippi Free Press. Hyde-Smith's campaign cut its own attack against Colom, calling him the "transgender defender" and naming him the "most radical Senate candidate of our lifetime." The ad played over 2,800 times across Mississippi and Memphis, Tenn., television markets in the 30 days since its Sept. 10 debut, costing the senator's campaign over $854K, per AdImpact. Hyde-Smith's campaign appears to have pulled back on the ad, spending less than $150,000 to air it between Oct. 19 and Oct. 26. The bottom line: Hyde-Smith is still expected to win, but the race is far tighter than anyone expected. As President Trump said during a rally for Hyde-Smith in Corinth, Miss. on Monday: "I'm here because Cindy is doing great, but I've just got to make sure."

26f497c3a961.text: Democrats will happily tell you how good they feel about retaking the House on Tuesday — just as soon as they stop hyperventilating into a paper bag. Why it matters: They've been burned too many times on Election Day to feel anything more than "nauseously optimistic," as one House Democrat put it to Axios. The polls point to a decisive Democratic victory on Nov. 3, yet fears of a massive polling error or some other eleventh-hour disaster are giving party members sleepless nights. "One woman at a rally in New Jersey told me last week that she was 'nauseously optimistic,'" Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) told Axios. "That may capture a lot of people's last-minute jitters." A House Democrat who has spoken to leadership told Axios: "They feel optimistic. You know, guarded. Guarded optimism. Where we're going to end up, you never know." State of play: Democrats are targeting dozens of Republican-held seats they think could flip, some of which President Trump carried by 10, 15, even 20 percentage points in 2024. Democrats' House Majority PAC, for instance, went on the air Wednesday in retiring Rep. Elise Stefanik's (R-N.Y.) district, which Trump won by 21 points. They also began spending against Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.), who won his last reelection with 60% of the vote. HMP is so bullish it has moved money out of the races to replace retiring Reps. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) and Darrell Issa (R-Calif.), which they believe Democrats are on track to win handily. "I am cautiously optimistic we win between 20-25 seats," Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) told Axios. Democrats' landslide scenario puts them closer to 40 or 50 pickups, which would be a historic night for the party. Yes, but: Mid-decade redistricting in Republican-controlled Southern states is all but certain to cut into those gains. The GOP is expected to easily flip redrawn seats in Tennessee and Louisiana where the incumbent Democrats chose to retire rather than face uphill reelection battles. Democratic leadership is also nervous about several Democrats who opted to run in their new seats, including Reps. Kathy Castor (D-Fla.), Darren Soto (D-Fla.) and Shomari Figures (D-Ala.), according to three lawmakers familiar with their thinking. What they're saying: All of the nearly 20 House Democrats who spoke to Axios on Wednesday expressed some degree of confidence about the election. "I've been to 26 states this campaign, and I'd say Democrats have been riding a wave of tremendous optimism and activism over the last several months," said Raskin. Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Mich.) told Axios she is feeling "legitimately good" and that "the cautious optimism is there only because of … history." "The optimism is real and I think for good reason," said Rep. Johnny Olszewski (D-Md.). But virtually everyone also offered reasons for keeping their expectations tempered. "Dems have been burnt by good polling before," Rep. Dave Min (D-Calif.) told Axios. Min also said Democrats are "hyper-aware of the election tampering that Trump and his goons are engaging in right now," something several other lawmakers echoed. "We're bracing for all manner of drama before, during and after the election," said Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.). The other side: "The Democrats are trying to deflect from the revelation of their secret, corrupt plan to stack Alaska's ballot," said White House spokesperson Lauren Bis, referring to a New York Times report about the drafting of spoiler Senate candidate Dan J. Sullivan. The Justice Department has sued to delay certification of Alaska's Senate election if Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan narrowly loses. "If these are the types of tactics Democrats need to use to win elections, maybe they should reexamine their radical policies," Bis said. Other Democrats worry that an eleventh-hour spending spree by Republican donors and super PACs will give the GOP a critical boost in the final days of the campaign. "Elon Musk's $366 million infusion to Republican coffers ... has definitely filtered down into a lot of the close House and Senate campaigns and paid for a wall of propaganda," said Raskin. Another House Democrat told Axios that there is "some anxiety about the super PAC money from Rs," which is "mostly coming" from candidates in battleground districts. Zoom in: Lawmakers also pointed to race-specific dynamics that have helped certain Republicans outrun national headwinds. The battle between Democrat Cait Conley and Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) is "razor-thin close" despite Kamala Harris carrying the district in 2024, a House Democrat from New York told Axios. A House Democrat from Michigan told Axios that Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed's weakness atop the ticket is "hurting" Democratic campaigns in the state's battleground House districts. A House Democrat from Texas told Axios the party will likely fall short in several winnable seats there because of either poor recruitment or insufficient investment from the national party. The bottom line: "There are two ways to run — scared and unopposed," said Scholten. "We're running in tough elections all across the country, and we're going to run hard through the tape in every single one."

At least 300,000 people in parts of the Himalayan region could now be living in the path of potential disasters, a new study suggests.
Researchers found that the amount of built-up land in high-risk zones in northern Nepal, parts of south-eastern Tibet and a corner of India's Uttarakhand had grown by about 45% between 2016 and 2023.
In areas particularly threatened by flooding from glacial lakes, development increased even faster, rising by almost 78% over the same period, according to the peer-reviewed study published in Scientific Reports.
The team of scientists behind it said the true number of people under threat could be much higher, as they only analysed a specific territory and not neighbouring areas which face similar risks.
The study was carried out before August's devastating mass floods which left more than 1,400 dead and thousands missing in Nepal. More recently there have been several smaller incidents, including flooding along the Budhi Gandaki river on 11 October that damaged 200 houses, swept away five bridges and left five people missing.
Nine researchers from the UK, Nepal and India looked at areas up to 50km (30 miles) downstream from Himalayan rivers, as well as around 1,360 glacial lakes.
They found significant development in these areas - including an expansion of tourism facilities, infrastructure development and real estate.
It's clear in Pokhara, a major tourism hub at the foot of the Himalayas that's grown significantly in the past 30 years to cater for a massive increase in visitors.
Mayor Dhana Raj Acharya says it's a huge challenge to deal with the risk posed by the Seti Gandaki River, which stems from the Annapurna mountain range and flows right through the city. Many old buildings are just 5m (16ft) from river banks, he says, despite new rules requiring them to be further away.
"Where we move them, and how we do that, is the real challenge."
To the north is the world-renowned Annapurna trekking region that has also seen a major increase in settlements along river banks - some hit by recent floods and landslides.
Phurpa Chhiring Lama, who runs a homestay there, feels helpless. Normally all of his 20 rooms are occupied at this time of year - the peak trekking season - but now only five are. "We have been doing this business for more than 40 years, but we've never seen this kind of disaster."
Krishna Gauchan, whose hotel is close to the glacier-fed Modi river, is worried too. "This river can flood if the glacier collapses or if the glacial lake bursts out and we are living in constant fear."
Tourism investors promote some of these spots as destinations without factoring in the risks, suggests Khagendra Poudel, a geographer at a local campus of Tribhuvan University. It's similar to what's happening in parts of north India's Himalayan valleys which host major pilgrimages.
The president of the Hotel Association Pokhara admits tourism businesses have expanded "without any proper planning" in the region and been promoted "haphazardly".
"By the time disasters hit, it is too late," says Laxman Subedi. "As a professional body we are trying to create awareness among tourism entrepreneurs and investors."
But it's not just tourism. The regions surrounding the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers have seen a significant rise in the construction of hydropower plants.
"As river valleys become increasingly populated, development decisions being made today will shape disaster risk for decades to come," warns the study's lead author, University of Leeds glaciologist C Scott Watson.
And even more buildings may be under threat than those identified by the researchers.
The study categorised buildings at risk as all those that were within 50 vertical metres (164ft) of a river or glacial lake's surface.
But during the catastrophic flooding on 26 August, locals in Rasuwa district say the river level had risen by 70m (230ft) at some points - so even buildings that were relatively far from the river banks were hit and buried by debris-sludge.
The risks in all of these areas are largely driven by warming in the Himalayan region, which scientists say is happening at twice the global rate. This has sped up the melting of glaciers, icefields, snowpacks, and ground that's normally frozen all year.
This can, in turn, destabilize mountain slopes which are also frequently shaken by earthquakes, unleashing devastating disasters downstream.
The rapid melting is also filling up and expanding glacial lakes until they burst, causing deadly floods. Nepal alone has documented around 30 of these events since 1940.
Another issue is that rising temperatures cause rain to reach high altitudes where it used to only snow, leading to slope failures, rock and ice falls, and other disasters.
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah raised the dangers of climate change at his recent UN General Assembly speech, where he said his country was paying a "colossal price" for a crisis it did not create.
"Every major disaster threatens to erase years of development. And it forces a poor country to borrow money to repair damage it did not cause."
Alton Byers, a mountain geographer at the University of Colorado who was not involved in the study, says it should serve as a "springboard" to bring about more effective early-warning systems and other precautionary measures.
But achieving that will be a challenge. Campaigners say building regulations aren't implemented on the ground and through the years, development has been haphazard in too many places.
Roads, hydropower projects, hotels and market towns have expanded on the low, flat land along rivers, which is accessible and buildable, says Prof Surya Raj Acharya, an urban planning expert and registrar at the University of Nepal.
Those responsible have often ignored safeguards including keeping off the river bank, he adds.

d37326e03c17.text: President Trump headed to Ohio to rally voters in a race that could determine control of the Senate. That stop comes after dueling rallies in another key state offered a snapshot of the divisions shaping the midterm elections. Liz Landers reports. Amna Nawaz: President Donald Trump heads to Ohio tonight to rally voters in a race that could determine control of the Senate. Geoff Bennett: And that stop follows dueling rallies in another key battleground state, Texas, that highlighted sharp divisions driving this year's midterms. Our Liz Landers reports. Liz Landers: Last night, a political showdown in a usually deep red state, Trump and Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico holding rallies just miles apart in Lubbock. President Donald Trump: And the other guy does not deserve it. He doesn't represent your values. State Rep. James Talarico: On November 3, we are going to do something extraordinary. We are going to do something historic. Liz Landers: The president mocking the Democrat with insults and a nickname. President Donald Trump: Seven days from now, the people of Texas are going to defeat Democrat communist James Talafreako. Liz Landers: Talarico using the timing of the dueling rallies and that nickname to fire up the crowd. State Rep. James Talarico: I know that we're not the only show in town tonight, and I appreciate all 4,000 of you that showed up here this evening. (CHEERING) State Rep. James Talarico: That's a lot of Talafreakos in one room. So... (CHEERING) Ken Paxton: Let's go win Texas. Liz Landers: Talarico's opponent, State Attorney General Ken Paxton, also taking swings. Ken Paxton: So let me tell you about the other guy. I think you've heard of him, James Talarico, the most radical Democrat to ever run in Texas history. (BOOING) Liz Landers: All for a key seat in a state that is not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in more than three decades. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to retake the majority in the U.S. Senate. Another state that captures the fault lines shaping this year's midterms, Pennsylvania. Just two years ago, the state was central to Trump's return to the White House, but now anxieties over the economy and corruption have crumbled support for Trump and the Republican base. Linda Markle, Pennsylvania Voter: The Republican Congress does not have a spine. They've abdicated their powers to one person, one person only. And that's not democracy. Liz Landers: But for others, the president and his party still have their support. John Tim Betts, Pennsylvania Voter: Probably President Trump. I mean, I'm sorry people don't like him, but I think he's doing more for us than anybody else has. Liz Landers: But how big is the battleground for Senate control? A new New York Times/Siena University poll shows Democrats may be making surprising gains, in reliably red South Carolina, Republican Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill her late brother Lindsey Graham's seat, tied with Democrat Annie Andrews. Darline Graham in South Carolina today: Sen. Darline Graham (R-SC): Nobody outworks South Carolinians. That's the formula, and it's working, and we're going to keep it going. Liz Landers: In North Carolina, where a Democrat hasn't been elected to the Senate in nearly 20 years, former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper leads Republican Michael Whatley by double digits, centering his campaign on affordability. Fmr. Gov. Roy Cooper: And these tariffs are chaotic. They're not -- they're essentially a tax, folks. We need to overturn them. I will work to do that when I get to the United States Senate. Liz Landers: Also in North Carolina today, Vice President J.D. Vance making the case for Republicans. J.D. Vance: North Carolina, you send a message to Washington that we are sick of being ignored, we are sick of being left behind, and we are going to put America first for a change. (CHEERING) Liz Landers: Both parties have less than one week left to make their closing arguments to voters. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Liz Landers.

4611d1e054d0.text: By — Farnoush Amiri, Associated Press Farnoush Amiri, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/un-condemns-u-s-economic-embargo-of-cuba-though-more-nations-sit-out-amid-trump-push Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter UN condemns U.S. economic embargo of Cuba though more nations sit out amid Trump push World Oct 28, 2026 6:50 PM EDT UNITED NATIONS (AP) — The U.N. General Assembly condemned the U.S. economic embargo of Cuba for the 34th year on Wednesday, even as Washington's campaign to influence the outcome led to a number of countries voting against the resolution or sitting out the decision for the first time. WATCH: Trump at GOP rally in Florida revives idea of military intervention in Cuba after Iran The vote was 130-17, with 25 abstentions — a notable decrease in support from last year, when more than 160 nations supported the measure and only 12 abstained. While such resolutions at the U.N. General Assembly are not legally binding, they do reflect world opinion. For the first time in 34 years, Western countries like Germany, Italy and Latvia were among those that refrained from voting. Bosnia, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Lithuania, Morocco, North Macedonia, Paraguay and Slovenia are among those member states that voted no — most for the first time. It marks a stunning shift in international support at a time when the small island country weathers outages, shortages and other deepening financial troubles as the Trump administration looks to force changes to Cuba's political system by increasing an already punishing economic campaign. President Donald Trump last week once again raised the specter of U.S. military intervention, saying American warships could stop over in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war. "A great power is attacking through economic war a member state of this organization," Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez said ahead of the vote. "Cuba is not a threat. The blockade is a threat." U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz told member nations that, "your vote today is the only thing standing between the corrupt, kleptocratic communist regime and using this body and your vote for another propaganda victory at the expense of the Cuban people." Tensions between Washington and Havana have spilled over into fiery public spats at the United Nations. On Tuesday, Waltz and Rodríguez got into a shouting match on the floor of the General Assembly while debating the embargo resolution. Watch the clip in the video player above. Shortly after Waltz had begun his criticism of the socialist government, Rodríguez walked down to the podium where the U.S. envoy was addressing the hall and called him a liar while trying to get a point of order from the official presiding over the session. "This individual needs to back away from this podium. He's not going to intimidate me in the United States of America," Waltz said as U.N. security and personnel tried to intervene. "You understand who you're dealing with? This is America. Back up." In a post on X, Rodríguez reminded Waltz where he was making his remarks, saying he's at the U.N., not at a national security meeting at the White House. "With his crude lies at the UN General Assembly, the U.S. government has launched another desperate attempt to justify its economic aggression against Cuba and its criminal energy blockade," he continued. On the sidelines of the GA hall, Waltz accused a member of Cuba's delegation of attacking an American diplomat who was filming him. He said Secretary of State Marco Rubio has ordered the official sent home. The State Department on Wednesday confirmed to the AP that the individual accused has left the U.S. A week earlier, a similar interaction between Waltz and his Cuban counterpart, Ernesto Soberón Guzmán, took place outside a U.S.-hosted panel with Cuban dissidents and former prisoners that sought to highlight allegations of the oppressive behavior of the island's government. It all reflects a clear break from the traditional diplomatic decorum expected at the U.N. and the new phase of contentiousness between the U.S. and Cuba. The U.S. embargo against Cuba was first imposed in 1960 after Fidel Castro led a revolution that toppled dictator Fulgencio Batista and nationalized properties belonging to U.S. citizens and corporations. As a result, the Caribbean country has spent decades facing the dire impact of longtime economic and financial troubles and is now being pushed to a breaking point after Trump announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to Cuba. The warning has effectively cut off fuel to the island, leading to widespread power outages that impact basic services such as water supply and internet and telephone services. Associated Press writer Matthew Lee in Washington and Dánica Coto in San Juan, Puerto Rico, contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Farnoush Amiri, Associated Press Farnoush Amiri, Associated Press

765210bfec18.text: In Israel, nearly all the votes have been counted in Tuesday's election. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies emerged as the largest bloc, but lost seats and fell short of the majority needed to form a government. The results leave Israel facing the prospect of political gridlock. Nick Schifrin reports from Tel Aviv. Geoff Bennett: In Israel, nearly all the votes have been counted in yesterday's election. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies emerged as the largest bloc, but lost seats and fell short of the majority needed to form a new government. The results leave Israel facing the prospect of political gridlock. Nick Schifrin joins us now from Tel Aviv. So, Nick, last night the opposition bloc was leading based on exit polls. Now that the votes have been counted, where do the party stand? Nick Schifrin: Well, you're right, Geoff. The polls essentially inverted the final results. As you said, Netanyahu's Likud Party won the most seats of any party, and his coalition also won the most seats, even if, as you pointed out, they did lose their majority. Now, as of now, with the vast majority of votes counted, they -- Netanyahu's bloc has 53 seats, well short of the 61 it needs for a majority in the Parliament or Knesset, but more than the 48 seats that the opposition Change bloc won. One of the most significant outcomes of this election is the 19 seats that as of now the Arab parties won. They are also anti-Netanyahu. So you could conclude that the majority of the country rejected the current government, but that is not how Israeli politics work. It is Netanyahu's coalition that has the most votes, which means, as of now, there's not only weeks ahead of us of negotiations, but there's no clear direction that the country has chosen to go, even though, Geoff, voters on all sides told us that the country is at a crossroads. Geoff Bennett: And what are the scenarios, Nick, for what could happen next? Nick Schifrin: So, next week, Israel's president will invite one of the blocs to try and form a majority government. When it comes to Netanyahu, he would have to persuade one of Eisenkot's coalition partners to defect. But a Netanyahu official told me today they consider that impossible. Or he could form what's known as a unity government with Eisenkot. This has been done before, especially in times of war. But Eisenkot and all of his allies have ruled it out. They are vociferously anti-Netanyahu. Now, Eisenkot does have his own path. Note again, the Change bloc in blue and the Arab parties in green combined have more than 61 and could create a government together. But Israelis have been resistant to Jewish parties needing Arab parties to be part of the ruling coalition, especially after October the 7th, and Eisenkot calls his coalition -- quote -- "Zionist." But we will see what happens because there is a technical way for those Arab parties to support Eisenkot from the outside. As for Netanyahu today, his campaign accused Arab voters of -- quote -- "stealing the election," an allegation police responded to by saying there is no investigative substantiation to the claims. And last night, Netanyahu called for the Arab parties to be excluded. Benjamin Netanyahu, Israeli Prime Minister (through interpreter): We must form a right-wing national strong government. That is what must be done. We must not, must not endanger Israel and establish a government that is backed by anti-Zionist Arab parties. Nick Schifrin: Finally, Geoff, the fourth and perhaps most likely scenario at this point, one that many Israelis do not want, neither side gets to form a government or neither side succeeds in forming a government, and Israel heads to more elections. Geoff Bennett: And what might all of this mean for Netanyahu and his political future, Nick? Nick Schifrin: Well, Netanyahu stays prime minister, even if he's supposed to act with restraint. But analysts here say that he could choose to take the country to war. A U.S. official confirms to me that Netanyahu pushed for attacks on Iran before the Israeli election. Israeli defense officials have also said that, and that led to this extraordinary warning last night from Gadi Eisenkot. Gadi Eisenkot, Israeli Prime Minister Candidate (through interpreter): I call on the heads of the security establishment and the civil service, remember that you serve only the state and the interests of the Israeli citizens. Stand firm against any attempt to challenge you. Netanyahu, do not dare use Israel's security for your own political needs. Nick Schifrin: Now, U.S. officials have also said, including President Trump in public, that the U.S. could go back to war with Iran after the U.S. midterm elections. And that would presumably give Netanyahu more leverage as these coalition talks play out, and which shows, really no matter what happens, Geoff, whether Netanyahu is able to form the coalition or not, we are still in a country dominated by Netanyahu and the opposition's inability to sell a majority of the country on the idea of a post-Netanyahu Israel. Geoff Bennett: Nick Schifrin reporting again for us from Tel Aviv. Nick, our thanks to you.

d01e894acb39.text: There is shock, anger and mourning in Spain after the second fatal train crash this year. At least 68 people have died in what is now the deadliest collision there in more than a decade. William Brangham reports. Amna Nawaz: In the day's other headlines: There is shock, anger and mourning in Spain after the second fatal train crash this year in what's now the deadliest collision there in more than a decade. At least 68 people have died. William Brangham has our report. William Brangham: A normal morning train journey in Central Spain today ended in a field of twisted steel. Near the town of Urda, about 90 miles south of Madrid, a high-speed train bound for Seville slammed into another train that was stopped, knocking them both off the tracks and shearing at least one apart; 147 people were aboard the stopped train. From inside, survivors could see out the windows at the destruction they'd narrowly missed. On the other train, nearly 400 passengers were thrown into chaos. Rafael Barcelo, Train Passenger (through interpreter): We were having breakfast, having a coffee, and we felt a huge impact. We were all thrown into the air. I am reasonably OK. My friend is quite worse. William Brangham: Many are now looking for their loved ones. Woman (through interpreter): My husband was in the train that left Madrid, and we just rushed here as soon as we heard about the accident. We came here and no one tells us anything. I don't know anything. William Brangham: Firefighters and a military unit climbed through the wreckage, digging by hand through shattered seats and crushed steel. Authorities said this is Spain's deadliest rail accident in more than a decade, but it's not the first one this year. In January, on the same high-speed line, a train operated by the same carrier derailed and struck another, killing 46, and ignited a debate over whether Spain is doing enough to keep its railways safe. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who faces national elections next month, went to the scene and promised action. Pedro Sanchez, Spanish Prime Minister (through interpreter): We are going to get to the bottom of this. If there were failures in the safety system, we will address them decisively. William Brangham: All high-speed service between Madrid and the southern province of Andalusia has been suspended. But in a country that built one of the world's larger high-speed networks, with the promise that its cities could be linked quickly and safely, today, that promise lies in pieces for the second time in a year. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm William Brangham.

Political action committees funded by technology companies, the state’s major utilities and other corporate interests have spent nearly twice as much to pass a ballot measure that would greenlight major development projects with minimal environmental or public review as public interest and labor groups have spent opposing it.
Developers and other corporate interests aim to streamline the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA, which requires public agencies to identify, disclose and mitigate a development project’s negative impacts on a wide range of environmental resources, including wildlife, air and water quality and tribal cultural resources.
Proposition 45 shifts who determines the scope of environmental review from public agencies and communities to project developers by rewriting the state’s foundational environmental law to fast-track major projects.
Supporters of Prop 45, sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, have spent more than $56 million to pass the measure, the most recent state records show. Opponents, led by a coalition of more than 550 labor, health and environmental organizations, have spent close to $30 million to defeat what they say will give polluters a free pass.
“Prop 45 will modernize the approval process for essential projects by establishing clear, enforceable timelines for agency decisions and court challenges,” the chamber said in promotional materials, “while keeping environmental protections intact and preserving worker protections, tribal protections and local control.”
Critics say Prop 45 will gut the state’s primary vehicle for allowing people to learn about plans for polluting developments in their neighborhoods and propose alternatives.
“It undermines basically every stage of that process,” said Woody Little, the spokesperson for No on Prop 45.
Little and his allies say the 41-page ballot measure was written by corporations who have paid to get their special interests on the ballot to create loopholes that favor polluting industries like recently regulated data centers while limiting the input of communities and local tribes.
Critics of CEQA, signed in 1970 by then-Gov. Ronald Reagan, blame the law for hobbling home construction and driving housing and cost of living increases in California, which are among the highest in the nation.
Prop 45 will lower housing and utility costs by reducing “endless” bureaucratic delays and protect taxpayers by reducing waste and cost overruns, Yes on Prop 45 materials argue.
Yet there is no requirement in the measure to reduce housing costs or utility bills. And the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that Prop 45 could leave state and local governments paying $100 million or more a year, partly to cover fast-tracked projects’ environmental impacts.
“The housing issue is a smokescreen for all these other polluting projects,” said Little.
California passed laws last year that significantly streamlined CEQA by exempting urban and mixed-use housing construction from its provisions as well as certain infrastructure and clean energy projects.
“I would hope that 100 percent of Californians would see this radical reshaping of California’s environmental law for the dangerous thing that it is. A wolf in sheep’s clothing.”
— Woody Little, No on Prop 45
None of the grassroots groups that promote “yes in my backyard,” or YIMBY, policies to build more housing and public transit in urban and suburban areas support Prop 45, Little said. Most are neutral, he said, while others oppose it.
Expanding housing beyond already developed areas means building new freeways, water connections and other expensive infrastructure that taxpayers ultimately pay for, Little said. And these projects often encroach on the wildland-urban interface, raising wildfire risk just as climate change is making fires more destructive.
At a time when California is already seeing the catastrophic costs of climate-fueled fires, Little said, the state should be requiring more environmental review around developments to assess and mitigate risk, not less.
What’s “Essential”?
Prop 45 covers nine types of “essential” projects, among them housing, water systems, clean energy (including carbon capture and storage), transportation, wildfire risk reduction and broadband internet access. All related and “ancillary” infrastructure is also covered.
Whether “ancillary” includes data centers, which typically require broadband infrastructure, has been a major point of contention.
Prop 45’s proponents have insisted the measure does not cover data centers, but legal experts disagree, pointing to $2 million in donations from just three data center builders and language buried in the measure’s 41 pages. Eligible projects include “broadband internet access projects,” defined as “mass-market retail service … that provides the capability to transmit data to, and receive data from, all or substantially all Internet endpoints,” a recent analysis found.

That definition includes facilities that house the physical infrastructure used to transmit consumer data to and from the internet—which describes many data centers.
Yet data centers are conspicuously absent from the list of excluded controversial projects, which includes high-speed rail, the Delta Conveyance Project, nuclear power and oil and gas facilities.
