From the moment Ryua first walked into her rental apartment in Tokyo she believed it to be haunted.
"When I visited the place for a viewing there was a man standing there, glaring at me," she says.
"Since the estate agent couldn't see him, I realised he must be a ghost."
While someone more squeamish would probably have quickly left the flat never to return, Ryua chose to go ahead and move in.
"I'm a bit of a contrarian, so I decided I wanted to become friends with this glaring male ghost," adds Ryua, who works as an aidoru, a young entertainer, and who doesn't wish to share her surname.
Four years later, and still in the same apartment, she says she continues to experience paranormal activity on a daily basis. She says she hears endless footsteps and the ghost talking.
Although Japan has increasingly marked Halloween, external in recent years, many Japanese people take ghosts seriously all year round. The country has a word, "yuurei", which means a lingering, troubled spirit.
These are the ghosts of people who died in violent or tragic circumstances - those who were murdered, killed themselves, or simply were lonely and died alone. If they died at home, then the belief is that their yuurei won't go away.
For house hunters who are not superstitious or squeamish it means there are big bargains to be found. There is a whole category of dwellings called jiko bukken, which means "stigmatised" or "incident" properties.
Under guidelines issued by the government in 2021, Japanese estate agents must disclose suicide, murder, death by fire, and any death where the body was not discovered for an extended period of time.
For rental properties this information must be disclosed for three years, and it must be revealed indefinitely for any property offered for sale.
By contrast, in the UK there is no legal requirement, external to reveal that a person died in a property. And in the US, it differs from state to state., external For example, in California you have to reveal if a person has died in the property in the past three years, while in Arizona and Oregon you do not.
Ryua was told that a man had killed himself in her apartment. It meant that she gets an almost 30% discount on her rent on her tiny, 25 sq m bedsit in the fashionable ward of Setagaya. She says she pays 45,000 yen ($285; Â£213) a month, instead of what should have been 62,000 yen.
While a house where there had been a murder or suicide would probably be harder to sell or rent out anywhere in the world, Tokyo estate agent Erik Oskamp says that Japanese people are particularly superstitious and averse to stigmatised properties.
"[Even] an apartment next to a cemetery will be difficult to rent out, especially if you can see the tombs from the kitchen," explains Oskamp. "The worst thing is if a suicide has happened in the apartment. Even if somebody has jumped from the roof, many renters will move out. Other issues are a serious crime or a lonely death."
The latter issue, that of a person dying alone, would not generally affect the price of a property in, say, the UK or the US.
But in rural Kagoshima, in Japan's southwest, it enabled Diane Tincher to buy a large three-bedroom house for about half of what would have otherwise been the asking price.
'If there is a ghost I'm thankful to her'
The 79-year-old American has lived in Japan for nearly 40 years, working as a tour guide. She says that the estate agent had been straight with her â there was a heavy discount as an elderly lady had died alone, thereby stigmatising the property.
Tincher paid 20m yen for the house, in a location where similar properties usually sell for up to 45m yen.
"I don't believe in ghosts. But I know that the Japanese are very superstitious," she says. "If there is a ghost I'm thankful to her every day... to live in such a splendid and affordable home."
Researching the house, Tincher had found it on a website called Oshimaland, which lists jiko bukken properties, giving details of the events that occurred. It was launched in 2005 covering Tokyo, before expanding across Japan and then internationally in 2011.
It is crowdsourced, meaning that members of the public add the homes and their details.
Teru Oshima, the founder of Oshimaland, says that in the past such properties were "not very attractive options" in Japan.
Yet as house prices have surged in the country in recent years, as well as a big increase in the wider cost of living, one 2025 survey found that more than half of Japanese people would now rent a jiko bukken if it was cheap., external
Back in Setagaya, Ryua says she is happy living with her ghostly flatmate. "I believe that ghosts were once living human beings, so they deserve our respect," she says.

978403e153a0.text: Vice President Vance sent a letter to Iran's national security chief stressing that any negotiations to head off U.S. military strikes "require discussions on the nuclear issue," a U.S. official said. Why it matters: The letter to Mohsen Rezaei, which focused on the possibility of restarting negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, is the most senior-level outreach by the U.S. to Iran in several months. It comes as President Trump considers resuming major combat operations in Iran after the midterm elections. Behind the scenes: Vance suggested sending the letter to Rezaei, who is one of the top national security officials in Iran and has a direct line to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. "The President was enthusiastic about the letter," said the U.S. official, who declined to say when it was sent. The Wall Street Journal first reported the letter. Zoom out: One of the key sticking points in efforts to relaunch negotiations is Iran's demand that the U.S. first lift its naval blockade, release frozen funds, and allow oil sales. The U.S. wants Iran to restart nuclear negotiations before receiving any sanctions relief. What he's saying: Trump told reporters Wednesday that Vance's letter was about helping Iran obtain needed medical supplies. "Basically, it's getting supplies in to help people that are not well," he said.

The Republican governor of Alaska has ordered an investigation into an alleged "scheme" which led to two Dan Sullivans standing in the state's US Senate race.
Governor Mike Dunleavy said he was responding to a New York Times (NYT) story, external which said the team of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola worked with people who tried to recruit spoiler candidates in the Senate race.
The governor's post on X said he would investigate "whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws". He did not say which laws he had in mind.
Dan Sullivan, the incumbent Republican senator running for re-election, and allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters. Peltola's team deny any wrongdoing.
They say they did not encourage the second Dan Sullivan, a retired teacher who lives in a remote fishing village, to stand. He has denied any links with the Peltola campaign.
The Alaska race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest of the upcoming US midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress. Americans head to the polls across the country on Tuesday.
Dunleavy's statement, which did not name the Peltola campaign, said the NYT reporting had supported findings by the state Division of Elections earlier this year.
"I am therefore directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted," he wrote. "The evidence will determine what happens next."
The NYT report alleged that people connected to Peltola's campaign, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), worked to try to recruit Sullivan the schoolteacher to stand in the Senate race.
This was part of a broader effort to encourage other would-be "spoiler" candidates to enter the race and dilute the support of the sitting Republican senator, the newspaper reported.
The paper said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the NYT's reporting.
The ballot paper is set to list the two men as Dan S Sullivan, who will be described as the incumbent Republican senator, and Daniel J Sullivan Jr.
Senator Dan Sullivan told Fox News on Wednesday night that Peltola should "come clean" and described it as a scandal of the highest order.
His fellow Republican senator in Alaska, Lisa Murkowksi, accused the Democratic campaign of engaging in a "pattern of lies". President Donald Trump has called for Peltola to be barred.
Previous efforts by the Republicans to remove Sullivan, the retired teacher, from the ballot have already been rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court which found no state laws had been broken by him running in the race.
The Trump administration filed a federal lawsuit last week aimed at preventing the certification of the result if the Trump-backed Sullivan loses, arguing that the presence of both of them on the ballot could confuse voters.
Some legal experts expressed scepticism of the merits of the lawsuit, and their chances of success given Alaska's courts had already allowed the second Sullivan to remain on the ballot.
The actual legal arguments the justice department made were a "frivolous theory," Rick Pildes, an election law expert at New York University, told the BBC.
He noted the lawsuit did not cite a specific provision that the government wanted to enforce, merely a general preamble taken from a sweeping US voting law.
Alaska election officials asked a federal court to dismiss the lawsuit "because the complaint has no legal basis".
The justice department has pledged continued legal action in the wake of the New York Times' reporting.
"They are cheating, let's call it what it is," Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Fox News on Wednesday.
In a series of Truth Social posts, Trump too pointed to the report and made a variety of allegations against Peltola, who he argued should be removed from the ballot. He repeated his endorsement for Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican senator, writing: "Dan is a GREAT man, has ALWAYS delivered for Alaska."
Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box.
The battle threatens to delay the full picture of nationwide results following the midterm elections. The ultimate question of which party controls Congress will have a significant bearing on the remaining two years of Trump's presidency.
A statement from an Alaskans for Mary spokesperson, written prior to Dunleavy's call for an investigation, said: "Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any DC politician will keep her away from that fight.
"The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign."
In a statement given to US media, the DSCC likewise denied that it had been involved in any such scheme.
Peltola earlier this week paused campaigning activities in order to recover after she and her family sustained "minor injuries" in a car crash.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has laid out her vision for what an "associate membership" status for Canada to the EU would look like as officials gather in Montreal to discuss closer ties.
It is "a partnership that comes close to membership than anything we have done before," she said on Thursday's remarks at the two-day Canada-EU summit.
She added it is a type of relationship that would be open "only to our closest partners outside of Europe who are ready to open a new frontier together."
It includes close alignment on governance and policies, and partnering in research and innovation.
For decades, Canada-EU summits took place without much fanfare - but that's not the case for this year's meeting in the Canadian city.
Thursday and Friday's summit is being closely watched for details on how Canada and the European bloc deepen their ties.
Von der Leyen first proposed "opening the door" to Canada last month for what she called an "associate membership" - a status that does not currently exist.
The overture came after Prime Minister Carney addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg, telling EU lawmakers that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".
Carney and many EU member states welcome closer ties, but not all are on board with what to call this new relationship.
Some, like Germany, are questioning the "associate member" term, fearing that Canada is getting preferential treatment ahead of other nations who also want in.
According to reports by multiple news outlets, Germany and other nations successfully lobbied to remove mention of the title in a draft statement ahead of the summit, opting instead for softer language that references an "ever closer association".
Germany's ambassador to Canada, Matthias LÃ¼ttenberg, told CTV News on Tuesday that some member states were "a little surprised" by von der Leyen's announcement last month.
While there is broad support for closer ties, the concept of "associate membership" is something that is not clearly understood as it pertains to Canada, he said.
"Germany has been using the term of associate membership for something completely different, which is the relationship of the EU to Ukraine and potentially Moldova", he said, both of which have been trying to join the bloc for many years.
Despite some opposition, von der Leyen has continued to use the term has not addressed the disagreement over the term.
Later on Thursday, Carney and von der Leyen and business leaders from both Europe and Canada will gather for a business forum.
Canadian officials said they also expect agreements to be hammered out on defence, critical minerals, research and trade over the two days.
Speaking to reporters earlier this week, European officials downplayed the possibility of a major announcement on Canada's new relationship with EU, saying much will be sorted in the coming months.
But both Canadian and EU officials have provided some clues on what the relationship could look like, including closer business ties and allowing more students to study on either side of the Atlantic.
Canada also does not plan on paying a membership fee similar to other EU nations, Canadian officials have said. Instead, it is looking at participating in different EU programmes that would benefit both Canada and member states.
And despite some disagreement about the wording, both have signalled they are fully on board with deepening ties.
"The wording is emblematic of the ambition," said one senior Canadian official who was granted anonymity to speak to reporters at a briefing ahead of the summit.
Since taking office last year, Prime Minister Carney has pushed Canada closer to Europe as his country continues to deal with an ongoing trade war with the US, its neighbour and largest trading customer.
US President Donald Trump has called the idea of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU "laughable", and has threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe if he considered it a "hostile act".
Canadian officials stressed on Wednesday that their pivot to Europe is not meant to offend anybody, but rather to build on work that was already underway.
Canada recently signed an agreement that gives its defence companies procurement access to the EU's Security and Defence Partnership programme.
It also signed a landmark energy deal with Germany in May that would see the first-ever long-term shipments of liquified natural gas from Canada to Europe in the coming years.
On Thursday, Canada released its new National Security Strategy, the first in two decades, which underlines supporting security and stability in Europe as a priority.
As for what this new relationship status will be called, Carney has said the "nomenclature" does not matter.
"What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians," he said.

DoorDash will acquire grocery delivery firm Instacart in a $17bn (Â£12.8bn) deal, creating a behemoth that will bring more meals, quick-need purchases and big weekly shops directly to customers.
DoorDash said the deal, expected to be final in about a year, will expand options for customers and let more sellers use the companies' services.
Instacart shoppers will be able to buy from 150,000 stores, up from the current 100,000, while DoorDash will reach beyond restaurants into retail, the firms said.
"Together, we can accelerate innovation across the grocery industry and make online grocery more seamless and affordable for the millions of households we serve," Instacart's chief executive said.
"Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more," CEO Chris Rogers also said.
For DoorDash, the acquisition will allow it to use Instacart's grocery selection and substitution expertise, the company's co-founder and chief executive, Tony Xu, said.
"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you'd choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts," Xu said.
He added that "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day".
The deal, expected to be done by the end of 2027 or first six months of 2028, is DoorDash's biggest acquisition to date, and could help it take on delivery giants like Amazon.
Morningstar analyst Martin Szumski told Reuters that the growth area in food delivery was shifting.
"Restaurant delivery is maturing, and growth now lies in more frequent, higher-value orders: weekly grocery shops, convenience items, and retail," he said.
In the agreement, DoorDash will acquire Instacart for a value of $65 a share, which would be a 26% premium on the closing price of Instacart stock on 22 October - the price before news of the potential merger first emerged. The deal will be at least 75% cash, DoorDash said.
DoorDash plans to keep Instacart's brand, app, and technology products. The delivery services will keep operating as independent companies until the deal is concluded.
The merger may raise antitrust issues with government regulators, Reuters also reported.
New York City's commission on consumer and worker protections, which last month reached a $131.5m settlement with DoorDash over allegations of underpaying workers, said in a statement: "This proposed merger continues a troubling trend of mega-corporations consolidating."
"Whether or not this merger proceeds, we will fully enforce delivery workers' rights," it added.

The defeated candidate in Brazil's presidential election, FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, has referred to himself as "leader of Brazil" in a letter he published on social media after leaving the country for the United States.
Bolsonaro lost to his left-wing rival, Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva, in the run-off on Sunday by a difference of 4.4 million votes, but has not conceded defeat.
In the letter, Bolsonaro alleges, without offering evidence, that he was the victim of "electoral fraud" and says that he will lead the opposition from the US.
He left Brazil on Tuesday after failing to comply with an order to surrender his passports, a decision which Lula described as "a shameful act".
Bolsonaro starts his letter, which he posted on his X account, saying "I address the Brazilian people and the international community as the leader of Brazil".
However, he had posted a previous version, that was later deleted, in which he wrote: "I address the Brazilian people and the international community as the rightful president of Brazil."
Both versions repeat the allegation that Bolsonaro first made on election night, that an extension of polling hours on Sunday had benefited his rival.
In the letter, he says it was "an electoral fraud unfolding before my eyes".
The extension was requested by both Lula's and Bolsonaro's campaign teams, and the head of Brazil's electoral authority has said that the vote proceeded normally and in full accordance with the country's laws and constitution.
An analysis of election data conducted by BBC Brazil and BBC Verify has also found that only around 34,000 people voted during the extended hours - far lower than the 4.4 million votes that separated Lula from Bolsonaro.
In his letter, Bolsonaro also addresses his departure from Brazil - which caused confusion after he disappeared for more than 24 hours.
It later emerged that he had gone across the land border to Argentina, and from there flew on to Florida, following a brief refuelling stop in Ecuador.
Bolsonaro left after failing to hand in his passports to police - in defiance of a Supreme Court order, which had been issued as part of an investigation into alleged money laundering.
He has not been charged as part of the money laundering probe and denies any wrongdoing, calling the investigation a "politically-motivated witch hunt".
Bolsonaro added that he had never intended to leave Brazil, but argued that he was the victim of "political persecution".
He ended the letter by saying: "I left Brazil but I haven't abandoned Brazilians".
While FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro said that he planned to lead the opposition from the US, it was not clear how he planned to do that.
His party recognised the election result and while some of its politicians have described Bolsonaro as a "political exile", the Liberal Party's leader RogÃ©rio Marinho stated on Wednesday that "there is no evidence" of the electoral fraud that Bolsonaro alleges took place.
It is also not yet clear where Bolsonaro intends to stay or for how long.
His younger brother, Eduardo, has been in self-imposed exile in the US since March 2025, saying he was the victim of political persecution. The two siblings posted a photo of themselves holding a Brazilian flag on Wednesday.
The Trump administration has provided visas for FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro and his family but did not say what kind of visas they were.
The US president did not explicitly endorse Bolsonaro in the run-up to the election and told reporters he "won't get involved" when asked about Bolsonaro's allegations of election fraud.
Earlier in the week, he had said that "it looked like another rigged election," without providing any evidence.
And on Thursday, Trump told reporters that "the election was a very great embarrassment to the people of Brazil".

At least 14 people have been killed after a Russian jet-powered drone hit a crowded platform at the main railway station in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, local officials have said.
Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said at least 14 others were wounded in the attack, including an 11-year-old boy.
Ukraine's state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said a passenger train headed for the southern city of Zaporizhzhia was at one of the platforms in Dnipro when the drone hit.
Russia's military has not publicly commented. It has repeatedly hit Ukraine's large railway network, but Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians.
In Dnipro, an elevated threat level was announced ahead of Thursday's strike, according to the railway operator chief, Oleksandr Pertsovsky.
"But unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform" when the drone struck, he said.
Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov said the incident was a tragedy, adding that a drone hit an electric civilian train.
Pictures from the Ukrainian rescue services show a large hole in a platform that is strewn with blurred-out bodies, near a blast-damaged train with smashed windows.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said "the Russians used a drone to attack a platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing."
He called for further US, European and G7 sanctions on Russia and repeated his criticism of a controversial deal that was struck earlier this month between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, which eased some sanctions on Moscow, allowing the US to import Russian diesel.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, two girls aged 15 were killed in a Russian missile attack on the centre of Chernihiv city, in the north of the country, regional head Vyacheslav Chaus said. At least 25 others, including four children, were injured, he added.
Chernihiv will hold a day of mourning on Friday.
In the city of Kremenchuk, in the central Poltava region, three people were killed and 28 injured in a Russian drone attack that hit residential buildings and a school, regional head Vitaliy Diakivnych said.
The latest Russian strikes came during efforts to uphold a fragile ceasefire in the besieged city of Oleshky, which has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and where residents have been trapped without food, water, medicine and electricity for years.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, wrote on Telegram that the truce was holding into a third day.
Meanwhile, the Kremlin has condemned Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow whilst the city hosts the Russia-Africa Summit, the Tass news agency has reported. The two-day event is attended by African leaders and government delegations from 48 countries.
The mayor of Moscow said 613 Ukrainian drones were launched overnight towards the region, most of which were shot down during their flight.
Russia's defence ministry has always denied targeting Ukrainian civilians and says its attacks on railways target the infrastructure used to transport military personnel and equipment.
However, the dangers to passengers are very real, and attacks on Ukraine's train infrastructure have risen sharply.
Of the 521 locomotives hit since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, almost 60% have been hit this year, according to statistics released by Ukrzaliznytsia supplied to AFP news agency.
Overall attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.
There appears to have been a wider assault on Ukraine's infrastructure in recent weeks, with two bridges attacked in the capital Kyiv, and a metro train hit during one of the strikes.

Philippine police have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from the former home of Thomas Markle, father of the Duchess of Sussex.
Earlier this month, it was reported that hundreds of images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Thomas Markle Sr, 82, had been found at the property in the Philippines.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes, were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week. However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they could examine the items.
Thomas Markle Sr, who is now in the US, has strongly denied the allegations made by his son, describing them as "sick lies".
Cebu Regional Prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC that Thomas Markle Jr was "adamant" that the case should be investigated, and that he felt his father "has to answer for it".
Last week, the Sun on Sunday reported that Thomas Markle Sr's ex-wife, Roslyn Loveless, had sent a letter to the Metropolitan Police about the 2019 allegations, which was shared with the Duke and Duchess of Sussex at the time.
Loveless, who has since died, is the mother of Meghan's two half-siblings. She divorced Thomas Markle Sr. in 1975, before he married the duchess's mother.
The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.
In a statement shared on Friday, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".
Speaking to the Sun, Thomas Markle Jr also apologised to Meghan for initially siding with her father during their long-running estrangement, and said he had "been protecting the wrong person for the past nine years".
Thomas Markle Sr moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May.
He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.
The police say they must identify how the material was obtained before they can consider any criminal charges.
Campaigners describe Cebu as a known hotspot for the sexual exploitation of children, and authorities say they take any such allegations very seriously.

A decade ago, an electric vehicle with more than 300 miles of range would have cost you nearly $100,000.
Today, 300 miles of range sits in the middle of the market and consumers can expect at least 200 miles in even the least expensive models, based on the latest 2027 model-year data on fueleconomy.gov.
This increase in range reflects falling battery costs and technological improvements. It’s helping boost the appeal of owning an EV by reducing range anxiety—the fear of being stranded mid-trip with nowhere to charge.
According to BloombergNEF, the global average price of a lithium-ion battery pack was $108 per kilowatt-hour in 2025, down 8 percent from the prior year and down more than 90 percent since 2010.
That’s “an astonishing number,” said Pavel Molchanov, managing director for renewable energy and clean technology at the financial services firm Raymond James, in an interview.
Molchanov covered rising battery range in a recent report on the EV market, noting that 500 miles of range may be regarded as normal by 2030.
Let’s zoom out to what this may mean for oil demand. EVs accounted for 25 percent of the global market for new cars and light trucks, though they were less than 10 percent in the United States, according to the International Council on Clean Transportation.
At current ownership levels, electric cars and light trucks reduce global oil demand by 2.2 million barrels per day compared with what it would otherwise be, according to the Raymond James report. That’s 2 percent to 3 percent of global demand.
Molchanov expects this share to more than double by 2030, which is one of the reasons he thinks global oil demand will have peaked by then.
Demand is down this year compared to 2025 because of the Iran war, and is likely to rebound when the war ends, he said. But he acknowledges that demand may never recover because of geopolitical changes in response to the war and rising EV market share.
“It is not inconceivable that 2025 was the peak,” he said.
The 2027 model with the most range is the Lucid Air Grand Touring AWD with 19-inch wheels, which can go 512 miles on a charge, according to fueleconomy.gov. Its base price is $114,900, which puts it well outside what most people can afford.
Lucid, based in Newark, California, says it achieves high ranges because its motors, batteries and other components are designed for high efficiency. The efficiency is evident in its ability to go five miles per kilowatt-hour of battery capacity, which is much higher than is typical.
So that’s the top of the list. How about the middle?
The median range is 311 miles, which includes the Audi S6 e-tron and the Hyundai Ioniq 9 AWD Performance. They have base prices of $79,600 and $71,250, respectively.
That’s still too expensive for most buyers, but several other models stand out with long ranges and lower prices: The Chevrolet Equinox FWD has a range of 319 miles and a base price of $36,795, and the Toyota bZ XLE FWD Plus has a range of 314 miles and a base price of $37,980.
The model with the least range in the database is the VinFast VF 7 Plus, with 209 miles. VinFast, a Vietnamese brand that is building a U.S. dealer network, no longer lists the VF 7 on its website, but the VF 8 has 256 miles of range and a base price of $40,400.
To gauge how much batteries have improved, I looked at ranges from a decade ago.
At the top was the Tesla Model S AWD-100D, with 335 miles and a base price of $94,000.
At the bottom was the Smart Fortwo Electric Drive Convertible, with 57 miles and a base price of $28,750.
Looking further back illustrates the scale of improvement, according to Department of Energy data.
In 2011, there were just four models: the BMW 1 Series ActiveE, the Nissan Leaf, the Smart Fortwo Electric Drive Coupe and the Smart Fortwo Electric Drive Cabriolet. The BMW had the most range with 94 miles.
Now there are more than 100 models and the median range continues to increase.
I don’t think range anxiety is dead, but it’s fading fast because of battery innovation and the expansion of public charging networks. That said, chargers are still rare in some states and regions. But these gaps in the system are less of an issue when a typical battery has enough range to cross an entire state.
Let’s put this in practical terms. For me, EV range reached an important threshold at 240 miles.

South West Water has been given the lowest possible environmental rating by the Environment Agency over high levels of pollution.
The regulator downgraded the firm from two stars out of a possible four to one, meaning it is now considered a "poor performing company" for its environmental impact.
It said it had performed "significantly below target" for sewage pollution incidents for the 15th year in a row.
South West Water, which has 1.8 million customers across Devon, Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly and parts of Dorset and Somerset, said it knew there was "much more to do" and was taking action to improve areas that "matter most" to customers and the environment.
The annual Environmental Performance Assessment grades England's nine water and sewerage companies largely on how often they pollute rivers, streams and the sea.
For 2025, South West Water was among four companies rated as poor performing, or one star, while four others were rated as requiring improvement, two stars.
Severn Trent Water was the only company to achieve the highest rating of four stars.
The Environment Agency's report card comes a month after South West Water was fined almost Â£8m for a series of pollution-related offences over six years.
In the last year it also recorded the sharpest rise in customer complaints of any water company.
Serious incidents in the past year include pollution in St Austell River, killing thousands of fish, while pollution at Exmouth meant beachgoers had to leave the water.
Industry regulator Ofwat said the company met seven of its 23 targets in 2025-26, with below target performance for "most areas".
It noted its performance in relation to water supply interruptions "deteriorated substantially" and, despite improving annual performance by 38%, said the company's total pollution incidents performance remained more than double its target.
Customer satisfaction also remained challenging, ranking 15 out of 17 in the sector.
While storm overflows performance improved by 19%, it still fell short of its target, the Environment Agency said.
'Under new management'
It was, however, the only company to have met its target for internal sewer flooding, or how often wastewater enters a property, every year since 2020-21.
A spokesperson for South West Water said: "We are under new management with a renewed focus on improving our performance.
"We know there's much more to do and although it will take time, we are taking action and making progress in the areas that matter most to our customers and the environment."
They said the firm had "reduced spills from storm overflows by 17% last year alone, with spill duration down by 25%, and we have insourced over 40 new leakage specialists".
"We are working hard to build on the progress we're making, backed by record levels of investment across the region," the spokesperson said.
"We are transforming our network to improve long-term resilience of our water supply; protecting the environment and tackling leaks as part of our multibillion-pound plan to deliver the long-term improvements our customers and communities expect."
A separate report from the Drinking Water Inspectorate, the Environment Agency, Natural Resources Wales and Ofwat said South West Water's drinking water quality "remains exceptional, and consumers can be confident that their water is safe to drink".
It noted although its internal sewer flooding performance had deteriorated, "it is still performing better than the industry average".
However, it said overall environmental performance "is poor".
In a summary, the report said overall water supply interruptions "remain a significant concern, and it is one of the worst performers in the industry".
To improve the company needed to reduce interruptions and complete a transformation programme to address the root causes of its failures and "substantially improve customer interactions and overall experience", it said.
Surfers Against Sewage described the latest performance ratings as "another league of shame for water companies" but she added they were "a mere slap on the wrist that means absolutely nothing".
Head of campaigns Jo Morley said: "What is the point in these environmental performance ratings when year after year water company behaviour gets worse?"

feb9333d5e53.text:
Timâs view
US President Donald Trumpâs apparent handout to Big Oil this week is really more of a favor for small producers, and may actually hand more regulatory sway to Europe.
At a campaign event in Texas on Tuesday, Trump said the Environmental Protection Agency will scrap âexpensive and unnecessaryâ Biden-era restrictions on methane emissions from thousands of low-producing oil and gas wells. The move, which is in keeping with the administrationâs numerous other environmental rollbacks, was framed as another solution to the countryâs energy price woes, even though the EPAâs own analysis concluded it will, at best, reduce gasoline prices next year by about 0.14%.
Methane is a nuanced challenge for the oil and gas industry. Itâs a super-potent greenhouse gas and linked to local health effects. Itâs also the main component of the very product â natural gas â the industry sells; letting it leak or burn away has always been understood as a necessary waste that lacks cost-effective measures to divert it. Now the world needs more gas than ever, and methane emissions abatement measures, from better pumps to satellite monitoring, have proliferated. Top oil CEOs and trade groups, including during the Trump administration, have frequently advocated for some form of methane regulation and propounded the need to take voluntary action.
The new rules also create issues over market access: Europe, which since the invasion of Ukraine has become a crucial market for US gas, is in the process of erecting trade barriers that will penalize high-emissions energy products. The Trump administration succeeded last week in pushing Brussels to delay those rules â leaning again on energy security arguments â but the delay âcan hardly be considered a win for industry,â Columbia University researchers wrote, because the EUâs ultimate emissions goals are unchanged. That means Exxon and its peers are still undertaking methane cuts for the sake of appeasing Brussels, and in preparation for a Democrat-led White House, no matter what Trump does. Gutting US regulations will only erode their competitive advantage against small producers that are less interested in global markets, less concerned about their environmental reputations, and more burdened by the costs of compliance.
Notable
- Leading Democrats are divided on whether to press forward now on a bipartisan permitting reform bill, which a former climate advisor said would enable Trump to push through fossil fuel projects, or wait and try for more concessions after the midterms.

A record 33 members have been expelled from China's Communist Party as it concluded a major annual political gathering, which had the most empty seats ever seen.
The fifth plenum was attended by 279 Central Committee members, compared to 315 at the fourth plenum in October 2025 and 364 at the third one in July 2024.
While recent plenums focused on economic reforms or social and development issues, party discipline took centre stage at this week's gathering.
Xi Jinping has made the fight against corruption a central pillar of his rule since he took the reins in 2012, calling it the "biggest threat" to the party.
Anti-corruption purges continue
Sixteen of the 33 members expelled are from the military, according to a communique issued on Thursday, which marked the end of the four-day closed-door gathering held at a hotel in Beijing.
It's unclear what specific charges these members face beyond "serious disciplinary and legal violations". Such broad allegations have become routine under Xi's anti-corruption campaign.
It has now become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", says Chong Ja Ian, a non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
"In this case, the campaign will continue and expand depending on how secure Xi feels rather than any real issue with corruption."
In its statement, the party said it has "squarely confronted the grim reality that party leadership had at times weakened or hollowed out" and that it will continue to "enforce strict party self-governance, including turning the knife inwards to... curb disorder".
The latest expulsions bring the total number of members removed under Xi's third term to a record 51, up from 35 and five in his first and second terms respectively.
Beyond the plenum, China's top anti-corruption watchdog reported that 680,000 people across the party apparatus have been disciplined in the first nine months of this year.
This is also the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300. The current Central Committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 members.
Observers argue that Xi views corruption not just as graft but also ideological impurity and, crucially, disloyalty.
In January, he warned against "two-faced cadres" who profess political loyalty but defy orders and act in their self-interest.
Who are the key figures purged?
Among the high-ranking officials expelled are former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui, and ex-top generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. Official statements announcing their removal this year said they "seriously violating [the party's] discipline and rules", which is widely read as a euphemism for corruption.
The culling of the military's top brass has been particularly significant, with Neil Thomas, Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang from the Asia Society Policy Institute describing it as "in a category of its own".
"It raises serious questions about organisational leadership and combat readiness, even as China continues to unveil formidable new military hardware," they wrote.
Zhang was also vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces. The seven-member commission has since been whittled down to just two members: Xi as chairman and Zhang Shengmin vice-chairman.
Ma and Zhang Youxia were former Politburo members. Their removal, along with former general He Weidong in 2025, meant the powerful 24-man Politburo was at one point left with 21 members.
Zhang Shengmin was promoted to the top decision-making body at the fifth plenum, bringing the number to 22.
Former prominent diplomat Liu Jianchao, who disappeared from public view in July last year, was also named among those who have been purged.
"Xi has few qualms about removing people he promoted," Chong says. "That he does so at will with little opposition underscores how unassailable his position is at the moment."
Xi's plans for the future
Analysts believe one reason for the increased empahsis on discipline â which many interpret as loyalty â is next year's Party Congress, when the CCP will vote again for its next leader.
A leadership reshuffle is due in 2027 and many analysts expect Xi to hold on to the top job for a fourth term and beyond. No leader has served that long except Mao Zedong, the founder Communist China.
Xi has reason to "scrutinise the next cohort more closely" given the fall of so many officials from the current committee, Thomas says.
"Today's rising stars tend to be relatively young, boast technocratic backgrounds, and have connections to Xi's political network," he says, adding that "provincial leadership ranks are a promising place to look".
Observers say that ultimately, Xi is expected to dominate personnel selection at the 21st Party Congress, which will further cement his grip on the party and the country.
"Xi's focus is further consolidating power around himself... The readout from the plenum suggests he intends to be at the centre of China and the Communist Party for the foreseeable future," Chong says.
"However, further down the road, such concentration of power may pave the way for a more serious power vacuum when Xi ages and slows down."

Lizâs view
There is a lot of money in the world. Is it enough for AI? One player in the great spend-a-thon of 2026 provides us with two different answers.
Apolloâs deal to buy a stake in Abu Dhabiâs government-backed asset manager, Mubadala Capital, is a bet that the real shortage facing Wall Street right now isnât capital, but places to invest it. Apolloâs retirement arm takes in $1 billion a week that it has to find something to do with, and its origination engine canât keep up. By investing in Mubadala, it gets first dibs on a steady stream of deals. The takeaway is that an oversupply of capital is chasing too few opportunities.
Apolloâs $40 billion chip lease to SpaceX suggests the opposite. When we checked in on SpaceXâs financing six days ago, the riskiest piece appeared likely to find takers at about 3.5 percentage points over a baseline US Treasury rate, steep but reasonable. By the time it closed this week, the spread had blown out to 3.95 points â outrageously expensive for SpaceX, which carries an investment-grade rating. Those eye-watering terms make clear that while the AI money is there, it now costs a lot more than it did a few weeks ago.
Capital providers are wising up to the risks of the AI trade, even if they have the money to burn. âI wonât say they were dumb until four weeks ago, butâ¦â said one Wall Street executive, âtheyâve gotten a lot smarter, fast.â
Notable
- âWhile we are proud of the privileged position âwe play in the AI investment cycle, no one knows how the demands for capital and compute will evolve as the broader AI ecosystem matures,â Goldman Sachsâ CEO David Solomon said on a recent call with analysts. âThat will only become clearer as technology and markets continue to develop.â

7de8ac18f2b2.text: Data: Resources for the Future; Note: Central RFF scenario ; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios The Senate permitting plan would cut emissions from power plants in the near term and help keep electricity prices down, a new analysis finds. Why it matters: The study from scholars at Resources for the Future, a nonpartisan think tank, offers some of the most detailed independent modeling yet of the bill 's effects. It will help inform lobbying and advocacy around the bill ahead of a test vote looming on Nov. 9. Driving the news: The analysis models how the bill would affect the power sector compared with current law and policies. Among the findings from its central scenario: It would drive "robust" transmission expansion ( see above ), enabling "use of additional clean energy and existing resources of all types." Overall electricity system costs are an estimated 3.5% to 7% lower each year through 2041 compared to a no-bill baseline, saving over $350 billion total through 2050 in present-value terms. That should translate into lower electricity bills for people, co-author Kevin Rennert tells Axios, though the study does not directly model retail prices. The bill would boost the build-out of renewables, partly enabled by expansion of transmission, with added clean energy displacing fossil fuels even though additions of gas-fired capacity still occur. CO2 from the power sector would initially drop as more coal is edged aside, and then climb over time — but remain below levels projected without the bill. By the numbers: In 2028, there's roughly 60 gigawatts more clean energy capacity on the grid in the study's central outlook compared to a baseline of current law and policy. Data: Resources for the Future; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios The intrigue: The RFF analysis shows how it sees the bill initially pushing power plant emissions downward. Even that eventual upward trend is hardly guaranteed. This kind of study is by definition packed with assumptions and variables that the authors acknowledge — the future being the future and all. For instance, it uses a "high-electrification demand scenario to represent the rapid increase in demand from data centers and other sources." Yes, but: The study — which uses a model developed by the Energy Department's National Laboratory of the Rockies — doesn't attempt to analyze every aspect of the wide-ranging bill. For example, it does not capture how changes in environmental laws would affect mining, pipelines, and various activities outside the power sector. Catch up quick: There's a lot of other analysis flying around in the intense public and closed-door lobbying over the bill. A new White House study finds the bill would eventually boost GDP by $82 billion to $164 billion annually and provide substantial savings on power bills. And Punchbowl News reports that the Solar Energy Industries Association is circulating an analysis on Capitol Hill showing that under the bill, solar and wind would together provide over 37% of power generation in 2035 vs. around 20% under "obstructed permitting." What we're watching: Emissions, renewables deployment, and costs are several factors in the permitting bill battle, but hardly the only ones as some environmentalists and other critics take aim at the bill. Other contested terrain includes the effect on consultation with Native American tribes, historic preservation, and more. The NAACP, for instance, is out with a new document strongly criticizing the bill. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

The environmental performance of water companies worsened again last year despite industry investment, according to the first joint report by the regulators.
Eight of the nine companies in England were rated as "poor" or "requiring improvement", with only Severn Trent receiving the highest rating.
Companies were praised for reducing service disruptions but serious pollution into the environment remained a "major concern".
The chair of the environmental regulator, Alan Lovell, said the results showed the industry continued to "fall well short of the standards rightly demanded by both us and the public".
"I'm very angry," he told BBC News. "I think it's extremely disappointing to see the level of pollution incidents... and I completely sympathise with the public."
Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said she was "demanding answers from the companies that are failing" and would be "shining a spotlight on the worst offences around the country".
Four different regulators currently oversee water companies in England and Wales - the Environment Agency (EA), Natural Resources Wales (NRW), Ofwat and the Drinking Water Inspectorate - and this marks the first time they have come together to assess the industry.
It is a nod to the commitment made by Sir Keir Starmer's government to merge the organisations covering England into a single body as part of efforts to streamline regulation.
But it is on environmental performance that the report is most critical.
Serious pollution incidents in 2025 were a "major concern", the Environment Agency said, and remained at similarly high levels to those seen in previous years.
Overall, England's water companies were awarded 16 out of a possible 36 stars for environmental performance - the worst total on record.
The EA said this was due to "declining performance in some areas but also due to our tighter performance standards".
And in Wales, DÅµr Cymru Welsh Water was given a two-star rating, out of four, by NRW.
Industry body Water UK acknowledged that "the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough".
But it also pointed out that more than half of all pollution incidents were as a result of "blockages or vandalism, which are not in the direct control of the water companies".
"It will take time, but record investment will help secure water supplies, support growth, and end sewage entering rivers and seas," a spokesperson said.
Today's report did highlight some "strengths to build on", with UK drinking water quality remaining "among the best in the world".
And the regulators also noted that "leakage has reduced over the long term" but said improvement was still needed.
Will record investment deliver improvement?
Water companies have committed record levels of investment up to 2030 to upgrade their networks and sewage treatment works. But customer bills are expected to rise 36% on average between 2025 and 2030 as a result.
There has already been Â£5bn invested over the last five years to try and tackle environmental pollution.
But Alan Lovell from the EA said: "Not all companies have delivered the environmental improvement schemes they have been funded for."
In September, it was reported that the number of complaints made by households about water companies to the Consumer Council for Water (CCW) rose by 84% in a year - the highest in 20 years.
Mike Keil, chief executive of the CCW, said that "many customers have not noticed any improvement in customer service or performance" despite recent bill rises.
"People support investment and understand it takes time to bear fruit," he said, but added that "bill payers are already questioning whether their money is being well spent".
The government is planning to introduce new legislation next year to overhaul the structure and regulation of the industry - including combining the regulators in England.
The Welsh government plans to set up a new regulator alongside Natural Resources Wales.
In his Labour conference speech last month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced that a strengthened Water Bill would also remove limits on government ownership of shares in England's major water companies.
He also promised new powers for local leaders. The BBC understands further details on the idea of "regional bodies" to oversee water companies are likely to follow in the coming weeks.
Water consumption fails to fall, risking supplies
The joint report, published on Thursday, also found that household consumption in England and Wales in 2025 remained similar to the previous year, at 137 litres per person per day.
Government advisers have said that demand for water will likely have to fall to safeguard future supplies, which are facing pressures from climate change, a growing population and historic underinvestment.
Hosepipe bans remain in place across large parts of England and Wales as companies have sought to shore up supplies following drought this summer.
Mark Owen, head of fisheries at the Angling Trust, said the industry also needed to take more responsibility and cut leakage rates further.
"Every litre lost has already been taken from the environment while our rivers, fish and wildlife are under immense pressure," he said.

One of Mars’ strangest clouds may rely on unusual physics to emerge.
The Red Planet’s ribbonlike cloud — which stretches as long as four Grand Canyons laid end-to-end — may form without a speck of starting material to seed it, researchers report October 7 in Nature Geoscience. This manner of forming clouds, called homogenous nucleation, was thought to be possible on paper but not to occur naturally.
Tiny particles such as dust or salt floating in the air seed typical clouds on Earth. But that cloud physics doesn’t seem to apply to the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud. Beyond its impressive length, this wisp of water ice is remarkably consistent, forming daily in the same spot roughly 45 kilometers high on the slope of a Martian volcano for several months each year.
The team tried and tried but couldn’t reproduce the cloud’s formation, including its lengthy tail and consistent cycle, with computer models employing standard cloud physics, says François Forget, an astrophysicist at the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique, or LMD, in Paris.
There’s no shortage of dust on Mars. The trouble is that high up in a thin Martian atmosphere, few cloud-forming dust particles stay suspended. Instead, they probably clump together and eventually fall, says planetary physicist Jorge Hernández-Bernal, who did the work at LMD. This left cloud formation without seeds as the most convincing explanation, he says.
Nailing a Mars cloud’s features
Every day during some seasons on Mars, a long wispy cloud emerges along the flanks of the Arsia Mons volcano, as seen in the observations video spanning three Martian hours. How that cloud forms has been a mystery. A new simulation, bottom, included unusual physics, in which clouds form without starting material. That approach replicated the shape and timing of Mars’ Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud for the first time.
The team’s model suggests that the eye-catching plume originates when air flowing across the volcano triggers a rapid lifting of a moist parcel of air. The decrease in pressure at that altitude lets the air parcel expand, rapidly cooling it.
The newly cooled air now has 100,000 times more moisture than it can hold, the team’s model suggests. This excess moisture undergoes homogenous nucleation, rapidly forming more stable ice crystals. Winds sweep the forming cloud outward, creating the cloud’s distinctive long shape.
While the model doesn’t perfectly match satellite observations, it does capture how the phenomenon that leads to the cold air pocket reoccurs day after day, just like the real cloud does.
The study was surprising because “homogeneous nucleation is generally treated in our field as this theoretical concept,” says Samuel Atwood, an atmospheric and planetary scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., who was not associated with the study.
“It’s a pretty compelling story that they’re telling with the model, but it’s only one view or one perspective on it,” Atwood says, adding that future measurements supporting the team’s finding will provide more certainty. Hernández-Bernal says that he plans to validate the study by testing alternative explanations.
Even beyond Mars, the study provides food for thought. Previous studies have suggested that on Earth, meteor smoke provides particles for cloud formation in an upper layer of the atmosphere called the mesosphere, though a few studies have suggested homogenous nucleation could be responsible. Now that scientists are proposing homogenous nucleation on Mars, Hernández-Bernal says, “maybe there will be an increased interest in investigating this on Earth.”

Plans to introduce "bee bus stops" aimed to boost biodiversity in urban areas have been approved for Peterborough.
Peterborough City Council said 34 bus stops could include Living Roofs, mini-gardens planted on top of bus shelters that are made up of wildflowers and other vegetation.
The initiative was included in its new plan for the city's bus stops, which will also see "comfortable seating" replace existing perch seats.
At a meeting of the cabinet, external on Tuesday, the plans were discussed and approved.
The council will award a new contract to Bauer Media Outdoor UK to manage the city's bus stops.
The agreement includes the company providing the council with an annual income of Â£140,000 from the sale of advertising space, plus 2.5% of its quarterly gross revenue.
The contract is expected to run for a minimum of 10 years, with options to extend it, and could provide the authority with Â£2.8m over 20 years.
There are more than 350 Living Roofs across the UK, including in Birmingham, Glasgow and Northampton.
Chris Wiggin, the council's Liberal Democrat cabinet member for environment, said: "We need to do everything we can to support biodiversity and support bees and other pollinators because without those there is no other life, so I'm very happy to see these [plans] come forward."
Other planned changes to the city's bus stops include providing up-to-date passenger information and installing digital advertising screens at most bus stops.

The United States has imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry over its alleged support for the M23 rebel group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, increasing pressure on Kigali to withdraw its troops and halt support for the rebels.
"Rwanda must halt its support for M23 and withdraw its troops from eastern DRC," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
The sanctions come months after Rwanda and DR Congo signed a US-brokered peace agreement aimed at ending the conflict.
Fighting has continued in eastern DR Congo since early 2025, when M23 seized the cities of Goma and Bukavu. Rwanda denies backing M23.
The US Treasury says Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training.
The M23 has seized mineral-rich areas, including gold-mining sites in South Kivu and Rubaya, a major coltan-producing area in North Kivu. Washington says minerals from rebel-held territory enter Rwanda's supply chains, alleging that Rwanda exports more minerals than it produces.
The sanctions are intended to reinforce the Washington Accords, signed by the Congolese and Rwandan presidents in December 2025 under US mediation. The deal aimed to end the conflict and expand regional trade and investment, but fighting has continued.
On 24 October, ahead of the sanctions announcement, DR Congo President FÃ©lix Tshisekedi urged the international community to increase pressure on Rwanda.
"We must firmly demand that the international community impose concrete sanctions against Rwanda and exert increased pressure, so that we may finally secure a lasting peace in our country," he said.
In a statement to Reuters, DR Congo foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions and urged Rwanda to honour its commitments under the Washington Accords, respect the UN Charter and withdraw its troops from Congolese territory.
"The Washington Accords contain clear commitments regarding Rwanda's security, specifically the neutralization of the DR Congo-sponsored FDLR genocidal militia, which are wholly unmet, and with no accountability," Rwandan government spokesperson Yolande Makolo told the BBC.
The FDLR is a militia linked to perpetrators of Rwanda's 1994 genocide. Kigali considers it a security threat and cites its presence in eastern DR Congo to justify its military posture.
"Rwanda remains ready to fully implement the Washington Accords, concurrently with the willingness of the DRC to fulfill those commitments, and with the mediator holding all parties accountable," she said.
The US also sanctioned Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a popular bank and financial institution serving Rwanda's security services.
Washington alleges it facilitated tens of millions of dollars in transactions for M23 and its political wing, the Congo River Alliance, helped pay for military equipment for Rwandan forces from China and enabled gold to be transported from rebel-controlled areas to Kigali.
The sanctions freeze the designated entities' assets under US jurisdiction and generally prohibit US individuals and businesses from conducting transactions with them, unless authorised or exempt. Violations can result in penalties for US and foreign parties.
The measures follow earlier US sanctions against Rwanda's army and four senior military commanders in March 2026. The US imposed further sanctions on Gasabo gold refinery and three mining companies accused of smuggling conflict minerals in June 2026.
Pressure is also mounting over Rwanda's international sports partnerships. Two US senators have urged the National Basketball Association (NBA) to reconsider its commercial relations with Kigali, questioning whether it aligns with the league's stated commitment to human rights.
In a letter sent to NBA commissioner Adam Silver on 23 October, senators Jeff Merkley and Marsha Blackburn questioned the league's continued partnership with Rwanda amid allegations of human rights abuses.
The NBA has yet to issue a substantive response to the letter.
Rwanda has used sports high-profile sports sponsorship to raise its international profile. Early this month, it secured a 10-year deal to host Formula 1's African Grand Prix in the early 2030s.
The country's sponsorship of Arsenal ended in 2026, while Bayern Munich has also ended its commercial partnership with Visit Rwanda.
The M23 has recently joined a new rebel coalition, known as the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) and led by former Congolese President Joseph Kabila, which wants to oust Tshisekedi's government.

Audio recordings published in Spanish media reveal conversations between train drivers and a railway control centre in the minutes leading up to a deadly train crash that killed at least 69 people and injured dozens.
Officials are investigating the cause of the disaster, which occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Seville barrelled into a stationary train on Wednesday morning.
Three audio recordings between the control centre in Madrid and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another some 25km (15 miles) up ahead had stalled.
Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez, who travelled to the area of the crash, said authorities were working "day and night" to "get to the bottom of every last detail of this tragedy".
The release of the recordings comes as Spain begins three days of national mourning for one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history.
One train, run by state-owned operator Renfe, had 397 passengers on board. Ahead of it on the same line was a train run by private operator Iryo, with 147 passengers.
A reported issue with the automatic signalling system - a computer failure - had forced all trains to halt on the affected stretch.
But later the Renfe train was ordered to proceed in "error", according to Spain's transport minister.
Audio recordings published by Spanish news outlets including El Pais and RTVE reveal the conversations that took place between the two train's drivers and the control centre in the Spanish capital ahead of the crash.
In one recording, a control centre operator is speaking to the driver of the Renfe train, which was travelling behind the other train and was having some technical difficulties.
After some exchanges, the control operator tells the driver: "Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation."
The driver replies, "At normal speed?" To which the controller says: "Yes."
The Lateral Signaling Block is a back-up or alternative train system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.
The driver of the other train - operated by Iryo - says in another audio recording that communication with the train-control system has been lost and it is not moving.
The train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda", the driver tells the control centre operator. After a series of exchanges, the driver is then told to "resume the journey" normally.
The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.
The latter recording suggests that the controller had been notified that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached.
Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by the other train.
Spain's transport minister Ãscar Puente said on Wednesday that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".
The leaking of the audio recordings has been criticised by some Spanish politicians.
Posting on X, Alberto IbÃ¡Ã±ez, a member of Congress for the left-wing Sumar platform, described the leaks as "despicable".
Irene Montero - the prime ministerial candidate for the left-wing Podemos party - said responsibility for the crash should not be placed on one worker, adding that train drivers and experts have been warning against the liberalisation of the railway sector for years.
From the crash site, SÃ¡nchez said: "We are working day and night not only to support the victims' families, but also to establish every last detail of this tragedy and strengthen safety measures to ensure it never happens again."
Most Spanish politicians have cancelled all public engagements and suspended their campaigning ahead of a snap election on 29 November.
The exception is the far-right party Vox. Its leader, Santiago Abascal, said his party would not take part in what he described as attempts to "use mourning to silence criticism" of the country's rail infrastructure.
Overnight, around 1,500 people gathered outside the Spanish Transport Ministry building in the capital, according to Spanish broadcaster TVE, which reported that demonstrators were largely calling for the resignations of SÃ¡nchez and Puente.
Police used tear gas to disperse crowds after protesters hurled bottles and flares. No injuries or arrests were reported.
Rail drivers went ahead with a planned strike on Thursday, with the Spanish Union of Railway Drivers (Semaf) saying the strike action was being held "in defence of railway safety".
The leader of Spain's main opposition People's Party Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o said: "Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure."
At the crash site, emergency crews worked through the night under powerful floodlights to cut open metal carriages in the search for victims, with many of those killed in the crash still to be identified.
Hundreds of personnel have been deployed to the disaster site to assist with recovery efforts, according to Spain's interior ministry, with drones and helicopters being used to find victims and remove rubble.
A spokesperson for the Spanish Civil Guard told the BBC they had deployed more than 900 people from different specialist departments, and the priority now was identifying remains.
They said they did not know how long this would take, but urged those with missing family members to go to one of the local centres which have been set up to offer DNA samples.
Witnesses of the crash described seeing people crying and bleeding, passengers trapped in their seats and smoke billowing throughout the carriages, one of which caught fire.
Late on Wednesday, relatives were still trying to gather information about passengers who were on either of the trains.

HONOLULU—Soldiers in the Pacific need technology that works when networks are attacked and connectivity isn’t guaranteed, said Gen. Xavier Brunson, the commander of U.S. Forces Korea.
“If the service tells you who they are and what they're going to do, and you choose not to try to meet the requirements of how they're going to fight—that's going to be a problem. Because in the future, our networks will be fully under attack. I think in the future we'll have to operate disaggregated and distributed. I think in the future, things will happen so fast, they'll happen so fast that we won't know sometimes what's happening to us,” Brunson warned during a keynote Tuesday at the TechNet Indo-Pacific conference here.
“There will be plans that will change before we even get in the theater…And if your product can't operate on the edge, then it's not a product that's going to be able to help the Army fight the way the Army's going to fight, much less the joint force.”
Brunson’s comments come as what’s known as the Davidson window, a 2027 timeline for when China’s leader has told its military it must be ready to invade Taiwan, draws near.
But while there’s no expectation of a war with China next year, it’s something the military is still preparing for, Gen. Ronald Clark, commander of U.S. Army Pacific Command, said in his keynote address.
“There are 157 days between today and 2 April. So that mark on the wall for us in our headquarters is to ensure that we are in position, postured forward to deter war in a window in which our adversary may find it to their advantage to attack Taiwan. But again, it's not a date that we think that conflict will happen…But we'll continue to prepare. We'll continue to modernize. We'll continue to posture ourselves for the business of deterred war well beyond [2027].”
Congress and the lack of a 2027 budget could stymie some of those modernization efforts unless lawmakers pass a full budget by December.
Working under stopgap funding is the “biggest challenge” that affects “plans for new starts and being able to fund some of the programs that we know are going to yield benefit to the soldier,” Clark told reporters earlier this month.
Examples include experimentation and some efforts to improve the mission partner network, he said: “You can't start that contract if you don't have new money. So it's a challenge that, again, we have to overcome…we have more experience operating under a [continuing resolution] than we do with an appropriation.”

The Navy needs more continuous monitoring solutions for systems on ships and ashore, including products that scan for vulnerabilities, Richard Williams, who manages command, control, communication, computers, and intelligence platforms for the U.S. Pacific Fleet, said Tuesday.
- “I would offer that we are in a zero day today.
