The News
A number of national political figures are looking svelte these days. But it doesnât do to rifle through public figuresâ medicine cabinets. And only a few of them are saying much about the policy implications of the new class of miracle drugs that promise to reverse Americaâs obesity epidemic: GLP-1s.
So I called up the only national figure who has both talked openly about his own treatment and taken concrete steps to expand coverage of the drugs to include weight loss: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker.
Pritzker was diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes in 2024 and began taking insulin. A doctor added a GLP-1 to his treatment protocol a few months later. Heâs since lost about 80 pounds and no longer takes insulin.
He was feeling good when we spoke this week: He said he has more energy, he goes for walks, and heâs stepped off a lifelong ârollercoasterâ of struggling with his weight.
âWhen I think about all the ill effects of obesity across the population, and the costs that come with it âÂ and Iâm talking about personal cost as well as financial cost âÂ it feels to me like we may have stumbled onto something,â he marveled. âAs the price drops, we really ought to be offering this to everyone.â
Illinois extended its coverage of the drugs â from covering them for just diabetes to also covering them for obesity â for state employees in 2024. About 32,000 Illinois state employees and their family members are currently on the drugs, at a total cost of $149 million âÂ a sum that Pritzkerâs office says makes up 18% of the stateâs prescription budget. For perspective, 41% goes to coverage of other brand-name specialty drugs taken by 6,500 employees.
GLP-1s touch nerve centers of US healthcare politics, from populist fury at big insurers and pharmaceutical companies to worries about government spending and a growing awareness of the toll of chronic illness.
But even as President Donald Trump pushed Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk to lower prices and states, the 2028 campaign, which effectively begins after the midterms next week, will be the first presidential race during which the drugs will no longer be a novelty.
Pritzker hasnât committed to running in 2028, and heâs not ready to make sweeping political claims or to push private companies to cover the drugs.âIf the cost savings bear themselves out, then I think you can campaign on it,â he said.
2028 Math
The policy questions around GLP-1s are red-hot in state Medicaid and health plans â and in corporate boardrooms, where CEOs and human resources executives are balancing demand from employees with a hit to the bottom line.
Depending on expansion criteria, more than 40% of Americans under age 65 with private insurance could be clinically eligible for GLP-1s, a 2024 KFF study found.
Those costs would add up: Americans taking a GLP-1 spend an average of $1,528 per year on their medication, including those with insurance coverage and without it. For cash payers, the cost can be far higher. Novo Nordisk, which makes Wegovy and Ozempic, advertises list prices ranging from $149 per month to $399 per month, depending on the dose.
This year, seven states that expanded Medicaid coverage of GLP-1s for weight loss either dropped the benefit or added restrictions to limit eligibility. (Illinois did not extend coverage to Medicaid enrollees.) Medicaid cuts passed in a 2025 tax bill set to take effect next year are expected to exacerbate statesâ problems.
A key question is time: When does better health save healthcare money? The median job tenure in the US is about four years, while the federal government evaluates health outcomes on a 10-year timetable.
Pritzker said his state is carefully monitoring the savings GLP-1s bringÂ and thinks they can at least defray some of the price tag. (It may help that âin state government, we have quite a lot of people who stay for a reasonably long period of time,â he said.)
Others argue that narrow actuarial questions are a distraction from the larger political issue. âWe borrow against our future for far worse reasons than the health of our citizens,â the CEO of the direct-to-consumer health care company Ro, Zachariah Reitano, told me.
The cost of the drugs there and in the private market limits their use, the philanthropist and former energy trader John Arnold notes.
âDrugs donât work if people canât access them. This class of drugs should be broadly available at a fair price,â he said.
Benâs view
About 32 million Americans take GLP-1s, a higher number than there are American Jews and Muslims combined. About twice as many Americans take drugs as pay for artificial intelligence subscriptions.
Many are paying out-of-pocket sums comparable to expenses like gasoline. (I pay Eli Lilly $454 a month for 30 milligrams of Zepbound and some small needles, and would certainly be receptive, as a voter, to Pritzkerâs or, say, JD Vanceâs plan to save me a few bucks.)
And the politics of GLP-1s are unsettled. Pritzker rolled them out quietly, and it seems possible that voters concerned about the growing cost of government (not to mention the small but influential minority of thin people) may have qualms about broader expansions.
But itâs also obvious that anyone seeking the American presidency in 2028 will have to figure out a response to the challenging policy questions around the jabs. This is particularly true in states like West Virginia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Oklahoma, and Texas, where medication usage (and diseases like obesity and diabetes) are among the highest in the country.
People active in the space have some suggestions: Arnold called on Congress to block loopholes Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly could use to delay competition from generic GLP-1s. He also noted that the most obvious and effective solutions, like mandating public and private programs to cover GLP-1s for obesity, will be expensive.
Roâs Reitano suggested using the governmentâs scale to negotiate lower prices, and to structure programs that pay for patients staying on the trea

b3d2ad1af20f.text: Call it a new Apollo moment: Rocket launches from Cape Canaveral, Florida, are now outpacing those of the Cold War-era space race that first made the launch site famous. Why it matters: U.S. leaders are rushing to grow the number of rocket providers at America's busiest spaceport amid a space and arms race with China. Beijing plans to send a crew to the Moon by 2030 or sooner and is rapidly building up its satellite and rocket fleets. What they're saying: "There's nothing really comparable in the background of my career to what we're experiencing today," Space Force Col. Brian Chatman, the commander of Florida's rocket range, told Axios in an exclusive interview. Behind the scenes: The Cape is busy expanding to meet President Trump's mandate for the nation to support 1,000 annual launches by 2030. Chatman said with all the contractors on base, inspection backups and parking chaos abound. A rundown of some major projects Chatman is overseeing: SpaceX is expanding its footprint on the Cape for its Starship super heavy-lift launchpads. Newcomers Relativity Space and Stoke Space are setting up their facilities and are aiming to launch rockets for military and commercial customers sometime in late 2026 and 2027 . NASA is preparing for next year's Artemis III testing missions, and the Artemis IV voyage that aims to return astronauts to the Moon by 2028. Blue Origin is rapidly rebuilding its launch complex after its New Glenn rocket exploded in May. Jamie Draper, the Cape Canaveral Space Force Museum's director, told Axios there's been "boom and bust" cycles throughout the base's history. "We're definitely in one of those boom cycles right now," Draper said. By the numbers: Last year, Space Launch Delta 45, the military command overseeing the Cape, supported 109 orbital liftoffs from the base — the most in its history. In April, Space Launch Delta 45 oversaw five different rocket launches for unique missions, breaking a record set at the height of the U.S.-Soviet space race in the 1960s. Space Force officials estimate that the number of Cape launches could rise from the 109 it reached in 2025 to "approximately 1,200 by 2036" annually, according to the service's vision plan . Reality check: There's only one other military spaceport in the U.S. — California's Vandenberg Space Force Base — and the two can't fully handle the anticipated surge in commercial and military demand. Top military leaders stress the need for a third U.S. port. Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant, the head of Space Systems Command, told reporters last week that another spaceport was likely needed by 2030. Enter SpaceX: The newly public Elon Musk-controlled company plans to start building another site off the Louisiana coast next year, with its first Starship launch planned for 2029. That site, known as Starbase, would "relieve quite a lot of the pressure" on Cape Canaveral, said Brian Weeden, director of civil and commercial policy for the Aerospace Corporation's Center for Space Policy and Strategy. The bottom line: Until new spaceports arrive, Cape Canaveral will remain the linchpin of the nation's rocket enterprise. "We have a prime piece of real estate here that maximizes launch opportunities," Chatman said. "But the reality is, there's so much demand for launch in the future that we just need more sites."

A fake medical emergency, an audacious jailbreak and a 36-hour search operation that ended with 17 prisoners being recaptured.
Those are the highlights of a story from India's Tamil Nadu state that has captured headlines across the country.
It began on Monday night after 17 men escaped from a prison in Theni district in the southern state after overpowering guards, and ended almost two days later with police catching them in batches.
The incident has drawn attention to overcrowding in Indian prisons. Police say the Theni prison was housing 334 inmates against a capacity of 200, leaving authorities unable to maintain control once chaos broke out.
The state police said it has suspended nine staff at the prison for alleged negligence in connection with the incident.
All the men who escaped were undertrials - inmates on trial or awaiting one - and 18 of them were in one cell at the prison in Thekkampatti in Theni.
On Monday night at 2230 local time (17:00 GMT), one of the prisoners acted like he was going through a seizure. The other cellmates shouted for help and a jail official responded. He was soon overpowered by the prisoners, police said.
The prisoners then got out of the cell, reportedly attacked two other jail guards and took away keys which they used to open the main gate and flee. While 17 escaped, one returned to the prison immediately.
Several prison personnel were injured in the attack.
Police sources told BBC Tamil that they were examining the possibility of collusion between some prison officials and the escaped men.
Sandeep Rathore, Director General of Police for Prisons in Tamil Nadu, said in a press briefing that the jailbreak was caused by "human error".
"There was a clear breach of security protocol as the prisoners managed to pass through a three-tier barrier manned by security personnel," he said.
On Thursday, he was replaced as the head of state prisons and transferred to a different department.
At the time of the incident, only four guards were on duty, far below the staffing required to maintain the prescribed 1:6 guard-to-inmate ratio recommended by the state - which should have worked out to 34 guards against the approved strength of 200 prisoners.
The police then launched a manhunt, calling forces from across the state.
"Advanced technology, drone surveillance, CCTV footage analysis, and the tireless efforts of police personnel played a crucial role," the department said in a statement on X.
Four men were arrested at a bus station in a nearby village, and the fifth was caught while he was travelling in a tuk-tuk.
A drone search of a forest near the prison led to eight more escaped prisoners being caught. Videos of the arrests showed the men obeying police instructions even as they did not answer questions from reporters who were also seen at the scene.
Two more were captured with the help of drone surveillance, police said, while the last two men surrendered on Wednesday.
News agency PTI reported that all 17 recaptured prisoners have been moved to high-security correctional prisons.
Rathore told media that all prisons across the state would be audited to check if rules were being followed.
The incident evoked memories of one of the biggest jailbreaks in Tamil Nadu in 1995 when 43 suspected militants escaped from a special camp after digging a 153-foot-long tunnel beneath a historic fort. Some of them were never recaptured.
While the investigation is going on, the incident has sparked a conversation on overcrowding in Indian prisons. The National Crime Records Bureau's last Prison Statistics India report from 2023 showed a national occupancy rate of 120.1%.
Data shows that undertrial prisoners - individuals who are detained while they await police investigation or court trials - make up more than 73% of India's total prison population. Human rights groups and legal experts have also raised concerns about delays in investigations and trials that lead to people languishing for years behind bars.
Additional reporting by Siraj and Prabhurao Anandhan

0f55efbab49a.text: President Trump seems to think he can save a vulnerable Ohio Republican senator's ass by talking about how strong it is. Why it matters: Republicans are getting hammered over the war in Iran, gas prices and data centers. But they're playing along with Trump's ogling of male candidates, which he's described as an election strategy. "I don't do this with men very often. I started examining his body because I didn't know he was a great athlete. And I looked and I watched up and down and I looked at his ass," Trump said of Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) at an Ohio rally. "My wife and I have a good sense of humor, and we know he's doing all he can to help us win," Husted told Axios. "We have made sure to hit the gym during the busy campaign to uphold the high standards the president has set for us." Zoom in: In five rallies over three weeks across the country, Trump gave a head-to-toe appraisal of his most vulnerable Republican senator. "His ass was like a big piece of muscle," Trump said in Michigan last week. "Then I looked at his legs and I said, 'Man, his feet are big,' " Trump said in North Carolina. Polling has shown Husted narrowly behind or tied with former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D), and Republicans view him as the most vulnerable GOP incumbent. Zoom out: Husted is getting the most love, but he's not alone. "You know, he's a very handsome guy," Trump said about Sen. Tim Sheehy (R-Mont.) at a Montana rally earlier this month. "I like the white hair, I like the big, strong build. Big, strong guy." Trump said of Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), who is running for Senate in Georgia. Trump called him "all man." "I actually think that Rick Jackson's a very handsome, distinguished, beautiful-looking guy," Trump said about the Republican gubernatorial candidate in Georgia. "Look at this beautiful guy," Trump said of House candidate Ed Gallrein (R-Ky.). Trump called him: "Central casting." Between the lines: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has also joined the fun: "I know that Husted gets a ton of attention, but I think Bernie is kinda eye-candy too," he joked during an event Tuesday. Thune was referring to Husted's fellow Ohio Republican senator, Bernie Moreno. "They both got it going on when it comes to that," Thune said. The other side: Trump has questioned the looks of Democratic senators and candidates. "I don't think he's a good looking man," he said of Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), who he frequently refers to as Pee-wee Herman. He has called Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico a "weird looking dude," comparing him to Alfred E. Neuman — though Trump hasn't been much kinder to Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton. The bottom line: Trump argued at a rally in Texas this week that "the audience loved" his description of Husted's body. "By the way, he went up 12 points that day. He went from being down to being up," Trump continued. "Maybe I should do that with Ken Paxton, but I'm not sure your body is gonna qualify."

Data Center Health Worries Animate Midterm Campaigns
PAGE, Ariz. — Doug Herrera still lives in the house his father built, though his dad died some time ago from cancer. Herrera wonders if that illness could have been linked to pollutants from nearby uranium mining. Now, he worries that a possible new neighbor — a proposed $10 billion mega data center — could imperil his health.
“I’m a patriot, but I’m highly against the data center,” Herrera, 64, said from his front porch near a yard sign that reads “No Data Centers.”
“There is light pollution, sound pollution. The temperature is going to rise,” he said.
Page is a gateway to iconic Southwestern landscapes of arid desert studded with Joshua trees and towering red-rock formations. While the City Council approved the sale of land for a data center, the developer needs zoning and other approvals. Residents concerned about possible health effects have signed petitions and mobilized to oppose construction.
The boom in data centers is dividing communities such as Page and turning future construction into a flash point in the midterm elections. The leading candidates in the close race for Arizona’s 1st Congressional District are at odds over any new centers there, and the state’s attorney general has called for a pause on new approvals and building.
Emerging research into data centers’ possible health effects is adding grist to the various state fights, giving ammunition to Democrats and some Republicans who’ve broken party ranks to oppose the sprawling complexes.
It has also put some incumbent politicians who have supported data center expansion in unexpectedly vulnerable positions in reliably red states like Ohio and Texas, where the megabuildings now operate by the hundreds.
“Two years ago, a lot of these data centers went up and there was not an organized, watchful opposition,” said Lee Hannah, a political science professor at Wright State University in Dayton, Ohio.
“That opposition has come up in a grassroots way so quickly that decisions made a year ago by local officials or state governments to get behind a data center are suddenly career-ending.”
The hyperscale centers house infrastructure to power AI, with servers that sprawl over tens of thousands of square feet or more. The city of Page approved the sale of 500 acres for the proposed data center, though the location within that acreage hasn’t been decided. The area sits on open land studded with blackbrush and native grasses near Horseshoe Bend, an iconic curve of the Colorado River that has long been popular with tourists.
Data centers gobble up electricity and rely on backup gas generators during times of peak energy demand. The resulting air pollution has been linked to heart conditions, respiratory issues, and elevated cancer risks, according to a number of environmental studies.
Emissions from the centers could cause nearly 1,300 deaths annually by 2030 and an annual public health burden of more than $20 billion in 2028, based on modeling led by researchers at the University of California-Riverside.
Cooling components can contain what are called forever chemicals, synthetic substances that accumulate in human tissue, according to advocacy and environmental groups. And the hum and whir of generators and heating and air conditioning systems can exceed 90 decibels, which can harm hearing.
Data centers are lit up for operations and security, creating light pollution that can increase the risk of chronic disease, the groups say. The megafacilities also create what are known as data heat islands, which are higher-temperature zones caused by intense energy demands.
“We’re just starting to see the very early edge of the wave of the research into health impacts of data centers,” said Alison Steele, executive director of the Environmental Health Project, a nonprofit public health organization. “By the time we have a substantial volume of research it’s going to be too late, because the decisions are being made now.”
A trade group for the data center industry said a review of the largest data center market — Virginia — found that use of backup power sources, including diesel generators, is minimal, and that existing state and federal regulations limit potential emissions or impacts.
“Data centers are committed to being responsible partners where they operate,” said Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs at the Data Center Coalition.
It Cuts Across Politics
Mounting concerns about data centers are dividing candidates and pitting some GOP contenders against President Donald Trump, who supports the facilities’ construction as vital for economic growth.
Two in 3 Americans oppose the construction of new data centers in the U.S., according to an October Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll.
Such political standoffs are happening largely in states that Trump won in 2024, where most new data center capacity has been proposed. About 1,400 data centers operate in the U.S., and an additional 2,000-plus are planned.
Sixty percent of data center capacity under construction is in states Trump won by five percentage points or more, according to Cleanview, a market intelligence company. Excluding Virginia, 92% is in states the president won.
Hannah said the uptick in construction has put Trump’s coalition at particular risk because data centers are often built in rural areas, where the president has often enjoyed insurmountable margins of support.
“This is where most of the data centers go,” Hannah said. “They go into red states, because Republicans are less critical of economic opportunity. If it promises jobs and money, they’re all in.”
In Page, signs opposing construction pepper front yards.
The opposition to more data centers in the state could pose political risks for GOP House candidate Jay Feely, who won his primary with an endorsement from Trump. He says they are key to keeping up with China. Democratic opponent Amish Shah wants a pause on new construction in th

Stephanie Rowell was standing on her parents’ front porch in July when a wasp stung her left arm.
She said that almost immediately her arm felt like it was “on fire,” her body started itching all over, and her face became swollen and red.
Rowell, 53, took Benadryl, and her father started driving her to the nearest emergency room, about 25 minutes away. But after driving for 10 minutes they spotted a TruHealthNow urgent care facility in Purcellville, Virginia, and decided to stop, hoping she would get help faster.
“I thought I was going to die,” she said, recalling that she felt her throat tighten and found it harder to breathe.
Rowell, a manager at an agritourism business who lives in Round Hill, Virginia, has been uninsured since 2025, when she said she could no longer afford to buy coverage on her own.
After she checked in and disclosed that she did not have health insurance, Rowell said, a nurse practitioner saw her in an exam room and quickly diagnosed anaphylaxis, a severe and potentially life-threatening allergic reaction.
She said the nurse practitioner advised her that she needed a shot of epinephrine to reverse her symptoms.
Then the bill came, via a medical assistant.
“The medical assistant apologized and said I had to pay $400 for the shot up front,” Rowell said.
The Medical Service
Epinephrine is a naturally produced hormone, and a synthetic version is used as an injectable medication to treat severe allergic reactions, typically delivered via a single-dose prescription device called an EpiPen. It can prevent anaphylaxis from developing into anaphylactic shock, a life-threatening condition that occurs when the reaction causes a dramatic drop in blood pressure.
Because patients sometimes experience a recurrence of anaphylaxis after the initial reaction, it is recommended that patients be monitored in the hours after receiving epinephrine.
In addition to the injection, the urgent care’s staff checked Rowell’s vital signs, including her blood pressure, and a medical assistant monitored her for 30 minutes after she received the shot, according to Manbir Takhar, TruHealthNow’s medical director.
The Bill
$605: $400 for the medication, a $40 fee to administer it, and $165 for the visit to the urgent care center.
The Billing Problem: Emergency Care or Urgent Care?
Rowell said she was stunned that she was expected to pay before she received the shot of epinephrine. She returned to the waiting area to retrieve her wallet from her dad.
After she handed over her debit card, she said, the medical assistant gave her the shot. Within a few minutes, she could feel her throat loosening and her symptoms eased.
“I asked, ‘If I didn’t have the money, would you have just let me die?’” Rowell said. “And they said, sorry, that is their policy.”
Officials at TruHealthNow, which privately owns and operates eight urgent care centers in Northern Virginia and Maryland, said Rowell was told its policy in emergencies is to first provide treatment before handling billing. “Our policy is we give the shot and worry about the money later,” Preet Takhar, TruHealthNow’s CEO, said in an interview with KFF Health News.
The company officials confirmed Rowell was asked to pay before she received the shot. They said the nurse practitioner first determined Rowell’s condition was stable and that she was asked for payment as the injection was being prepared.
The request for payment did not delay administering the shot, said Manbir Takhar, who is married to Preet Takhar.
“The patient was stable, and that is why we took the payment then,” she said.
Federal law requires hospital emergency departments to stabilize anyone who shows up, regardless of ability to pay. But urgent care centers generally don’t fall under that law unless they are owned by hospitals, said Barry Furrow, director of the health law program at Drexel University in Philadelphia.
Urgent care centers have proliferated across the country in recent years, offering quick access to care, especially for people who don’t have a regular physician or can’t immediately see one, and particularly after hours and on weekends. The clinics usually take insurance and charge patients who don’t have coverage.
More than 15,000 urgent care centers handled about 185 million patient visits in 2025, according to the Urgent Care Association, a national trade group.
Urgent care centers offer a wide range of primary care services, treating conditions such as sore throats, flu, sprained ankles, and minor cuts. While services vary, they are not intended to treat life-threatening emergencies such as heart attacks or traumatic injuries.
Yet people sometimes show up at urgent care centers when they need emergency care, usually because they do not realize the seriousness of their condition, said Alan Ayers, an urgent care industry consultant.
While urgent care centers, like most doctors’ offices, ask for an insurance card or payment up front, that should not happen for patients needing emergency help, he said.
“Collecting a copay at check-in is standard across outpatient medicine, and it’s a separate question,” Ayers said. “For a sore throat, it doesn’t matter much. For anaphylaxis, it should never come up.”
Doctors also face an ethical obligation to treat patients facing an emergency if they have the capability, without asking for up-front payment, said Arthur Caplan, professor emeritus and past head of the medical ethics division at the New York University Grossman School of Medicine.
In a lifesaving situation, “you don’t need to have a patient go fumbling around for a credit or insurance card,” he said. “If you have the skill to take care of someone, you should.”
Medical experts say patients should generally know when to seek care at a hospital instead of an urgent care facility. For example, if they have trouble breathing or are experiencing chest pain, they should head to the ER. But some cases are not as clear-cut.

The Campaign To Defend Trans Healthcare in Missouri Is Slow Going, on Purpose
CREVE COEUR, Mo. — Reneé Luckfield tries not to knock like a cop.
In fact, the 29-year-old spends a lot of time thinking about how to make strangers comfortable when she shows up at their door to talk about transgender healthcare. A syncopated “tap — tap-tap-tap” sounds friendly even when she knocks loudly. In each encounter, she masks her own unease.
“Honestly, it’s not something that I’m entirely comfortable with,” Luckfield, a transgender woman, said while walking door to door in this affluent St. Louis suburb. “And it’s not fair that we have to do this work.”
Transgender issues have become a major theme in this year’s midterm elections, especially in Missouri, where voters are weighing a proposed constitutional amendment to bar minors from gender-transition surgery, cross-sex hormone therapy, and puberty blockers. The potential ban is part of a proposed amendment to reinstate a near-total ban on abortion in the state.
Voters in four other states will also decide on transgender issues this year: a proposed ban on transgender health care for minors in Colorado, and proposed restrictions on transgender athletes in youth sports in Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska, and Washington.
Luckfield is part of an effort by the LGBTQ+ advocacy organization PROMO Missouri to defeat the Missouri measure by knocking on 100,000 doors across five of the state’s largest metro areas before the election — an ambitious target the group is trying to reach with a mixture of full-time canvassers like Luckfield, the St. Louis lead, and volunteers who show up on weekends. About one out of every 10 knocks turns into a conversation, and they’re aiming to have 10,000 conversations before Election Day. The group celebrated reaching 6,000 in early October, but the process is slow going, intentionally, as canvassers aim for open-ended, “transformative” conversations with potential voters.
The technique, “deep canvassing,” has a history of changing people’s perspectives on difficult political topics, including a 2012 campaign that overturned a gay marriage ban in Maine and a 2021 campaign for police reform in Minnesota that, while defeated, triggered new debate. Now organizers in Missouri hope it can help stave off the latest effort in the state to permanently ban gender-affirming care for minors.
In 2023, Missouri’s Republican-dominated legislature permanently blocked minors’ access to gender-affirming surgeries and temporarily blocked their access to new prescriptions for puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for four years. The state is one of 27 that enacted restrictions on gender-affirming care for minors in the past five years.
The deep canvass in Missouri began in 2024, as transgender healthcare was becoming a focal point of state and national elections. President Donald Trump’s campaign, and pro-Trump groups, spent millions of dollars that year attacking Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris over transgender issues, such as one declaring, “Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you.”
And in Missouri that year, an amendment to add abortion protections to the state’s constitution passed by fewer than 100,000 votes. Opponents argued the measure would also enable the state’s ban on gender-affirming care for minors to be overturned. “NO TAX PAID CHILD SEX CHANGE SURGERY” read a sign opposing the amendment.
This year’s amendment to reinstate the state’s abortion ban and codify the ban on trans healthcare for minors is polling neck and neck, with 43% supportive of the bans, 44% opposed, and 13% undecided, against a margin of error of 4.09%. This most recent poll doesn’t ask separately about abortion and gender-affirming care, but polling from February showed stronger support for abortion access. The deep canvassers are trying to reach voters who are against banning abortion but are more ambivalent on trans issues. That means not spending too much time talking to people who are already very opposed or very supportive of the proposed bans.
To discern people’s views, canvassers are trained to ask the person they’re speaking with to place themselves on a scale from 0 to 10, with 0 being totally opposed to banning abortion and 10 being totally in favor of it. Then they ask the person to use the same scale to rate their feeling toward banning “gender-transition procedures for trans minors” — language similar to what voters will see on the ballot. After each of those questions, canvassers ask why the number the person chose is right for them.
On an overcast Saturday morning in late September, with Missouri’s summer heat seemingly broken at last, the sounds of lawnmowers and leaf blowers filled the air as Luckfield began knocking doors in a neighborhood 20 miles west of the Gateway Arch.
The first person who opened their door was a 10/10 in canvasser shorthand — in favor of banning abortion because of her Christian faith and in favor of banning gender-transition procedures for minors because she doesn’t think children are equipped to make those decisions and doesn’t think parents should either.
“I hear you,” Luckfield replied. “That’s everything I need from you today. Thank you very much for your time.”
The exchange wasn’t unusual, Luckfield said. Neither was a conversation she had later that morning with Carol Parsons, who said she was opposed to banning both abortion and gender-transition procedures for minors — a 0/0. Luckfield acknowledged Parsons’ support and asked if she had any questions about the process kids go through to get care.
“I do feel that they need to be old enough to realize that that is life-changing,” Parsons said. Surgery is the thing she’s not sure about, she said.
“It is tricky, and it is scary to think of that happening for young kids,” Luckfield acknowledged. “The phrase ‘transgender procedures’ — that’s, I think, very deliberately chosen language to stoke that fear of surgeries in particular.”

Tanja Konwinski thought the Constitution pipeline was dead.
When her husband bought 82 acres in Schoharie County, New York, in 2023, she knew Williams Cos. held an easement on the property for the proposed natural gas pipeline. But the state had rejected the project’s water quality permit application in 2016 and courts upheld that decision. She assumed it would never be built.
Now, the 125-mile pipeline, which would stretch from Pennsylvania to upstate New York, is back in the federal regulatory process, backed by the Trump administration’s push to expand domestic energy production. The U.S. Department of Energy has announced plans to direct up to $42 million to the project under the Defense Production Act, a 1950 law that allows the federal government to support private-sector production in the interest of national security.
For New Yorkers, the pipeline’s revival has implications beyond the fate of a single project. It’s the latest flashpoint in the state’s debate over how to balance energy costs and supply with its climate commitments—and the debate is taking center stage in the state’s governor’s race.
Incumbent Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul is trying to weigh the state’s climate commitments against concerns about rising electricity and heating costs.
Hochul’s Republican challenger, Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, argues that expanding natural gas infrastructure would increase energy supplies and lower utility bills. Blakeman has floated the idea of repealing New York’s 2014 fracking ban, which was enacted due to concerns over public health and environmental risks.
While Hochul has said she will not allow fracking, her administration has approved a previously rejected pipeline and delayed a major climate target. Even if Hochul wins this November, environmental advocates question whether the state will maintain protections they fought for years to secure.
A recent poll conducted by Quinnipiac University, shows Hochul leading Blakeman by 14 percentage points.
Pipeline Problems
There is currently no proposal for the Constitution pipeline before New York, said Ken Lovett, a spokesperson for Hochul.
Late last year, Williams, the energy infrastructure company, withdrew its state permit applications after the Department of Environmental Conservation determined that three of them were incomplete.
The company says it is still pursuing state permits. Public records also show it has asked the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, which regulates interstate gas pipelines, to reinstate the project’s 2014 construction approval and waive the requirement for a New York permit.
While the Department of Energy has pledged to help Williams pay permitting development costs under the Defense Production Act, environmental groups and state regulators have questioned whether the project can lawfully proceed without New York’s approval.
Joshua Sewell, director of policy and research at the budget watchdog group Taxpayers for Common Sense, said using the law to support energy development is not unprecedented. Former President Joe Biden invoked it to strengthen domestic renewable energy supply chains.
But Sewell sees the Trump administration’s approach as part of a broader effort to bypass established safeguards.
The Constitution pipeline is one of two major gas projects Williams is pursuing in the region. The other, the Northeast Supply Enhancement (NESE) pipeline, would wind through New Jersey into New York Harbor.
Williams says the projects would help address regional gas supply constraints and deliver reliable, affordable energy “while supporting economic growth and emissions reductions,” company spokeswoman Cherice Corley said in an email.
New York rejected NESE’s permit applications twice over water-quality concerns. The project resurfaced last year after the Trump administration briefly halted construction on Empire Wind, an offshore wind farm near New York City. A few months later, NESE received permits from New York and New Jersey—though an appeals court subsequently cancelled New Jersey’s approval.
President Donald Trump has claimed Hochul agreed to allow pipelines to proceed in exchange for federal support for offshore wind projects. At a June press conference, he said Hochul agreed to allow construction, but was now “holding up” the Constitution pipeline. Hochul’s spokesperson denied that she made such a deal, saying the governor is open to gas projects when they meet state regulations.
The dispute reflects the tension in Hochul’s “all of the above” energy policy, which aims to combine natural gas and nuclear power with investments in renewable energy. She has directed the state power authority to develop at least one gigawatt of nuclear power and pledged state funding for clean energy development.
“The Governor’s all-of-the-above approach to energy is designed to increase New York’s energy supply in a variety of ways to keep the lights on and costs down for New Yorkers,” Ken Lovett, a spokesperson for Hochul, said in an email.
But Hochul has also pushed back the state’s original deadline to cut greenhouse gas emissions to 40 percent below 1990 levels by a decade, while increasing the eventual reduction target to 60 percent. She said the original timetable would have driven up energy costs.
Environmental groups say the pipeline approvals and delayed climate goals risk are undermining the state’s progress on environmental issues.

“We have to be in a new kind of social contract that includes nature … we don’t want this land to be collateral damage,” said Karenna Gore, executive director of the Center for Earth Ethics.

In 2016, current Democratic candidate for Congress Leticia Gutierrez lived six miles from a refinery owned by the Brazilian oil company Petrobras in Pasadena, part of the greater Houston area. The plant accrued thousands of dollars in fines from the Texas Commission on Environment Quality for violations including the release of dangerous air pollutants like sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides that coated the significantly Hispanic area bordering the plant, where Gutierrez and her two children lived.
Her eldest son developed an upper respiratory illness as a child and, according to Gutierrez, it wasn’t until she spoke to several pediatricians that she was able to identify the source of her son’s ailment as pollution from the nearby petrochemical facilities along the Houston Ship Channel. A decade later, the same environmental issues that plagued Gutierrez’s community have become central to her campaign platform as she makes a bid in a newly redrawn congressional district that is reliant on fossil fuel to power its local economies by providing more than one million jobs.
“I’m all for making money, but it shouldn’t be on the backs of our children’s health,” Gutierrez told Inside Climate News.
As Election Day approaches, Gutierrez and her Republican challenger, Alex Mealer, have taken clear stances on the industry and its impacts. Gutierrez has focused much of her campaign on the disparate health and environmental ramifications that spawn from living near petrochemical facilities. Mealer, a former oil and gas finance executive, emphasizes her plans to expand employment at those facilities and strengthen the district’s fossil fuel businesses.
This will be the first general election since Texas’ 9th district was redrawn to favor Republicans last year. The election could determine control of the House. A recent poll from the University of Houston shows Mealer, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump in the primary, with a six point lead over Gutierrez, and 10 percent of voters still undecided. Mealer defeated state Rep. Briscoe Cain in the Republican primary runoff. Gutierrez secured her own party’s nomination against five opponents in March.
According to Renee Cross, the senior executive director and a lead researcher behind the poll at the University of Houston’s Hobby School of Public Affairs, the gap between the candidates is considerably narrower than expected, particularly in a newly redrawn district.
“It went from a +26 Democrat district to a +9 Republican. Well, +9 is not tremendous, but it still gives the edge to Republicans,” Cross said. “So the fact that Gutierrez is only 6 points behind is pretty remarkable, not only based on those voting trends but also based on the amount of money that Mealer has had to advertise to get people aware not only of her, but aware of her opponent’s alleged weaknesses.”
Gutierrez and Mealer fall on opposite sides of the oil and gas industry, with Mealer alleging that Gutierrez’s concerns for refineries’ effects on public health will undermine job growth in the oil and gas sector that powers the state of Texas. Gutierrez has denied the assertion.
“My response has always been the same, even as I’ve been doing this work prior to me campaigning: advocating for cleaner air and cleaner environmental standards actually creates jobs,” Gutierrez said. “It doesn’t do away with them. As a matter of fact, this Trump administration’s rollback of a lot of the protections have been put in place for decades by Republicans,” she said, referencing former President George H.W. Bush’s 1990 amendments to the Clean Air Act.
Mealer has expressed plans to expand domestic energy production in an effort to knock down gas and electricity costs and boost local economies. She’s also announced plans to grow the Houston Ship Channel, which accounts for 18.5 percent of the state’s GDP.
Throughout the campaign, Gutierrez has courted working class families, drawing on her background as a single mother and the immigrant daughter of farm laborers. She has pledged to tackle affordability and environmental issues, like the disproportionate impact of poor air quality near Port Houston. Labor organizations, including the Texas Gulf Coast Area Labor Federation and the Texas chapter of the Service Employees International Union, have endorsed her.

The Texas Health and Environment Alliance declined to comment on the election but said the organization has worked with Gutierrez for years and witnessed her advocacy in the Houston area.
Though Gutierrez has never held public office, in her role as government affairs director at the advocacy group Air Alliance Houston, she supported legislation designed to improve environmental standards in the region, including Senate Bill 763, which called for a more efficient review of air quality standard permits.
In her role at Air Alliance, she also supported HB 1730, which proposed a collaborative health study from the University of Houston to determine the health outcomes caused by forever chemicals in partnership with the Railroad Commission of Texas, the TCEQ and the Department of State Health Services. According to Gutierrez, following a fire at a storage tank in 2019, chemicals from the foam used to combat the blaze seeped into the Houston Ship Channel, raising the contamination level above that allowed by the EPA.
Mealer, who did not respond to requests for comment, has remained relatively quiet on climate and environmental issues in her own campaign, a decision that Cross said makes sense given that, while Mealer has maintained a strong positive position toward the oil and gas industry, residents in the 9th district still grapple with its health effects, including higher cancer risks.

Reeling rods, pulling pots and hauling nets this summer, fishermen from Greece to the U.K. discovered unexpected visitors popping their heads above the surface.
In the Aegean, it was silver-cheeked toadfish—an invasive pufferfish with powerful, prominent teeth. In the English Channel, it was the unprecedented arrival of uncommon common octopuses. And in the Adriatic, it was the aggressive and aptly named blue crab.
Across the continent’s seas and straits, warming waters and decades of overfishing are throwing marine ecosystems off kilter and sending species swimming in new directions. For the fishermen landing unfamiliar tentacled and scaled sea creatures, the novel arrivals haven’t always been welcomed on deck.
“The fisheries I found 30 years ago were more or less the species that archeozoologists found in [archaeological] remains many thousands years back. But today, this is changing really fast,” said Anastasia Miliou, the science director at Archipelagos Institute of Marine Conservation, a Greek nonprofit.
“Fishermen are [already] having a hard time because of a lack of fish. Changing temperatures and the new invasive and alien species don’t make it any easier,” said Miliou, noting the surprising spikes in certain stocks were adding financial pressure for artisanal fishermen struggling to survive.
This summer was Western Europe’s warmest on record. Above the waterline, a wave of wildfires, droughts and heat-related deaths ravaged the continent. The blue-jewelled depths of the Aegean and even the more-bracing North Sea and Baltic basins also experienced mass heat.
Globally, June to August 2026 saw the highest mean sea surface temperature on record. In Europe, this included sea surface temperatures more than 3.6 and 5.4 degrees Fahrenheit (2 or 3 degrees Celsius) above the last three-decade average.
As global ocean heat content rises for the ninth consecutive year, “ectothermic” fish—species unable to regulate their own temperature that depend on finding suitable surrounding conditions—are on the move.
These newcomers across the continent have brought economic challenges to fisheries who have, at times, struggled to adapt.
In Greece, the arrival of the fatal-if-consumed toadfish and their large, sharp gnashers has significantly damaged fishing gear as the rabbit-like front teeth chomp nets.
“It’s got to the point where we might go out fishing one day and then spend the next three days fixing our nets,” Giorgos Kyriakakis, a Cretan fisherman, told Greek public broadcaster ERT in June. “They eat our catch and damage our nets—that’s very costly.”
Over the summer, Greek fishermen were offered almost $6.00 (€5.33) per kilo to catch the invasive species by the Agriculture Ministry.
Off Britain’s southern shores, eight-legged, suction-cupped common octopuses have arrived from breeding grounds in the Channel Islands and northern France in record numbers. The largest population bloom in 75 years, the arrival is tied to temperature increases, according to researchers at the Marine Biological Association.
The newcomers have proven both a blessing and a curse. Staggeringly lucrative catches have been recorded for those able to catch the creatures. But for traditional shellfish fisheries, the landings of brown crabs, European lobster and king scallops have dropped dramatically.

With octopods expected to stay in U.K. waters, the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs held its first “octopus conference” earlier this month.
“They are both a threat and an opportunity for fishermen and a massive challenge for fisheries management,” said Mike Cohen, CEO of the National Federation of Fishermen’s Organisations, at the event. “The sudden arrival of this fast-growing, short-lived and highly predatory species into British waters upends a lot of our established knowledge and expectations about our coastal ecosystems.”
In many cases it’s more than just warming water. It’s also the consequences of rampant overfishing.
“We forget to put in the equation the human [fishing] impact because in the Mediterranean, and especially here in the Aegean Sea, our seas are very overfished,” said Miliou, explaining that this creates gaps in the ecosystems.
“When the new species arrive here, they find a lot of space to grow because the native species are no longer there,” added Miliou, highlighting that many invasive species hitch a ride in the ballast water of ships transiting the Suez Canal.
Europe’s not alone.
More than 125 fish species in Japanese waters were found to have moved north to cooler waters, according to an eDNA study released this week by the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology.
“Fishermen across Japan are already finding differences in the types of fish they reel in compared to a few decades ago,” said the paper’s lead author Timothy Ravasi in a press release.
“A sudden influx of new types of fish means you need new techniques, tools, and knowledge to catch them, which is especially hard on small, family-based fishing businesses,” Ravasi said, noting people might not be able to make their culturally or historically significant dishes.
With European fish moving north to cooler confines—and also deeper to colder, darker depths—fisheries management will have to adapt. And as El Niño hits the Pacific Ocean, fish stocks are likely to be further disrupted the world over.
“Healthy marine ecosystems have their own mechanisms to restore balance and resist the spread of invasive species,” said Miliou, who remains optimistic.
“Nature will remake the balance as long as we let it. Right now we’re not letting it.”

As the most heavily forested state in the country, about 94 percent of Maine’s forests are privately owned, so focusing on their carbon benefits has both immediate ecological and economic effects.
By creating specific programs and collaborations, the state has been strategic in using its resources to reach its climate goals and has made thoughtful partnerships for years ahead. The story of Maine demonstrates how individuals can collectively make a greater impact and how international alliances can contribute toward global stewardship.
In a four-year climate action plan called “Maine Won’t Wait,” the state sets out four pillars to focus on: drastically reducing greenhouse emissions, strengthening resiliency by adaptation, protecting jobs at risk from climate change and creating clean energy jobs and supporting all of Maine’s residents, even in rural communities.
On the economic side, Maine’s Forest Products Council reported that in 2024 the state’s timber industry produced $8.3 billion for Maine’s economy, representing 3.45 percent of the state’s GDP. Maine’s paper and timber industry also accounted for 29,000 jobs across 16 counties.
But Maine’s 18 million acres of forests also protect the watershed, soil and biodiversity as the largest unfragmented tract across the eastern United States, essential for species migration.
One thing is certain: Maine’s forests are indispensable. In 2021, the state created the Forest Carbon Task Force and implemented a range of programs and legislation to support Maine’s forests and build climate resiliency. Now, as reporting deadlines are approaching, the state can see exactly how successful these conservation efforts have been.
In March, the Maine Forest Service introduced the WoodsWISE Resilience Program, which supports private woodland owners and encourages climate-focused stewardship. The program, which works alongside an existing program called the WoodsWISE Incentives Program, is now funded by two grants totaling $9 million from the Inflation Reduction Act and the U.S. Forest Service Landowner Support Program. One grant requires documentation of pre- and post-treatment inventory and carbon modeling.
Nicole Rogers, formerly the Maine Forest Service landowner outreach forester, said that through the WoodsWise program, landowners can apply for eight approved practices that have climate or carbon benefits. To participate, woodland owners need 10 to 1,000 acres of forest and must agree to work with a practice plan focused on the area of practice implementation that meets their forest’s specific needs for 10 years.
“Our program is a tool for landowners wanting to take action in their own forest,” Rogers said in an email. “By offering financial incentives, landowners have the opportunity to do thoughtful silviculture with a reduced financial burden.”
According to Rogers, since March, more than 150 landowners have participated in the WoodsWISE Resilience Program. Through this program, a trained consulting forester works with each landowner on a plan specific to their forest’s needs so they can gain support while navigating the changes from climate change.
The program focuses on good stewardship, which can mean many things, depending on the forest. It can range from invasive species removal and thinning an overcrowded, young forest; to removing specific trees to encourage regeneration, or removing trees that carry disease or fungus.
“These practices can be costly for a private landowner, so the program aims to reimburse 60 to 90 percent of the financial burden for landowners based on their underserved status by creating an indiviudalized plan the woodland owner agrees to follow for the next 10 years. This could result in up to $20,000 per participant and another program is set to open later this year with a higher landowner cap. With programs like these, the state of Maine could see a collective benefit.”
By purposefully using landowners’ forests, Maine has an advantage in reaching carbon neutrality. According to research by the University of Maine, the state’s forests offset at least 60 percent of overall greenhouse emissions annually. Philip Bartlett II, the former chair of the Maine Public Utilities Commission, said that electricity generation in Maine is already fairly clean, with a mix of renewables in use throughout the state.
Bartlett said it’s important to look long-term when meeting climate goals, and agrees that good forest management practices are key for Maine. He said that, to his knowledge, no fast clear-cutting is being done, and forests are managed for growth and harvesting, creating opportunities for carbon sequestration.
The challenge, he said, is the state’s vastness, which makes residents rely on fuel for transportation and oil to heat their homes. Bartlett said recent international dynamics have emphasized the need for a diversified portfolio of renewable resources to stabilize electricity prices.
“I think what we’re seeing now is that reliance on fossil fuels is really what is driving a ton of volatility and really high prices during certain parts of the year. So the only way you’re going to tackle that is to figure out how to diversify that portfolio,” he said.
Catherine Wolfram, a professor of energy economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Sloan School of Management, said Maine’s implementation of carbon markets aligns with how Europe and other countries are operating.
She said that while compliance markets run by governments in which polluters are essentially taxed for carbon emissions are “extremely robust and extremely effective,” much of the criticism of carbon markets comes from the voluntary markets where companies buy and sell carbon offsets without formal monitoring, with corruption and manipulation sometimes a factor.

Ethiopia has received 12 Su-35 fighter jets from Russia, as fighting intensified in the northern Tigray region neighbouring Eritrea.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who is attending the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow, described the acquisition as a "milestone" that would boost Ethiopia's defence capacity.
He said Ethiopia and Russia had agreed on the deal several years ago and the warplanes had come ahead of schedule. He also said that Ethiopia had plans to acquire four S-400 air defence systems from Moscow.
The Ethiopian leader said the military hardware was essential to protect the country from external threats.
Abiy, who described Russian President Vladimir Putin, "as a close friend of Ethiopia", said Ethiopia had now become the first country in subâSaharan Africa to own this kind of "advanced combat technology".
"If we fail to build this capability, surviving as a country in our region will become difficult. Countries with sufficient preparation are not easily defied," he said.
Russia and Ethiopia have signed several military agreements in recent years, including a deal in 2021 to train and improve technology for the military.
Abiy explained that Ethiopia signed an agreement with Russia several years ago to procure the Suâ35 jets and Sâ400 systems, citing global air force trends and security threats facing the country.
The Suâ35, he noted, was equipped for both airâtoâair and airâtoâground combat, with the ability to detect and neutralize incoming cruise missiles at distances of up to 200km (124 miles).
Military intelligence analyst Qalaab Segatu told BBC Amharic that Ethiopia's acquisition of additional warplanes was a key indication that "it was preparing for possible wars with other countries, not just internal conflicts".
According to him, the jets are highly manoeuvrable and capable of covering large areas, with radars capable of ensuring air superiority and long-range scanning.
When combined, the fighter jets and air defence systems "create a significant capability to protect and defend major cities and critical infrastructure such as the Renaissance Dam, providing key strategic air superiority", Qalaab said.
Abiy said in addition to the advanced capabilities of the aircraft from Russia, the use of drones was equally important in strengthening deterrence.
Ethiopia has extensively used military drones, including those sourced from Turkey and China, in recent conflicts.
"We need to build capacity not only with drones, but also with the fourth generation capabilities of the Su 30 and Su 35 [aircraft]," Abiy said.
The latest acquisition of military hardware from Russia comes after the current conflict in northern Tigray started last month between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).
Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended a civil war.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing the TPLF, which it denies.
Tensions between the two countries have also persisted as Abiy terms Ethiopia's lack of direct sea access an "existential question", which Eritrea views as a direct threat to its sovereignty.
Eritrea gained independence in 1993 after a decades-long war with Ethiopia, with the latter losing access to the sea.

9bab8b48cf61.text: By — Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/hegseth-fires-the-pentagons-top-military-planner-even-as-trump-considers-new-iran-strikes Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Hegseth fires the Pentagon's top military planner even as Trump considers new Iran strikes Politics Oct 29, 2026 4:51 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired the Pentagon's top military planner, a defense official said Wednesday, the latest in a series of generals to be ousted and one that comes even as President Donald Trump is weighing renewed strikes on Iran in the eight-month-long war. Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff. He is the second general to be ousted from the post, known in military circles as the "J5," under Hegseth. His predecessor, Lt. Gen. Joseph McGee, was forced to retire last October. Please check your inbox to confirm. The defense official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters, said there is no immediate replacement for Sylvia and no reason has been given for the firing. The move was reported earlier by The Atlantic. A spokesperson for the Joint Staff said "the Chairman, the Joint Staff, and the Joint Force extend our deepest gratitude to Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia and his family for their 32 years of distinguished service to our nation" and they "wish him and his family the best." WATCH: A look at Hegseth's attempts to reshape the Pentagon Typically, the J5 director and their staff are responsible for generating and coordinating military plans with both the chairman of the Joint Chiefs and the president. Sylvia's firing comes as Trump has repeatedly floated starting new military operations against Iran. Trump has vowed to "finish the job" in Iran after launching the war with Israel eight months ago and said new strikes are an option after the midterm elections next week. U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action after Tuesday's elections as well as for the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, two diplomats briefed on the matter said. They say Trump has not made a final decision on new strikes. A third U.S. aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are making their way to the region. Before arriving at the Joint Staff, Sylvia served as the commander of the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, until May 2025, according to his official biography, which has now been taken offline. He also previously served as the vice director for the J5. He is the latest in nearly two dozen generals, admirals and other military leaders to be fired, forced to retire or otherwise depart under Hegseth's tenure — almost all of which have not been publicly explained by the Pentagon. That includes the civilian secretaries of the Army and Navy as well as some top uniformed officers for the military services. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment late Wednesday. Hegseth said last month that he ordered the military to double the cuts to the overall number of top officers to a 20% decrease to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027. There are currently roughly 800 flag and general officer positions. "I call it accountability and long overdue," Hegseth told junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps Base Quantico on Sept. 30. Some members of Congress have criticized cuts to the ranks of generals as a "purge" that will take years to rebuild. "He's got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military," Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a former Navy combat pilot who has been critical of Hegseth, said last month. "He's purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it's going to take a generation to recover from it." Associated Press writers Aamer Madhani in Washington and Samy Magdy in New York contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 1149d7eccad6.text: The 2026 midterms already face a messy pileup of lawsuits and ballot battles, raising fears about election confidence before voters even finish casting ballots . Why it matters: Election challenges aren't unusual, but as the Trump administration continues to make false claims about widespread voter fraud, officials are juggling fights over voter lists, mail-ballot rules and election certification challenges. What they're saying: "The types of challenges that we are seeing pre-election, this close to election day, are very unusual, and mostly because they are coming from the federal government," Jonathan Diaz of the Campaign Legal Center told Axios. "These lawsuits are frivolous," Diaz said, adding they could "create doubt in the minds of the public about the legitimacy of the election process." "It shouldn't be allowed to happen, and it was done in conjunction with Schumer and everybody else. It's called VOTER FRAUD. It should not have been allowed to happen." The other side: The White House referred Axios to comments President Trump made to the media. The Department of Justice did not respond to Axios' request for comment. Here's some of the ways chaos and uncertainty have shaped the 2026 midterms: California In the Golden State, the Trump administration asked state election officials to set aside ballots from roughly 20,000 registered voters whom the DOJ suspects are noncitizens. A federal judge rejected that push Wednesday night, warning that the administration lacked sufficient evidence to justify potentially disenfranchising eligible voters. The judge noted that the DOJ had made similar claims in neighboring Nevada, where election officials determined that 185 voters the DOJ had flagged as noncitizens were actually U.S. citizens. Diaz told Axios that, from his perspective as a voting-rights advocate, the California battle is "not a real lawsuit. It's a political press release that they just happened to submit to the court." The other side: The White House directed questions about the ruling to remarks Trump made Thursday, in which he said "California is very corrupt," and the state's elections are "extremely corrupt." He did not provide evidence for his claims. Washington On Monday, the two U.S. attorneys' offices in Washington state asked the state to set aside ballots from more than 400 people they allege were illegally registered to vote. The letter mirrors similar demands sent to California before the Trump administration sued. Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs fired back Wednesday, tearing into the U.S. attorneys for making the request so close to Election Day and calling the timing "profoundly disappointing." Hobbs said a preliminary investigation confirmed that the federal list includes U.S. citizens and is unreliable. He asked prosecutors to provide individualized proof of ineligibility. North Carolina Nearly 4,000 mail-in ballots, or about 6%, processed in North Carolina through Oct. 24 have been flagged for problems that, if not fixed, could invalidate voters' choices. Time is running out for those voters to address the issues, and hundreds have yet to respond to notifications about their ballots. The rejections appear to stem in part from new guidance issued by the GOP-controlled state Board of Elections requiring the inner ballot envelope to be sealed, even if the outer envelope is already sealed. Alaska In Alaska's Senate race , two men named Dan Sullivan are on the ballot, Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan. New reporting from The New York Times on Wednesday alleged that aides to Democratic candidate Mary Peltola helped recruit the other Dan Sullivan in an apparent attempt to confuse voters and siphon votes away from the incumbent senator. Peltola's campaign denies any involvement. Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation Wednesday for investigators to determine whether the alleged scheme violated Alaska law and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted. The DOJ has separately sued to delay certification of the Senate election if the incumbent loses and votes for the other Sullivan could have changed the outcome. Go deeper: Trump is pulling every lever to reshape U.S. elections

Sir Patrick Stewart: The life of a legendary actor
Legendary Star Trek actor Sir Patrick Stewart has died, aged 86. Stewart died at his home in Los Angeles on 28 October after suffering with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia, according to a statement shared on his social media.
âHis sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre,â the statement reads.
In a career that spanned seven decades, Sir Patrick won multiple Emmys and Golden Globes, a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and a knighthood from Queen Elizabeth II.

Sir Patrick Stewart, who has died at the age of 86, was a stage and screen great who balanced Hollywood stardom with an equally stellar career in classical theatre.
While many actors are typecast, he moved effortlessly from Shakespeare and Dickens to the command of the USS Enterprise and his famous wheelchair in X-Men.
In a career that spanned seven decades, Sir Patrick received multiple awards, a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and a knighthood from Queen Elizabeth II.
One of the world's most versatile actors, he mastered both comedy and tragedy, science-fiction and historical drama - despite the entertainment industry's traditional dislike of bald heads.
Patrick Hewes Stewart was born in Mirfield in the West Riding of Yorkshire on 13 July 1940.
His mother Gladys was a textile worker. She was active in amateur dramatics and encouraged her three sons to take part.
His father was a former Sergeant Major in the Parachute Regiment whose experience during the wartime evacuation of Dunkirk had shredded his mental health.
"My father was a very potent individual," Stewart later recalled. "It was said that when he strode on to the parade ground, birds stopped singing."
But Alfred Stewart had become a quick-tempered man, suffering from what would now be called post traumatic stress.
He was prone to drink and often took out his frustrations on his family - although Patrick himself was never the target of his fists.
Young Patrick's love of drama developed at school when one of his teachers introduced him to Shakespeare and encouraged him to perform.
His first public performance was in a local church production of Cinderella.
He found the predictability of dramatic performances a welcome change form the turmoil of his home life.
He left school at 15 and eventually got a job as a journalist and obituary writer on the Dewsbury Reporter.
He also threw himself enthusiastically into the flourishing local theatre. "I used to recite Shakespeare from memory," he said. "I just learned all these big speeches."
But he found it impossible to concentrate on both his job and his acting. Eventually his editor told him to choose between journalism and the "foolhardy" acting.
Stewart picked up his typewriter and walked out.
At the age of 18, he had the traumatic experience of losing all his hair, a huge blow to an aspiring actor and self-conscious teenager - who worried that girls would no longer find him attractive.
He won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic and later joined the Royal Shakespeare Company - playing a variety of roles across the company's repertoire.
And when not appearing as Oberon or Enobarbus, he made his TV debut as a fireman in a 1967 episode of soap opera Coronation Street.
His Broadway debut came in 1970 as Snout in Peter Brook's critically acclaimed production of A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Over the next two decades, Stewart appeared in a variety of television roles without threatening to become a major star.
In 1974, he played Lenin in the BBC's 13-part drama series The Fall of Eagles.
He was a conspiratorial Roman soldier in the hugely popular I, Claudius and a Soviet spy in Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy and Smiley's People.
In 1984, Stewart left the RSC and moved to the National Theatre. Now in his mid-40s, he had only ever been unemployed for three weeks, but was rarely cast as a main character.
He'd landed a number of minor film roles: including playing Guinevere's father in Excalibur, a minstrel in Dune, and a riding instructor in Little Lord Fauntleroy.
And he was the voice of a small character in the animated film of Richard Adams' novel The Plague Dogs.
But even he described the first half of his career as "sound but never spectacular".
Then came the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard.
A producer named Robert L Justman was intent on reviving the Star Trek franchise, and was looking for a successor to William Shatner's legendary James T Kirk.
He had hoped to find a sexy, hirsute Frenchman to play the role - but chanced upon Stewart giving a lecture to his wife's Shakespeare class in Los Angeles.
Justman turned to his wife. "I said I think I've found our new captain," he said.
Stewart was intrigued but dubious.
He knew nothing about the original Star Trek and his great friend Sir Ian McKellen, told him not to throw his stage career away on a wild goose chase into space.
But in need of a boost to his finances, Stewart signed a six-year contract, firmly believing the show wouldn't last and he'd be back on the boards before long.
"Everybody told me it would be a flop," he recalled. "A friend of mine said, 'Get a suntan, make some money, go home.'"
He was, however, pleased that the producers didn't mind his baldness.
He'd tried wearing a wig in early screen tests, but it looked ratty and - in the end - Star Trek's founder Gene Roddenberry told him to ditch it.
"In the 24th Century, they wouldn't care if Picard was bald," he said.
Stewart, who was billed by the New York Times as "an unknown British Shakespearean actor", found it hard adapting to his new job.
After his stage experiences, he found the 20 hours a day on set tiring, and he also struggled to work with a fairly laid-back and fun-loving US cast.
His decision to call his fellow actors together and give them a lecture about behaving more seriously failed to gain him popularity.
"It was really awful, being dressed down by the captain," said Brent Spiner, who played Data, the android. "We really thought, 'Well, please, get over it'."
Eventually Stewart softened, insisting that every member of the cast told at least one joke a day.
Despite his initial scepticism, Star Trek: The Next Generation both survived and prospered - making its star a very wealthy man.
Captain Picard was supposed to be French, but displayed a surprisingly English regard for both Shakespeare and Earl Grey tea.
And, after playing all those Shakespearean princes and dukes on the London stage, Stewart became fiercely proud of him, and of the show's ability
