The Ukrainian city of Kherson has known its first two days of quiet after many years, as a US-brokered temporary ceasefire has allowed residents rare moments of respite from the constant Russian aerial attacks that plague the front line region.
Videos posted on social media showed people strolling down streets covered in anti-drone nets and gathering in the city's squares - ordinary activities that usually mean keeping one eye on the sky and one ear out for incoming drones.
"Ever since the ceasefire was announced, there's been total silence," said Olga, 42, speaking by phone from Kherson. "We are all, of course, overjoyed."
"I don't even know what to call it," she added, her smile coming through in her voice. "It's as if everything has finally come to an end."
Since Tuesday, Kherson has "literally come back to life," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
"People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. What for some is ordinary everyday life, for residents of the Kherson region today is the greatest desire."
The temporary pause in hostilities - due to end on Sunday - is the result of efforts by US First Lady Melania Trump to broker a safe passage out of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which lies on the other side of the Dnipro river from Kherson.
For several days, Russian forces have been working to clear the road of mines, ahead of a planned evacuation of Oleshky's civilians on Friday.
But there are fears that, alongside carrying out the well-publicised "humanitarian operation" â which some American journalists will be invited to witness â the Russians are using the truce to bolster their forces in the area ahead of a renewed onslaught of Kherson from next week.
"They are... using this lull to strengthen their positions, bring in more military supplies, weapons, ammunition, and drones, and carry out some redeployment of their forces," an anonymous source working in local government told the BBC.
Petro Andriushchenko, Director of Ukraine's Center for Studying the Occupation, says Kherson locals have told him that they witnessed a military build-up around Radensk, some 20km (12 miles) from Oleshky.
Its residents will be saved but "we are simultaneously giving the enemy an opportunity to exploit the ceasefire for its own military purposes," he said. Once the ceasefire ends, the situation may be "worse than we saw before, because Russia's units will be stronger. They have enough time to prepare to prolong this action."
Though Kherson residents are clear-eyed about what lies ahead, for a brief period this week the city caught its breath.
No violations have been reported on either side since Tuesday. There have been other ceasefires in the past, but these were generally not respected, Kherson resident Dima said.
"This is the first time the shelling has stopped, people don't quite believe it," he told the BBC. "They are going to the shops, drinking coffee, walking around... The city is alive."
On social media, a woman named Yulia wrote about her unusually uneventful trip to the supermarket with an edge of disbelief. For once, she said, she returned home from the shops "whole and calm, not as usual - scared, sweating from the horror and with a lump in my throat."
This week, dozens of people were also able to access their belongings and homes in the so-called "red zone" of Kherson â an area so exposed to drones and artillery attacks that it has become unlivable.
"Some are venturing into places where nobody has dared to go for years, filming areas where simply being present has meant - and will once again mean - almost certain death," said Denisa Bohackova, a Czech volunteer who lives in Kherson.
Dima described scenes of "girls, boys, parents, grandmothers" walking down the streets of the red zone carrying suitcases and bags, returning to their flats to see what they could retrieve.
Some of those who returned to the red zone found buildings reduced to charred, empty shells; in other cases, homes had been looted. The scale of destruction in some of these places, Bohackova said, is "breathtaking".
Others were rushing back for reasons beyond material concerns. Angela Dobrovolska's husband Serhiy was killed two years ago by a grenade dropped by a piloted Russian drone - an instance of a "human safari" attack of the kind that Kherson has become sadly infamous for.
On Thursday, Angela headed back from Kyiv to Kherson to visit his grave for the first time in months. "They say that all the people have rushed to Kherson," she said. "And I'll be going to the cemetery to my husband."
The population of Kherson has dwindled from over 250,000 to about 65,000 since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which will enter its sixth year in February.
Though civilian life in the city never stopped, Bohackova said, it also carried on under the conditions of an active battlefield, with schools, theatres, kindergartens and hospitals moved underground.
"An ordinary civilian from Kherson has experienced more of this war than many soldiers," Bohackova said.
Olga, who is raising two children, described regular blackouts, mines dropped by drones and concealed by fallen leaves, drone fragments ricocheting, and a city that typically shuts by the afternoon.
But since silence fell on the city, Olga has been able to live a normal life. She drove to a different town and took the bus to another district to visit her grandmother with her son. Around her, the shops were full, as were the cafes. After years of quiet streets, "there was even a small traffic jam," she smiled.
But the clock is ticking.
The evacuation of nearby Oleshky is due to be completed by Sunday, after which the ceasefire will be over. "The concern is that, starting Monday, things could turn truly chaotic," Olga said.
"We know the strikes will resume, and that they will increase," said Dima, as he and his wife prepared to visit their flat in the red zone for the first time in several months

9e4e991dc3fd.text: Alaska's tight Senate race is facing a new controversy over two candidates named Dan Sullivan appearing on the ballot — a twist that's drawn attention from President Trump . The big picture: The controversy is adding uncertainty to one of the nation's most competitive Senate contests, with control of Congress on the line in next week's midterm elections. Catch up quick: The New York Times reported this week that Democratic operatives with ties to Mary Peltola's Senate campaign helped recruit a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan to challenge Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan. Trump accused Peltola and Democrats of election fraud and called for criminal prosecution, though the Times did not establish that any laws were broken. Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation into Peltola's campaign over the NYT report. House Republicans are also launching an Alaska Senate race probe. Though the presence of two Sullivans in the Senate race has been known for months, the Times' report adds a new wrinkle to a dispute that's already reached the courts. Here's what to know about the controversy. The same-name Senate race controversy The controversy centers on two candidates with nearly identical names appearing on Alaska's Senate ballot: Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan and unaffiliated challenger Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. The ballot will show registered Republican "Sullivan, Dan S." and unaffiliated candidate "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr." Peltola and Republican Gerald Heikes will also be on the ballot. The challenger initially filed as a Republican but later changed his registration to undeclared. He will appear on the ballot without a party label. Flashback: Concerns about the duplicate names have existed for months. In June, a top Alaskan election official ruled that candidate Daniel J. Sullivan was ineligible to run on the state's primary ballot. The official said she found the candidacy was "filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot's fairness or neutrality," per the Associated Press. The Alaska Supreme Court later ruled that state election officials lacked the authority to disqualify Sullivan based on their concerns about his motives, allowing him to appear on the ballot. The court did not determine whether his candidacy was intended to mislead voters. Trump reacts to Alaska controversy Flashback: Last week, the Justice Department sued Alaska, seeking to block certification of the Senate election if the incumbent loses by a margin potentially attributable to voters confusing the two Sullivans. Both Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have asked a federal judge to dismiss the case. Alaska officials are seeking dismissal of the lawsuit, arguing that it has no legal basis and that the federal government lacks authority to intervene in a matter governed by state election law. Zoom in: The new NYT report , published this week, cited texts, interviews and documents showing that Peltola's aides worked with Democratic operatives to recruit candidates who could siphon votes from the Republican senator. Per the report, a staffer was told to review every "Dan Sullivan" in the state, leading the team to Dan J. Sullivan, the retired schoolteacher who was registered as a Republican. Peltola's campaign and the DSCC denied recruiting Sullivan, per NYT. The latest: The NYT report sparked a reaction from Trump this week, who wrote on Truth Social that the recruitment by Peltola's campaign was done "in order to defraud, confuse, and obfuscate the Election," in his call for Peltola and the other Sullivan to be prosecuted. Gov. Dunleavy ordered a state investigation on Oct. 28 into the allegations, and House Oversight Chair James Comer launched a congressional probe on Oct. 29. What they're saying: "Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any DC politician will keep her away from that fight," a spokesman for the Peltola campaign tells Axios. "The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign." The other side: In a statement to Axios, Nate Adams, a spokesman for Dan S. Sullivan, accused Peltola, her advisers and Democratic operatives of coordinating with the DSCC to recruit candidates to deliberately confuse voters. "We always knew this was a coordinated effort to mislead Alaskans, and Mary Peltola was counting on it staying buried until after the election. Now that she's been caught red-handed, she still won't come clean," Adams said. "Instead, she's doubling down on the lie and is now attacking the same media outlets she's been misleading for months." How Sullivan confusion could affect the Alaska race Why it matters: Alaska's ranked-choice voting system could limit the impact of voter confusion for the two Sullivans. How it works: Ranked-choice voting allows voters to rank multiple candidates in order of preference. If no candidate wins a majority of first-place votes, the lower-performing candidates are eliminated and their supporters' votes go to the next-ranked choice. If Dan J. Sullivan is eliminated, ballots listing the incumbent as the next remaining choice would transfer to him. But voters who mistakenly select Dan J. Sullivan without ranking the incumbent could still cost the Republican votes in a close race. By the numbers: Dan J. Sullivan received 2.5% of the vote in Alaska's August primary, compared with 41.4% for the incumbent and 49.5% for Peltola.

77cbe8745971.text: By — Mark Kennedy, Associated Press Mark Kennedy, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/patrick-stewart-star-of-stage-and-star-trek-dies-at-86 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Patrick Stewart, star of stage and 'Star Trek,' dies at 86 Arts Updated on Oct 29, 2026 4:52 PM EDT — Published on Oct 29, 2026 4:02 PM EDT Patrick Stewart, the classically trained actor who added Shakespearean gravitas to the "Star Trek" and "X-Men" franchises, has died. He was 86. Stewart died Wednesday in Los Angeles, following "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said. Stewart's diagnoses had not been previously disclosed. WATCH: Patrick Stewart reflects on his life and legendary career in new memoir, 'Making It So' While best known as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the "X-Men" and "Star Trek: The Next Generation" series and films, respectively, Stewart spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise. Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of "A Christmas Carol" and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter's "No Man's Land" and Samuel Beckett's "Waiting for Godot" in repertoire with buddy Ian McKellen. He achieved some of the best reviews of his career when he finally tackled Macbeth for the first time. The production, under the direction of Rupert Goold, debuted in May 2007 at England's Chichester Festival Theatre, switched to London's West End and then moved to the Brooklyn Academy of Music before transferring to Broadway in 2008. Stewart's performance earned him his sole Tony Award nomination. The Times of London said his Macbeth was "an enthralling creation of frailty, appetite, egotism and grim humor." The Daily Telegraph said he had turned in "a truly great performance" and The New York Times said it was "a must-see." "Nearly 50 years I've waited," Stewart told The Associated Press in 2008. "I learned it when I was 14. I memorized all the soliloquies just because I thought they were great. And they stuck, so I didn't have to learn those bits of the play, which is a blessing, because learning lines has now become the one curse of this job." Starship commander grew up without a toilet Raised in Mirfield in Yorkshire, a working class corner of northern England, the future 24th century commander of a starship grew up without a bathroom in his house. Stewart joined an amateur drama group at 12 and memorized Shakespeare for fun as a teen. He won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, launching a career as a character actor. He had been bald since he was 19 — alopecia runs in his family. His father, a former regimental sergeant major in the British Army, was prone to outbursts of "repeated violence against my mother," as Stewart wrote in a newspaper piece. "Violence is always a choice a man makes and he alone is responsible for it." In his memoir, "Making It So," Stewart wrote about how he and his older brother Trevor braced for the nights when their dad came home drunk and angry, and attacked their mother. "Sometimes it was with an open hand, other times a closed fist. Always he aimed for her head." The son would later become a patron for Refuge, an organization that provides shelter for domestic abuse victims. Loving Shakespeare proved fruitful as Capt. Picard "The stage would prove to be a safe space, a refuge from real life in which I could inhabit another person, living in another place and time," he would write. Stewart was accepted into the Royal Shakespeare Company and stayed for 14 years, playing everything from Mark Antony to Henry IV to Shylock to Oberon. "People who were not in the company would say to me, 'Give it a break. Why don't you go somewhere else?' And I would say, 'To do what?'" he told the AP. "Telly?" Stewart eventually left to look for more varied work, including the 1981 film "Excalibur." He had just done a production of "Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?" in 1987 when an interesting offer came along. "I found myself in Hollywood shooting a syndicated science fiction series, which I was assured would fail." It didn't, of course. Thanks to Stewart's rich baritone and noble bearing, the "Star Trek" franchise ran for seven years, 178 episodes and produced four feature films. He was known for his slogan "Make it so." His adoration for Shakespeare would serve him well when he began to play Jean-Luc Picard, a 24th century starship commander. "There is a formality to the way they speak and comport themselves that remind me of numerous Shakespearean situations I'd been in onstage. I should play Jean Luc, I realized, as if he were a character in 'Henry IV,' which is about brave men," Stewart wrote in his memoir. Despite the Borg and Klingons, Stewart still managed to make room for blank verse. He established the Paramount Shakespeare Company, a workshop on Saturday and Sunday mornings for any actor interested. (Stewart revisited Picard in the TV series "Star Trek: Picard.") Stewart died just a few days after Walter Koenig, another "Star Trek" icon, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov on the original NBC TV show from 1966 to 1969. The show gave him higher visibility, which led to more work, including roles in the films "Conspiracy Theory," "L.A. Story" and on Broadway, where he starred in "The Tempest," "The Caretaker" and David Mamet's "A Life in the Theater." He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in June 2010. Stewart was also an ambassador for the International Rescue Committee. A brave and commanding persona. But sexy? In July 1992, he and supermodel Cindy Crawford were on the cover of TV Guide's "Top Turn-Ons," based on a readers' poll. In his memoir, Stewart wrote: "Absurd." Stewart was first introduced as the character Xavier in the original X-Men trilogy, appearing in three films from 2000 to 2006. He later returned i

7a625e82e517.text: By — Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/judge-blocks-trump-administrations-medicaid-work-requirement-rule-forcing-proof-of-medical-frailty Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge blocks Trump administration's Medicaid work requirement rule forcing proof of medical frailty Politics Oct 29, 2026 3:53 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Chronically ill people on Medicaid won't be bound by new work requirement rules that the latest Trump administration guidance requires in order to qualify for "medically frail" exemptions, a federal judge ruled Thursday. U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns in Boston gave a partial victory to a coalition of 25 states and the District of Columbia, which sued the Trump administration in June over the new Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services guidance linked to the 2025 law known as the "One Big Beautiful Bill." READ MORE: As states face stricter Medicaid work requirements, Nebraska is an early test The law says the definition of medically frail must include people who are blind or disabled, have substance use disorders or disabling mental disorders, have certain disabilities that significantly impair daily activities, or have serious or complex medical conditions. But the CMS rule went further, requiring people in those categories to show that their conditions also "significantly impair" their ability to comply with the law's work requirements. The plaintiffs argued that the stricter rule would prevent eligible Americans from accessing the care they need — and oversteps the text of the law itself as well. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "The states have met their burden of showing irreparable harm for which monetary damages would provide inadequate compensation — they face the burden of costly and intensive alterations to their eligibility verification systems," Stearns said in his 16-page ruling. Notably, while the ruling will make it easier for some Medicaid recipients with qualifying medical conditions to obtain an exemption from the new work requirements, Stearns' decision does not strike down the work requirements as unlawful. Additionally, Stearns upheld two other federal restrictions on how states can verify medical frailty: including the requirement that states reject proof of patients' medical frailty if the diagnosis is more than a year old. He also upheld a policy allowing states to accept only one self-attestation per continuous period of enrollment. Explaining why he upheld the portions in favor of the government, Stearns said "the government provided a non-frivolous rationale for adopting each provision and explained why it did not find the States' concerns of disenrollment compelling." Representatives from the Department of Health and Human Services and CMS did not immediately respond to an Associated Press request for comment. The new Medicaid restrictions are part of Trump's big tax and policy law in 2025. The change affects those covered through an expansion in most states that gave more lower-income people access to the government's safety net healthcare program. Starting Jan. 1, expansion enrollees aged 19 to 64 must show that they work or do community service at least 80 hours a month, or are in school at least half the time. There are exceptions for those considered medically frail or in addiction treatment programs, among others. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. With less than a week to go until the US midterm elections, which will determine which party controls Congress for the next two years, more than 43 million Americans have already voted.
Data from the University of Florida Election Lab indicates that four to five million early votes have been cast each day, representing a much higher rate than in most previous elections.
Texas has seen the highest above-average turnout rate so far, says Prof Mike McDonald, who runs the Election Lab database. Hispanic communities are also seeing a much higher turnout than usual.
Overall turnout appears on track to outpace 2020, or even 2018, which beat the 1914 record for overall turnout in a midterm election.
Texas has already surpassed its 2022 numbers by around 1.75 million voters, says McDonald. More than 5.8 million ballots have already been cast in the Lone Star state, which has emerged as a key battleground that could decide which party controls the Senate for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
Data from states that require voters to register a political affiliation indicates an increase is votes cast by Democrats, while Republican early voting numbers remain generally similar to 2022.
Early voting is also up among voters who chose to not register with a specific party, McDonald says, however the data does not show which candidates they chose.
Figures on Thursday, external show that 44% of early ballots have been cast by Democrats, and 31.2% by Republicans. A further 24.7% were attributed to voters who had no party affiliation. However, that's just for the roughly half of states that require voter affiliation.
Three states require voters to submit their race when they register - North Carolina, Georgia and Florida. Data from these states shows an increase in votes cast by Hispanic and black communities, while voting among white people is on par with 2022 early voting figures.
"That makes sense because communities of colour are more frequently part of the Democratic coalition, and whites are more frequently part of the Republican coalition," McDonald says.
Texas does not require voters to provide party affiliation or race. But the data still shows a surge in voting by some counties on the border with Mexico, which are comprised of more than 90% Hispanic people.
"When I look at those counties, what I see is some of them are going to beat their 2022 turnout in just the early vote alone," says McDonald.
Early voting has boomed in recent years, driven by the Covid pandemic when more states began offering early voting options, including both in-person and by mail.
In the 2020 election, when voters were picking both the next president as well as their lawmakers, more than two-thirds of all ballots were cast early. Half of those early votes were also cast by mail.
Voters increasingly prefer to vote in-person, even when voting early, says McDonald. They are also returning their ballots earlier than in previous elections.
He adds that he believes this could be due to concerns about postal voting, but says there is not data to indicate what could be causing this. Postal votes are more likely to be disqualified due to errors, he notes, and says some voters could be concerned about meddling in the US Postal Service.
Some officials have already confirmed records being broken. On Thursday, the city of Minneapolis said that it has set an early voting record for a non-presidential election.
Early voting will soon taper off, as states start cutting off early voting as an option in the days before the election on Tuesday, 3 November.

Republicans wonât attach their names to this prediction, but many of them expect Tuesdayâs midterms to hand Democrats at least one chamber of Congress. And theyâre already bracing for President Donald Trumpâs healthcare agenda to get bogged down by a divided government.
The slowdown could happen in a number of ways, GOP aides working on health policy told me â depending on how big an election night Democrats have. At a minimum, Republicans anticipate that a new House majority will haul Trump administration health officials into oversight hearings on a litany of topics, like the still-growing measles outbreak, the presidentâs slashing of global health aid, and the implementation of Medicaid work requirements.
Those hearings would be designed to trip up administration officials. But even if they donât yield embarrassing headlines, Republicans are prepared for healthcare policymaking to get hairier. âPreparing for oversight and obstruction from Democrats will take 50% of our time and mean less ability to push for reforms and regulation,â a former GOP congressional staffer said.
Two top Trump health officials have left in the last week alone: Senior health adviser Calley Means and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Deputy Director Jennifer Shuford. The midterms could complicate the confirmation prospects of several others still awaiting their Senate votes, including Chris Klomp, tapped as No. 2 at HHS, and Heidi Overton, picked to lead the Food and Drug Administration.
The former Republican staffer put it bluntly: âGod forbid we lose the Senate â weâre not getting any nominees in.â
Even a tiny Senate GOP majority could hand outsized power over health confirmations to a single Republican, like abortion-access supporter Lisa Murkowski of Alaska or libertarian-leaning Rand Paul of Kentucky.
Healthcare bills with bipartisan potential, like measures on hospital price transparency or food labeling, might still find room to break through. But as one former health official told me, itâll be âmostly gridlock.â

5c7e5a4ad6d4.text: By — Tim Sullivan, Associated Press Tim Sullivan, Associated Press By — Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/how-trumps-immigration-crackdown-sparked-a-backlash-that-could-undermine-republicans-campaigns Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter How Trump's immigration crackdown sparked a backlash that could undermine Republicans' campaigns Politics Oct 29, 2026 3:23 PM EDT MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — When Donald Trump was running for president two years ago, Americans' television screens were filled with images of migrant chaos. There were tent camps on both sides of the border, caravans of people trudging through Central America and concerns about newcomers overwhelming social services. Please check your inbox to confirm. That turmoil faded as President Joe Biden tightened immigration enforcement after Trump clamped down even more. Now any chaos is on American streets, where violent and even deadly clashes have defined a deportation campaign that's designed to fulfill hardliners' goals of uprooting anyone in the country illegally. The shift helps explain why Trump's effort to fulfill his promises has turned into a backlash, undermining one of the core issues that fueled his return to the White House. While Trump maintains some support for his handling of the border, polling shows voters disapprove of his approach to immigration, a striking turnaround that could undermine Republican attempts to maintain control of Congress in the midterms. WATCH: How immigration policies shaped America and evolved throughout its history "The American people supported strong border security," said Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat who has become a prominent critic of the administration's policies. "What they got instead was shredding the Constitution, mass deportations and killing American citizens on the streets of Minneapolis." Trump's allies say the president is the victim of his own success. "The disaster at the border and the impunity of people just walking over and being released into the country was hard to ignore," said Mark Krikorian, executive director of the Center for Immigration Studies. Trump dramatically reduced illegal border crossings, Krikorian said, "and that's often politically bad." Krikorian praised Trump for adopting low profile but highly effective sweeps that have achieved month after month of record arrests. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers arrested almost 51,000 immigrants in the country illegally in August, according to the Department of Homeland Security, up from 49,000 in July and 43,000 in June. An estimated 660,000 people have been deported in the past fiscal year, according to the Migration Policy Institute, short of the administration's goal of 1 million annually. Biden's immigration policies remain a regular target for Republicans this year. Trump said at a recent Florida rally that Democrats let migrants "pour across our borders from all over the world." "If they win in the midterms, they'll do it again," he warned. Trump returned to White House with deportation pledge In 2024, Trump warned repeatedly of an immigrant "invasion." "They're poisoning the blood of our country," he said of people crossing the border illegally. He insisted, falsely, that immigrants were behind spikes in crime and eating household pets. Even as Trump drew criticism for his rhetoric, his focus on the issue resonated with voters who had seen illegal immigration soar during the Biden administration, with border arrests from Mexico reaching a record 250,000 in December 2023. Trump's victory seemed poised to reshape immigration politics. Forty-six Democrats in the House and a dozen in the Senate joined Republicans in voting for the Laken Riley Act, a bill named after a Georgia student killed by a man in the country illegally. The law requires detention without bond for noncitizens accused of murder and other violent crimes. After Trump took office, he cranked deportations into higher gear. Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland resident, was one of the people caught up in that net. Despite a court order forbidding it, the administration sent him to his native El Salvador, where he was confined to that country's notorious central prison that was also used to house other Trump deportees. The U.S. Supreme Court directed the administration to "facilitate" Abrego Garcia's return, and Van Hollen flew to El Salvador to meet with him. Some Democrats questioned the wisdom of confronting Trump on an issue where the president was so popular, the senator recalled. Now his party is more emboldened on the issue. "We've gone from some of that sniping on the sidelines to a clear vote among Democrats to defund ICE," Van Hollen said. Minneapolis crackdown leads to backlash The early face of the Trump crackdown was top Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino, who swaggered through raids in tactical gear and deployed forces to Los Angeles and Chicago, where he led a helicopter raid on an apartment building. But Minneapolis was the turning point. More than 2,000 federal officers were sent to the city, and scenes of masked agents spilling from convoys of unmarked vehicles became commonplace. Tens of thousands of protesters took to the streets. Two U.S. citizens — Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both 37 — were killed during confrontations with agents. In the weeks that followed, the White House pushed aside Bovino and Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem. Michael Pretti, Alex's father, said this week that the family is still troubled by the bystander videos of the shooting. A man who had already been found guilty of firebombing a group of protesters advocating for the release of Israeli hostages in the US state of Colorado has now plead guilty to federal hate crime charges.
Prosecutors said Mohamed Sabry Soliman threw Molotov cocktails at the group of demonstrators in June 2025 - injuring at least 12 people, one of whom died.
He plead guilty in May to 101 state charges, including first-degree murder - resulting in a sentence of life in prison - but initially pleaded not guilty in the federal case.
Prosecutors want Soliman to be sentenced to life in prison plus 50 years over the federal charges, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
He is due to be sentenced in January.
United States Attorney Peter McNeilly said the sentencing recommendation was driven by what the victims wanted.
In light of the plea, McNeilly said Soliman had dropped motions seeking to keep his family from being deported from the US in case they needed to be witnesses in his case.
Authorities said Soliman planned the attack for a year, watching videos on explosives before driving from his home in Colorado Springs to the Boulder protest.
While he hurled the Molotov cocktails at the crowd on 1 June, 2025, he shouted "Free Palestine". The group were members of Run for Their Lives in Colorado, which met weekly to support the release of Israeli hostages taken by Hamas during the 7 October attacks.
Karen Diamond, 82, died from injuries caused by the attack three weeks later. Her family said her husband, Lou, was also severely burned and had to recover for a month in a hospital burn unit.
Soliman, an Egyptian national, told police after he was arrested that he wanted to "kill all Zionist people", according to court documents.
He came to California in 2022 on a non-immigrant visa that expired in February 2023, according to CBS.
The firebombing escalated concerns about antisemitic violence in the US, taking place shortly after a fatal shooting outside a Jewish centre in Washington DC.

A Toronto jury has found self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski guilty of fraud, after hearing evidence he stole millions of dollars of investor money and spent it on private jets and other luxuries.
The jury quickly reached its verdict on Thursday, convicting the 27-year-old with one count of fraud over C$5,000 ($3,600; Â£2,900), after just hours of deliberation.
Throughout trial, Crown prosecutors called over a dozen witnesses, including investors whom Pleterski had cheated, and accountants and financial experts who testified on his scheme.
Pleterski pleaded not guilty and represented himself at his trial, cross-examining only one witness. He presented no evidence and did not testify.
The Canadian man was charged in May 2024 with one count each of fraud and money laundering following a 16-month joint investigation between Durham Regional Police and the Ontario Securities Commission.
The laundering charge was later dropped.
At the time, Durham Regional Police Chief Peter Moreira said it was potentially the biggest-ever fraud case in the region.
During Pleterski's trial in Ontario's Superior Court, Crown prosecutors presented ample evidence of his lavish spending using investor funds, according to local media.
He is believed to have taken more than C$36m from investors, and spent about half.
They said he used the money sent to his company AP Private Equity Limited to buy multiple trips on private jets and spend about C$5.6m on luxury vehicles.
Prosecutors also said he used the money to spend C$45,000 a month on a lakefront mansion in Burlington, Ontario, while racking up C$4.9m in credit card bills.
Bankruptcy proceedings had shown Pleterski also bought a McLaren and BMW for his parents - who had given him C$50,000 as a crypto investment - along with a Louis Vuitton bag, Burberry coat and a 2017 Bentley Bentayga.
Crown prosecutor Akshay Aurora said during closing arguments on Wednesday that "Pleterski was no 'Crypto King'".
"He was a thief. A thief who stole investor money and used it as he pleased," Aurora told the jury, according to CBC News.
Things came crashing down for Pleterski ahead of his May 2024 arrest.
In December 2022, he was kidnapped in the middle of the night in downtown Toronto, with his captors demanding a large sum for his release.
"I'm sorry, I really am, I didn't want to or mean to ruin anyone's life," a bruised and bloodied Pleterski said in a video obtained by CBC News.
He was released three days later, after being tortured, including with waterboarding, cigarette burns and beatings with golf clubs.
He returns to court on 13 November for a sentencing hearing.

Army pilots are trying virtual reality to stay more alert in flight
The 101st Combat Aviation Brigade is testing the NeuroTrainer as a possible readiness tool for their aviators.
The 101st Combat Aviation Brigade is testing a virtual-reality headset to see if it can make helicopter pilots more alert.
For the next eight months, the unit will incorporate the Oculus-based NeuroTrainer into their flight-training regimen, to measure whether pilots’ reaction times improve.
“In the 101st Combat Aviation Brigade, our pilots operate in unpredictable environments where split-second decisions dictate mission success,” Col. Anthony Marston, the unit’s commander, told Defense One. “By putting our aviators through the targeted exercises using the NeuroTrainer, we want to see if it can measurably improve their processing abilities.”
Pilots will do three headset sessions a week, playing two games for at least six minutes. One game requires them to catch orange balls while dodging projectiles, and the other challenges them to identify a robot teammate outside of their immediate field of view, then swat a ball in that teammate’s direction.
“All the VR-based exercises are designed to challenge and improve reaction time, situational awareness, and quick-decision making,” said Capt. Drew Lightsey, a spokesman for the 101st CAB.
During the initial phase of the program, unit pilots will do a round on the NeuroTrainer and then get in a helicopter simulator to measure their cognition, a news release said.
“It had a little bit of a learning curve to start,” said Chief Warrant Officer 2 Eric Low, a CH-47 Chinook maintenance test pilot. “Once you start to get the hang of it, it felt like a video game. I like how it challenged different aspects of hand-eye coordination and the ability to track multiple objects at the same time.”
The second phase begins at week 15, when 70 pilots will be evaluated on their long-term results.
“Evaluators will consider the speed at which aircrews perform emergency procedures in the simulator and a qualitative assessment asking open-ended survey questions on how participants felt they improved after using the system over time,” Lightsey said.
Down the line, the NeuroTrainer could become a tool for pilots to use on days when they aren’t flying, or for staff pilots who don’t fly frequently but need to keep their skills sharp.
“I think this device could bring awareness to some of the underlying issues affecting our pilots,” said Victor Rodriguez, cognitive performance specialist for the 101st CAB’s Holistic Health and Fitness program. “The performance results could help us recognize when to discuss stress, oversaturation, or emotional regulation with them to help them improve.”
The press release said that similar headset tests are taking place at Navy Fighter Weapons School, Air Force Special Operations Command, and the 75th Ranger Regiment.

dbd4958f3611.text: By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press By — Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trumps-justice-department-pushes-a-spate-of-politically-sensitive-cases-as-midterm-elections-near Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump's Justice Department pushes a spate of politically sensitive cases as midterm elections near Politics Oct 29, 2026 2:03 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — A crucial and contentious midterm election arrives next week, and President Donald Trump's Justice Department has been scrambling with a blitz of headline-making actions and cases that defense lawyers, Democrats and other critics say is no coincidence and reeks of politics — in both the timing and the targets. READ MORE: Trump administration charges former FBI Director James Comey for the third time This month alone, the Justice Department escalated an investigation into Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar with a search of her home; brought criminal charges against two former FBI officials accused of falsely downplaying their knowledge of investigations involving Hunter Biden; revealed a fresh attempt to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey; and made an unsuccessful attempt to indict a former White House aide who delivered dramatic but disputed testimony about Trump's efforts to overturn the 2020 election. That's on top of lawsuits in Alaska and California related to next week's voting. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The moves are notable not only because of the timing but also because they largely have been directed at outspoken critics of Trump or issues that have animated the Republican's base. The Justice Department has also employed unusual maneuvers to lock down charges, bypassing grand juries to file what are effectively placeholder cases against Comey and the ex-FBI officials in the heavily Democratic nation's capital — where prosecutors over the past year have repeatedly struggled to secure indictments. READ MORE: Blanche says Trump isn't trying to meddle with Alaska election results by suing over Senate race "Never in the modern history of the Department of Justice has there ever been such a brazen disregard for time-honored norms and protocols in conceiving of or undertaking politically sensitive investigations," said David Laufman, who served as a senior Justice Department official across Democratic and Republican administrations and helped oversee the Hillary Clinton email investigation. The Justice Department, in a statement, said it is "following the facts and the law, not anyone's political timetable." The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid major action before an election The law enforcement agency has a long-accepted practice of avoiding overt investigative actions against candidates in the weeks before an election, or other public steps that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome. It's such a foundational principle that successive attorneys general have issued departmentwide memos during election cycles reminding employees not to make an investigative move designed to help or hinder any particular candidate. Responding to questions about the recent investigative moves, the Justice Department said in a statement that it was an informal practice, not a written rule, to avoid overt actions within 60 days of an election. The practice is meant to prohibit prosecutors from choosing the timing of an action to affect an election, the department said. "The standard is purpose, not proximity to Election Day. Department policy does not require the Department to stop ongoing work during an election season," the department said. That practice was famously tested in 2016 when Comey, then the FBI director, told Congress 11 days before Election Day that the bureau was revisiting its investigation into Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton's handling of classified information because of newly discovered emails. Comey has said he felt he picked the least destructive option available, but his decision-making was harshly criticized by Democrats — and the Justice Department inspector general. Attorney General Todd Blanche, for his part, has not been shy about his view that the Justice Department does not exist independent of the White House and has insisted he is no different from his predecessors in serving a president. He has denied that the department's investigative decisions are political. Yet even before this month, the Justice Department had initiated multiple inquiries into the president's perceived adversaries. That includes a Florida-based investigation that Trump allies had hoped would prove a right-wing theory that former law enforcement and intelligence officials who scrutinized the president over the last decade had conspired against him. That investigation has shown signs of faltering amid a spate of staff turnovers and delays. Investigators in recent weeks have put off scheduled grand jury testimony of multiple witnesses, according to multiple people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation. A 'little sideshow on top of a sideshow' Among the most politically delicate moves this month came when federal agents searched the home of Omar, one of the most outspoken congressional critics of the president. She is on the ballot Tuesday for another term representing Minnesota's 5th District. Federal agents seized Omar's phone in the search and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, as investigators probe issues related to her immigration paperwork. Jet lag isn’t just for travelers hurtling across time zones. Migratory birds may get it, too.
Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus) fly fast enough to experience jet lag, researchers report October 29 in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the sun’s position and veer slightly off course.
For animals crossing vast oceans, the sun can help them determine which direction to fly. But because the sun’s position in the sky changes throughout the day, these animals need an internal clock synchronized with natural local sun time to use it as a compass. This circadian rhythm helps them compensate for the sun’s apparent movement and stay on course.
But when birds zip east or west, local time shifts faster than their internal clocks might adjust. Scientists have long predicted that this mismatch could confound the birds’ sun-based compasses, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.
Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometers away. The team focused on the return journeys, isolating 1,837 continuous homeward flights.
Assuming the seabirds’ internal clocks were synchronized with local time at sunrise, the researchers calculated how flights should throw off their sun compass and compared those predictions with GPS tracking data. The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction.
“But what really surprised us is that the small orientation errors … continue to be visible even when the birds were in sight of presumably familiar land,” Guilford says. While following a coastline, the birds should be able to use it as a guide to keep their course. But they either veered closer to shore or farther out to sea in line with their predicted sun compass errors. The pattern suggests that the birds use the sun compass alongside coastal cues, even when the two point in different directions.
The errors are small enough that they add only a few kilometers to the journey, not enough to prevent the Manx shearwaters from finding their way home.
This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India. The findings, Rani says, hint at an ability that could serve these feathered fliers well as climate change and human activities alter familiar landscapes: The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.
“After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani says. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”

64ce921a4adf.text: After his far-right coalition lost 11 seats in the election, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is trying to discredit the results by claiming there was mass voting fraud in Arab communities. Why it matters: Netanyahu appears to be trying to spook the opposition bloc out of cooperating with Arab parties to form a new government. But the opposition is concerned he has an even more ambitious goal: To prevent the results from being certified at all. That would block the swearing in of a new parliament, in which he would lose his majority. Driving the news: Netanyahu and his Likud party started the campaign to delegitimize the Arab vote days before the elections. Half of Netanyahu's social media posts on Election Day cast suspicion on the unprecedented turnout in Arab communities, an apparent attempt to drive his supporters to the polls. Arab voters cast ballots in historic numbers, winning 19 seats between their two parties. On Wednesday, Netanyahu's Likud party issued a statement claiming the "elections were stolen" by the Arab parties through bribes and fraud. Its claims were based on the arrest of three activists from the Arab Ra'am party who were suspected of paying a small number of voters in one of the Arab cities. The Israeli police said there was no evidence to support Likud's claims of a "stolen" election. Behind the scenes: The situation escalated dramatically on Thursday when a letter sent to the director of the Shin Bet domestic security agency was leaked to Israel's Channel 12. It was written by the supreme court judge who heads the Central Elections Committee. The judge ordered the Shin Bet director to immediately investigate suspicions of election interference by foreign countries and submit conclusions within a week. Shortly after the letter leaked, Israeli media outlets identified Qatar as the country in question. The allegation is that it funneled money to one of the Arab parties to propel turnout in their communities. Over the past year, several of Netanyahu's closest advisers have been investigated by Shin Bet for allegedly being paid by Qatar to improve its image among Israelis. Zoom in: At a press conference on Election Day, the Shin Bet director, who is a far-right Netanyahu political appointee, said the elections were "safe and secure." He did not mention any suspected foreign interference. But the next day, the director met the head of the Central Elections Committee and briefed him on intelligence that suggested foreign countries sent money to one of the Arab parties to increase turnout. Later that day, the Shin Bet director briefed Netanyahu on the intelligence, but not his opponent Gadi Eisenkot. Eisenkot was briefed by the Shin Bet only after the letter leaked. Later on Thursday, the director also briefed outgoing opposition leader Yair Lapid. Sources with knowledge say the Shin Bet had the intelligence weeks before the elections. In a statement on Thursday, Shin Bet said the head of the Central Elections Committee was the only one outside of the security agency who knew about the investigation ahead of the elections . Zoom out: Shin Bet said in its statement that the investigation is "focused and narrowly defined" and made clear it doesn't cast doubt on the vote of the Arab minority. "The investigation should not be used to cast suspicion on or accuse an entire sector of society that exercised its democratic and legal right to vote. Only those who acted unlawfully will be held accountable," the statement read. What they're saying: But Netanyahu and Likud nevertheless seized on it. After the letter leaked on Thursday, they called it "an earthquake" and again claimed without evidence that "the elections were stolen." "This is an attack on democracy aimed at enabling a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel, and the overthrow of right-wing rule in order to bring about an Israeli withdrawal and the defeat of the IDF on all fronts — first and foremost in Iran," the Likud said. It also said that "no Zionist party should cooperate" with the Arab parties in replacing the Knesset speaker after the new parliament is sworn in or in establishing a new government. The other side: Eisenkot said the suspicions of foreign interference in the elections must be immediately and thoroughly investigated. But the swearing-in of the Knesset must proceed as scheduled, he said. "Netanyahu is leading an illegitimate influence campaign targeting the Israeli public, aimed at delaying the publication of the election results and manufacturing a false narrative to delegitimize the new Knesset," Eisenkot said. What to watch: The vote count ended on Thursday with the opposition parties winning 67 seats and Netanyahu's coalition winning 53. The results are expected to be certified next week, with the Knesset being sworn in several days later. The opposition plans to immediately replace the current speaker of the Knesset and start passing laws — first and foremost, establishing a national commission to investigate the security failures that led to the October 7 attacks. Netanyahu has blocked efforts to launch such an inquiry for three years. Yes, but: While the opposition's majority will allow it to take over parliament, it's not clear whether it will be able to assemble a government. Can inertial navigation make ground-robot swarms real?
Two startups are equipping small wheeled robots with a GPS-free nav package.
Two startups, working together for just under a week, may have found a way around the biggest obstacle to deploying swarms of ground robots: the need for GPS-free navigation in a small package.
Swarmbotics AI, which makes 100-pound autonomous robots, is teaming up with TERN, whose navigation software doesn’t need GPS, the companies announced Wednesday.
The Army has been seeking alternatives to the spoofable, jammable satellite-based system for years.
“The current environment has taught us that GPS is the first thing that gets canned on the battle space,” William Shuart, a program manager for the Army’s Pathfinder3D program, told Army magazine in January.
So the service is fielding jam-resistant GPS cards for munitions and is also working on ALTNAV, which uses a different satellite constellation. But its plans for a robot-forward ground force require a position-navigation-timing system that can get by without a satellite signal at all. The self-driving car industry, with its reliance on GPS and unstealthy LiDAR, hasn’t been much help.
Enter TERN, whose PNT system needs no signals from space, and Swarmbotics AI, an Arizona robotics company whose four-wheeled FireAnts fit roughly into a two-foot cube.
“Our teams integrated the TERN system on site here in Phoenix into the FireAnt in less than a week, which I think is really impressive. So we went from never having really spoken to these guys on a technical level at least to having the system fielded in a week,” said Drew Watson, co-founder and CTO of Swarmbotics AI.
TERN’s Independently Derived Positioning System, or IDPS, combines input from the vehicle’s own sensors, including “wheel speed, steering angle, and 3D motion data,” with onboard map data.
“We’re using the motion of that vehicle all the way down to something as as compact as a FireAnt, and through that successive motion, we're able to output latitude and longitude at the same rate that GPS could, or twice a second,” said Shaun Moore, co-founder and CEO of TERN.
Next up: sharing that information, which Watson described as “a building block to something else.” The team wants to move toward coordinated swarm maneuvering, with teams of robots sharing data with one another in a mesh network. If each member of the swarm understands where it is and where its teammates are, that data can add value to other sensor data, such as camera or radar feeds about threats.
“The way that's working is that each one of these FireAnts is giving a line of bearing to an enemy tank, for instance. Those are triangulated into a position of that enemy tank via multiple firings. The quality of that identification, the position of that enemy tank, is based on the position of the firings…It improves the automatic target recognition,” said Watson.
Both companies have already drawn Army attention. TERN received a $11.26 million contract in September, and both have participated in the service’s Operation Jailbreak tech demonstrations.

da0b9ab94110.text: By — Laurie Kellman, Associated Press Laurie Kellman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/cnn-msnow-and-politico-ask-court-to-make-trump-access-order-permanent Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter CNN, MSNOW and Politico ask court to make Trump access order permanent Politics Oct 29, 2026 1:10 PM EDT Three news outlets have beefed up their legal complaint against the White House over access, saying it is continuing to defy a judge's orders by refusing to let them return to covering President Donald Trump in the Oval Office and on Air Force One — thus violating their free speech rights by continuing to keep them out of the rotating press "pool." CNN, MSNOW and Politico said Wednesday that the president is retaliating against them for reports he does not like, which violates U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly's previous orders for the administration to allow reporters for the outlets to fully return to the pool of journalists covering the president. WATCH: Attorney for banned outlets on legal fight over White House press access Even after those orders, the White House was continuing to block reporters for those outlets from covering Trump in "the very locations that the president most frequently engages with the press," Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., the outlets' attorney, said in a statement. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The most recent filing asks the court to make those previous orders permanent. At issue is whether the president, or anyone, can punish news outlets for the content of their reports. The news organizations say that doing so is "viewpoint discrimination" forbidden by the First Amendment's free-speech protections. READ MORE: Judge extends order blocking Trump from banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from White House Trump insists that he doesn't have to let news outlets whose reports he dislikes onto White House grounds, on Air Force One or other areas. The White House had not responded to the amended lawsuit as of Thursday morning. "Every news organization now faces the risk of similar punishment for coverage the President deems insufficiently favorable," the outlets wrote in their filing, "and the public is deprived of current and complete information about its government." The filing comes about two weeks after Kelly ruled that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are likely to succeed in the extraordinary case pitting the president against the news outlets that cover him. READ MORE: CNN says it was left off Air Force One for Trump's Saturday trip to a college football game In a victory for the journalists, Kelly expanded a previous, temporary ruling that the administration had violated the news outlets' Fifth Amendment right to due process. On Oct. 13, Kelly also sided with a second argument by the outlets: that Trump's ban breached their First Amendment right to free speech. Kelly rejected Trump's reasoning that the ban was driven by policy goals, such as protecting national security. He argued the ban was the result of Trump's stated belief that the outlets' reporting was inaccurate and biased. "Simply put," Kelly wrote in the opinion, "That is unlawful viewpoint discrimination" — the government taking action against types of speech or coverage it does not like. These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.
With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.
The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).
“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.
To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.
Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.
“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.
As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.
It’s possible that the smaller size could have long-term impacts on the population, says Emma Stone, a conservation biologist at the University of Bath in England. “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years,” she says. Changes in the animals’ physical traits or adaptations caused by human pressures might make the bats less able to respond to environmental, climate or disease stresses.
The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.
“These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”

Health officials from 45 African countries met Wednesday to coordinate a continent-wide response to an Ebola outbreak that has killed nearly 5,000 people in DR Congo and spread to Kenya and Nigeria, as an assessment presented at the meeting showed only three of 31 countries evaluated were adequately prepared to respond.
âOur member states, they agree and they commit to implement all actions that we discussed today, including strengthening the preparedness efforts,â said Jean Kaseya, head of Africa CDC, the continentâs public health agency. Kaseya told Semafor in an interview last week that he feared content-wide spread was possible. 1f1b043426ef.text: By — Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/inflation-heats-up-again-days-before-midterm-elections Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Inflation heats up again, days before midterm elections Economy Oct 29, 2026 12:24 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — An inflation gauge closely monitored by the Federal Reserve accelerated last month, showing that prices remain elevated less than a week before midterm elections in which the uncomfortably high cost of living for millions of Americans has become a central issue. Consumer prices rose 3.6% in September from a year earlier, the Commerce Department said Thursday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, prices climbed 0.5%, up from 0.3% in August and the highest figure since May. READ MORE: U.S. economy grows at brisk 3.4% pace in third quarter on strong consumer spending and AI investment Rising gas prices drove much of the inflation increase as renewed violence in the Middle East has kept oil prices above $100 a barrel, up from below $70 before the Iran war. But prices also rose outside of fuel costs. The cost of services such as shipping, hotel rooms, and utilities increased rapidly from August to September, a sign that inflation is spreading and growing more entrenched. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "The inflation outlook has become more concerning," Ksenia Bushmeneva, an economist at TD, a bank, wrote in a commentary on the report. "Price pressures are showing signs of heating up. Elevated gasoline prices are keeping headline inflation hot, but underlying pressures are also broadening." WATCH: Warsh holds briefing after Fed leaves key interest rate unchanged Polls show that the rise in inflation has soured most voters on the economy, leading them to give President Donald Trump poor marks on handling rising prices. Trump campaigned in 2024 on lowering the cost of living, including bringing the cost of gas below $2 a gallon. It currently averages about $4.25 a gallon nationwide. Excluding the volatile energy and food categories, core inflation also picked up last month. It increased 3.1% from a year ago in September, up from 3% in August, the Commerce Department said. And from August to September, core prices rose 0.3%, the same as the previous month. Separately, the government also said the economy grew at a strong 3.4% annual rate in the July-September quarter, much faster than the 2.2% growth in the April-June quarter, as consumer spending jumped and business investment rose, fueled by spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure. READ MORE: Trump promised to stop inflation. Now Republicans may pay the price in the midterm elections Consumer spending climbed 3.8% at an annual rate in the third quarter, the second straight quarter of strong growth and far above the 0.7% increase in the first three months of the year. Yet there are signs that consumers may struggle to maintain that level of spending. Inflation is eroding their incomes: In September, inflation-adjusted incomes, after taxes, declined 0.3% from the previous month. Consumers appear to be dipping into savings or relying on credit to fuel much of their consumption. "Together with higher borrowing costs, these headwinds are likely to weigh on consumer demand in the coming quarters," Bushmeneva said." The reports come a day after the Federal Reserve, the agency tasked with combatting inflation, left its key interest rate unchanged. Yet strong economic growth and persistently higher prices could mean more pain for Americans when the Fed meets in December. The Fed is much more likely to hike its key interest rate, which could lift borrowing costs across the economy. Thursday's inflation data comes from the personal consumption expenditures price index, which typically echoes the better-known consumer price index published earlier this month. The Fed more closely monitors the PCE index because it puts less weight on housing prices and allows for changes in consumers' shopping habits. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 9ea74f06ca6c.text: By — Cara Anna, Associated Press Cara Anna, Associated Press By — Julia Frankel, Associated Press Julia Frankel, Associated Press By — Koral Saeed, Associated Press Koral Saeed, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/netanyahus-party-claims-israeli-election-stolen-as-results-show-him-losing-majority Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Netanyahu's party claims Israeli election 'stolen' as results show him losing majority World Oct 29, 2026 8:44 PM EDT JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party on Thursday amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had "stolen" the election, potentially with foreign assistance, as final results showed his bloc had lost its majority in parliament. The opposition accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population after a historic showing by Arab-led parties in an attempt to delegitimize the election. If the rest of the opposition teams up with Arab parties, a rare and politically risky move, they could potentially form a majority government in parliament, the Knesset. Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu's party were accusing Qatar — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas, the Gaza-based militant group. Qatar issued a quick denial, calling the allegations "ridiculous and dangerous." In a video statement, the commission's acting director general, Dean Livne, did not elaborate, but warned that reports about the probe had been "entirely unfounded." "It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population," he said. "They are doing this because they lost," he said. Eisenkot ridiculed the accusation of foreign interference with a tongue-in-cheek statement, saying: "I welcome the fact that Netanyahu is finally condemning Qatari involvement in the State of Israel." Netanyahu has long faced accusations that former top aides of his accepted money from Qatar. By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be positioning himself to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for Eisenkot to join with Arab parties, who could potentially give Eisenkot the backing he needs to oust Netanyahu. The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to "cast aspersions" on an entire section of the population that "exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner." The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament. It said that even though an investigation was taking place, "allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless." The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within a week. Those campaign attacks, along with anger over the divisive Netanyahu and his far-right government, brought outraged Arabs to the polls like never before. On Thursday, Yair Golan, head of the Democrats party, accused Netanyahu of "attempting to undermine the election results through an ugly delegitimization campaign directed against the will of the public — and against the Arab public in particular." "Netanyahu is working to steal the election," the Arab-led Joint List party asserted Thursday. President Isaac Herzog called it a "sensitive moment" and called for a full investigation.
