17b6c0241a01.text: Crypto exchange Binance is investigating what could be the biggest crypto hack in history as users saw upwards of $5.7 billion in funds drained from wallets Thursday afternoon. Why it matters : The suspected hack comes after a wave of high-profile cyberattacks and data breaches during so-called "Black October," when a series of hacks and AI-discovered bugs triggered fears of a global crisis. Driving the news: Binance co-founder Changpeng "CZ" Zhao, who is no longer an executive at the company, said on X that the crypto exchange appears to have been hacked, although a company spokesperson says it's still investigating the matter. Analysts and traders who follow the crypto markets closely estimate that $1.7 billion to $5.7 billion was taken during the suspected cyberattack. "This is unprecedented," said Kevin March, a co-founder of JPEG Trading, a cryptocurrency trading firm that closely tracked the hack to monitor market conditions. Zoom in : Binance limited withdrawals and platforms including Tether and Circle froze more than $1 billion in cryptocurrencies, per Zhao. Such a step that would limit the scope of customer losses. Zhao and a Binance spokesperson said user funds are safe. The Binance spokesperson said the exchange's security teams are "reviewing all relevant information with urgency." The big picture: If estimates hold up, the suspected Binance hack would be the biggest crypto attack in history. In 2025, North Korea-linked hackers stole about $1.5 billion worth of crypto from the Bybit exchange. The country has turned hacking and scams into an industrial-scale scourge, focusing on crypto heists and a widespread practice of tricking Western companies into hiring North Korean workers . Between the lines : Crypto is a relatively common hacking target, but massive attacks can leave smaller exchanges vulnerable to collapse due to the potential for panicked withdrawals. Binance's size makes it more insulated, March said. "If this happened to any other business in crypto other than Binance, it would've been catastrophic." The exchange is capable of covering potential losses through its insurance and balance sheet, he said, although broad reverberations in crypto markets and prices remain possible. The intrigue: Reports of a breach came just hours after Polymarket confirmed it was facing a cyberattack, prompting the decentralized predictions market operator to pause trading for an hour after an attacker made off with at least $2.7 million in user funds. Researchers at Hudson Rock tied the Polymarket incident to a breach involving third-party website monitoring tool DebugBear , which said earlier Thursday it was responding to its own security incident. What to watch: Binance has yet to confirm who may be behind the attack and the total value of the currencies suspected hackers made off with.

9f8728e73761.text: Democrats' main Senate super PAC is privately telling top donors that Texas offers their best shot at flipping a deep-red Senate seat, followed by Ohio, where the race remains close. Senate Majority PAC also sees victories in Iowa and Alaska as within reach, though the outcomes could take longer to become clear. Why it matters: Democrats are increasingly confident about Election Day on Tuesday — and sharing their qualified optimism with their biggest donors. To retake the Senate, Democrats need to win two of those four states — all of which Trump won by double digits in 2024 — flip North Carolina and Maine, and avoid an upset in Michigan. JB Poersch, president of Senate Majority PAC, projected confidence that Democrats will wrest control of the Senate from Republicans during a private donor briefing this week as he walked through the races state by state. He also reminded donors that Kansas, where even Republicans are deeply worried, is a state Trump won by roughly 16 points in 2024. But it's in play . What they're saying: "This matches what we've been saying publicly and privately for weeks. There are signs of optimism in Texas, but it remains a toss-up, as do Iowa, Ohio and Alaska," said Lauren French, a spokesperson for SMP. "There is positive movement for Democrats, but it is critical to remember that every seat on the battleground map voted for Donald Trump by double digits," she said. "These are deep red states and we're focused on bringing them over the finish line so the Senate can work to provide real relief to families who are being crushed by the cost-of-living crisis." The big picture: Texas hasn't elected a Democratic senator since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988. Democrats thought they'd end the drought in 2018 and let themselves fall for then-Rep. Beto O'Rourke, who lost to Sen. Ted Cruz by 2.6 percentage points. Four years later, O'Rourke tried again to prove a Democrat could win statewide in Texas. He lost the governor's race by nearly 11 percentage points. This time around, Democrats have state Rep. James Talarico, who's narrowly led recent polls against Republican nominee Ken Paxton. Zoom in: During this unseasonably sunny week in Washington, private polls and scraps of data are flying from phone to phone at outdoor cafes as both parties search for a story to tell themselves, their candidates and their donors. At every table, there are essentially two camps: The pessimists find reasons to dismiss every glimmer of hope. Republicans are worried about a "red scream." The optimists blow past inconvenient facts that might kill their victory vibes. Some Democrats are "nauseously optimistic." In reality, optimists and pessimists — in both parties — are flying without instruments. Internal polls contradict each other by a point or three, door-knocking data is noisy, and early-vote numbers can be spun to tell almost any story. The bottom line: On some level, big-dollar donors know they lack the omniscience to read the political landscape with the same clarity they once brought to an IPO's S-1 filing. But they also believe they deserve better data and analysis than what's publicly available. At the very least, they want private briefings to give them a clearer picture than is epistemologically possible. Hence the flurry of briefings. The challenge for the super PACs is to return all the calls — and give donors hope without making promises they can't keep.

4f6272861312.text: By — Dante Chinni, The Conversation Dante Chinni, The Conversation By — Ari Pinkus, The Conversation Ari Pinkus, The Conversation Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/new-survey-finds-more-than-two-thirds-of-americans-believe-their-country-is-in-decline Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter New survey finds more than two-thirds of Americans believe their country is in decline Nation Oct 29, 2026 7:37 PM EDT This article originally appeared on The Conversation. Inflation is causing real economic pain. Worries about healthcare costs have jumped sharply. And 7 in 10 Americans believe the country is in decline. That is the landscape for the 2026 midterm election, according to a new survey from the American Communities Project at Michigan State University, which I direct. READ MORE: What our final poll before Election Day says about midterms and Trump The findings, which follow up previous data work the American Communities Project has done in 2023, 2024 and 2025, come from a survey of 2,155 American adults over two weeks in September 2026, conducted by the survey research firm SSRS, using an online panel and telephone, with a margin of error of +/- 2.4 percentage points. The American Communities Project studies 15 types of communities. Taken as a whole, the national numbers reveal an electorate that is unsettled, gloomy and likely looking for change. Inflation: Deepening concern Cost of living is a unifying concern for all Americans. For the past four years, when given a list of 20 issues – including abortion, climate change, gun violence, drug addiction, education, healthcare, housing, immigration and taxes – respondents have consistently reported that inflation is the No. 1 issue in their community. But the new data shows something more significant. Almost half of Americans, 47%, say they are experiencing real pain from rising prices – a sharp rise from previous years. In 2023, 2025 and 2026, we asked respondents whether they were experiencing "serious financial problems" due to price increases. In July 2023, 27% answered yes. In 2025, 30% said yes. In 2026, 47% said yes. This significant swing underscores that many Americans across the country are really hurting in this economy. For some groups, concern about costs reached well above 50%. For those ages 18-29 – members of Gen Z – 61% said they are dealing with serious financial problems because of price increases, the highest percentage among the four generational cohorts, including ages 30-49, 50-64 and 65+. Cost of living was also a particular concern reported among people of color. Overall, 65% of Hispanics and 63% of Black Americans said they are experiencing serious financial problems because of price increases. Healthcare: A rising issue Healthcare emerged as a top issue in our new survey. In 2025, 20% of respondents said it was a top concern in their community. This year, 30% cited healthcare as a top concern, a 10-point jump. That shift also made healthcare the No. 2 issue in this survey, after inflation. For some demographic groups, concern about healthcare in their community reached above one-third of respondents. Among those whose income falls between US$75,000 and $99,999, 36% said healthcare is a top issue; among Black Americans, 35% said so. This tracks with the policy changes and public health challenges since our 2025 survey. Many have lost health insurance, hospitals have closed, and disease outbreaks have affected communities. It also may be tied to increasing costs overall. The pain people feel from inflation in healthcare can be especially acute because the dollar amounts can be large. The United States in decline The 2026 survey data also showed a 15-point jump in the percentage of Americans who agree with the statement: The United States is in decline. The number is at 70% this year, up from 55% in 2025. In some ways that number makes sense. Consider the other numbers mentioned here – pain from inflation and concerns about healthcare – and the mood of Americans in general. READ MORE: Americans' opinion of economy drops to lowest level since 2014 But there is another important point in the data. That number, 70%, is exactly what it was in 2023, the first year the American Communities Project did a survey. In 2025, the "decline" number dropped to 55%, and that change was largely driven by communities that voted for President Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election. It was a measure of hope for the future, and it showed in massive improvements in the general hopefulness in communities such as the evangelical hubs, concentrated heavily in the South, rural middle America and the middle suburbs. The fact that the "decline" number is back to 70% suggests those same Trump-supporting communities have seen their hopes take a hit – and a deeper analysis of the data on the American Communities Project website shows just that. At the very least, the data suggests a very disillusioned electorate. Times and attitudes change It's important to keep the 2024 election in mind as the 2026 midterm elections near. It's a sign of how opinions and attitudes can change – and quickly. The data here represents this moment in time, and it will likely move after November, which is why we will field this same survey again after the new Congress is seated. On Oct. 26 we released our more detailed community-level findings on the American Communities Project website. This data explores how opinions and attitudes differ depending on where and how people live. This articl

A golden eagle chick has become the first to fledge from a nest on a managed grouse moor in the south of Scotland.
The bird - Beaky Junior - hatched in a nest in a secret location in the Moffat Hills, at a site used for recreational gamebird shooting.
It comes after a Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) report revealed that two-thirds of UK persecution incidents involving birds of prey had occurred at similar sites.
And it is being considered a "hugely significant milestone" by those running a project to boost golden eagle numbers in the region.
Dr Cat Barlow, chief executive of Restoring Upland Nature (Run) which is behind the scheme, said they had received "incredible support" from landowners and gamekeepers.
The project to relocate birds from the Highlands to a secret location in the Moffat Hills started in the summer of 2018.
Numbers in the south of Scotland had fallen to a handful of breeding pairs but they are now at a record level of more than 50 - despite some setbacks.
Birds have been shot at or killed and that is why the birth of Beaky Junior - one of five golden eagle chicks successfully fledged in the area this year - is being seen as so significant, since it happened on a managed grouse moor.
Earlier this year, the RSPB report highlighted 182 confirmed persecution incidents involving birds of prey in Scotland over a 10-year period.
It said they were widely scattered across the country but the majority - 64.3% - had occurred on land managed for gamebird shooting.
Against that backdrop, the efforts in southern Scotland to encourage estates and conservationists to work together are seen as particularly important.
Beaky Junior was even named by local gamekeepers in recognition of the "key role" they have played in helping golden eagles thrive.
Barlow explained: "It is wonderful to see a golden eagle hatch, fledge and fly freely from the newly-established nest of a translocated golden eagle that has made its home on a managed grouse moor in the Southern Uplands.
"This reflects the incredible support we have had from landowners and gamekeepers â from translocations in the Highlands, to continued monitoring and protection of birds and eyries on their lands and estates.
"Indeed their support has been absolutely vital to our success in restoring the population of golden eagles to record numbers."
She said the fledging of five chicks from the nests of birds they had translocated to southern Scotland was a "hugely significant milestone".
Barlow added that it gave "genuine hope" in the battle to reverse biodiversity decline and ensure future generations across Scotland, England and Wales could experience the "incredible sense of awe" when seeing a golden eagle.
Michael Clarke, who chairs Run, said individuals from "all walks of life" had helped the birds to thrive.
He added that they would continue to monitor the impact of the golden eagles on the area "with support of land managers, gamekeepers, farmers and the wider community".
The chief executive of landowner body Scottish Land and Estates, Sarah-Jane Laing, said it was thrilled to hear gamekeepers had named the chick.
"Beaky Junior's arrival serves as a powerful example of what can be achieved when land managers and conservationists unite behind a shared vision, grounded in trust and genuine partnership," she said.
"Seeing this magnificent species return to and flourish in these landscapes is something we can all take pride in."
The gamekeepers involved asked to remain anonymous in order to protect the location of the bird.
Speaking on their behalf, Mark Ewart, regional co-ordinator at the Southern Uplands Moorlands Group, added: "It is incredibly rewarding to see gamekeepers celebrated for the important role they have played in the success of Run's South of Scotland Golden Eagle Project.
"Monitoring and providing the right habitats for golden eagles and other species to flourish is an important part of what gamekeepers do on a day-to-day basis.
"To encounter golden eagles daily is the ultimate indicator of the success of the project-gamekeeper partnership."

be4c9200ec5b.text: By — Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/judge-denies-federal-request-to-segregate-california-ballots-says-it-would-wreak-havoc-on-voting Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge denies federal request to segregate California ballots, says it would 'wreak havoc' on voting Politics Oct 29, 2026 6:57 PM EDT LOS ANGELES (AP) — A federal judge rejected on Wednesday a Trump administration request to stop California from processing the ballots of up to 20,000 people over allegations they are likely noncitizens, warning it would "wreak havoc" on the midterm elections. READ MORE: California election officials frustrated, rattled by DOJ demand to sequester 'noncitizen' ballots The ruling by U.S. District Judge David O. Carter comes as more than 3.7 million people have already voted in the state. "Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable. Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred," Carter wrote. "If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process." Prosecutors for the Justice Department said they would immediately appeal the decision. The decision is the latest legal setback for President Donald Trump in his efforts to expand federal control over state-run elections ahead of voting that will decide control of Congress for the rest of his term. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The Republican administration sued election officials in the Democratic state in mid-October, accusing the officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a list of 20,000 people it alleged were likely noncitizens on the state's voter rolls. The administration had asked the judge to require the state to wait to count those ballots until the voters' immigration status could be verified. The Justice Department made a similar request in Washington state this week for the state to sequester ballots submitted by hundreds of people it suspects are not U.S. citizens. Meanwhile, another lawsuit filed in Alaska last week seeks to delay certification of the vote if the Republican incumbent running for U.S. Senate doesn't win. All three states have House or Senate races that will help determine the balance of power in Congress. Judge says Justice Department's request violates civil rights laws Carter's order was a forceful rebuke of the federal government's demand, arguing that segregating ballots at this time in the election would require counties to develop new methods for sorting ballots and "risk disenfranchising an untold number of voters." In other words, Carter argued, it would have the same effect as purging voters and therefore violates the National Voting Rights Act, which prohibits changes to voter rolls within 90 days of an election. The federal government's request, Carter wrote, "would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens." California mails ballots to all 23 million registered voters. Court filings show over 500,000 ballots had already been processed by this week, meaning their envelopes had been verified and the ballots removed. That would make it virtually impossible to know which ballot belonged to a particular voter, Los Angeles county officials have testified. Carter, an appointee of former Democratic President Bill Clinton, also rejected the Justice Department's argument that California was impeding the federal government's ability to enforce the law. He argued that prosecutors already demonstrated the ability to enforce election law when they arrested 28 noncitizens who had allegedly voted or registered to vote illegally. Carter previously said in court that he was inclined to appoint a special master to vet the government's data processes. His Wednesday order appeared to reverse course, and he did not establish one in his order denying the Trump administration's demands. Justice Department will appeal decision The federal government said it would file an appeal in the case for the second time on Wednesday evening. The USA's first appeal was denied by the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, since it preempted the district court's decision. Two of the three judges also expressed overwhelming skepticism about the merits of the lawsuit itself. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli doubled down on the lawsuit's arguments Wednesday. "Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials," Essayli wrote on social media following the ruling. "This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution." Essayli, who argued on behalf of the federal government on Tuesday, has previously said the federal government's request wouldn't impede the election. Instead, he argued that the Justice Department was trying to prevent the "dilution" of the vote with noncitizen voters. "Segregating a ballot does not prevent it from being counted later," Essayli said. "It is designed to preserve the status quo and prevent the infection of our election with illegal ballots." California's decision echoes national trend Election law experts following the case have said the ruling is consistent with a broader change. David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said the district court's ruling "confirmed what we already know: states, not the federal government, run elections." He said the DOJ's demands of California election officials, so close to Election Day, seemed "designed to cause chaos." 5c1351a0b711.text: By — Deema Zein Deema Zein By — Bryan Gallion Bryan Gallion Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-how-does-the-associated-press-call-2026-midterm-election-winners-4-things-to-know Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: How does The Associated Press call 2026 midterm election winners? 4 things to know Politics Oct 29, 2026 6:55 PM EDT The Associated Press has tracked voting in U.S. elections for 178 years, and it's gearing up to make thousands more race calls in midterm contests this Election Day. Watch the video in the player above. Along with gathering ballot returns to declare winners, for the first time in a major general election the AP is now partnering with broadcast news networks to survey the electorate for the new Voter Poll. This questionnaire is an updated way to analyze voter demographics and motivations, and it will offer results in every state where there's a statewide election. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Here's how the AP's election processes work. How does the AP know ballots are counted? The AP will tabulate results for nearly 7,000 races, including national congressional contests, state legislative and gubernatorial races, as well as some local elections for mayor, city council and school board, according to David Scott, the AP's vice president for U.S. election services. About 4,000 journalists working for the AP will collect results from local voting precincts and election offices across the country. Around 1,000 vote-entry clerks will answer calls from those AP workers to enter candidates' vote totals into the news agency's election night reporting system. READ MORE: A guide to the key ballot measures voters will decide on Election Day That data is matched to election returns posted on county and state websites or delivered by electronic feeds to ensure accuracy. The AP's Decision Team then analyzes those results to determine who won. "We like to say that what we do at AP on election night is the single largest act of journalism there is," Scott said. How and when people vote has changed over time, and the AP's data collection has followed suit. Back in 1972, Scott said, about 95% of Americans voted at a polling place on Election Day, compared to less than half of Americans now. Most people are casting their ballots before Election Day, by mail or through in-person early voting. How does the AP call election winners? The AP's Decision Team is comprised of journalists, data analysts and political science experts who study elections full-time. A race won't be called until a candidate has reached the point where competitors no longer have a path to victory. "Not until that moment," Scott said. "Our certainty is our standard." WATCH: 2026 midterms preview, plus your questions on voting Many races are called on election night, but some take longer. The AP called the 2020 presidential election for Joe Biden four days later, for example. And it didn't call the 2000 race between George W. Bush and Al Gore, sticking by its assessment that the margin in Florida was too close to declare a winner. Out of more than 11,000 races in which the AP declared winners during this year's primary elections, Scott said his team made three mistakes, citing incorrect information from election officials and a technical issue. What is The Voter Poll and what does it tell us? The Voter Poll will interview voters in person about whom they voted for and what issues mattered to them when they cast their ballots on Election Day, similar to traditional exit polls. But the survey is also interviewing people who voted early — reaching them online, by phone or by mail. The AP used its own system, AP VoteCast, to gather insights about the vote in general elections from 2018 to 2024. It partnered with ABC News, CBS News, CNN, Fox News, MS NOW and NBC News last year to develop this new poll, and the broadcast networks will join in conducting the research this year. READ MORE: What our final poll before Election Day says about midterms and Trump About 75,000 voters are being surveyed before Election Day, and around 25,000 more will be interviewed at polling places in 15 states on Nov. 3. The survey will also analyze the demographics of states and of their electorates to see how they align. While races can't be called from this data, it can provide a sense of what direction an election could be going. Scott said voter demographic shifts in 2024 "pointed early in the night to success" for Trump. The rise in voting ahead of Election Day led to this updated survey method. "Really what we've tried to do with our colleagues at the broadcast networks is design a methodology that reaches Americans, no matter how you cast your ballot," Scott said. "You have the opportunity for us to ask you questions so we can understand the fullness of the American electorate." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Deema Zein Deema Zein Deema Zein is a digital anchor, correspondent for PBS News/ PBS News Hour. By — Bryan Gallion Bryan Gallion

af31a5876058.text: Alaska's governor is ordering an investigation into Democrat Mary Peltola's Senate campaign over reports that it recruited a spoiler candidate to dilute Republican votes. That’s as President Trump repeated calls for Peltola's prosecution during a trip to another deep red state where his endorsed candidate is facing headwinds. Liz Landers reports. Geoff Bennett: With Election Day just days away, the battle for control of the U.S. Senate is intensifying, and so are allegations of political dirty tricks. Alaska's governor has ordered an investigation into Democrat Mary Peltola's Senate campaign over reports it recruited a spoiler candidate to siphon votes from Republicans. Meantime, President Trump is campaigning in South Carolina, another Republican stronghold where his endorsed candidate is struggling. Our Liz Landers has more. President Donald Trump: Thank you. Liz Landers: President Trump rallying for his handpicked Senate candidate today in a state he won by nearly 20 points in the last presidential election. President Donald Trump: And five days from now, we're going to elect Darline Graham to the United States Senate. (CHEERING) Liz Landers: The president attacking Graham's opponent, Dr. Annie Andrews, with a false slur. President Donald Trump: But we can't have tranny Annie. If you have one or two victories, you're going to have communists in control of the U.S. Senate. The reason is that the other Democrats, there aren't too many sane ones to start off with, I will be honest. Most of them are horrible. Their policy is so bad. Liz Landers: Graham's bid to succeed her late brother for a full term may be on shaky ground, a recent New York Times/Siena poll showing her race against Andrews in a dead heat. That's evident on the ground at early voting sites, where even Republicans are fed up with the affordability crisis and the war in Iran. Brent Chaplin, South Carolina Voter: Most people would get fired. You would get fired from your job if you don't perform. So it's time to -- like Donald Trump says, you're fired. It's time to fire some people. Jaime Walker, South Carolina Voter: Do I love the current administration and everything they do? I like a lot of things, but there's some things I don't like. However, for me, voting is more like against the other -- the other party. Liz Landers: En route to the Palmetto State, the president continued to question how officials are administering the election in another state, Alaska. President Donald Trump: It's called voter fraud. Should not have been allowed to happen. Liz Landers: A New York Times investigation found that the campaign of the Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, recruited a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan to run against the incumbent Republican, Dan S. Sullivan. Trump suggested Peltola should be criminally charged. President Donald Trump: It's hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run. Liz Landers: For her part, Peltola called the story a distraction. Rep. Mary Peltola (D-AK), Senatorial Candidate: It's another diversion. Every day it's some new look over here moment, not Dan Sullivan, registered Republican, incumbent, voted for this war in Iran 14 times. Liz Landers: Dan S. Sullivan, the incumbent senator, also weighing in by phone this afternoon. Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK): To the Alaskan people, don't let your ballot be thrown away. Don't let the dirty tricks of Peltola and her campaign trick you. Liz Landers: Alaska's governor now ordering an investigation into whether Peltola's campaign violated Alaska's laws. The Department of Justice already filed a lawsuit late last week, preemptively asking that the results of the Alaska Senate race not be certified if the Democrat wins. Last night, former President Obama used his star power in Georgia to rally for Democrats Jon Ossoff and Keisha Lance Bottoms. While Ossoff appears to be in a comfortable lead in the race to keep his Senate seat, polls show Bottoms neck and neck with her opponent, Rick Jackson, in the race for governor. If she wins, Bottoms would be the first black Woman governor in U.S. history. Barack Obama: I heard the president was not happy. Liz Landers: The former president also addressed a joke he made over the weekend that President Trump's renovations make the White House look like a Cheesecake Factory. Barack Obama: They mobilize a whole-of-government response to that joke. (LAUGHTER) Barack Obama: Not to inflation, but to that joke. They don't have solutions to actual problems. So they'd rather have the media and you talking about the Cheesecake Factory. Liz Landers: Outside the rally... Woman: No insult to Cheesecake Factory, because I do like them. Liz Landers: ... attendees said that, while they love the restaurant, they understand that the former president's joke gets at a larger issue. Darlene Webb, Georgia Voter: The rule of law does not apply to the Republican Party for some reason at this time. So I just want to make sure that we're out here trying to change and put good people in office that's going to support the people and not just their pockets. Liz Landers: The rule of law exercised last night in California, where a district judge denied the federal government's request to stop the processing of 20,000 ballots that they alleged were sent to noncitizens. The judge calling it an attempt to -- quote -- "coerce a state and local government to abandon their own constitutional elections procedures." The Justice Department also declared in a late filing Wednesday night that it would not send FBI or ICE agents or employees to serve as poll monitors. President Trump will continue his midterm blitz tomorrow with a rally in Florida. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Liz Landers.

829139e71d44.text: In our news wrap Thursday, a local ceasefire in Oleshky held for a third day with humanitarian aid set to enter the Russian-held Ukrainian city soon, the Pentagon is reportedly accusing a recently fired Army general of misconduct amid allegations that he leaked classified information to the media and stage and screen legend Patrick Stewart has died. Geoff Bennett: And we start the day's other headlines in Ukraine. A local cease-fire in Oleshky held for a third day with humanitarian aid set to enter the city soon. Roughly 2,000 people remain trapped in the Russian-held area. The Russian military began clearing land mines today. The explosives have prevented residents from leaving Oleshky, and it remains unclear whether they will be able to evacuate to Ukrainian or Russian-controlled territory. Meantime, local authorities in Central Ukraine say a Russian drone slammed into a train platform in Dnipro, killing at least 14 people. One woman who was waiting for her train described the terrifying moments after the attack. Svitlana Shcherbak, Train Passenger (through interpreter): I am simply lost for words with outrage. Why? Why on earth did Russia, that occupier, those bloody invaders, attack the civilian passengers on the commuter train? Why? What do the people have to do with this? Geoff Bennett: Meantime, Russian President Vladimir Putin says he's in close contact with Elon Musk as Russia develops its own alternative to his Starlink Internet service. Putin also praised the tech mogul as a genius. The reported contact raises questions about Musk's relationship with Moscow, given Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine and Starlink's critical role in Ukrainian military operations. The Pentagon is reportedly accusing a recently fired Army general of misconduct amid allegations that he leaked classified information to the media. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia from his position overseeing strategy, plans and policy for the Joint Chiefs of Staff. Sylvia is the latest senior military official ousted by Hegseth and the second general removed from that same post. The Pentagon has not publicly confirmed a reason for his dismissal, and Sylvia has not commented. A reporter asked President Trump today about the officer's removal, but referred to him only as Lieutenant General Sylvia. The president appeared not to realize the officer is a man. President Donald Trump: She's got problems. She's going to have big problems. She did. Well, we're very much looking for leakers. And she's going to have big problems, long-term problems. Geoff Bennett: Sylvia's removal comes amid reports that the Trump administration is considering renewed military strikes against Iran after the midterm elections. Spain started three days of national mourning today for the victims of yesterday's high-speed train crash. Cranes worked through the night to clear away crushed cars as search-and-rescue teams combed through the wreckage. Crews found one more body, bringing the death toll to at least 69. Dozens of others were injured, and families have been traveling to the area in a desperate search for their missing loved ones. Cesar Vicente, Son of Missing Train Passenger (through interpreter): We don't know anything. This is chaos. I have my father, and I don't know where he is. I hope to find him. Oh, my lord. I don't want this to happen to anyone. This is unbearable. This is hell. Geoff Bennett: This is Spain's second major train disaster this year, adding pressure to the government of Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez just weeks before national elections. European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde says she's stepping down in February, months before her eight-year term was set to end. Christine Lagarde, President, European Central Bank: I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future. Geoff Bennett: Lagarde announced her decision on social media, appearing with bandages on her face. The 70-year-old said she had undergone minor surgery to remove what she described as a little skin cancer. She later told reporters that she's stepping down to speak more freely about global affairs. Her departure sets off a process among European leaders to select the next president of the European Central Bank. Delivery giant DoorDash is buying Instacart in a $17 billion deal, pending regulatory approval. Instacart would retain its name and app while customers could order through either platform. Instacart shoppers would also gain access to 50,000 additional stores through DoorDash. The merger would help the companies compete with retail giants like Walmart, Costco, and Amazon. Shares of DoorDash jumped more than 5 percent today, though Instacart closed lower. Elsewhere on Wall Street, a sell-off of Google's parent company Alphabet weighed on stocks. The Dow Jones industrial average lost a quarter-of-1-percent. The Nasdaq dropped more than 1.33 percent. The S&P 500 also closed in negative territory. And we have two passings of note to report this evening, starting with Oscar nominee Barbara Barrie. Paul Dooley, Actor: What are we going to do about it? Barbara Barrie, Actor: I don't know, dear. We could always strangle him while he's asleep. Geoff Bennett: She was nominated for her role as a supportive mother to an Indiana teenager in 1979's "Breaking Away." Barrie was also a familiar face on television, appearing as the wife on "Barney Miller," and later as Brooke Shields' grandmother on "Suddenly Susan." She earned three Emmy nominations and a Tony nomination for originating the role of Sarah in Stephen Sondheim's "Company." Her daughter says Barrie died with medical assistance following a terminal cancer diagnosis. Barbara Barrie was 95 years old. And stage and screen legend Patrick Stewart has died. Patrick Stewart, Actor: Engage. Geoff Bennett: He brought gravitas to the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," a character he went on to port

b44390618601.text: U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of forces in the Middle East, briefed President Trump Thursday on the state of the Iran war, with a focus on the ongoing naval blockade , according to two U.S. officials. Why it matters: As he did before Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025 and Operation Epic Fury in February, Trump is pursuing dual tracks — trying to reach a deal to restart peace talks while also preparing for a possible resumption of major combat operations after the midterms. Behind the scenes: Trump wanted to hear directly from the CENTCOM head on whether the naval blockade is working, the U.S. officials said. Cooper also briefed Trump on the military operation for guiding oil tankers out of the Strait of Hormuz to global energy markets. And he updated Trump on the economic pressure campaign the military is conducting in concert with the Treasury Department. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, White House envoy Steve Witkoff and other senior officials also attended the meeting, the officials said. The White House and CENTCOM declined to comment. The Wall Street Journal first reported the meeting. Driving the news: A group of regional mediators led by Qatar is trying to get the U.S. and Iran to head off a resumption of war after the midterms in favor of negotiations. "The mediation is at a very sensitive stage," a regional source said. Qatari mediators recently delivered a letter from Vice President Vance to Iran's Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Gen. Mohsen Rezaei. Vance proposed restarting negotiations but stressed that any talks would have to address Iran's nuclear program. Trump and Vance met Wednesday to discuss a possible gesture of goodwill toward Iran, such as sending humanitarian goods like food and medicine, according to a source with knowledge. Later in the day, Trump publicly backed the idea. What they're saying: U.S. Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack told CNN on Thursday that the U.S. and Iran are "very close" to a deal to deescalate tensions. "I think we're very close to finally getting to a place where we can say, 'Let's just have a timeout,'" he said. "We're not going to have an overall solution immediately, but we can allow the region to find its own pace." The other side: Iranian officials on Thursday continued to demand the U.S. take a series of steps — such as lifting the blockade, releasing Iranian frozen funds and allowing Iran to sell oil — before resuming negotiations on their nuclear program.

Four are in Pennsylvania, where President Trump and Republicans made significant gains in 2024. Now Democrats are betting that the president's low approval rating and frustration over high prices will shift the political landscape. d20c526d9b5e.text: By — Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/doordash-offers-17-billion-for-instacart-in-what-would-be-big-grocery-delivery-consolidation Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter DoorDash offers $17 billion for Instacart in what would be big grocery delivery consolidation Economy Oct 29, 2026 6:41 PM EDT DoorDash is offering $17 billion to buy Instacart in a deal that could consolidate the grocery delivery business in the U.S. and abroad. The companies say the tie-up would combine DoorDash's global reach and expertise in logistics with Instacart's purpose-built technology and long relationships with grocers. It could also help the companies better compete with rivals like Amazon. READ MORE: Instacart ends program where users see different prices for the same item at same store But it could also lead to less competition in the delivery space, which could raise prices for consumers and give grocers fewer partners to negotiate with. "They were competing for a share of consumers' wallet," said Randall Sargent, a partner specializing in grocery and retail at the consulting firm Oliver Wyman. "As a general economic principle, less competition and more consolidation tends to be worse for consumers." The deal is expected to be finalized by the end of 2027 or in early 2028 if it's approved by Instacart shareholders and government regulators. Instacart's name and app will remain Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the U.S. and Canada. DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app would remain, and Instacart's 600,000 shoppers — who are independent contractors — would be able to continue fulfilling orders as before. Consumers who are currently paying $9.99 per month for separate DashPass and Instacart+ memberships, which give them free delivery on most orders and other perks, would be able to pay one fee instead of two, DoorDash said. Instacart customers would also have access to 50,000 additional stores that are on DoorDash's platform. Grocers would also be able to choose either delivery platform. Tony Xu, DoorDash's co-founder and CEO, said the deal could help local grocers compete with larger players. Walmart is the largest U.S. grocer, with 21% share of spending, followed by Costco and Amazon, which each have 8% share, according to Numerator, a market research company. "Over the past decade or even two decades, what you see is the largest companies are only eating more and more of the pie. Why is that? It's because they've invested aggressively into capabilities like a modern technology stack, like fast delivery, like new fulfillment models," Xu said Thursday during a conference call with investors. "That's what this combination is really about, where DoorDash and Instacart can give every retailer a fighting chance at competing in the modern-day era." The deal would also help DoorDash and Instacart fend off rivals like Walmart, which has been moving into restaurant delivery. Walmart partnered with Subway, its largest in-store restaurant tenant, this past summer and has since expanded to select locations at Dunkin' and Papa Johns. The company said it now has 2,400 restaurant locations on its restaurant delivery platform. DoorDash has been growing its grocery business DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food, electronics and many other products. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3 billion orders last year using a network of 9 million independent delivery workers. That dwarfs Instacart, which fulfilled 338 million orders last year. DoorDash has a market value of $73 billion. DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores. The partnership expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 U.S. Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco. DoorDash's move into grocery has hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on U.S. delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company. DoorDash's share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats' share held steady at just under 20%. Combined company could attract more ads, but also scrutiny Sargent said a combined DoorDash and Instacart could potentially attract more ad revenue from food companies. Right now, Instacart can only share what consumers put in their baskets, for example, but a combined company could also show them what customers ordered for takeout lunch. "Food companies want to spread their ad dollars around and reach customers efficiently," Sargent said. "The more you can hand them an audience that you know all about, the more formidable a challenger this new company is." But the tie-up will also be subject to scrutiny from antitrust regulators in the U.S. and elsewhere, particularly at a time when consumers are agitated about food price inflation. Ethan Litwin, an antitrust attorney and partner with New York-based Shinder Cantor Lerner, said it could be problematic if DoorDash controls Instacart's technology, since many grocers use that technology to power their online storefronts. "DoorDash could therefore cut rivals off, outmatch them on targeting and logistics, or monitor competitors' pricing and discounting in real time, which could facilitate coordination on pricing," Litwin said. "I expect that the parties will call these efficiencies, but an advantage big enough to build a monopoly will not stay consumer-friendly for long." Acquisition was discussed for a while Apoorva Mehta

81a0adef426b.text: As candidates make a final push to win over voters ahead of Election Day, Lisa Desjardins takes a deep dive into the battle for the House of Representatives. Geoff Bennett: And Lisa Desjardins joins us now at the super screen for a deeper dive into the battle for the House of Representatives. So, Lisa, this is an expensive contest for the House. Where does it all stand? Lisa Desjardins: Expensive and expansive. Look at this map of all the races. These are the 81 somewhat to very competitive races that we are tracking. Now, The Cook Political Report lists a lot of competitive races. It's important to also know this number, three. This is the magic number. Democrats need to flip three seats on net in order to take over the House. So I don't want to just look at this large map, but let's look at the most competitive seats that are toss-ups or leans. These 50 dots represent those 50 seats that may determine the fate of the House of Representatives. What's important here is who occupies them now. Look at this. It's mostly Republicans, 39 of these seats occupied by Republicans. They are on defense. Remember that magic number three? So, essentially Democrats need to pick up three seats right here -- this is the line -- in order to flip the House. Now, The Cook Political Report already forecasts that Democrats are likely to flip some seats. How many? Ten. So, if you remember this line that determines control of the House, Democrats have already put themselves in position to pass that. And, right now, Republicans need to push back. But they are in a good position at this moment, Geoff. Geoff Bennett: And on the substance of all these races, the economy is the top issue, per usual. But how and where is that playing out? Lisa Desjardins: Right. I love looking at this the substance. Let's talk first of all, about housing, that issue that we found in Northeastern Pennsylvania. These are the places where housing is particularly an issue in the campaign. You see it in Florida, in Nevada, in Southern California. But let's talk about the issue that a lot of Americans also feel, gas and fuel prices. It is everywhere, but I want to point out these races where they are particularly facing record high fuel prices, or like in Maine or Alaska, where they are more dependent on diesel or heating oil. And let's focus on one race in particular where this is a factor. Let's go to Colorado's Eighth District. This is a situation where the gas prices have still been rising this month. The Democrat, Manny Rutinel, says that the issue is Iran and tariffs. He says he had pushed back against President Trump. But the Republican, Gabe Evans, says, no, it's the problem of regulation, and he has supported President Trump. So this is a factor in this race. Geoff Bennett: And what about the other issues driving these midterm races? Lisa Desjardins: There's one more I want to talk about because a lot of the country is, and that is data centers. Here's an example of four of the races where that has become a campaign issue this year. And I want to focus on one. This is Central Michigan, Michigan's Seventh District. The Democrat, Will Lawrence, won his primary in part because he campaigned so hard on a ban, at least temporarily, on data centers. This is a district where we just saw a $10 billion data center put on hold because of protests from locals. Now, Tom Barrett, the Republican incumbent, he has a different tact. He instead says each locality should be able to decide whether they want the data center or not. This race is a good test of how far voters want to go when it comes to data centers. And all of these issues, of course, around the country do have ties to the economy. And it's important to see how that layers in. Geoff Bennett: Lisa Desjardins, our thanks to you, as always. Lisa Desjardins: You're welcome.

cfbfc7ba37d7.text: Israel is facing political uncertainty after an election that produced no clear governing majority. But what do the results reveal about how Israelis want leaders to confront the country's challenges? Nick Schifrin discussed that with Tamir Hayman, former chief of Israeli military intelligence and current executive director of the Institute for National Security Studies. Geoff Bennett: Israel is once again facing political uncertainty after an election that has produced no clear governing majority amid competing allegations of voting fraud and irregularities. But beyond the political maneuvering, what do the results reveal about how Israelis want their leaders to confront the country's mounting challenges? For that, our Nick Schifrin spoke with retired Major General Tamir Hayman, former chief of Israeli military intelligence and current executive director of the Institute for National Security Studies. That's a leading Israeli think tank. Nick Schifrin: Tamir Hayman, thank you very much. Welcome to the "News Hour." Regardless of whether Benjamin Netanyahu stays prime minister or Gadi Eisenkot becomes prime minister, is there an overall agreement on how Israel should approach its national security since October the 7th? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): It seems like Israelis are still in the trauma after post-October 7, and they are reluctant on going to any kinds of concessions in the Palestinian-Israeli conflict. Most parties argue for a very hawkish, proactive approach in terms of the next state needed in confronting Hamas and Iran, et cetera, et cetera. So it seems like, in that aspect there's a proactive, hawkish military, security approach that is accepted, and we are not entering a zone of agreements or a peace-aspiring environment. Nick Schifrin: You write that pursuing peace is considered a danger, and -- quote -- "War is necessary and preventive war is preferable." Does that mean Israel is set to be in a perpetual state of war? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): Let me just emphasize that, in this article, I wanted to provoke a discussion, so I exaggerated a little bit in order to be able to observe trends. But it seems to be describing trends that are in the consensus. Nick Schifrin: And where Israel is going? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): And where Israel going, if not diverted. We are headed right now, brings us into very dangerous place. Nick Schifrin: Does Israeli leadership believe that a perpetual state of war is better? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): They do not believe that peace is a viable or tangible solution right now. Most Israelis will consider any form of a peace as weakness, naive approach, trusting the Arabs, trusting the enemies. The general sentiment is, we trusted the Arabs, and they betrayed us. So what left is an ongoing state of confrontation. Nick Schifrin: You describe, even if it's exaggerated, this severing with the United States. And, again, I will I will read it, knowing that you say it's exaggerated, but it's very provocative. "The United States is a declining power, and, given its ongoing social and political shifts, will soon abandon Israel. In any event, excessive dependence on the U.S. exposes Israel to the influence of a progressive American value system incompatible with Israel's Jewish character." I mean, it's an understatement to call that controversial among American Jews, but is that where we're headed? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): It seems like we are losing our position as a consensus among Americans, and we are losing the bipartisan approach. We have already lost the bipartisan position, and we are going to be maybe homeless in the political spectrum of United States. Secondly, the fact that we are dependent on our national security on capabilities and backing from United States create vulnerabilities. So, what is the rational outcome? We must rely on ourselves. Nick Schifrin: Netanyahu has referred to Israel as super Sparta, basically being self-reliant on weapons, as you have been describing. He's even suggested that Israel might have to rely on Bitcoin because of future sanctions. How isolated, in your opinion, is Israel? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): The idea that if Israel will be ever isolated, it is an existential threat to the existence of Israel, OK? The economy is based on high-tech and an advanced science. That cannot be established in an isolation mode based on crypto. Second, there's a true threat of isolation and sanctions. But the way to handle it is to approach the causes of that. Nick Schifrin: But given the results of this election, even if we don't know exactly the numbers, in which Netanyahu and his bloc maintained the lead over the opposition bloc, doesn't that suggest that these trends are accelerating, that many Israelis have embraced these ideas that you're critiquing? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): The political spectrum map is moving right. The problem is that there is radicalization in the right-wing establishment after October 7. Nick Schifrin: And back to the concept that you write about. And again, acknowledging that you say that you're exaggerating, there's one fundamental conclusion that you have, and that it's that the consensus is to -- quote -- "guarantee Israel's continued existence as a Jewish state, even at the cost of eroding its democratic values." Explain that in simple terms. Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): The whole article asks critical question, whether it's good for Israel to move in that path. Of course, it is wrong. And that's what -- that's the whole purpose of this idea. Why do I emphasize the tension between democratic and Jewish values? Because if we're not going to do anything in the Palestinian arena, and we will annex the Palestinian territories, we will annex the West Bank into Israel, we will not have a Jewish majority. And the only way to maintain a Jewish statehood is by eroding democracy. This is an, again, existential threat to the identity of Israel as a Jewish democratic state

In less than two weeks, U.S. Senate leaders plan to take an initial vote on the divisive permitting reform bill aimed at easing regulatory barriers that can delay energy projects. As the date nears, some of the country’s leading environmental groups are ramping up their opposition, arguing that the measure would do more harm than good.
A new report from Resources for the Future, a research nonprofit, projects that the bill’s power-sector provisions would cut carbon emissions by 1.8 gigatons by 2041 and reduce annual electricity-system costs by an average of 3.5 percent to 7 percent compared to a scenario without the bill.
But the projected benefits are unlikely to convince the bill’s critics, partly because the analysis doesn’t address the provisions that have drawn the most opposition, including changes to the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.
The debate over the bill, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, has divided environmental and clean energy advocates and threatens to unravel a compromise between the bill’s Democratic and Republican co-sponsors.
On one side, clean energy business groups and advocacy organizations praise the bill’s approach to accelerating timelines for building transmission lines and renewable energy projects. On the other side, key environmental advocacy groups say the proposal would speed up fossil fuel infrastructure buildout and remove current tools to oppose projects.
“Over the next two years, BAAJA would create more legal runway for this president to make corrupt deals and greenlight harmful projects of all kinds, and it would constrain any future president from repairing the damage,” said Abigail Dillen, president of Earthjustice, an environmental law nonprofit, in a commentary posted on Tuesday.
The same day, four Senate Democrats sent a letter to the bill’s co-sponsors saying they have concerns that President Donald Trump’s administration cannot be trusted to follow through on promises that were made during negotiations.
“Beyond consideration of the actual text, the promise of BAAJA will only succeed if President Trump takes care that it is faithfully executed,” reads the letter from Democratic Sens. Tammy Duckworth of Illinois, Ed Markey of Massachusetts and Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden, both of Oregon. “The Trump administration’s record gives us no basis to assume that he will.”
The senators cite the Trump administration’s cancellation of already-approved clean energy grants and loans and evidence that decisions were made with intent to harm states that voted for Democrats. They said the administration should reinstate all canceled awards and commit in writing to no longer basing grant decisions on the political affiliation of a state’s elected officials.
If the administration doesn’t comply, the senators have threatened to oppose a motion to proceed to debate on the bill at a vote scheduled for Nov. 9. Losing the support of four senators who have been vocal advocates for environmental protection could make it harder to secure the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster.
In a statement, a Trump administration spokesperson said the White House supports the bill because it will deliver jobs and investment.
“The text of the legislation has been published, and all that is left to do is vote,” the spokesperson said. “We are in direct conversations with the lead negotiators in the Senate and are looking forward to action on this historic legislation to unleash more energy in the United States.”
A co-sponsor of the bill, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-Rhode Island, has also expressed concerns that the Trump administration will go to extraordinary lengths to oppose renewable energy even if the bill becomes law.
“We await real signs of regulatory good faith,” he said in a post on X, along with a link to a Bloomberg article about the administration’s recent contradictory actions on wind power.
Meanwhile, a coalition of conservative groups, many funded by the petrochemical billionaire Koch family’s network, urged the Senate this week to pass the bill to “protect property rights, promote energy abundance, and restore America’s ability to build.”
Emissions Cuts, But an Incomplete Picture
The new analysis by Resources for the Future follows several by other organizations that also show substantial cuts in emissions resulting from the power-sector provisions of the bill.
Resources for the Future is a leader using economic models to estimate the effects of complex legislation. Among the findings:
- The bill would increase the country’s transmission line capacity by 30 percent by 2041, meaning more power can be transported on interstate power lines. A lack of transmission capacity is one of the main factors impeding construction of new wind, solar and battery projects and more lines would allow more of those systems to be built.
- Building new, cleaner power sources would help displace some of the older, more polluting sources on the grid, adding 60 gigawatts of clean power capacity compared with a baseline scenario without the bill. The analysis also found that removing existing constraints would lead to a small increase in combined-cycle natural gas plants, though that effect would diminish over time.
- Power-sector carbon dioxide emissions would be lower under the bill than without the bill, although both scenarios show emissions growth over the study period. Adopting the bill would reduce cumulative carbon emissions by 1.83 gigatons through 2041. In the final year, emissions would be 6 percent less than the baseline level.

c50d26d44b33.text: Journalist and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa chronicled her fight against the Duterte regime in the Philippines in her 2022 book, “How to Stand Up to a Dictator.” She detailed attacks on her reporting and her newsroom's struggle to defend press freedom and democracy. In a new book, Ressa warns of other threats to those same freedoms. Amna Nawaz spoke with Ressa about “The Fight Back." Geoff Bennett: Journalist and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa chronicled her fight against the Duterte regime in the Philippines in her 2022 book, ""How to Stand Up to a Dictator." She detailed years of attacks in her reporting and her newsroom's struggle to defend press freedom and democracy. Now, in a new book, Ressa warns of different threats to those same freedoms. Amna Nawaz spoke with her earlier today. Amna Nawaz: According to Maria Ressa, there's a dual threat now by autocratic leaders and big tech companies weaponizing information and algorithms to create new crises for democracy and humanity. That's all in her new book called "The Fight Back: A Citizen's Guide to Standing Up to Dictators." And Maria Ressa joins me now. Welcome back. It's good to see you. Maria Ressa: Good to see you. Thanks for having me, Amna. Amna Nawaz: You talk in the book about what you call an unholy alliance between state power and platform power. What do you mean by that? Maria Ressa: A decade of harms from artificial intelligence, right? We're only talking about the tail end of it. But we have talked a lot about my two dictators in the Philippines. It was Rodrigo Duterte, who won as president in 2016 with the help of Facebook. And my second dictator, who I would argue is more powerful is Mark Zuckerberg, because, at that point, 93 percent of Filipinos on the Internet were on Facebook. Facebook is our Internet. And here's the part. They both act with impunity, but Rodrigo Duterte is now waiting at The Hague for his trial to begin, his charges of crimes against humanity, while, from 2016 to today, Mark Zuckerberg is still acting with impunity. He's not been elected for anything. And the three phases of harms that we have had from the attention economy, the tech that hacks our biology, right, when lies become facts, so the attention economy in social media, chatbots, and the harm, the intimacy that is taken from us, and the last one is agency itself with the agentic and multi-agentic world. Amna Nawaz: We have seen that battle for facts, battle for the truth play out here in the United States. As we talk here, we're days away from another critical midterm election. You break it down in the book to talk about the convergence of three crises, truth, order, and accountability. Maria Ressa: Yes. Amna Nawaz: How similar is all of this to what you saw under Duterte in the Philippines? And be specific to what we're seeing here in the U.S. now. Maria Ressa: What we lived through in the Philippines is that we found out we needed to leave the virtual world to come to the real world, right, and because I was getting an average of 98 messages per hour. When we came into the real world, that was how we had a whole-of-society approach that ultimately led to the arrest of Rodrigo Duterte. And then we had just recently Brazil. Brazil, if you remember, right, they have the same two dictators we had in the Philippines in 2016. President Trump, similar, right?The state and Meta, Mark Zuckerberg under a different name now. And what the -- after the first run-off elections, when it looked like President Lula was going to lose, I'd never sensed such a desperation in Brazilians. And they used WhatsApp to mobilize in the real world. And they mobilized the largest ever out, same thing that happened in Serbia. This time, the students, they moved from the virtual world to the real world. I don't see that same kind of desperation yet in America. But I do see an awareness that AI and, more importantly, data centers are something Americans don't want. And that seems to be bipartisan. But, having said that, this is the moment, right? The world is looking at America. What choices are you going to make? Amna Nawaz: You offer very specific, tangible steps at the end of each of your 10 chapters that you want people to try to follow just to be aware of the role that they play in the spread of misinformation... Maria Ressa: Yes. Amna Nawaz: ... in the maybe falling apart of accountability in many ways too. The very first chapter, step one, you say track your screen time for seven days. Maria Ressa: Yes, absolutely. Amna Nawaz: Why is that important for Americans to do? Maria Ressa: Because think about it. The more time you spend on here, the less time you spend in person with someone else. And this is not meant to educate you or to build real intimacy, real connections. HUNTSVILLE, Ala.—Candidates for Alabama’s second-highest office took the stage Wednesday for what was the first major-party debate for a statewide office since 2010, the year Republicans took the reins of government from Democrats for the first time in the modern era.
In a debate hosted by WHNT, a Huntsville-based television station, state Rep. Phillip Ensler, a Democrat, and former Republican Party Chairman John Wahl answered questions from moderators and engaged in significant back-and-forth for about an hour, including on a couple of environmental and energy issues.
One major sticking point in the debate was the impact of data centers on Alabamians, their communities and their energy bills.
Asked whether he believes data centers are good for Alabama, Wahl said he thinks the facilities are inevitable but that he shares the concerns of some residents about their impacts.
“Data centers are a necessary evil,” Wahl said. “We already have them. We all like our YouTube, our cloud, our streaming services. But the question is when these are moving into communities, we have to make sure that those communities are protected.”
The demand for data centers in Alabama and across the country has been driven largely by the spread of artificial intelligence tools like large language models, not by the use of services like YouTube or Netflix, according to experts. If built to full capacity, data center campuses proposed in Alabama would consume more energy than all of the homes in the state combined, an Inside Climate News analysis found.
“We want the capital investment,” Wahl said. “We need data centers, but we need to do it the right way.”
Ensler, the first statewide candidate to propose a moratorium on new data center construction, said he’s met with residents across the state who have made their views about the facilities clear.
“There are residents all over that are very concerned about the lack of transparency. They’re concerned about data centers being forced on their communities,” he said. “They’re concerned that Alabama Power is [jacking] up their prices.”
An Inside Climate News investigation found that Alabamians paid the highest average residential electricity bills in the nation in 2024, the latest year with complete data at the time.
Ensler has made data centers and concerns around Alabama Power, the state’s powerful electric utility, a focal point of his campaign. Ensler, from Montgomery, has visited Lowndes County, whose residents are fighting a proposed hyperscale data center, five times.
Hours before the debate, and in the days leading up to it, Ensler stood in solidarity with Fenn Church at his home in Shelby County. Church has been in a months-long legal dispute with Alabama Power over its use of eminent domain to lay transmission lines across his property.
“Alabama Power thinks they can just walk over anyone and everyone,” Ensler has said of the situation. “They’re just trying to flex their muscles and intimidate people, and if they can do that to him and do it here, they can do it anywhere.”
In a statement, a representative of Alabama Power said that the utility understands “that property is personal, and we remain committed to treating property owners fairly and respectfully.
“The Alabama Supreme Court’s decision allows work on this section of the transmission line to move forward, supporting a project that is an important investment in the security and reliability of the electric grid for the customers and communities we serve,” the emailed statement said.
Church had won a temporary victory against the utility in lower court earlier this year, receiving a preliminary injunction from a Circuit Court judge that prevented Alabama Power from accessing the property while the lawsuit moved forward.
Last Wednesday, the Alabama Supreme Court granted a motion from the utility to stay that decision. Since then, Fenn and the utility have been at a stalemate.
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
Church has said he’s attempted to have U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, the Republican candidate for governor, act as a mediator between himself and Alabama Power. But Ensler, Church said, is the only candidate who has come to his property to stand toe to toe with the utility.
“And I so appreciate him for it,” Church said. “It’s not about Republican or Democrat. It’s about what’s right.”
The topic of the Public Service Commission, the state’s utility regulator, arose at the debate when Wahl accused Ensler of supporting an effort to take away Alabamians’ right to vote for lieutenant governor by having the governor and lieutenant governor run as a ticket.
Alabama lieutenant governor is primarily charged with presiding over the state Senate. If the office of governor becomes vacant, the lieutenant governor assumes the state’s highest office.
Ensler and Doug Jones, the Democratic candidate for governor, have said they would support a state constitutional amendment that would have voters elect their governor and lieutenant governor on the same ticket, the method used by most states with both roles and similar to the way federal elections for president and vice president work.
“I think that’s a bad move,” Wahl said. “I don’t like it.”
Ensler responded that any changes like that would have to be approved by Alabama voters through a constitutional amendment. Ensler then brought up the Public Service Commission overhaul.
“Who has taken away the right to vote from people is Republicans who pushed a bill to change the Public Service Commission and take away people’s voices for a very important body at a time in which utility rates are going up,” Ensler said. “So if we’re concerned about taking away the voice of the people, that was done by Republicans when it comes to the Public Service Commission.”

Paul Solman reports for our higher education series, Rethinking College. But in an era increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence, one of the oldest skills taught on college campuses may be more valuable than ever. Paul Solman reports for the next installment in our higher education series, Rethinking College. Paul Solman: Isolated by COVID, bombarded by social media, screen-swamped in general, and headed for an all-bets-are-off job market, no wonder today's students feel, to use a lament from my college days, as if they're up a tree, that is, precariously perched. Well, most of us remember from college learning to fend for ourselves by making friends outside the safe bubble of home and high school. But nowadays, with all the job pressure today's students face, is learning to socialize still as crucial? Jill Barry: I think, for me, it is one of the most important aspects, because when you're in college, you're meeting all these people of different backgrounds and you want to be able to use that knowledge once you graduate into a job. Paul Solman: Is it the single most important aspect of college, learning to live on your own, be with other people? Kosi Chugbo-Junius: Yes, I think it is like the single most important. (LAUGHTER) Paul Solman: We started this story last spring at Michigan universities, where the emphasis from the top was crystal clear, not so much socializing as reorienting college to get students jobs. Paul Solman: Eastern Michigan University President Brendan Kelly. Brendan Kelly: We have to understand that our business is rooted in the student, and then has to be connected to their participation in the economy after graduation. Paul Solman: We heard the same thing from new MSU Itzel Segovia. Itzel Segovia: So I met people from all different backgrounds, and I will catch myself, like, on a Tuesday morning eating pho because of the friend that I made, and she's from Vietnam. So I think that it's essential to create those relationships in college, because that's one thing that will go with you through life. Paul Solman: And we didn't just hear it in Michigan; 800 miles east at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, same story. Kosi Chugbo-Junius: I came here, I didn't know a single person. Paul Solman: Senior Kosi Chugbo-Junius. Kosi Chugbo-Junius: Everything I have here, every resource I lean on is someone that I had to form like a social connection with. Like, I rely on that every day. Paul Solman: Seniors Jill Barry and Ben Luu. Jill Barry: When you're in college, you kind of develop a sense of self and you become more yourself, and you know how to communicate with people, and you're more confident in who you are. Paul Solman: When you first came here, how freaked out were you about, say, meeting other kids or meeting girls? Like, when -- if you were to ask me in freshman year if I were to ever be an R.A., like, I would have never even dreamt of it. But as... Paul Solman: Would you have talked to me when you were a freshman if I came to you at a table? Ben Luu: Probably not. I would probably run away or something. I was a very shy kid in high school. Paul Solman: Shy, isolated. So many higher ed students these days actually report feeling lonely. Betsy Cracco, University of Massachusetts Amherst: We start to see the erosion of social skills because people are spending so much time in virtual world. So when they come to campus, it might be the first time they're really immersed in a community. Paul Solman: Betsy Cracco runs the student well-being initiative at UMass Amherst.
